Pope Leo XIV set for first official visit to France, with huge crowds expected in Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:19:58 UTC
06:19:58 KST

The trip will mark the first official papal visit to Paris since Benedict XVI in 2008.
Pope Leo XIV is making his first official visit to France from 25 to 28 September.
In the French capital, excitement is building.
According to the police prefecture, up to 250,000 people are expected to line the streets along the route of Leo XIV's procession through the streets of Paris. Around 80,000 people have also bought tickets to attend the youth mass that is set to be held at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis, in the north of the city.
Paris has not welcomed a pope since 2008, when Benedict XVI visited.
“Pope Francis visited Strasbourg, Marseille, and Corsica, which are on the outskirts of France,” said Charles Mercier, director of studies in the history and sociology of Catholicism at the École pratique des hautes études (EPHE) in Paris.
"But coming to the capital is a big event because it hasn’t happened in a long time. It fuels people’s enthusiasm, and I think that’s one of the reasons for the success of this visit.”
Another reason for the enthusiasm is the pontiff’s popularity, which extends far beyond French Catholics. Elected in May 2025, Leo XIV has presented himself as a pope who is connected and attentive to everyone.
Leo XIV will be in Paris and the wider Île-de-France region for two days.
He is due to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée palace on Friday. He is also set to meet with "the authorities, civil society and the diplomatic corps" before heading to UNESCO.
On Sunday, he is expected in Lourdes, where he is due to speak with seven victims of sexual abuse within the Church.
Among them is a former pupil at the nearby school of Notre Dame de Bétharram. In 2024, more than 230 victims filed complaints over corporal punishment and sexual abuse at the Catholic institution in southwestern France.

Man convicted of attempted murder in shooting of three Palestinian students in Vermont

Man convicted of attempted murder in shooting of three Palestinian students in Vermont
WASHINGTON, Sept 21 - A man was convicted by a jury of attempted murder in the late 2023 shooting of three Palestinian American students in Vermont, two of whom were wounded and one was left paralyzed from the waist down, prosecutors said on Monday.
Jason Eaton was found guilty on three counts of attempted second-degree murder for the shootings of Hisham Awartani, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid on November 25, 2023, in Burlington, Vermont, prosecutor Sarah George, the Chittenden County state's attorney, said in a statement.
The conviction rejected Eaton's insanity defense and he will be sentenced at a later time, George said. A jury trial commenced in the Chittenden Superior Court a week ago and lasted till Monday.
Eaton faces a sentence of up to life without parole, with a presumptive minimum term of 20 years to serve on each count, George said.
The three Palestinian American students, who grew up in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, were walking in Burlington when Eaton approached and shot them, prosecutors and police said.
Awartani was paralyzed from the chest down and now lives with paraplegia, his family said. Aliahmad was struck in the chest and Abdalhamid was struck in the glute while running away, according to prosecutors. Aliahmad and Abdalhamid were visiting Awartani's grandmother over a Thanksgiving break from school.
All three were 20 at the time and wore black-and-white Palestinian keffiyeh scarves while conversing in a mix of English and Arabic when the gunman confronted them, prosecutors said. Their families said on Monday justice "has been rendered" and that they feel relief.
Though Eaton pleaded not guilty, he did not dispute being the shooter. His legal team said he should not be found guilty due to insanity, referring to his claims that US and Israeli intelligence ordered him to carry out the shooting through radio and that God asked him to protect Jewish neighbors.
US rights advocates have noted rising anti-Arab, anti-Muslim and anti-Jewish bias since the start of US ally Israel's devastating assault on Gaza following a deadly October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel.
Some fatal incidents that have sparked alarm include a 2023 deadly stabbing of a 6-year-old Palestinian American child in Illinois whose killer was sentenced to 53 years in prison and died in custody, and a 2026 San Diego mosque shooting that left five dead, including two teenage suspects. REUTERS

“The “I” that considers is very different from the “I” that has fears. To have fears, to…

“The “I” that considers is very different from the “I” that has fears. To have fears, to have, specifically, the fears on which Keats dwells, is to be immersed in acute sensation. The fear that one will cease to be is unlike the state of chronic fearfulness we call timidity. This fear halts and overtakes, it carries intimations of change or closure or collapse, it threatens to cancel the future. It is primal, unwilled, democratic, urgent; in its presence, all other function is suspended.”
— Louise Glück, Proofs and Theories

Putin’s United Russia remains in power. What should concern the West is how it got there - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:12:48 UTC
06:12:48 KST

Unsurprisingly, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party won a vast majority of seats in the State Duma elections.
Preliminary results released on Monday indicated that United Russia won 355 of 450 seats in the state’s lower house of the legislature, or approximately 57.8% of the vote, Russia’s Central Election Commission announced.
Notably, at least 86 veterans of the war in Ukraine are expected to take seats in the Duma, the Moscow Times reported.
This does not include the hundreds of regional officials who were elected in the world’s largest landmass. The final results will be released no later than October 5, the CEC said.
United Russia’s victory was an unfortunate but obvious conclusion. It is concerning that this election maintains Putin’s hold on power and could lay the groundwork to further escalate the war in Ukraine, especially as many fear another round of draft orders. However, it is vital to understand why this election turned out this way in the first place.
Some analysts and exiled journalists called this election Russia’s most uncompetitive election in its modern history, not only because of the way politicians campaigned, but also because of how easily the Kremlin manipulated the results
Firstly, the way that Russia conducts its elections already makes any results easier to distort.
Russia offered electronic voting in 33 of its 89 federally recognized regions. The election was also spread over three days. Both of these factors make it much easier to tamper with results in an already rigged election.
Secondly, Putin manipulated the fact that Russians even have elections in the first place as proof that his citizens support his increasingly authoritarian actions.
In several appearances before the elections, he pointed to the fact that Russia is having elections despite the conflict in Ukraine as proof of three different things. His primary unspoken claim is that Russia is still democratic, or at least a “managed” democracy. His second claim is that Russians are supportive of the “special military operation” in Ukraine (Putin’s government does not call the war a war in an effort to delegitimize Kyiv and control the domestic narrative within Russia). Finally, he uses the fact that Ukraine has not had an election since it declared martial law over four years ago as proof that Zelensky runs a fascist regime.
“We have to stand for election, not be afraid to run for office,” Putin said in June. “And I would advise everyone to do the same. Especially in Ukraine.”
This is Russia’s first parliamentary election since it began the war in Ukraine. Over the course of election season, Putin  he also framed elections as a way to show support for the war.
“Your choice and resolve will show once again that millions of people stand behind our fighters,” Putin said last week. “Participating in the elections is our shared contribution to Russia’s victory.”
United Russia’s public approval rating was at a notable low of 33% before Friday
However, United Russia’s public approval rating was at a notable low of 33% before ballots were cast on Friday, according to Russia’s Public Opinion Foundation, which is regarded as Kremlin-friendly.
Still, Kremlin-friendly paper Kommersant claimed that this year had the highest voter turnout since the early 2000s, at about 60%.
This is part of the reason why, if the claims are true, it is so interesting that there was also notably little campaigning in this year’s State Duma race.
In more than one instance, Russian state TV channels were set to moderate a debate between candidates, none of whom showed up.
"Good evening, and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," one Russia state TV News anchor said in one clip circulating online. The camera then cuts to six empty podiums.
"The candidates haven't turned up. So, it's goodbye from me."
It’s worth noting that Putin has never participated in a televised electoral debate during his near 20 years in office. It’s fair to assume that other members of his party have since followed suit.
However, the fact that this happened more than once shows that Russian politicians know that there is little competition. United Russia will take most of the seats in the federal government as well as state and local elections, and a few opposition candidates will make the cut to maintain a veneer of democracy.
Only four other parties cleared the electoral threshold
In the 2026 election, only four other parties cleared the electoral threshold: the Communist Party, the Liberal Democratic Party, New People, and A Just Russia.
Put together, they have 89 seats.
It can be hard to distinguish between these parties. Some obviously tilt more to the right or left, but in terms of the “special military operation,” they all vote the same way, and therefore function as systemic opposition.
The Kremlin, under Putin’s tenure, has been eliminating dissenting parties from the ballot. Russians now have only 17 registered political parties that can run in elections, down from around 100 in the 1980s.
A prime example of this is Yabloko, a left-leaning party that explicitly called for a ceasefire in Ukraine, was eliminated from the ballot this summer.
Some individual candidates have run, but 29 of at least 36 opposition candidates barred from the elections were Yabloko candidates, according to reporting by the Moscow Times and the independent Russian-language outlet Vyorstka.
Notably, some Yabloko candidates were fined for interacting with materials involving slain Russian activist Alexei Navalny. While they have denied the charges, they were still disqualified, fined thousands of rubles, and in some cases were declared “foreign agents”, the Kremlin’s label to brand someone a traitor with foreign influence.
This election in Russia has not changed anything. Because there is no way to see the real breakdown of the data, there’s no way to know how Russians actually feel about their government. That, in and of itself, is the biggest indicator of how rotted Russia’s political system is.
So United Russia will take another supermajority in the State Duma, the so-called opposition will continue to play by the Kremlin’s rules, and ordinary Russians will continue to live under a “managed” democracy.
No one ever thought the Kremlin would lose in this election. But it has shamefully signaled to its citizens and to the world that it’s not going anywhere.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met US CIA chief John Ratcliffe at Shannon Airport in Ireland, two people familiar with the matter said.
The meeting took place on Monday, one of the sources said. The other source said the pair spoke informally while their planes were being refueled without specifying a date. Both sources, who requested anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, declined to disclose details of their conversation.
The meeting happened as Zelensky was traveling to New York to take part in the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations. Ratcliffe was on his way back from meeting Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, one source said.
Ratcliffe's meeting with Zelensky comes less than a month after the CIA chief traveled to Moscow to meet with Russia's top intelligence officials.
Putin, Zelensky meetings with CIA not publicly disclosed
Neither Ratcliffe nor the CIA has publicly disclosed what was discussed in Moscow. One of the sources, who confirmed the Zelensky meeting to Reuters, said Ratcliffe had been in Moscow to discuss Ukraine, but they declined to elaborate.
The New York Times reported last month that Ratcliffe used his trip to share his bleak assessment of the state of the Russian war against Ukraine and to urge the Russians to cut a deal before their position weakens.

Irish athletes group urges national team to boycott matches against Israeli soccer team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:12:37 UTC
06:12:37 KST

More than 160 Irish sportspeople have signed an open letter asking the Ireland national football team to boycott their upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures against Israel, the Irish Sport for Palestine Group said on Monday.
Ireland are due to play Israel on September 27 in Hungary before the reverse fixture in Serbia on October 4. Both matches are set to be staged at neutral venues and behind closed doors after protests by players and fans over the war in Gaza.
Irish Sport for Palestine said the signatories included Olympian Ciara Mageean, former footballer Louise Quinn, former rugby flyhalf Tony Ward and boxers Tyrone McKenna and Eric Donovan.
"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.
"Not playing the game would be the most sporting thing you could do. Through your leadership and courage, it would show the power of sport to unite, remind us of the shared values that connect us all, and have an impact far beyond the game."
Irish soccer players urged for boycott against Israel
In May, leading Irish footballers joined celebrities in a campaign urging Ireland to boycott the Nations League matches against Israel.
Ireland has been one of the European Union's most outspoken critics of Israel's conduct during the Israel-Hamas war, and Football Association of Ireland (FAI) members voted overwhelmingly in late 2025 for its board to request that UEFA immediately suspend the Israel Football Association from European competitions.
The FAI later committed to playing the fixtures, citing possible sanctions that could affect the national team and the association.
Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said last week he had spoken individually to players about facing Israel and that "none of us feel comfortable playing in these games."
Reuters has contacted the Israeli FA for comment.

Trump approval drops to career-low 32% as GOP support erodes over Iran war, inflation - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:12:13 UTC
06:12:13 KST

US President Donald Trump's approval rating fell to 32% - the lowest of his political career - as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living amid the unpopular Iran war, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
The poll, completed on Sunday, was conducted over a four-day period that saw Trump throw three major news organizations out of the White House and muse that Washington's iconic Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts - named after slain President John F. Kennedy - could be torn down if Trump's own name could not be added to it.
It found voters leaning away from supporting Trump's fellow Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
Trump's overall approval was down from a reading of 35% in last week's Reuters/Ipsos poll, with support among his own Republicans down to 73% from 82% a week earlier.
Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 on promises to tame inflation and end foreign wars. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the hours after he was sworn in, he enjoyed a 47% approval rating.
Just 17% of respondents in the new poll approved of his handling of the cost of living - the top issue Americans say will determine how they vote in November.
Iran takes a toll
Dissatisfaction among Republicans on inflation has been growing since Trump launched the war on Iran in February, which has pushed gasoline and diesel prices sharply higher. Now for the first time, Republicans who disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living outnumber those who give him a thumbs up - 51% to 44%.
Trump's approval rating is lower than any recorded for his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, whose presidency was also marked by surging inflation and who ultimately ended his reelection bid after a poor debate performance heightened concerns about his age. Biden's low was 35%, reached in late October 2024.
Only 34% of the most recent poll respondents approve of the strikes on Iran. The conflict has cut the world off from a significant slice of the oil and gas produced in the Middle East, and threatens to stoke higher inflation in the US and elsewhere as businesses pass on higher fuel costs to consumers.
Trump initially said the conflict would last a few weeks and that Iran needed to be bombed to stop it from developing nuclear weapons. Earlier this month, the Republican leader pledged the war would end "immediately after" the election. But Iran has shown no sign of giving up, and in recent weeks Tehran and its allies have threatened further disruptions to oil markets.
Some 82% of poll respondents - including nine in ten Democrats and three-quarters of Republicans - said the conflict would likely go on for an "extended period of time."
Democrats trump Republicans in midterm polls
The Reuters/Ipsos poll showed registered voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans - 43% to 35% - when asked how they would vote in the midterms. The 8-point gap was the biggest lead for Democrats in Reuters/Ipsos polling this year. For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his term.
The poll results on congressional voting plans provide an overall view of which party Americans nationwide want to see in charge in Congress, though the results don't capture all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House of Representatives.
Trump remains popular among Republicans on the issue of immigration - with 79% of his party backing him - but only 36% of Americans overall support his approach to the matter, and 55% disapprove. Some Republican allies in Congress have warned that his aggressive campaign to deport people in the country illegally risks alienating voters with family who recently immigrated to America, like some Hispanics.
Some 35% of poll respondents approve of Trump's approach to fighting crime, compared to 50% who disapprove.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online and gathered 1,277 responses from US adults nationwide. It had a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

Federal politics live: Bragg to reignite super fight with housing plan

Follow all the updates in our live blog.

Live updates
Government not considering DV royal commission
The government is not considering a royal commission into violence against women and children, Treasurer Jim Chalmers says.
Advocates for an inquiry stepped up their call for the government to take action after four separate alleged domestic violence incidents in New South Wales over the weekend.
Chalmers told ABC's News Breakfast the incidents were "absolutely horrific" but the governent was focused on boosting resources over calling an inquiry.
"We've chosen instead to increase the resourcing for child and family violence, domestic violence. We do acknowledge that this has a number of sources and we're trying to deal with the sources of all this violence, whether it be more security in the housing system, whether it be monetized misogyny that we see online," he says.
"We do acknowledge, that all of this violence is obviously entirely, unacceptable. It's horrific in every way. That's why we've increased the resources, and that's why we all need to do better, to do everything we can to make a difference here."
If you or anyone you know needs support,call Lifeline on 13 11 14, Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, or 1800 RESPECT on 1800 737 732.
Australia joins international push for AI safeguards
Anthony Albanese and more than a dozen world leaders have issued an urgent plea for global guardrails to ensure AI remains "under human control", in a demonstration of middle powers flexing their collective muscle, as the US and China fight for global dominance.
In an alarming statement — issued on the eve of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York — the 22 signatories warn "the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks" and efforts to ring-fence it are failing.
First flagged by Albanese on Saturday, the declaration warns capable AI systems have already managed to circumvent testing safeguards and gain unauthorised access to real-world systems.
"The rapid development of frontier AI models poses serious risks to safety and security if not appropriately managed," the statement reads.
The coalition of middle powers — including Australia, Finland, Norway, Canada, Singapore and the European Commission — calls on AI companies to develop transparent safety protocols and governments to develop and coordinate common standards.
Read more about the statement at the link below
Bragg to reignite super fight with housing plan
A plan for Australians to use their superannuation to make it easier to secure a home loan is set to be floated by Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg.
The proposal, which has not been adopted as Coalition policy, would allow individuals to use their retirement savings as collateral for a mortgage or to increase the size of a loan.
Bragg will make the pitch in an address to the Financial Services Council today. He first floated the idea a couple of weeks ago after One Nation released its own superannuation policy.
"Why should we live in a nation where big institutions own houses by virtue of government policy but people can’t use their own money to get a home or reduce their own mortgage?" he's expected to say, according to a copy of his speech.
The Coalition went to the last two elections with a proposal to allow individuals to withdraw up to $50,000 for a first home deposit.
Bragg stressed none of the options floated in the speech were opposition policy but the Coalition has an "open mind".
"They are options worthy of a debate in a country like Australia," he's expected to say.

UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:09:05 UTC
06:09:05 KST

The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.
The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil.
Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world.
The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government.
On the flight to the United Nations in New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.
The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating.
“We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said.
The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK, where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result.
“Of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part,” Burnham said when asked if he would raise the issue in talks with Trump.
As well as the focus on the Middle East, other major international challenges, including the war in Ukraine and artificial intelligence, are expected to dominate Burnham’s meetings at the UN general assembly.
The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak: European leaders have warned that Russia could launch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within months to test the strength of the alliance.
Burnham’s speech to the UN is expected to focus on harnessing the power of AI, amid concerns at home over the safety of the rapidly advancing technology. He will be accompanied on the trip by his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.
The prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump is a significant moment, with the US president still said to be angry over the UK’s refusal to support his military action in Iran, and ongoing tensions over levels of defence spending.
Burnham will attempt to highlight the importance of the security partnership after the UK and US launched a heavyweight torpedo, designed to sink ships and deep-diving submarines, in British waters last week from a Plymouth-made drone named Excalibur.
Government insiders, however, are taking some solace from Trump’s low-key response to UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after weeks of diplomacy with the White House over the summer.
They are also hoping to avoid a clash over energy policy. The prime minister is expected to signal to Trump that he is in favour of more drilling in the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield that is likely to get the green light within weeks.
Analysts believe the balance of risk for the bilateral relationship has shifted since Keir Starmer was in office, given the Republicans face a difficult set of midterm elections and the US president’s personal ratings are plummeting.
Trump is also likely to be more focused on his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and his address to the UN, which comes shortly before the talks on Tuesday.
Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.
Asked whether he felt he could trust Trump, Burnham said: “Yes, of course, we trust our allies. Of course, we do.” Pressed whether this applied to the US president personally, he repeated: “Yes.”
Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to use his UN meetings – which will also include the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – to “drive opportunity and deliver hope”, making progress on areas with the potential to deliver for people at home.
Burnham has focused on domestic issues since his arrival in No 10, despite Starmer warning that it would be impossible to separate them from global affairs, given how the Ukraine war is weighing heavily on UK security and the Iran conflict on the economy.
On the flight Burnham acknowledged they were inseparable. “[Starmer] was right to say it’s about how we deliver back at home and the situation in the Middle East is a very clear example of that. It is a very big driver of the cost of living pressures that we’re currently facing,” he said.
Before the trip, Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “The British people at home are at the forefront of the prime minister’s mission in New York this week. Because to deliver at home, we must ensure we are leading international efforts to brighten a darkening global picture …
“To give people the breathing space they need, he is clear we must work with our international partners to face up to the biggest challenges of our generation. So this week at [the UN general assembly] he will be leading the charge on the global issues that impact people’s lives at home.”
Burnham will tell world leaders the UK will focus on AI and climate change when it hosts the G20 in Manchester next year, potentially causing ripples with Trump, who has previously criticised the UK’s stance on global warming.
The meeting gives Burnham an opportunity, however, to host international allies on his home turf, although the location of the summit was chosen under the Starmer administration.
Burnham has been accompanied on the trip by his wife, Marie-France van Heel, who No 10 said would be meeting her international counterparts and supporting the prime minister, whose father, Roy, died last week.

UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:09:05 UTC
06:09:05 KST

UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support
LONDON, Sept 21 - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday he had agreed to a request from Saudi Arabia to provide defensive air-to-air refuelling for a limited time period, a move he described as helping to stabilise the wider region.
Riyadh requested support after the Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a new front in the wider war that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
"We have received a request from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support, and on the advice of the defence secretary and the foreign secretary, last night I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling," he told reporters as he travelled to New York for a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly.
"Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attack... and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request," he said.
Britain and Saudi Arabia have been close military allies for decades, with Britain serving as one of the kingdom's largest arms suppliers.
Earlier this year, Britain deployed its Sky Sabre air defence system to Saudi Arabia to help protect it from Iranian missile attacks during the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran.
For the new air-to-air refuelling support, Britain will deploy one Voyager plane in the coming days.

Ukraine Breaches Bunkers at Russian Droneport Built to Store and Launch Strike UAVs

Militarnyi reported the damage on September 21, citing satellite imagery published by the Telegram channel Absolutely Reliable.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Tsymbulova site, near the village of the same name in Russia’s Oryol region, is a dedicated base for storing, preparing, and launching Russian strike drones.
Construction of the facility began in August 2024, and investigators believe the first drone launches may have taken place as early as that autumn.
By 2026, the complex had expanded substantially. Satellite imagery reviewed by Militarnyi showed new launch positions, storage facilities, and support infrastructure for several types of Russian strike UAVs.
By August, the site had 10 launchers for Geran-5 jet-powered drones, 6 for Geran-4 UAVs, 4 for Geran-3 drones, and 3 for standard Geran-2s.
The droneport has repeatedly come under Ukrainian attack.
On the night of August 30, Ukrainian Defense Forces struck storage and launch facilities at the same complex, damaging a Geran launch position and a storage facility for strike UAVs.
The expansion of Tsymbulova coincides with Russia’s broader expansion of its drone production infrastructure.
At its Alabuga complex in Tatarstan, Russia's largest drone-manufacturing operation, construction crews have been excavating underground production halls, with roughly 42,000 square meters of subterranean space already built for planned Geran lines.

An inconvenient truth: Why the EU could lose twice to Alisher Usmanov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:01:17 UTC
06:01:17 KST

An inconvenient truth: Why the EU could lose twice to Alisher Usmanov
The EU is divided over a deal to un-sanction Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov. Brussels’ allies in Kiev aren’t happy, but the alternative – a legal showdown – could call the bloc’s entire sanctions regime into question.
Ambassadors from EU member states met on Monday to discuss Usmanov’s case. According to Euronews, France pushed for Usmanov’s removal from the blacklist, in exchange for Azerbaijan freeing two alleged French spies.
Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency, proposed that Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, another Russian businessman, be delisted on the condition that the EU renew its anti-Russian sanctions regime for 36 months instead of the usual six.
After a second round of talks on Monday that stretched into the night, EU envoys failed to agree to remove Usmanov and Fridman from the list. Meaning no agreement has been reached on extending the bloc's sanctions.
Usmanov is at the centre of a discussion that could undo a central pillar of the EU's personal sanctions policy.
Why was Usmanov sanctioned?
A highly successful entrepreneur in the final years of the Soviet Union, the Russian-Uzbek businessman snapped up metal and mining businesses during the rapid privatization of the 1990s, breached into media with his acquisition of Russia’s Kommersant newspaper in 2006, and expanded his wealth with a series of savvy investments in Apple, Twitter, and Facebook over the following decade.
Usmanov, believed to be Russia’s seventh-richest person with a net worth of more than $16 billion, was sanctioned by the EU four days after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
The EU’s sanctions ledger declared that Usmanov “has particularly close ties to the President of the Russian Federation, Vladimir Putin,” has “acted on behalf of the President of the Russian Federation in a number of business deals,” and gave former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev “personal use of luxurious residences” controlled by his companies.
“Kommersant under Usmanov’s ownership published a propagandist anti-Ukrainian article by Dmitry Medvedev” the entry continued, concluding that “therefore he actively supported the Russian government’s policies of destabilization of Ukraine.”
EU media: Unreliable sources
According to Usmanov’s lawyers, Brussels sourced all of its “reasons and evidence” for sanctioning the billionaire from “mass media and social media publications.” In a letter to the European Council last month seen by Intellinews journalist Ben Aris, Usmanov’s legal team argued that this evidence has been proven false in courts in all 27 EU member states.
Back in 2022, Usmanov launched a sweeping campaign of litigation against newspapers and other media outlets incorrectly reporting his business links to the Russian government and characterizing him as “Putin’s favorite oligarch.” Usmanov won judgments against Germany’s Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ), which claimed that he used his wealth “in the interests or at the direction of the Kremlin,” against German state broadcaster ARD, which connected him to a “bribery scheme,” and against Luxembourg’s Mediahuis, which named him as the owner of a sanctioned superyacht impounded in Hamburg.
Among his other legal victories were judgments against Forbes, Germany’s Der Tagesspiegel, Austria’s Kurier, and Switzerland’s Blick, all of which used false claims by deceased anti-Kremlin activist Alexey Navalny to back up their stories of Usmanov’s ties to the Kremlin.
The European Council could stand accused
Since 2022, his lawyers reportedly claimed in the letter, more than 3,200 articles about Usmanov have been corrected and 1,300 deleted, in 60 countries. Almost 100 cease-and-desist letters have been issued and 58,000 pieces of online content and ads about the businessman have been pulled down, many of which “relied on the Council’s narrative.”
The European Council, meanwhile, has quietly removed at least 18 documents from its “evidence packs” against Usmanov, the letter claimed.
The wave of retractions and deletions – issued by the same sources used to back up the sanctions decision – “must be accepted as exculpatory evidence,” Usmanov’s lawyers wrote. “To sum up, the allegations used to maintain Mr Usmanov’s designation have been discredited and refuted in 27 out of 27 EU Member States.”
The EU’s dilemma
The EU’s Court of Justice has already dismissed two attempts by Usmanov to appeal his blacklisting. In rejecting the second attempt last September, the court ruled that the council’s decision to sanction Usmanov was based on a “specific, precise and consistent” body of evidence.
However, even Politico, the Brussels elite’s leak-factory of choice, has reported that the “evidence packs” used to justify sanctioning figures like Usmanov are often “hastily compiled” and based on “shaky evidence.”
On shaky grounds: The secret, slipshod evidence the EU uses to sanction Russian oligarchs.#tomorrowspaperstodaypic.twitter.com/uATyU0YjCO
— POLITICOEurope (@POLITICOEurope) September 20, 2023
In 2023, Politico found that evidence against Russian businessman Grigory Berezkin was drawn from articles written by an AI chatbot, and a website called ‘Russian Crimes’ written by journalists that didn’t exist. Another evidence pack cited an advertisement in a Russian lifestyle and cooking magazine. Yet another cited a Ukrainian gossip site. Berezhkin was removed from the EU’s blacklist that September.
More than a dozen individuals have since been removed from the list. Some, like Formula 1 driver Nikita Mazepin, had been sanctioned over the alleged offenses of their relatives. At least six – including Pavel Ezubov, cousin of metals magnate Oleg Deripaska, and former e-commerce tycoon Aleksandr Shulgin – were delisted after taking legal action against the EU.
Keeping Usmanov on the list could open the EU up to more legal challenges from the billionaire, which could make more of the council’s classified evidence packs being made public. Confirmation that much of the evidence is spurious may have emboldened the almost 3,000 individuals and entities sanctioned by Brussels over the conflict to launch challenges of their own. Fridman also certainly believes the bloc is engaged in significant overreach.
To the envoys who met on Monday, cutting Usmanov loose may have been seen as a necessary sacrifice to preserve the legitimacy of the sanctions regime.
National interest
The push to delist Usmanov began in Slovakia this March, when Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar argued that there were “very strong legal arguments” against the sanctioning of him and Fridman. Uzbekistan and a number of other Turkic countries – including Türkiye – reportedly lobbied Bratislava to push for his removal from the blacklist.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico is a vocal critic of EU sanctions against Russia, but Slovakia found an ally when France unexpectedly began advocating for Usmanov’s delisting, citing unexplained “national security” interests. According to multiple media reports, France has been negotiating behind the scenes with Azerbaijan, where President Ilham Aliyev has apparently agreed to release two imprisoned French citizens in exchange, one of whom was jailed for spying on the country’s military on behalf of French intelligence.
Why did Luxembourg back off from Fridman?
According to Reuters, Luxembourg backed the delisting of Fridman, who has sued the duchy for $16 billion over its freezing of his assets in 2022. Luxembourg reportedly argued that its case against Fridman would be weakened if Usmanov alone was let go, and insisted that the two billionaires be treated as a package deal.
EU diplomats took to Politico to vent at the French last week, with one complaining that “if France goes ahead with this, others will come forward with their own oligarchs that should be delisted ... [then] the house of cards starts to fall.”
What nobody in Brussels will admit on the record is that if Usmanov is un-sanctioned, politicians and publishers across Europe will likely breathe a sigh of relief that their media outlets – many of them government-funded – will not be dragged into a legal showdown that could result in massive payouts and the collapse of the sanctions system itself.
What does Usmanov’s case tell us about the EU?
The case exposes cracks in the EU’s “united front” for Ukraine, as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put it during her State of the Union speech last week. As France and Luxembourg demonstrated, no EU member is above breaking ranks when their national interest is at stake, and the EU is sometimes capable of putting its own members’ needs above Ukraine’s.
Is the Kiev tail wagging the EU dog?
Kiev remains incandescent at the thought of its EU masters going off-script. “How can anyone seriously discuss sanctions delisting while Russia’s war continues?” Vladimir Zelensky’s sanctions adviser, Vladislav Vlasiuk, complained on Monday.
“Usmanov and Fridman were listed because they are part of Russia’s aggressive regime waging a war of aggression against Ukraine,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sybiga wrote on social media. “Delisting is unacceptable and would send the wrong signal to Moscow at a time when pressure needs to increase.”
Usmanov and Fridman were listed because they are part of Russia's aggressive regime waging a war of aggression against Ukraine. 
What has changed? Nothing. Delisting is unacceptable and would send the wrong signal to Moscow at a time when pressure needs to increase. 
On the…
What does this tell us about the EU's info-culture?
No matter how unsavory a character Brussels finds him, Usmanov’s string of legal victories against Western Europe’s most prestigious news outlets – seen in Moscow as paranoid pillars in an increasingly hysterical echo-chamber – sends an important signal to the EU: As long as it believes what it tells itself about Russia and Russians, the legal ground it stands on is incredibly shaky.

Former ‘death squad’ leader appears in military trial in The Gambia
Sanna Manjang faces a military court for deserting the country’s army in 2017 after the end of Yahya Jammeh’s 20-year rule.
The former head of the Gambian paramilitary unit known as the “Junglers” has appeared in a military court to face charges of desertion.
Sanna Manjang is accused of deserting the armed forces when the lieutenant colonel fled the country in 2017 after the end of the 20-year rule of President Yahya Jammeh.
The case in the capital, Banjul, marks another official bid at accountability for killings which happened when Jammeh was in power, after a murder case against Manjang was dropped in July.
He is facing trial for an absence of “a continuous period of nine years with the intention of deserting”. Manjang was arrested in Senegal last November and was repatriated to The Gambia a month later.
The Junglers armed group, which operated independently from the Gambian army, has long been accused by the United Nations of extrajudicial killings and torture.
Longtime leader Jammeh was forced into exile after losing power in 2016 to Adama Barrow, then opposition leader and now president.
Following Jammeh’s departure, the country established the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission (TRRC). It investigated alleged crimes under his rule and found that between 240 and 250 people were killed by the state. It also found evidence of widespread extrajudicial killings, torture, kidnappings, witch hunts and other abuses.
Several of Jammeh’s accomplices, including Junglers, have been detained and sentenced abroad in Germany, Switzerland and the United States.
Murder charges dropped
Manjang was previously charged with four counts of murder, including that of AFP journalist Deyda Hydara in 2004, but the charges were dropped in July as The Gambia struggled to summon witnesses, some allegedly members of the death squad.
In addition to Hydara’s shooting, Manjang was accused of killing three other men, including one he personally decapitated.
After the charges were dropped, Manjang was charged separately for the assault of two other men in an ongoing trial.

What a Trump order to put political appointees in charge of NIH funding would mean for science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:54:01 UTC
05:54:01 KST

President Donald Trump’s reported plans to establish a committee to oversee—and possibly veto—scientific grants issued by the nation’s top health agency via an executive order would undermine U.S. science and innovation leadership, advocates and scientists say.
The planned executive order was reported by the New York Times and Politico and has yet to be released.
“Scientific grants should be judged by scientific expertise, not political ideology,” says Jennifer Jones, director of the Center for Science and Democracy at the Union of Concerned Scientists. If finalized, she says, the reported plans would “upend the way we do science in this country.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The move would overhaul how federal money is allocated to science—a similar rule change was already proposed by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which garnered significant criticism from scientists and national science organizations. Earlier this month Congress temporarily blocked the regulations from going into effect.
Under the reported executive order, an appointed committee would sign off on grants issued by the U.S. National Institutes of Health, which has a budget of more than $40 billion. The NIH funds research on cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, heart disease, and more—“the kind of biomedical research that touches everybody’s lives,” Jones says.
The committee would reportedly include OMB director and Project 2025 proponent Russell Vought and NIH head Jay Bhattacharya. The Washington Post first reported on discussions among Trump officials about such a panel.
Historically, the NIH has followed a “gold standard” practice of independent peer review for federal grants, says Arthur Caplan, an emeritus professor at the New York University Grossman School of Medicine, who previously served on NIH advisory committees. The process requires researchers to submit a lengthy proposal and go through multiple rounds of screening and review by independent experts.
“I think it’s a very, very dangerous and bad idea to layer in an ideologically driven, new oversight board to the process,” Caplan says. “I don’t think peer review at the NIH is broken. So what are we fixing, unless it’s imposing a political agenda?”
Colette Delawalla, founder and CEO of Stand Up for Science, a scientific advocacy nonprofit, says the Trump administration’s reported plans appear to be designed to exert political control over American scientists.
“It’s extremely obvious that Russell Vought is not going to stop trying to dismantle the American scientific ecosystem and the American higher education system,” Delawalla says. “Is the NIH going to continue to be the gold standard of scientific review if a nonscientist whose singular task is to destroy science is the one that all grants have to pass through? I don’t think so.”
Trump’s second term has been marked by repeated efforts to cut federal funding for research, particularly in fields examining racial disparities in health, LGBTQ+ issues and climate change. At the same time, the administration has targeted universities and other institutions in moves that have included a largely unsuccessful attempt to freeze federal funding for Harvard University over alleged failures to address antisemitism on campus.
When asked for comment, an NIH spokesperson told Scientific American that “NIH remains committed to its mission of funding biomedical research to benefit the health of the American people.”
The OMB did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Spain's Tax Agency and French customs seized the drugs in the Atlantic and arrested four crew members of the yacht and the ringleader based in Girona.
The interception of a sailing boat carrying more than two tonnes of cocaine in the Atlantic has led to the dismantling of a logistics network for drug trafficking. The joint military and customs operation off the Galician coast ended with the arrest of the crew on the high seas and of the network's leader in Girona, marking one of the biggest seizures from the drug cartels' maritime routes.
Operation Doncella, conducted by Spain's Customs Surveillance Service together with the French customs authorities, resulted in five arrests and the seizure of more than 2,000 kilos of cocaine some 400 miles off Galicia.
The investigation was launched in February in Girona to look into a suspicious yacht.
Boats for Eastern European and Balkan mafias
It focused on a 14-metre yacht flying the Polish flag but some of the paperwork raised questions and it emerged that its owner had been convicted of theft.
The evidence confirmed that the network was supplying foreign-flagged leisure boats to organised crime groups from Eastern Europe and the Balkans. A
fter gathering information in Poland via the Intelligence Centre for Counter-Terrorism and Organised Crime, officers located the yacht in Roses, Girona and kept it under surveillance until 11 July, when it put to sea with its tracking system switched off in order to avoid being monitored.
Five suspects arrested
With help from the US Drug Enforcement Administration, the UK's National Crime Agency and Portugal's Maritime Analysis and Operations Centre for Narcotics, a Spanish patrol vessel tracked and located the smugglers 400 miles off Galicia.
After the boarding operation in the early hours of 14 September, officers found 70 bales containing 2,100 kilos of cocaine stowed across the deck. The operation led to the arrest of four crew members — of Argentinian, Uruguayan, Colombian and Albanian nationality — with the Albanian suspect allegedly responsible for overseeing delivery to buyers in the Balkans.
While the Petrel I was towing the yacht to Vigo, police in Girona arrested the ringleader of the network, a Chilean national in charge of sourcing the vessels. The investigation remains open as officers seek to arrest a man in Barcelona believed to be responsible for the group's surveillance and logistics.
Those charged will appear before the National Court on counts of belonging to an organised criminal group, smuggling and drug trafficking as authorities look to crack dwon on the Atlantic cocaine route.

EU fails to finalize Russia sanctions deal, ambassadors to reconvene hours before deadline

EU fails to finalize Russia sanctions deal, ambassadors to reconvene hours before deadline
EU ambassadors failed late on Sept. 21 to finalize a deal on renewing sanctions against nearly 3,000 Russia-linked individuals and entities, with negotiations set to continue just hours before the measures are due to expire.
Coreper II, the EU ambassadors’ body, said talks would resume at 8 a.m. Brussels time on Sept. 22 "with the aim of finalising agreement."
"Given the deadline of tomorrow midnight for all legal procedures to be completed, it is important that we find agreement as soon as possible," the statement said.
The agreement had initially been expected to be confirmed by 8 p.m. on Sept. 21, and then by 10 p.m., but Latvia remained opposed to the proposed compromise, according to three national diplomats who spoke to the Kyiv Independent.
Under the deal negotiated earlier in the day, Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman would be removed from the EU sanctions list, while restrictions on roughly 3,000 other individuals and entities would be extended for 36 months — significantly longer than the bloc's usual six- or 12-month renewal periods.
read also
The individual sanctions, which include asset freezes and travel bans, require the unanimous approval of all 27 EU members. A temporary seven-day extension adopted last week keeps the existing measures in force only until Sept. 22, meaning failure to reach an agreement risks allowing the entire list to lapse. The dispute does not affect the EU's separate sectoral sanctions against the Russian economy.
Latvia was the sole country still withholding approval of the proposed compromise late on Sept. 21, according to the three diplomats.
The impasse follows weeks of disputes over Usmanov and Fridman. France joined Slovakia in pushing for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek billionaire, to be removed from the blacklist. Diplomats told Reuters that France's position followed pressure from Azerbaijan, which is holding at least two French nationals, although an Azerbaijani official rejected the characterization that Baku had pressured Paris. Luxembourg subsequently sought the removal of Fridman, according to Reuters.
Both men have challenged the EU sanctions imposed on them following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. When sanctioning Usmanov in 2022, the EU described him as having "particularly close ties" to Russian President Vladimir Putin. The bloc said Fridman had supported actions or policies threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence. Both men dispute the allegations underpinning the restrictions.
Ukraine has strongly opposed removing either businessman from the sanctions list.
"What has changed? Nothing. Delisting is unacceptable and would send the wrong signal to Moscow at a time when pressure needs to increase," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sept. 21.
Ukraine's sanctions envoy Vladyslav Vlasiuk similarly argued that lifting restrictions while the war continues would signal that sanctions could simply be waited out.
"Delisting without a fundamental change in conduct sends exactly the wrong signal: pressure is temporary, accountability is negotiable, and sanctions can simply be waited out," Vlasiuk said.
Ukraine's ambassador to the EU, Taras Kachka, also criticized the proposed compromise, saying that "compromise only invites Moscow to raise the stakes."

California declares state of emergency ahead of El Nino
LOS ANGELES - California’s governor on Sept 21 declared a state of emergency as the US west coast readies for what is expected to be a damaging El Nino.
Forecasters say the coming months could bring powerful and damaging storms to the region because of this weather pattern, with the threat of higher-than-usual tides that could trigger coastal flooding.
Governor Gavin Newsom said the state needed to get ahead of problems instead of waiting for them to happen.
“This action is about giving communities the support they need, giving first responders the tools to do their jobs, and giving families the confidence that their state is ready,” he said.
“We are preparing for this El Nino early because every Californian deserves to be safe in their home, connected to their community, and protected when severe weather comes.”
The declaration on Sept 21 is procedural and intended to make it easier for state agencies to access resources, and to pre-position flood-fighting supplies like sandbags and pumps.
The proclamation also prepares the California National Guard to support flood response, search-and-rescue, engineering, and logistics missions when needed, officials said.
El Nino is the warming phase of a natural cycle in the tropical Pacific, known as the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), and comes along every two to seven years.
It sets in when east-to-west trade winds ease, allowing warm water which normally collects in the western Pacific Ocean to slide back east and rise to the surface.
When those warmer-than-average surface temperatures last for a few months, they cause more storms and clouds over the region, which in turn cause ripple effects through the entire global atmosphere: hotter and drier conditions in some places, cooler and wetter in others.
Human-caused climate change increases El Nino’s impacts. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so El Nino-linked rains can turn more extreme. It also dries out soil, deepening drought where El Nino brings it.
This year’s El Nino has a 69 per cent chance of becoming the strongest on record, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and is already unleashing extreme weather across the globe even though it is not expected to peak until October-December.
California’s coastline has already been battered by storms that have damaged or destroyed homes.
Coastal erosion also forced the cancellation of a music festival in Santa Monica that had been set to feature The Killers, Olivia Dean and Jack White. AFP

Novaya Gazeta Europe: United Russia would have won just 34% in State Duma elections without ballot stuffing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:44:52 UTC
05:44:52 KST

Novaya Gazeta Europe: United Russia would have won just 34% in State Duma elections without ballot stuffing
Without fraud, United Russia would have won about 34% of the vote in the State Duma elections. The party’s official result — nearly 58% — was about 1.7 times that figure. Novaya Gazeta Europe reached this conclusion using calculations based on election analyst Sergey Shpilkin’s method.
Shpilkin’s method rests on the principle that adding large numbers of votes for one candidate increases both that candidate’s vote share and overall turnout. On a graph, polling stations with typical results form a relatively even cluster, while anomalous stations — where ballot stuffing is believed to have occurred — form a “comet tail” extending toward higher turnout and a larger vote share for the front-runner.
“This year, the cluster of fraud-free polling stations is centered at 34% of the vote for United Russia. That is probably what the result would have been without fraud,” Novaya Gazeta Europe said. Two election analysts agreed with its calculations, according to the outlet.
Sergey Shpilkin, a physicist, began analyzing Russian election statistics in 2007 using an approach developed by American diplomat John Brady Kiesling. Despite its limitations, many political scientists and journalists have used Shpilkin’s method to assess election fraud. Shpilkin’s home was searched in 2022, though he was already outside Russia at the time.

Trial of six French Islamic State suspects opens in Baghdad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:44:05 UTC
05:44:05 KST

The suspects were part of a group of 47 French nationals transferred last year from Syria to Iraq, where numerous suspected IS members were already being held.
The trial of six French nationals suspected of belonging to the "Islamic State" (IS) group opened in Baghdad on Sunday morning, with the next hearing scheduled for 5 October.
They face the death penalty if they are found guilty of crimes "against Iraq and the Iraqi people."
Their lawyers are calling for them to be repatriated to France, arguing that the proceedings are being conducted too quickly and do not give their clients a proper opportunity to mount an adequate defence.
The suspects were part of a group of 47 French nationals transferred last year from Syria to Iraq, where numerous suspected IS members were already being held.
This group included, among others, the man who claimed responsibility for the Nice attack in 2016.
According to investigators, the six men joined IS after travelling via Turkey and then crossing into Syria. They were arrested by Syrian Kurdish forces between 2018 and 2019 during the collapse of the self-proclaimed "caliphate" of Daesh.
After they were transferred to Iraq last year, Iraqi authorities brought charges against them for membership of a terrorist organisation.
Fighters from the jihadist group carried out massacres in Syria and Iraq in 2014, reducing many women and girls to sexual slavery.
Iraq, backed by US-led forces, declared victory over IS in 2017. Two years later, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces said they had also defeated the group in Syria.
Iraqi courts have handed down hundreds of death sentences and life terms to people convicted of terrorist offences, including foreign fighters.
In 2019, 11 French nationals were sentenced to death before their sentences were commuted to life imprisonment.
Last February, more than 5,700 suspected IS members from over 60 countries were transferred to Iraq by the United States after spending several years in detention in Syria.
Iraq also returned two detained foreign nationals in April to their respective countries, one from Finland and the other from the US, after they were acquitted.
Iraqi PM visits France
The opening of the new trial comes a week after an official visit to France by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaïdi.
Al-Zaïdi travelled to Paris on 13 and 14 September to "consolidate the strategic partnership and the ties of friendship between France and Iraq," according to the Élysée.
At the end of the visit, the two nations affirmed "their shared vision for strengthening security and stability in the Middle East, based on respect for national sovereignty, non-interference, good neighbourly relations and territorial integrity."
Paris and Baghdad also called for "respect for international law and the use of diplomatic solutions to address the crises and shared threats facing the region."
The Iraqi PM expressed his thanks to France, conveying "his appreciation" for Paris' continued support to Iraq, particularly in the fight "against Daesh terrorism."
France and Iraq also pledged to step up "their cooperation on security and defence" and their shared commitment to "relentlessly combat terrorism and prevent any resurgence of Daesh, with full respect for each other's sovereignty."

FIFA President Gianni Infantino on Monday sent a letter to FIFA Council members and the presidents of all 211 member associations outlining his openness to dialogue over reform at world soccer’s governing body.
In the letter, seen by magazine The Athletic, Infantino addressed the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal and put forward two separate reform plans ahead of the FIFA Council meeting on Oct.15.

Regarding the FIFA president’s suggestions for reform, it will be up to the FIFA Council—FIFA’s main decision-making body of 37 members—to decide whether to take the proposals forward.
Infantino has faced growing pressure since launching this summer’s now-abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal, which involved selling stakes in a company controlling commercial rights to the World Cup and other FIFA competitions to private investors.

UN expert warns US boat strikes could amount to crimes against humanity

21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
UN special rapporteur Ben Saul has warned that US attacks on suspected drug-trafficking boats could amount to crimes against humanity and said there are reasonable grounds to consider the strikes unlawful under international law.
In a statement, he said US forces have killed at least 223 people in attacks on suspected drug-trafficking vessels since Sept. 2, 2025, in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific.
Washington has described the targeted vessels as being involved in drug trafficking.
Saul questioned the legal basis for using military force against suspected traffickers, saying drug trafficking does not by itself constitute an armed attack that would justify the use of force in self-defense under international law.
He said suspected traffickers should instead be dealt with through law enforcement measures and due process.
The UN expert also raised concerns over reports of covert operations in Mexico, including alleged targeted killings of cartel leaders and surveillance flights by foreign drones over Mexican territory.
The reports have not been independently verified, and Saul did not attribute the alleged operations to a specific country.
He warned that foreign military operations carried out in Mexico without authorization could violate the country's sovereignty.
The concerns come amid growing US pressure on Mexico over drug trafficking and organized crime. US President Donald Trump has advocated stronger action against drug cartels, while Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has rejected unilateral US military intervention in Mexico.
Saul and other UN experts have called for independent investigations into the deaths and accountability for those responsible if the strikes are found to have violated international law.
The UN special rapporteur is an independent expert appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, and his statements do not necessarily represent the position of the United Nations.

‘we are probably looking for the tension’: formafantasma on designing the exhibition space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:35:36 UTC
05:35:36 KST

formafantasma on research, design, and the exhibition space
For Formafantasma, the Milan- and Rotterdam-based studio founded by Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin, exhibition design starts with looking closely at the relationship between the artworks, the building, the institution, and the people moving through it. The duo’s research-driven practice often looks at materials, culture, and the relationship between tradition and contemporary production, and they bring the same curiosity to exhibition-making. They look for what they call ‘the tension’ in a project — the moments when the artworks, architecture, curatorial idea, and established ways of displaying art don’t quite line up.
‘There is no fixed methodology, because exhibition design is always relational,’ Formafantasma tells designboom. Research and design happen at the same time in the duo’s process. The studio looks at the artworks, their material and historical context, the building they will be shown in, and the conventions of display, while also testing walls, materials, sightlines, and other ways of organizing the space. Sometimes, a seemingly pragmatic decision can reveal the larger question. ‘An apparently pragmatic decision, a wall, a fabric, a particular sightline, reveals a conceptual question that becomes central to the project,’ they explain.
The Shakers: A World in the Making at Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein | image by Bernhard Strauss, courtesy of Vitra Design Museum
challenging the supposedly neutral exhibition space
That way of working also leads Formafantasma to question one of the most familiar conventions of contemporary exhibition-making: neutrality. The white cube can appear to disappear around an artwork, but the studio argues that its familiarity does not make it neutral. ‘A white plaster wall is no less designed than a metal or textile wall,’ they tell us.‘It has simply become so familiar within contemporary art that we have stopped seeing it as a choice.’
Their exhibitions of Caravaggio and Bernini at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam and Mike Kelley at Moderna Museet show how they approach this idea differently depending on the work. For Caravaggio and Bernini, they moved away from the darkness and theatrical lighting associated with the artists, using an exhibition language closer to the white cube. With Mike Kelley, they did almost the opposite, bringing the industrial character of the museum into the foreground through metal panels. In both cases, the architecture around the works is treated as part of the exhibition and not as something that fades into the background. ‘The response therefore cannot precede the question,’ Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin explain. ‘It emerges from looking very closely at what is already there.’
For the studio, the objective is to identify the particular spatial conditions that might make relationships within each project more visible or more complicated. ‘We are less interested in finding a visual language that will unify everything than in understanding what spatial condition might make the relationships within an exhibition more legible or more complex,’ the duo shares with designboom. This also explains their interest in the history of display itself. The way objects are exhibited is never simply a technical matter. ‘We have become increasingly interested in the exhibition itself as an object of inquiry: why a wall looks the way it does, why information occupies a particular position, why visitors are expected to move or sit in particular ways, why some materials appear neutral while others become immediately visible,’ they add.
The Shakers: A World in the Making at Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein | image by Bernhard Strauss, courtesy of Vitra Design Museum
turning curatorial ideas into spatial conditions
This relationship between concept and physical space is evident in Formafantasma’s work for the 2026 Diriyah Contemporary Art Biennale. Curators Nora Razian and Sabih Ahmed were thinking about movement, migration, oral transmission, and different forms of passage. The Biennale’s setting in the JAX district, meanwhile, consisted of very large industrial spaces.
Formafantasma introduced porous textile partitions and wooden structures that established boundaries without severing one space from another. Visitors could often perceive another work, room, or presence through the architecture. ‘The curatorial idea of movement therefore wasn’t represented symbolically; it began to affect how boundaries themselves behaved,’ the studio highlights. Instead of translating a curatorial idea into an obvious visual metaphor, Formafantasma allows it to influence the physical organization of the exhibition. The conceptual and the practical develop alongside one another, a process that applies to questions that might initially appear purely technical, such as whether a work can tolerate daylight, how much acoustic separation a sound work requires, what should be visible behind an artwork, where visitors can rest, and how much material should be introduced for an exhibition that will exist for only a few months.‘Conceptual questions and technical questions are not separate for us,’ they say. ‘The exhibition emerges through their negotiation.’
The Shakers: A World in the Making at Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein | image by Martin Schgaguler, courtesy of Vitra Design Museum
providing structure without prescribing interpretation
Visitor movement is another area where Formafantasma resists the idea of complete control. Sightlines, thresholds, concealment, and revelation can all affect what becomes visible and when, but the studio is wary of treating an exhibition as a choreography in which every visitor follows an intended sequence.‘We would resist thinking of movement as something we can completely choreograph,’ they explain. ‘Choreography can imply that the designer knows how the visitor should move and what they should experience at each moment. We are more interested in establishing conditions and possibilities.’
The approach changes according to context. At the Venice Biennale, where visitors encounter a high density of artworks and information, directing the gaze and creating moments of visual relief can become important. In a smaller exhibition, there may be greater room for wandering and ambiguity. For House of Nisaba: New Stories of Painting, curated by Hendrik Folkerts at Moderna Museet in 2026, Formafantasma deliberately avoided a central axis and prescribed sequence. From outside, the exhibition appears as a single architectural object. Inside, that unity fragmented into multiple routes and views created by straight and curved cardboard partitions. The architecture gave visitors orientation without establishing one narrative. ‘Perhaps the distinction is between providing a structure and prescribing an interpretation,’ Formafantasma says. ‘A structure can be precise while remaining open to other readings.’ The choice of cardboard sharpened this idea further. At a distance, the architecture could appear almost monumental, with a clear perimeter and threshold. Up close, however, the material was visibly fragile and provisional. ‘We liked that contradiction,’ they comment. ‘It was almost a cathedral made from cardboard: monumental but open to revision.’ Despite its monumental scale, the material could be cut, moved, and rebuilt, making the space feel more like a full-scale model.
Eccentrica at Centro Pecci | image by Marco Cappelletti
the artwork and its temporary ecology
Formafantasma describes this relationship between artwork and setting through an unexpected analogy: a nature documentary. ‘There is an animal in the foreground, which we understand to be the protagonist, and behind it there is a landscape that we somehow perceive as scenery,’ they say. ‘Ecologically, of course, this distinction makes no sense. The animal exists through its relationships with that environment.’ The same, they argue, is true of an exhibition. Artwork, architecture, neighboring works, texts, light, materials, visitors, and the institution form a ‘temporary ecology.’ Changing one element changes the relationships between the others.
This is why the studio rejects the idea of exhibition architecture as a passive background. Its role is to acknowledge that the conditions of display are already active. One of the projects that most clearly shifted Formafantasma’s understanding of this possibility was Oltre Terra, an exhibition that the duo both curated and designed. Investigating wool and the complicated relationships between humans, sheep, landscapes, agriculture, and extraction, the project also examined the history of the diorama as a device for isolating, reconstructing, and observing nature. Because Formafantasma was responsible for both the research and the exhibition apparatus, display could become part of the investigation. ‘The distinction between content and display became much less useful,’ they say.
The project helped the studio understand that exhibition design could do more than contain research. It could articulate an argument. That position places Formafantasma’s exhibition work within the broader logic of their practice, which moves between research, materials, objects, and users. The team uses the act of designing to expose the systems and conventions that shape what we encounter. ‘The conventions of exhibiting are extraordinarily powerful precisely because most of the time we don’t notice them,’ they conclude. ‘Making one of those conventions slightly unfamiliar can sometimes reveal the entire system.’
Eccentrica at Centro Pecci | image by Marco Cappelletti
Biennale Arte 2022 – The Milk of Dreams | image by Marco Cappelletti
Oltre Terra | image ©Gregorio Gonella
Oltre Terra | image ©Gregorio Gonella
Oltre Terra | image ©Gregorio Gonella

&quot;System&apos;s Agony&quot;: Every Third Vote May Have Been Rigged in the Elections to the Russian State Duma

"System's Agony": Every Third Vote May Have Been Rigged in the Elections to the Russian State Duma
Kyiv • UNN
Actual turnout may have been below 40%, compared with the official 59.32%. Analysts estimate the share of questionable votes at around 31%.
The actual turnout in the elections to the Russian State Duma may have been below 40%, instead of the 59.32% announced by the Central Election Commission, while about a third of the votes may have been falsified. This is evidenced by calculations by independent electoral analysts, The Moscow Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to preliminary official results, United Russia is receiving 57.83% of the vote—the party's highest result in its entire history. It may receive 347 seats in the State Duma.
Boris Ovchinnikov, co-founder of Data Insight, analyzed the first 20,000 published protocols, covering about a quarter of polling stations. In his estimate, turnout may have been falsified or artificially inflated at nearly 70% of polling stations outside Moscow, while around 31% of the votes overall may be questionable.
"The system's agony"
According to Ovchinnikov's calculations, the share of potentially falsified votes in United Russia's result may reach 55%.
Analyst Petro Zhyzhyn, who applied Shpilkin's statistical method, arrived at similar turnout estimates. According to his calculations, United Russia's actual support may have been around 35%, instead of the officially reported nearly 58%.
Electoral expert and former co-chair of the Golos movement Roman Udot called the results obtained "the system's agony." In his assessment, the Russian authorities have effectively exhausted their administrative resources, while the scale of the artificial increase in the result may amount to around 20 percentage points.
Analysts also allow for manipulation in favor of other parties. Electoral analyst Stanislav Andreychuk drew attention to the appearance of around 60,000 votes for A Just Russia in the Central Election Commission's system, after which the party managed to overcome the 5% threshold and enter the State Duma.
