Does Australia need another baby bonus as it faces a birth rate struggle?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:32:06 UTC
04:32:06 KST

in brief
- Australia faces a choice between higher immigration or having more babies to fix an ageing workforce and shrinking tax base.
- Experts say migration is the most effective strategy to staff essential sectors like aged care long term.
Australia will need to boost its population to support the elderly and the economy in the long term, experts warn, after the government's latest Intergenerational Report (IGR) found that people are expected to live longer and have fewer children.
The report landed as politicians float the idea of bringing back the Howard-era baby bonus and argue over the need to reduce migration.
Independent MP Bob Katter has recently suggested an up-front cash payment of $75,000 per child would reverse the declining birth rate, which is now expected to fall to just 1.34 children per woman by 2065.
The argument was dismissed by Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Nationals leader Matt Canavan, who said on Monday that family support policy should be more than just "here's some cash".
However, Australia does face challenging demographic questions, with experts saying the choice will come down to more migrants or more babies.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We will have a large pool of elderly people that we have to support," Dr Pelin Akyol, research manager at the economic think tank The e61 Institute, told SBS News.
"If we have a smaller pool of people working, then it will be a big fiscal problem in this country — and in every country."
Global and domestic surveys show that most people want to have more children than they end up having, owing to cultural, social, and economic constraints which are difficult to address.
"With AI and everything else going on right now, it is hard to know what will happen," Akyol said. "But what we know at this point is that it's going to affect the economy in a bad way".
The fertility illusion
While the IGR highlights a collapsing birth rate, demographers caution that official metrics paint a distorted picture of Australian family choices.
Peter McDonald, emeritus professor of demography at the Australian National University, told SBS News that the country's reliance on international students and temporary visa holders skewed the headline Total Fertility Rate (TFR).
Temporary migrants are often young adults aged 20 to 35 who are in higher education or the early stages of their career. While they are counted as potential mothers, they "hardly have any births," McDonald said, which drives the TFR down.
"That's one of the central reasons why Australia's fertility rate has been falling because the temporary population's been rising," he said.
The birth rate for women born in Australia is around 1.64, higher than the Australian Bureau of Statistics headline fertility rate of 1.48. While this is still below the replacement rate of 2.1, Akyol said the immigration influence on TFR is different in Australia than in other comparable nations.
"In Germany, migrants have higher fertility rate than natives," she said. "But in Australia, it is the opposite".
McDonald also warns against placing too much faith in the long-term projections of the IGR — which assumes net overseas migration will remain flat at 235,000 annually for the next four decades — and that immigration and total births can't be viewed separately as they are "not independent of each other".
"If you can tell me what the birth rate is going to be in 10 years, you're a better man than me," he said. "But if you can tell me what it is in 40 years, then you're a miracle worker."
Is a baby bonus the answer?
Katter's proposed return to former treasurer Peter Costello's cash payment for each newborn child would cost upwards of an estimated $22.5 billion a year for the present 300,000 babies born each year in Australia.
Akyol's research into the 2004 policy indicates that cash incentives do increase the fertility rate, but the effect is "not huge" and, given how different the world is today, "it is not guaranteed we will see a similar effect".
While a $75,000 payment is "huge" compared to the $3,000 of the original policy and "might have an effect", Akyol doubted this was the best use of money when other factors like support benefits also play a key role in family decisions.
McDonald said Australia's tax system has become too narrowly focused on early childcare, making raising older children harder for working families.
"Today, about 58 per cent of families get no family allowance for their children," he said. "It's not just about very young children... supporting families with children is also about supporting older children, and we've gone a long, long way away from doing that."
A median worker claiming both employer and state parental leave would already receive around $48,700 before tax, something McDonald said disadvantages those without full-time employment. Instead of re-introducing lump-sum payments, he calls for a broader review of child equity.
"I think there's a need for an inquiry into the system of child support payments, to deal with two issues: one is the inequity of the system for very young children, and two, the lack of support for older children," he said.
"Children are a social good.... so I think there is justification for supporting families with children; it's called horizontal equity."
"Horizontal equity used to be quite a big thing back in the 1980s ... I think it needs to be revisited."
A national trade-off
To offset a declining taxpayer base, the IGR highlights increasing older workforce participation and leveraging artificial intelligence to automate labour gaps.
However, McDonald questioned the feasibility of expecting Australians to work deeper into their 60s and 70s.
"A lot of people, particularly those who work in physically demanding jobs, do not want to work beyond pension age. They've had enough," he said.
"AI is going to make a big difference to future labour force needs, but AI is not going to wipe the bottoms of people in aged care."
Akyol said current debates around migration could soon flip as birth rates drop across the globe, including in key migrant origin countries such as China and India. With a shrinking global talent pool, nations could shift from seeking to restrict migration to actively competing for skilled workers.
"In the long run, there might really be a competition for getting the best migrants," Akyol said. "Because in all developed countries, fertility rate has been decreasing... and it seems like there is no hope that it will just turn back and increase again."
"There is no easy solution here. There is a trade-off with every kind of policy."
Relying on immigration is the most direct mechanism to address workforce shortages in sectors like aged care, which are already under strain, McDonald said — something he said the government has failed to communicate in its messaging.
"The IGR shows the advantage of a higher level of migration for the federal government's bottom line," McDonald said. "Migrants make our prospects of dealing with a future aged population much better."

MOS creates basket-like aluminium pavilion at Art Omi in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:30:38 UTC
04:30:38 KST

MOS creates basket-like aluminium pavilion at Art Omi in New York
US studio MOS Architects has used aluminium shingles to cover an egg-shaped pavilion at Art Omi in Upstate New York, creating a place to rest that draws stylistically on pre-modern basketry and mid-century futurism.
An experiment in form and material, A Dome with Four Oculi was installed on the expansive Art Omi campus as a place of shelter and rest.
The structure sits on stilts and consists of a shell that MOS compared to a crinoline dress.
It was then covered by aluminium shingles that overlap and are held in place by stainless steel bolts. Combined, the shell is around a quarter-inch thick. It has two portholes on the side that look out into the landscape and is open at the top.
MOS co-founder Michael Meredith told Dezeen that structurally it is like an "upside-down basket", connecting to both the studio's work in easy-to-assemble prefabricated aluminium structures and a focus on the potential for experimentation at small scales.
"We've been working for years with folded aluminium and basically using it like paper, almost like large-scale models," said Meredith.
It was designed to be put together with standard tools in just a few days.
Conceptually, the structure takes cues both from pre-modern basketry as well as from the Airstream trailer.
"There's something of woven architecture in it, almost pre-modern," said Meredith. "Woven structures have an economic use of material, lighter material in this case. There's something nomadic."
"But there's Airstream trailer quality too," he continued. "You can see a bunch of stuff in it."
Beyond the thematic elements, the structure also provides shelter and a place to sit in the fields of Art Omi, which hold dozens of rotating art and architecture installations.
The oculi on the sides of the structure also provide vistas across the field.
Triangular cutouts on the side provide access and give the structure as in a tent.
Viewed from elsewhere, the pavilion has a face-like quality. It almost looks like the top part of the head of the Iron Giant from the 1999 film.
"It's also, as everybody tells us, a little bit ridiculous," said Meredith, who said it was like a Buckminster Fuller dome reimagined by artist Philip Guston. He added that the woven nature of these structures makes it more practical than typical domes, as the sides could be modified and shaped as in basketry.
MOS is well known for its conceptual work and writings.
A Dome with Four Oculi relates to recent writings by the studio, such as its Smaller Architecture book, which calls for smaller architecture studios to experiment.
It was developed partly in response to what Meredith calls a "weird moment" for architecture. The prevalence and desire for bigness have left out an important space that architecture holds for expression.
"Architecture is in a weird moment in general. It used to be a more active part of cultural production," he said.
"At some point, though, it sort of shifted and just feels commercial. Everything just feels like a commodity," he continued.
"So that's what's nice about Art Omi. It's sort of outside the system, and it gives you a chance to reflect and think about something else."
The pavilion was part of Art Omi's fall architecture programming, which included TAELON7's Limbo Engawa pavilion.
Art Omi has been doubling down on its commitment to architecture and, in 2024, announced a series of 18 pavilions designed by established architecture studios such as SO-IL.
In London, Studio Saar created a shield-topped pavilion for London Design Festival, examining Britain's colonial history in India.
The photography is by Michael Vahrenwald.

Zelenskyy Responds to Trump: Ukraine Ready for Energy Truce if Russia Halts Strikes
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly responded on September 21 to US President Donald Trump’s social media statement, agreeing that Russia’s war against Ukraine “must be ended” and confirming that Kyiv is actively discussing diplomatic de-escalation frameworks with Washington.
Following his phone conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” citing the destruction and temporary shutdown of a large number of Russian refineries.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Trump called for an immediate end to the “ridiculous and never ending War,” arguing that “the whole World suffers” from the war and pointing to an estimated 25,000 monthly casualties as a primary reason to halt the fighting.
In a statement posted on X, Zelenskyy affirmed that Ukraine has sought peace since the onset of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and highlighted ongoing dialogues with the Trump administration aimed at formulating concrete steps to bring the war to a close.
He explicitly outlined Kyiv’s conditions for a partial energy and infrastructure truce, noting that matching Ukrainian de-escalation measures would depend on a complete halt to Russian attacks against Ukrainian civilian supply systems.

“It will no longer be the case that only the country under attack suffers,” Zelenskyy stated. “The nature of war is now such that the aggressor will suffer as well. Technology makes this possible”.
The Ukrainian leader’s remarks follow days of intense diplomatic exchanges over rising global energy prices, with Kyiv emphasizing that any halt to its deep strikes on Russian oil facilities remains contingent on reciprocal protection for Ukraine’s own energy grid and critical infrastructure.
Zelenskyy recently proposed a conditional energy de-escalation framework to Western partners, indicating that Kyiv is prepared to halt strikes on Russian refineries if international partners can secure and guarantee a complete end to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy, port, and logistics infrastructure.
In a statement, he emphasized that any mutual halt must be reliable, long-term, and enforceable rather than a brief operational pause. Expressing skepticism regarding Moscow’s willingness to abide by an agreement, Zelenskyy warned that Russia might seek temporary relief for its domestic fuel markets ahead of elections before resuming strikes.

Trump says U.S. is working on ‘major deal’ to replace Canadian potash with Belarusian supplies, but President Alexander Lukashenko says Minsk has none to spare
President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that the U.S. is working on “a massive Deal” to buy potash fertilizer from Belarus.
Trump, who is currently waging another trade war with Canada, said, “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.”
Just hours before Trump’s post, however, Alexander Lukashenko said that even if Belarus regained full access to Western markets for its potash fertilizer, it still could not supply them because all its potash was already under contract:
“As far as I know… We’ve managed to shift our exports eastward. Our negotiations with the Americans are proof of that. A lot of people here are making a fuss about potash. Even if we wanted to supply other markets — Western markets — we simply don’t have the volume. It’s all under contract.”
The U.S. relies on imports for nearly all its potash fertilizer. Canada supplies almost 80% of those imports and Russia another 12%.
Belarus is one of the world’s largest potash fertilizer producers, alongside Canada, Russia, and China. But sanctions have restricted its access to Western markets. The sanctions were imposed over the brutal crackdown on Belarus’s 2020 protests and the Lukashenko regime’s complicity in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
After Trump was reelected to a second term, the U.S. began improving relations with Lukashenko and, among other steps, lifted sanctions on Belarus’s potash industry. The EU, however, has kept its sanctions on Belarusian potash imports in place.

The ‘stab in the back’ that wasn’t: Why Stalin sent the Red Army into Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:23:02 UTC
04:23:02 KST

The ‘stab in the back’ that wasn’t: Why Stalin sent the Red Army into Poland
On September 17, 1939, Soviet troops crossed into eastern Poland. By that time, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth was about to collapse under the assault of Nazi forces. Soon, the Soviet military moved westward to meet the advancing Germans. Moscow and Berlin established a demarcation line according to which the USSR acquired parts of eastern Poland. Today, these territories belong to Belarus, Ukraine, and Lithuania.
This event still sparks debates both in Russia and Europe, and particularly in Poland. In Ukraine and Lithuania, political discourse has taken a surprising turn, suggesting that while the USSR was the aggressor state that invaded Poland on September 17, neither Ukraine nor Lithuania will yield any territory that they gained as a result of this aggression. For Lithuania, the situation is quite ironic, since it acquired its capital, Vilnius, precisely as a result of the Red Army’s Polish campaign.
Any commentary on this event provokes an intense and painful reaction from all sides that consider themselves victims of it. Nevertheless, it is essential to examine the circumstances surrounding the Soviet army’s invasion of Poland. For Russians, who lost countless lives during the Second World War, this topic is particularly sensitive; but the same holds true for Poles, who suffered comparable losses relative to their population size, and for Belarusians and Ukrainians, who found themselves in the middle of this significant territorial reallocation.
History can often be distorted by politics. From the late 1930s to the present day, interpretations of this event have evolved in various countries. It would be best to take a measured approach to assess what really happened, recognizing that each country has its own perspective shaped by its unique experience. We also need to remember that all parties had rational interests, yet none of them possessed enough information or the benefit of hindsight provided by post-war historians.
Buffer zone of discord
By 1939, both the Soviet Union and Poland were new states established on the basis of old nations. They had come into existence following the disintegration of the Russian Empire and the subsequent Russian Civil War. However, from the outset, there was a significant territorial dispute between Russia’s reincarnation in the form of the Soviet Union and Poland’s rebirth as the Second Polish Republic. The Poles laid claim not only to their own lands but also to all the lands Poland had once possessed, which included vast territories in Belarus and Ukraine. In Poland, this region is referred to as “Kresy Wschodnie,” which means “Eastern Borderlands.”
Overall, Poland’s ambitions extended even further. During the Russian Civil War, Polish forces advanced deep into Ukraine and captured Kiev before ultimately being defeated. The Red Army then launched its Polish campaign which also ended in failure a short way from Warsaw. Ultimately, the Poles acquired what they referred to as “Kresy” – the western regions of Ukraine and Belarus. For the most part, these territories weren’t populated by Poles, yet Poland had governed them before the territorial divisions of the 18th century and viewed them as its historical lands. During the interwar period, these regions underwent a process of polonization, with Ukrainian and Belarusian populations facing discrimination. One somewhat counterintuitive fact is that Ukrainian nationalist terrorism during that period was directed primarily not against the USSR, but against Poland.
Meanwhile, the Soviet Union regarded these lost territories as unjustly seized and was unwilling to relinquish its claims on them. In short, neither party was satisfied with such ‘peace’ and there was no warming of relations between the USSR and Poland.
The territorial dispute over the Vilnius region caused additional challenges. Poland seized Vilna (Vilnius), a city that Lithuania claimed as its historical capital and which was highly important to it both historically and culturally.
This atmosphere of ‘cold peace’ lasted throughout the 1920s. In the 1930s, the Nazis came to power in Germany. In 1938, Hitler annexed a significant part of Czechoslovakia (a few months later, he came to fully control the country). This crisis put the USSR and Poland at odds once again. The Soviet Union viewed the Nazis as a grave threat, and Moscow even considered intervening on behalf of Czechoslovakia. However, this required USSR troops to pass through Poland, which Warsaw resolutely rejected. It was opposed to any military cooperation with the USSR, even for transit purposes. Furthermore, during the German occupation of Czechoslovakia, Poland annexed the Teschen region (an area of 805 square kilometers with a population of 277,000) which was a small but notable territorial gain.
Throughout the negotiations regarding Czechoslovakia, the interests and positions of the USSR were overtly disregarded by Western allies – i.e. England, France, and Poland. The Soviet Union gained considerable political weight on the global stage only after WWII. Before that, its influence hardly rose to the level of a superpower. Consequently, Stalin had to swallow this bitter pill and prepare for the events to come.
Meanwhile, Hitler was determined to continue his aggressive expansion. The regime he constructed in Germany had a significant yet subtle flaw – its structure resembled a financial pyramid. The rapid growth of the country’s military industrial complex threatened to undermine its economy. The only salvation for the Third Reich lay in war or the unconditional submission of neighboring countries to its demands and threats. Poland was next on Hitler’s list of intended victims. He used the “Polish Corridor” – the strip of land separating mainland Germany from East Prussia – as leverage. The Germans maintained contact with this exclave solely by sea. Today, this area remains an exclave, but belongs to Russia: the current Russian city of Kaliningrad is the former German city of Königsberg. Additionally, Hitler demanded reconsideration of the status of Danzig, a city with a significant German population that had been designated a “free city” under the League of Nations’ protection.
Understandably, Poland wasn’t satisfied with these demands. The question was, how could it stand up to Germany, which was much more powerful. Clearly, the best option was to seek help from Western allies – Britain and France. They readily provided Poland with security guarantees and did indeed declare war on the Third Reich on September 3, just two days after it invaded Poland. However, what the Polish leaders didn’t realize was that their allies weren’t prepared to offer immediate assistance. Britain needed time to transport troops across the English Channel, while France had to mobilize and strategically deploy its troops. This couldn’t be done immediately, but it was uncertain whether Poland could hold out long enough.
Poland’s dialogue with Soviet diplomats was quite rude. Polish officials bluntly told People’s Commissar for Foreign Affairs Maxim Litvinov that they would ask for help “when it will be needed.” Throughout this time, the Polish government believed that “the dismemberment of Russia is at the heart of Poland’s eastern policy.”
It’s no secret that there were significant territorial disputes between the USSR and Poland, and that the two countries felt an aversion towards each other. In hindsight, Warsaw’s behavior appears reckless, but at the time, Poland believed that the guarantees from Western allies would suffice. They thought that by allowing even one Russian soldier into Poland, they could easily become hostages of such an ally. Strictly speaking, one can’t say that they were wrong. Nevertheless, the Soviet regime turned out to be a lot less strict than the German regime in Poland.
The USSR aimed to safeguard its interests in Eastern Europe. Moscow had no doubt that a large-scale war was imminent. And the USSR found itself in a vulnerable position. The key centers of Soviet power were located too close to the border. Leningrad (currently St. Petersburg) faced threats from both Finland and Estonia which it bordered, while Minsk and Kiev were dangerously close to the Polish border. The USSR wasn’t concerned about a threat coming directly from Estonia or Poland, but rather feared that a third party could use these regions as a launchpad for an attack on the USSR (by 1939, it was clear that this would be Germany). Stalin and his inner circle understood that the USSR would eventually confront Germany and were eager to secure the most advantageous position before the inevitable confrontation.
Mistrust and the fog of war
The USSR still had another option – direct negotiations with Western allies. Stalin was primarily interested in a coordinated plan of action against the Nazis. However, the Soviet Union had its own fears and biases. It’s important to note that, just like in the situation with Poland, neither British nor French leaders could foresee the future any better than their Soviet counterparts. And in 1939 they considered such an alliance no better than one with Hitler.
This might sound odd in 2026, but in the summer of 1939, Hitler wasn’t yet “the Hitler” that we’ve come to know. The Third Reich was still largely focused on repressing its own citizens. Anti-semitism with its discriminatory laws was abominable, yet not necessarily worse than the repressions in the US against African-Americans or the colonial practices of European powers. On the other hand, Stalin’s USSR, with its own repressions and ideology aimed at dismantling the capitalist world, certainly didn’t present itself as a beacon of virtue. This is why Moscow had its doubts about whether Britain and France were more reliable negotiating partners than Germany, and the same skepticism was shared by Paris and London in regard to Moscow. Additionally, Britain and France significantly underestimated the real weight of the USSR as an ally – and this was an error they would soon regret.
On August 11, an Anglo-French delegation arrived in Moscow. The problem was that the allies came with a very vague battle plan. The Soviet side insisted on including the term “indirect aggression” in the agreement, which implied using the territories of neighboring countries to wage war against the USSR. The allies believed that Stalin wanted free rein to act against the Baltic states, Finland, and wherever else he pleased. However, the Soviet Union needed this complicated wording to safeguard itself against a possible surprise alliance between Germany and Finland or the Baltic nations, leading to a potential invasion of the USSR from those territories.
Both sides distrusted each other and preferred to secure maximum guarantees with minimal commitments. Ultimately, the negotiations failed.
In response, the Soviet Union made a controversial move: it struck a deal with Hitler. On August 23, a non-aggression pact was signed between the USSR and Germany, outlining spheres of influence in Europe.
Under the famous Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the USSR aimed to buy time and establish a buffer zone in Eastern Europe. Moscow secured a significant condition – the incorporation of Eastern Poland (currently Western Ukraine and Belarus) into the Soviet sphere of interest.
Even today, this pact is often regarded as a deal with the devil. However, it did not serve as an immediate trigger for war. For Hitler, war was inevitable. Stopping the war would lead to the collapse of his entire foreign policy, and Germany’s bloated military system could not come to a stop without causing economic disaster. Moreover, Hitler did not regard the Soviet Union as a formidable opponent; he even devised plans of a complete military defeat of the USSR in three months.
Looking back, we may say that the 1938-1939 negotiations represent one of the greatest failures in the history of diplomacy. Had the world powers united against the Nazis in 1939 – or better yet, in 1938 – there might have been no WWII, but only a major clean-up of issues left over from WWI. However, there’s no way to change history.
The barrier to Blitzkrieg
Poland’s pre-war planning was based on several questionable assumptions. Poland believed that its army was sufficiently large and was capable of holding off the Nazis long enough for Western allies to come to its aid. Ideas to form a defensive line along the Vistula River and use the river as a natural barrier were ultimately dismissed. Marshal Edward Rydz-Smigly, who led Poland’s defense, aimed to cover all fronts and surrender nothing. However, in reality, Poland had far fewer military resources than the enemy and couldn’t seize the initiative. Moreover, after the annexation of Czechoslovakia, the Third Reich bordered Poland on three sides. Even without additional complications, this combination spelled disaster for Poland. Yet another problem existed: between the wars, the Germans developed a range of operational, tactical, and technical solutions known as “Blitzkrieg,” which prioritized rapid, decisive maneuvers. And Poland became the testing ground for this strategy in real-life conditions.
On September 1, 1939, Hitler invaded Poland, marking the start of WWII. On September 3, the Allies declared war on Germany. The Wehrmacht charged at the Polish army like a gorilla breaking free from its cage. Within the first week, the Polish forces retreated chaotically on all fronts, and some units became encircled. By September 5, the Polish government fled toward the border. On September 16, before the USSR entered the conflict, the Polish leadership was already negotiating with Romania regarding evacuation. The high command moved to Brest and lost contact with the main body of troops.
After September 10, there was no longer any centralized control of the Polish army. By September 16, German forces reached Bialystok, Brest, and Lviv. Most organized Polish units remained to the west and were encircled. The Allies were unable to assist Poland; French troops were slowly deployed and managed to carry out only a limited offensive that pushed the front back a few kilometers into German territory. The Allies could have saved Poland by 1940, if only it could hold out until then – but this was clearly an insurmountable task for the country.
Soviet political leaders decided that further delay was pointless. On September 6, Moscow announced “large-scale military exercises” which in reality meant that the country mobilized its armed forces. However, it soon became apparent that the Soviet military was not as combat ready as was anticipated. The troops weren’t ready for combat, military equipment required repairs, and there was a great shortage of additional vehicles.
Regardless of this, the Polish forces were completely disorganized and could not offer fierce resistance. The notion that the Soviets “stabbed Poland in the back as it fought” the Nazis sounds quite dramatic, but by that time, all that remained of the Polish army were some isolated battalions. Poland had lost all its industrial regions, mobilization was impossible, the army was defeated, and the remaining troops tried to defend Warsaw. In essence, there was no one to “stab in the back.” Formally, the Polish army still numbered in the hundreds of thousands of soldiers and officers, but in reality they moved around chaotically in the rear. There was no one to lead them into battle.
On the night of September 17, Stalin personally informed German ambassador to the USSR Friedrich-Werner Graf von der Schulenburg that the Red Army was about to start its operation. A similar note was delivered to the Polish ambassador to the USSR. The next morning, Soviet mechanized columns crossed the border into Poland.
The Polish government promptly fled the country. Commander of the Polish armed forces Marshal Rydz-Smigly ordered, “I command an immediate retreat to Romania and Hungary by the shortest routes. Do not engage in combat with the Soviets.”
The entry of the Red Army into Poland was accompanied by considerable disorder. Polish resistance was sporadic and was largely initiated by local junior commanders. The advance of Soviet troops was marked by confusion and there were many non-combat losses. In areas where the Poles put up resistance, the Soviet army fought, but generally for the Poles, it looked more like disarmament than defeat in battle. For instance, during the assault on Grodno, 57 Red Army soldiers were killed, while about 1,500 Polish soldiers and officers surrendered. During the campaign, an estimated 737-1,475 Soviet soldiers and officers died – many of them for non-combat reasons; and about 240,000 soldiers were taken prisoner.
While Polish soldiers and officers offered some resistance, the Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Jewish people often sympathized with or even assisted the advancing Red Army units. Poland’s ideology was one of triumphant nationalism, so non-Polish cultures found themselves in a subordinate position and were often openly discriminated against.
The Wehrmacht immediately halted its advance into territories that were claimed by the USSR. A few days later, the demarcation line was finalized. Tensions arose only in Lviv, where Soviet forces encountered German troops. As a result, all three sides – the Red Army, the Polish garrison, and the German army – lost both soldiers and equipment.
A separate story unfolded in Brest. On September 22, a Red Army tank brigade entered the city, which had been occupied by German forces. Depending on the narrator, this event is often described as either the passage of troops or a joint parade. Soviet commander Semyon Krivoshein and German General Heinz Guderian watched as German soldiers withdrew from Brest and Soviet troops took their place. The situation was all the more awkward since Krivoshein was Jewish and felt as uncomfortable standing next to a Nazi commander as Guderian did standing next to him.
By September 29, the Red Army’s campaign in Poland was essentially over. The Soviet Union expanded its territory by 196,000 square km (half of the territory of Poland) with a population of up to 13 million people. The Vilna region, including the city of Vilnius, was handed over to Lithuania, while areas populated by Belarusians and Ukrainians were assigned to the respective Soviet republics.
The fate of prisoners of war and the people detained by Soviet security agencies raised further questions. Many Polish officers were later executed at Katyn. But most captives were either sent home or fled to the West through third counties where they formed the Anders’ Army, which became part of the Western coalition. In western Belarus and Ukraine, Soviet authority was established, which caused certain upheavals that always accompany such transitions. Many people suspected of disloyalty were deported further east. However, considering the war which would soon break out, such exile often saved their lives.
Liberation for some, occupation for others
Setting politics aside and focusing on the actual circumstances surrounding the Soviet campaign and its alternatives, we see that the situation didn’t look flattering from any side.
Firstly, we need to dismiss the idea that Hitler would not have started the war without the pact or that the war was started jointly by the Nazis and the USSR. The Soviet Union lacked the diplomatic weight to impose its will on partners in negotiations. Indeed, the Nazis didn’t want more problems in the East. However, from Hitler’s perspective, he struck a fantastic deal: he resolved a potentially contentious issue and rid himself of possible complications by ceding territories that he considered worthless – that didn’t have any significant resources or industrial centers – to the Soviet Union.
For the USSR, this meant gaining a buffer zone in case of a future confrontation with the Nazis and reuniting two important national republics. Did the decision regarding Poland align with strict moral standards? Not really. But Poland had little reason to complain – after all, its army had forcefully seized the disputed territories a few decades earlier, only to lose them in another military conflict. And while we may vehemently denounce USSR aggression, we must also ask: what were the alternatives? In fact, there were only two viable options. The first one was to fight against Hitler with a weak military force and with no solid guarantees from Western allies. Negotiations on a joint action plan with those allies had just failed, so why would Stalin trust them?
As for Poland, it was outright opposed to an alliance with Moscow. Indeed, there was another option: to do nothing. This meant handing over the Kresy to Hitler. On September 17, 1939, the choice was not “Poland or Hitler” or “totalitarians or democrats”; it was simply “Hitler or Stalin.” Given this reality, it’s worth asking the moralists whether they consider Hitler a more legitimate or humane ruler of Lviv and Grodno than Stalin.
In this grim world of ‘realpolitik’, Poland’s position proved to be extremely vulnerable. The leaders of the Second Polish Republic consistently rejected any ideas of jointly fighting against Hitler with the USSR. Of course, they reasonably feared being drawn into Moscow’s orbit and ultimately finding themselves living in a socialist Poland. Ironically, by the end of the war, this is indeed what happened, but by that time Poland had lost one-fifth of its population due to the war and the Nazi occupation, and Warsaw and the entire country were in ruins. Should Poland have considered making political concessions to the USSR earlier instead of waiting until Moscow controlled Poland’s territory, army, and political institutions? That’s a question only the Polish people can answer. Indeed, it’s hard to shake the feeling that in 1939, faced with two evils, Poland chose to do nothing and simply perish. The idea of doing nothing in such a situation might look good in a novel, but it’s hardly practical in politics.
For Western allies, 1939 clearly became the year of lost opportunities. One could argue that an allied operation against the Nazis involving Britain, France, the USSR, and what remained of Poland could have been a better option than what happened in reality: Germany’s swift occupation of France, followed by Britain and the USSR fighting Germany on their own – Britain at sea and in the air, and the USSR on land. However, at the time, deep mutual distrust and a poor understanding of the situation played a fatal role in forming an alliance between Western democracies and the Soviet Union.
The USSR ultimately benefited from the events of September 1939, but not as much as it had hoped. Its territorial gains included western Belarus and Ukraine, and this was soon followed by the annexation of the Baltic states. Since a larger war loomed on the horizon, this territory became valuable only as square kilometers. These buffer zones proved crucial in 1941 when the USSR entered the war against Germany. The issue of Finland’s status, which the USSR declared war on several months later, remained unresolved.
Most importantly, Stalin hoped that he would gain far more time than he actually did. The USSR had hoped that it would have several years to prepare for war, while France put up active resistance. In reality, the defense of France collapsed in the summer of 1940, and the USSR gained only one year and nine months of breathing room. And rather than becoming weaker, the Wehrmacht grew even stronger in the course of the conflict against Western allies.
In 1939, politicians gave more candid and sensible assessments of the situation. Winston Churchill observed:
“Russia has pursued a cold policy of self-interest. We could have wished that the Russian armies should be standing on their present lines as the friends of the allies in Poland, instead of as invaders. But that the Russian armies should stand on this line was clearly necessary for the safety of Russia against the Nazi menace. In any case, this line exists, and this means that an Eastern Front has been established that Nazi Germany would not dare attack.”
The Soviet Union operated within the framework of ‘realpolitik’, which didn’t look either nice or noble.
But in less than two years, the Russians found themselves engaged in the greatest war in history, which was a battle for their very survival. And undoubtedly, the Soviet Union used every means at its disposal to strengthen its position before that day arrived.

SDA Seeks to Expand Ground Architecture for Future Missile Tracking Satellites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:22:49 UTC
04:22:49 KST

The Space Development Agency is opening a competition to expand its ground architecture to support a growing fleet of missile warning, tracking, and defense satellites.
The agency issued a solicitation Sept. 18 requesting bids from companies to develop ground entry points for its missile defense satellites at locations around the world. By early next year, SDA plans to choose a single company to build, install, and maintain up to eight new ground entry points and to perform upgrades at current sites.
The ground segment expansion will support Tranche 3 of what SDA calls its Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture, a low-Earth orbit constellation envisioned to include hundreds of data transport and missile tracking satellites that will be refreshed every two years with new capability. So far, SDA has launched just eight missile tracking satellites as part of what it calls “Tranche 0” to demonstrate the viability of space-based missile tracking in LEO. The agency is in the midst of launching Tranche 1, which will feature 28 missile warning and tracking satellites. Tranche 2 will include 54, and Tranche 3 will have 108 spacecraft.
That proliferated space architecture requires a network of ground systems that can push data from satellites to military users who need it to inform decisions about how to respond to missile threats. SDA expects that distributing those ground systems across multiple locations will both improve the performance of the capability and make it more resilient.
For its first two operational tranches, SDA is requiring its satellite vendors to provide the ground stations needed to operate their spacecraft. General Dynamics Mission Systems is under contract to integrate those ground stations into ground operations centers, which serve as hubs for each tranche of satellites. SDA has awarded the company $816 million to date for that work.
For Tranche 3, the agency wants to transition to an enterprise model, according to a Government Accountability Office report issued in January. That approach would feature “new capabilities” and build on the earlier tranches. SDA has also selected SAIC to serve as a third-party integrator for Tranche 3, which GAO says should help address past challenges with ground system testing and operations.
SDA expects to start launching Tranche 3 satellites in late 2028 or 2029, but in the meantime it’s focused on populating Tranche 1. The agency has launched three batches of data transport satellites and has six missions left to complete the tranche. SDA Director Gurpartap Sandhoo told reporters Sept. 15 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that the first Tranche 1 tracking satellites should launch either late this year or early next.
The Space Force’s fiscal 2027 budget requests $3.5 billion for SDA’s LEO-based Resilient Missile Warning/Missile Tracking program. Budget documents indicate that fiscal ‘27 funding, if approved, will support early work on Tranche 3 ground entry points and other infrastructure to expand the “global footprint.”

Canada’s Jews shouldn’t need a fundraising campaign to pray safely - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:22:42 UTC
04:22:42 KST

Const. Jeff Smith of the Belleville Police Service was waiting in an unmarked car outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday evening when, according to Ontario’s police watchdog, a man with a shotgun opened fire on him.
About 25 people were inside for Kol Nidre, the service that opens Yom Kippur. The synagogue’s president, Norm Weddum, says the congregation had never received a threat.
Belleville is a city of about 55,000, roughly 110 miles east of Toronto, and Weddum describes its Jewish community as small. Somebody at the local police department decided that this synagogue, on this night, needed an armed officer outside anyway. Ontario Premier Doug Ford called Smith a hero who stopped a tragedy. I think Ford is right, and I’d like to know who put Smith there.
Here’s what happened inside, as Weddum tells it. He heard shots, some congregants went toward the doors, and then a second round came. He moved everyone back into the sanctuary, shut the wooden doors so no one could be seen from the entrance, and told people to get down on the floor. Bullets came through the windows. One stained-glass window has about 20 holes in it.
Doug Lobel, a congregant, told CP24 news station what they were thinking down there: “Was the gunman going to breach the doors and start targeting us?”
He didn’t get the chance. Smith returned fire; a second officer fired as well, and Smith and the man were both hit. Houses and cars on the street were damaged. Smith, a 13-year veteran, is in critical but stable condition. The suspect, 29-year-old Sean Ward from neighboring Quinte West, is in life-threatening condition. No one inside was hurt.
Read the statements slowly
The first statement from Belleville police said an officer had “encountered” an individual near an intersection. It didn’t say why an officer was there. Since then, the force has had nothing to add, because the Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that takes over in Ontario whenever police shoot at someone, has invoked its mandate.
Mayor Neil Ellis told CBC he hopes the SIU investigation gets to “the root cause.” I don’t doubt he was shaken; he said he cried when he heard the news. But the SIU’s job is to decide whether Smith and his colleague were justified in firing. Why a 29-year-old showed up on that corner with a gun isn’t its question. Someone else has to ask it, and nobody has said publicly who that is.
Police haven’t said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue was the target. The SIU first described the weapon as a rifle and later as a shotgun. At least three people fired on a residential street, and nobody has said whose bullets went through the stained glass. I’m not going to guess at Ward’s motive. Whatever it was, Smith was there first.
'It pains me'
In June, Prime Minister Mark Carney stood in Holy Blossom Temple, Toronto’s oldest Reform synagogue, and said, “Canada’s civic compact is failing Jewish Canadians.” It was an unusually blunt thing for a prime minister to say. He noted that more than two-thirds of religion-motivated hate crimes the previous year had targeted Jews, who are about 1% of Canadians, and he announced another $75 million for security. Then he added, “It pains me that we had to commit $75 million to this.”
I believe him. I wish he’d stop saying it.
When a prime minister describes security money as a painful concession, the program that spends it tends to read the same way. The $75 million went to the Canada Community Security Program. The program describes itself as time-limited funding for communities at risk of hate-motivated crime. It covers up to 70% of eligible costs; under the program it replaced, the government paid half. Anything spent before a funding agreement is signed isn’t reimbursed. Guards qualify only as “time-limited third-party licensed security personnel.”
Read those rules as the treasurer of a synagogue the size of Sons of Jacob would. You raise the other 30% yourself, fill out the application, and wait for a signed agreement before spending a dollar. Then you hire guards on a “time-limited” basis, as if somebody at Public Safety Canada knows when the threat expires. The program is built for communities that can show they’re at risk. By its president’s account, this one had never been threatened.
Ford said out loud on Monday what those rules imply. He told reporters he was thankful such an experienced officer had been posted at the synagogue, and then added: “We never have enough security.” He’s the premier of Ontario. If anyone in the province can decide what counts as enough, it’s him.
On Sunday night, Toronto’s mayor, Olivia Chow, said Jews “should not need police presence to observe Yom Kippur.” Nobody disagrees with her. It’s no help to that treasurer deciding whether to apply for a guard this year.
Where I might be wrong
The best argument against everything above is Chow’s, taken seriously. A country that answers antisemitism by stationing police outside synagogues has accepted antisemitism as permanent. A dollar spent on a guard is a dollar that isn’t spent stopping someone before he picks up a gun. People who backed the new federal hate law would say the law is for slower work. They may be right. None of it would have helped the people lying on the floor of Sons of Jacob.
The harder objection, for me, is the guns. On Yom Kippur last year, at Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation in Manchester, England, worshipers were trying to keep an attacker from getting into the building. Armed police shot him about seven minutes after the first emergency call. One of the two men who died appears to have been hit by a police bullet.
In Belleville, at least three people fired on a residential street. If some of the rounds that came through that window turn out to be police rounds, this column gets harder to defend. I’d still defend it. Manchester’s police had to get there after the attack started, and Belleville’s officer was parked outside before it began. Nobody inside was hurt.
Reading this from afar
In August, I complained in this column that Israeli politicians had boiled their message to world Jewry down to three requests: “Educate your children. Come home. Speak well of us.” Expect to hear the second one a lot this week.
Some of the people who lay on that floor may one day make aliyah – the Hebrew word for immigrating to Israel – and Israel should be ready for them when they do. That’s a decision about where to raise your children and build a life. Nobody should be making it from a sanctuary floor.
What the Jews of Belleville need from us right now is support while they press their own governments for something those governments owe them. An Israeli minister who uses Sunday night to pitch aliyah would be making that job harder.
Queen’s Park should commit to a police presence at every synagogue in the province on the High Holidays (Queen’s Park is the Ontario legislature, roughly the province’s version of a state capitol). The province should pay for it, with no threat assessment required. The commitment should cover Purim as well. In March, gunfire hit Toronto’s Temple Emanu-El while the congregation was marking the holiday.
Ottawa should drop the 30% match and the “time-limited” condition for small congregations. A synagogue with two dozen people at Kol Nidre shouldn’t need a grant writer to get a guard.
Ontario’s prosecutors, known in Canada as the Crown, owe the public an explanation either way. The Combatting Hate Act took effect on July 18. It made hate-motivated crime a specific offense and created a crime of intimidating people to keep them from a place of worship, punishable by up to 10 years. When shots hit synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto in March, before the act was in force, the charges were reckless discharge of a firearm, mischief relating to religious property, and conspiracy. If the evidence shows Ward acted out of hatred, charge him under the new law. If it doesn’t, say so and explain why.
And Belleville police should tell us why Const. Smith was parked outside Sons of Jacob on Sunday night: who decided, based on what, and whether the synagogue got a bill. Whoever made that call got it right. Nobody else in Canada can copy it until they know what it was.

Foreign companies continuing to provide services to Iranian airlines will risk facing US secondary sanctions starting on Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on Monday.

Ukraine says foreign defense suppliers owe country about $10.58 billion, including $1.7 billion already paid for goods delivered late or never at all
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:21:50 UTC
04:21:50 KST

Foreign defense suppliers owe Ukraine approximately $10.58 billion, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Finance. Of this amount, approximately $1.70 billion represents overdue receivables or funds that the Ministry of Defense has already paid to suppliers but for which the corresponding goods or services were either delivered late or not delivered at all.
Ukraine is seeking to recover these funds through the courts. However, in several cases, the statute of limitations is approaching or has already expired, potentially preventing the state from recovering the money.
A $22,400 legal bill could put $403 million in recoverable funds at risk
The government needs approximately $22,400 in legal fees to continue these proceedings. Without this funding, Ukraine could lose more than $403 million, roughly 18,000 times the amount required for legal services.
“The lack of funding for international disputes deprives Ukraine of the ability to forcibly recover these assets,” the Ministry of Finance said.
Funding shortfall could jeopardize legal cases and future financing
The ministry warned that a lack of funding could deprive the state budget of significant revenues, potentially force Ukraine to terminate contracts with foreign legal advisers already representing it, and delay the appointment of new advisers. It could also negatively affect Ukraine’s standing and make it more difficult to secure financing in the future, Ekonomichna Pravda reports.
Supplier debts to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry rise amid growing funding needs
The Ministry of Defense’s overdue receivables have been growing year after year. As of 1 January 2024, they amounted to approximately $886 million, rising to approximately $1.01 billion as of 1 January 2025.
In this context, receivables are amounts owed to the Ministry of Defense by suppliers for goods not delivered or services not provided on time, even though the ministry has already paid for them.
The Ministry of Finance raised these issues amid a funding shortfall for Ukraine’s Defense Forces in 2026, which the president has put at approximately $27 billion.

Turkish first lady urges global shift in consumption habits, calls for 'shared responsibilities' in climate action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:21:25 UTC
04:21:25 KST

- 'We must rebuild our relationship with nature on the principles of balance and justice'
Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, who chairs the UN High-Level Advisory Board on Zero Waste, called for a shift in consumption habits and stronger international cooperation to address the climate crisis.
“The Zero Waste movement has transformed individuals from helpless observers in the face of the climate crisis into leading actors in the solution,” Erdogan said at the opening event of New York Climate Week.
“It has demonstrated that seemingly small behavioral changes can evolve into a social culture when they become widespread, and into a lasting system when supported by sound policies,” she added.
Emine Erdogan attended the event in New York, alongside Turkish Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas. The Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change and the Zero Waste Foundation were among the event's main sponsors.
She was welcomed at the venue by Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum, Zero Waste Foundation Chairman Samed Agirbas, Climate Group CEO Helen Clarkson, senior board member Emma Cox and other officials.
Beginning her remarks by conveying the Turkish people's greetings and respect, she thanked the organizers for their hospitality.
“Climate change is one of the most visible consequences of the heavy burden that human activities have placed on the Earth,” she said.
“Of course, we know the role of fossil fuels, industrial processes and high emissions in this crisis. But we must also ask ourselves: Are fossil fuels alone responsible for bringing us face to face with such a massive crisis? Is it large-scale industries? Or is it an unlimited demand for consumption that forces all of these to continuously produce more?”
'We must rebuild our relationship with nature on the principles of balance and justice'
Emine Erdogan said climate change was, above all, a result of a transformation in humanity's moral outlook.
“We have established a system that accepts from the outset that everything we produce has a short lifespan and that every object will one day become waste,” she said.
She noted that approximately 9.2 billion tons of plastic had been produced worldwide since the 1950s, with 7 billion tons becoming waste, describing the figures as a clear indication of the costs of this approach.
“Moreover, this burden is not distributed fairly across the planet,” she said. “The environmental costs generated by high levels of consumption are often left on the shoulders of societies that contribute the least to that consumption, vulnerable regions and future generations.”
“We must therefore begin by reducing excess in our habits alongside our waste, changing our mindset alongside our systems, and rebuilding our relationship with nature on the principles of balance and justice,” she added.
Erdogan said the Zero Waste movement emerged from this understanding, describing it as a moral stance that reminds people of limits and responsibilities at a time when consumption and waste have become normalized aspects of daily life.
'Zero Waste is the translation of this sense of stewardship into everyday life'
Erdogan said there was a fundamental difference between viewing nature as an unlimited reservoir of resources and seeing it as something entrusted to humanity.
“Zero Waste is the translation of this sense of stewardship into everyday life,” she said.
She explained that the first steps toward turning this awareness into behavior and ultimately a lasting system were taken in the Turkish presidential complex.
“Zero Waste practices that we launched at the presidential complex in 2017 soon spread to schools, hospitals, municipalities, public institutions and households,” she said.
“Our recovery rate, which stood at 13% at the time, has now surpassed 37%,” she added.
She reiterated that the Zero Waste movement had empowered individuals to become leading actors in addressing the climate crisis.
Erdogan also stressed that the approach would not diminish the responsibilities of governments and companies, but would instead expand and clarify them.
“Building infrastructure that makes it easier for people to make the right choices, designing products to be more durable, repairable and reusable, developing technologies that enable circular production, and establishing international cooperation for these efforts are our shared responsibilities,” she said.
“That is why I consider the journey of the Zero Waste movement from local to global to be extremely valuable,” she added.
'No target will be sufficient on its own; no technology will be a solution on its own'
Erdogan recalled that the Zero Waste resolution Türkiye submitted to the UN General Assembly in 2022 was adopted with broad international support.
She also noted that March 30 had been designated as International Zero Waste Day and that the UN High-Level Advisory Board on Zero Waste, which she chairs, had been established.
“We attach great importance to ensuring that the Zero Waste approach is addressed as one of the powerful tools of climate action at COP31, which we will host in Türkiye in November,” she said.
Erdogan said the discussion of Zero Waste at the opening of New York Climate Week was a meaningful indication of growing global ownership of the movement and a shared search for solutions.
“While I am delivering this speech, dozens of tons of waste have been generated in New York. The situation is no different in Istanbul or in many cities around the world,” she said.
“One thing is certain: As long as we continue the habits that produce today's problems while discussing the solutions of the future, no target will be sufficient on its own, and no technology will be a solution on its own,” she added.
Erdogan said the true value of the gathering would be determined not by what was said at the event, but by what participants chose to do differently after leaving.
“I hope New York Climate Week will lead to new habits alongside new ideas, and collective action alongside shared responsibilities,” she said.
Following her speech, Erdogan watched a live performance by contemporary marbling artist Garip Ay.
Editors-in-chief of newspapers and television channels, along with numerous other guests, attended the event.

Macron asks EU to ease fuel rules as France prepares new support measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:20:32 UTC
04:20:32 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron has asked the European Commission to temporarily ease some EU rules on fuel to increase supply and help contain prices, while the French government prepares new measures to support people affected by higher fuel costs, broadcaster BFM TV reported on Monday.
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Sept. 18, Macron proposed temporarily easing European fuel quality specifications, allowing greater flexibility on biofuel blending in diesel and delaying some new obligations for fossil fuel importers.
Macron said the measures could “strengthen our short-term import and production capacity” and “increase the supply available on the domestic market,” according to the letter.
He said temporarily adjusting fuel quality requirements could increase refinery output by between 5% and 20%, depending on the refinery.
The specifications cover factors including fuel density, vaporization limits and desulfurization requirements.
Macron noted that diesel used on US roads can contain up to 15 parts per million of sulfur, compared with 10 ppm under EU rules.
He also proposed greater flexibility on diesel biofuel blending.
The current B7 standard allows up to 7% biodiesel, while B10 allows up to 10%.
Macron said greater use of B10 could support diesel supplies and provide additional flexibility for the market.
The European Commission has said B10 has slightly lower energy content and could result in a very small increase in consumption.
Macron also called for a one-year delay to a requirement due to take effect Jan. 1, 2027, under which crude oil, natural gas and coal importers would have to demonstrate that suppliers meet EU-equivalent requirements for measuring and controlling methane emissions.
He said the new rules could create additional litigation risks for importers.
The European Commission has recommended delaying financial sanctions under the rules until the end of 2029.
Macron said the proposed temporary measures were needed amid disruptions to global oil supplies following the near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz since March, which he said had reduced global oil supply and changed hydrocarbon trade flows.
He said global oil stocks had fallen by more than 500 million barrels and warned that continued disruptions, including attacks targeting energy infrastructure in Russia and the Middle East and rising Asian demand, could further affect supplies.
Without the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the restoration of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, global crude oil supply could fall by at least another 4 million barrels per day, Macron said, potentially putting further upward pressure on prices.
Macron said Europe was particularly exposed to disruptions in refined petroleum products, with the EU relying on the Middle East for 36% of its kerosene imports and 18% of its diesel imports.
He also backed “a clear acceleration at the European level on electrification efforts” and “moderation of natural gas consumption, particularly for heating needs.”
Meanwhile, the French government is due to announce new measures Tuesday to support people affected by higher fuel prices.
The measures will be presented at a news conference at the Economy Ministry in Paris at 5 p.m. local time (1500GMT) by government ministers.
The announcement follows meetings on fuel prices at the prime minister’s office Monday.
The Elysee Palace said France was also working to facilitate the peaceful reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and secure energy supplies.

Brownlow simply latest chapter as Daicos continues rewriting AFL history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:20:09 UTC
04:20:09 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
analysis
Brownlow a short stopover as Nick Daicos continues rewriting AFL history books
When Nathan Buckley's decade-long tenure as Collingwood coach came to an end midway through 2021, there was a silver lining for the club amid the painful exit of the club legend.
Buckley's tenure had seen the Pies flirt with winning a premiership in 2018 and 2019 before ultimately failing, but by the time he wrapped up, Collingwood seemed well out of the premiership window.
The silver lining came in the form of a player who was yet to set foot on an AFL field: Nick Daicos, then a teenager touted as a generational prospect years before he was eligible to be drafted.
The AFL world was no stranger to the Daicos surname due to the exploits of Nick's famous father Peter, who had become immortalised at Collingwood as a member of the club's 1990 premiership side.
You did not need to be a Collingwood fanatic to know about Nick Daicos. Everyone around the game knew the kid was on his way because of his prolific exploits at the junior levels.
The weight of expectation that comes with the level of hype Daicos had as a draft prospect can prove crippling. Unfortunately, years of evidence support this.
Sometimes even the most hyped prospects can take time to fit into the AFL system, and it makes sense. These are boys coming to a man's game.
The more rigorous training regimes, expanded playbooks, media commitments, dietary requirements, and everything else that comes with being an AFL player can be too much. That is even before we get to the pace of the game being completely different.
That hasn't been the case with Daicos, who, as an audacious Nike advert claimed on the morning of the Brownlow count, has proven it inevitable from day one.
From his first game, Daicos showed an ability to bend the game to his will in ways not seen in teenagers, and we have all been blessed to witness it.
Daicos's arrival helped catapult Collingwood from second-last in 2021 to fourth in his first season in the AFL.
Collingwood fell one point short of a grand final appearance in Daicos's debut season, but went all the way in his second.
After collecting boatloads of the football across halfback while occasionally dipping his toes in the midfield as a rookie, Daicos supercharged the Pies engine room in 2023, helping them claim the flag, and he has not looked back since.
From very early on in Daicos's career, the Brownlow win appeared to be a question of when rather than if, but it was the one accolade he was frustratingly made to wait on.
Daicos followed up his premiership by polling a ridiculous 38 votes in 2024, the most by any player in the league's history up until that point, only for that year's winner, Patrick Cripps, to poll 45.
Last year, he was again a seemingly unbackable favourite before being stunned by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell.
Missing out on a Brownlow after being among the favourites for a few years can be something that follows you.
Marcus Bontempelli, despite being widely considered the best player of his generation, has yet to win the prestigious medal.
Buckley was famously made to wait year after year before eventually breaking through in 2003, his 11th season, while Gary Ablett Jr was even denied by his own teammate before his maiden Brownlow triumph. It is almost a rite of passage if you're an all-timer.
Despite Bontempelli, Zak Butters and Bailey Smith all challenging him at various points during the count, Daicos would not be denied this year.
Almost in revenge for the previous two seasons, this year, Daicos turned in an individual season that would ultimately prove impossible to ignore for the umpires.
Daicos broke Cripps's record with 47 votes and set a few more records along the way.
He is now the only player in league history to poll over 30 votes in three consecutive seasons, the only player to put together six straight three-vote games, and the only player to put together 13 three-vote games in a single season.
Given the ease with which Daicos has played from his first contest in the AFL four seasons ago, it was surprising to talk about the weight of expectation actually weighing on him after winning his elusive first Brownlow.
You get the sense that the weight of expectation might be the only thing that is capable of slowing him down, because efforts from his AFL counterparts to do so have so far proven futile.
For a player so metronomic and seemingly superhuman on the field, it was refreshing to hear Daicos admit he too deals with nerves and struggles with criticism, just like the rest of us.
Daicos admitted to the Brownlow win being a relief after being denied for so many years as a favourite, even saying he had given up trusting in betting markets.
Now that the Brownlow box has been ticked off, it is frightening to think of what an unburdened Daicos could potentially achieve.
Still just 23 years of age, Daicos has gone from being the precocious youngster to one of Collingwood's veterans, and he will act as the bridge from one era of Collingwood premiership contention to the next, just as Scott Pendlebury did.
He seems good enough to single-handedly wrench Collingwood's premiership window open for as long as he wants.
Adding premierships to his 2023 triumph will be at the top of Daicos's to-do list, and the hope will be that in the process of achieving that goal, his resume ultimately becomes undeniable.
The chance to be Collingwood's greatest player is in play. The chance to be the greatest player in league history is as well, as premature as that shout may seem.
The records Daicos set with his maiden Brownlow win will eventually be just another footnote for a player who is poised to rewrite the game's history books.
Like the commercial said: inevitable.

Putin's party wins record Duma majority in Kremlin-controlled elections as EU vows sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:17:03 UTC
04:17:03 KST

Five Western nations and Kyiv condemned the voting in occupied Ukraine as illegal, while a Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow on the final day of polling killed two people.
Vladimir Putin's United Russia party has won a record supermajority in parliament, preliminary results showed Monday. The tightly controlled three-day vote excluded every party critical of the Kremlin or the war in Ukraine.
Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said United Russia had secured 355 of the State Duma's 450 seats. That beats its previous record of 343, set in 2016, and is well above the 301 needed to change the constitution. Final results are due later this week.
The Communist Party came second with 40 seats, followed by the nationalist LDPR on 25, New People on 20 and A Just Russia on four. Pamfilova put turnout at more than 59 percent.
It was Russia's first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Criticism of the war is banned, and Yabloko, the only party calling for an end to the fighting, was barred from running for the national parliament, though it was allowed to stand in some regional votes.
"These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
United Russia told state media that 49 veterans who fought in Ukraine are expected to enter the Duma for the party.
Voting also took place in occupied parts of Ukraine, including Crimea and the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions.
On Sunday, the final day of voting, Kyiv hit Moscow with its biggest drone attack of the war, killing two people and setting an oil refinery ablaze. Russia's defence ministry accused Ukraine of trying to disrupt the vote and vowed to intensify strikes on Kyiv.
Russia's 'veneer of democracy'
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the Kremlin had "silenced dissent" and shut out international election monitors.
"The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia," she said. "The State Duma elections held by Russia on 18–20 September underscored the continued and deepening erosion of democracy in Russia, taking place in an increasingly authoritarian political environment."
In a statement on behalf of the bloc, Kallas said the EU would impose sanctions on those who organised the vote or stood as candidates in occupied Ukrainian territory.
"The European Union reiterates that it does not and will never recognise either the holding of these so-called “elections” in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results." the statement said.
Britain, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway said in a joint statement that holding the election in occupied areas was a "gross violation" of Ukraine's sovereignty and the UN Charter. They said the vote could not change the status of those territories under international law.
"These sham elections are part of a wider system of occupation: the imposition of Russian administration, law, media, education, language and citizenship, backed by coercion and repression," the statement said.
Ukraine's foreign ministry had earlier called the voting in occupied regions a "farce" and said it would not recognise the results.
The election brought one surprise. In the Novgorod region, where it was allowed on the ballot for regional elections held at the same time, Yabloko won just over six percent of the vote, enough to enter the regional parliament.
Putin's political opponents are in exile, in prison or dead. His main rival, Alexei Navalny, died in an Arctic prison in 2024.

Polo strengthens into hurricane, threatening Mexico’s Pacific resort towns
Polo strengthened off Mexico’s Pacific coast into a hurricane on Sept 21 and is forecast to rapidly intensify into a major storm, threatening floods, dangerous surf and strong wind gusts in coastal states and near major beach resorts.
Around midday locally (2am on Sept 22, Singapore time), Polo was located some 435km south-south-east of port city Manzanillo and 305km south-south-west of tourist town Zihuatanejo, packing maximum sustained winds of 130kph, the US National Hurricane Center said.
Forecasters said the storm could become a major hurricane by Sept 22 and continue strengthening through midweek. While its core is expected to remain offshore, the storm is likely to lash parts of south-western Mexico with torrential rain and hazardous seas.
The NHC said coastal parts of Guerrero and Michoacan states could receive 10 to 20cm of rain through Sept 24, with isolated totals of up to 30cm, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly in mountainous areas.
Private forecaster AccuWeather said the storm’s reach could extend out toward tourist hubs including Acapulco, Puerto Vallarta and Guadalajara, while southern Baja California Sur, including the Los Cabos area, could also see rough surf and strong gusts later this week.
Accuweather also warned that tropical moisture from Mexico is expected to push north through the rest of the week, threatening flash floods in the US South-west. REUTERS

Migrant child stows away to Spain under football bus
MADRID - A Moroccan boy travelled from Spain’s north African exclave of Ceuta to the mainland hidden under a visiting football team’s bus on Sept 21, sources at the club told AFP.

Club members gave him food, water and clothing before police took charge of him.
The authorities say conditions in Ceuta have deteriorated since the migrant influx, sparking angry demonstrations by residents. AFP

Porsche Becomes a Burden for Volkswagen Group — Media

Porsche, the carmaker, is becoming one of the Volkswagen Group’s biggest problems and is fading into the shadow of the Czech brand Škoda. Reuters writes, as reported by UNN.
Porsche, the manufacturer of luxury sports cars that was long Volkswagen’s most reliable source of profit, has become its biggest problem, creating an obstacle to CEO Oliver Blume’s restructuring plans at Europe’s largest automaker
Less than four years after its record-breaking stock market debut, Porsche has become a symbol of the problems facing the entire group: the company has lost its leading position in what was once a profitable Chinese market and suffered losses because of costly miscalculations during the transition to electric vehicles.
On Monday, thousands of workers protested against cuts at car plants across Germany, and this crisis extends beyond Porsche and the rest of Volkswagen’s sprawling empire, reflecting how Germany’s automotive sector is coming under pressure from Chinese competitors and U.S. tariffs.
On Friday, Volkswagen issued another profit warning, linking it to a €6 billion write-down on its 75% stake in Porsche - just weeks after approving extensive job cuts as part of the largest restructuring in the group’s 89-year history.
The write-down, which followed a €2.7 billion impairment a year earlier, points to a lack of proper oversight at Volkswagen, Jefferies analysts wrote, noting that, in their words, these were "endless surprises related to putting things in order."
Volkswagen attributed the write-down to poorer financial forecasts for Porsche, which made a high-profile stock market debut in 2022 in one of the largest IPOs on the continent in recent years.
In an internal memo seen by Reuters, Porsche CEO Michael Leiters stressed that the company remains committed to its medium-term profitability target of between 10% and 15%.
However, looking ahead, the company’s withdrawal from China, where it has reduced the number of dealerships, and pressure on its U.S. business from tariffs are raising questions about sales volumes.
Porsche has reportedly been going through difficult times for years, and Blume, who is leading the sports-car brand until the end of 2025, will oversee it during a crucial downturn while simultaneously serving as CEO of the group.
