Four years of “partial” mobilisation.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:13:07 UTC
01:13:07 KST

A send-off for mobilised men in Kazan, Tatarstan. Photo: Yegor Aleyev / TASS
Today marks the fourth anniversary of the “partial” mobilisation. Announced by Vladimir Putin in September 2022 following a series of military setbacks on the battlefield, the decree triggered the sudden conscription of hundreds of thousands of civilian men into the armed forces. The chaotic drive sparked a massive exodus, with hundreds of thousands of Russians fleeing across the borders to neighbouring countries to avoid being sent to the front. Over the past four years, the demographic makeup of the Russian military has shifted continuously, but the fate of those drafted in the autumn of 2022 remains one of the most opaque aspects of the war in Ukraine.
In our count of Russian army’s losses, we attempt to establish exactly how a person ended up in the war: whether they signed a contract before February 2022, enlisted as a volunteer after the invasion began, were recruited as an inmate from a penal colony, or were mobilised. Over time, information regarding mobilised soldiers has grown increasingly scarce: obituaries from the past two years most often omit any mention of how the deceased ended up at the front. Therefore, we consider our figure of 20,500 mobilised personnel killed to be our most conservative estimate and a significant undercount.
Assigning the “mobilised” status is further complicated by the fact that other types of recruitment can be identified through indirect signs. For example, a “volunteer” can be identified by their age, by social media profiles pointing to a civilian life prior to 2022, or by holding the rank of private at the time of death (if someone served in the army before the war, it is highly unlikely they would remain a private by 2026). The “inmate” status can be assigned if we locate an active prison sentence matching the deceased’s full name. For the “mobilised” status, however, there are no indirect indicators—only explicit mentions of mobilisation in an obituary.
Because of this lack of data, we cannot provide a full assessment of what has happened to mobilised men over these years. However, we have gained access to two major data leaks, which we have used to track developments over the past two years.
Mediazona and other media outlets obtained the first leak from a Russian military medic, Alexey Zhilyaev: the bulk of the dataset concerns patients in Defence Ministry hospitals, but it also includes the rosters of several military units and formations. These lists contain the names of around 40,000 mobilised men, predominantly covering the period of 2023–2024.
The second leak consists of the staffing rosters of several hundred military units, with records current as of July 2025. This leak contains data on more than 200,000 Russian servicemen, 16,000 of whom are designated as “mobilised”.
As usual, before working with the leaks, we verified their data against state registries and other open sources, and concluded that they are reliable.
From the first leak, we selected 2,515 mobilised soldiers—focusing exclusively on those who served in units mentioned in the second leak—and examined how their status had changed over the course of a year.
The discrepancy amounted to 1,152 men. The fate of 912 of them remains unknown: they could have been transferred to other military units for which we lack data, or discharged on medical grounds. The latter is more likely, as the core of our first list is based on records of the wounded.
Of the 1,152 men missing from the later rosters, 240 were killed.
In the July 2025 leak, 1,363 men remained. Of these, 972 entries on the staffing roster retained the “mobilised” designation. However, 355 men had changed their status, becoming contract soldiers (marked “fixed term”), with contract signing dates in 2024 and 2025.
Another 36 men were in the process of being discharged on medical grounds.
Out of the 1,363 men, only 21 became officers—specifically, junior lieutenants.
At the time of this summary’s publication, we have managed to confirm the deaths of 187 soldiers from the second list via state registries.
In total, out of the initial 2,515 mobilised men, we have confirmed the deaths of 427. Meanwhile, only 173 of these have been recorded via obituaries and added to our RUSSIA 200 database.
Based on these figures, we can assume that our data on killed mobilised soldiers underestimates the true losses in this category by at least half (and likely even more, given our classification errors). We are unable to estimate the number of wounded. Furthermore, even among those who remain on military unit rosters, at least a quarter have signed a contract and lost their “mobilised” status.

Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:12:51 UTC
01:12:51 KST

This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: September 21, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
September 21 marks the fourth anniversary of Vladimir Putin’s 2022 “partial” mobilisation, yet the true fate of the men drafted into the war remains highly opaque. Because recent obituaries rarely mention recruitment details and there are no indirect ways to identify the draftees, our current figure of 20,500 KIA mobilised soldiers is a significant underestimate. To overcome this lack of public data, we are now analysing two major military leaks to track what has actually happened to these troops over the past two years.
Read the report here:
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By September 21, 2026, the death of 7,692 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 241,600 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 244,700 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.

Trump’s deportation program sends Russian citizens to these four countries — not Russia — under secret agreements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:10:40 UTC
01:10:40 KST

Trump’s deportation program sends Russian citizens to these four countries — not Russia — under secret agreements
Since January 2025, Donald Trump’s administration has secretly deported more than 25,000 migrants from the U.S. to countries where they had no ties, according to an investigation by Forbidden Stories, a consortium of journalists.
Refugees International and Human Rights First say about 20,000 people were bused to Mexico. More than 5,000 others were flown to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean, and Central Asia.
Deportees were often sent from these third countries to their home countries, where their lives or freedom could be at risk.
The reporters say the U.S. has struck undisclosed agreements with at least 35 countries to accept deported migrants. Neither Russia nor Ukraine is among them. Twenty-eight of those countries are known to have already taken in people under the agreements, and the other seven have committed to doing so.
Forbidden Stories found that Russian citizens were deported from the U.S. to four countries: Costa Rica, Panama, the Central African Republic, and Moldova.
Among those deported from the U.S. were asylum seekers who feared persecution at home. In 2025, several “deportation” flights carrying Russian citizens left the U.S. They traveled via Egypt and Kuwait, among other countries.

Far-left leader pushing to lead Berlin says city has voted for change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:09:24 UTC
01:09:24 KST

Far-left leader pushing to lead Berlin says city has voted for change
BERLIN, Sept 21 - The far-left leader pushing to take over as mayor of Berlin promised on Monday to tackle unaffordable rents in the German capital, but faced early pressure to take action over accusations of antisemitism in parts of the local party.
Elif Eralp led the Left Party to their best result in Berlin where they displaced Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative party in the mayor's office and look set to head a coalition governing the city for the first time.
"Berlin has clearly voted in favour of a change in policy, for an affordable Berlin where everyone can live with dignity, regardless of income or background, and for the rent crisis to be tackled consistently at long last," she said on Monday.
PLAN TARGETS CORPORATE LANDLORDS
Famously described by former mayor Klaus Wowereit as "poor but sexy", Berlin has become increasingly expensive and its once famously cheap rents are now a thing of the past.
Eralp has pledged to expropriate more than 200,000 housing units from corporate landlords in a campaign which saw the party, whose roots lie in the former East German communist party, make gains in central and western areas of the city as well as its traditional strongholds in the east.
"I still stand by that," she said on Monday, despite questions about how to finance a move the centre-left Social Democrats estimated would cost some €20 billion ($22.94 billion).
She said she aimed to reduce the influence of corporate landlords such as Deutsche Wohnen and Vonovia. Vonovia Chief Executive Luka Mucic said the group was ready to discuss solutions to Berlin's housing shortage but that "socialisation doesn't create any new housing".
Merz, who said the policy would have "devastating effects" on foreign investment if it were ever implemented, said he expected swift legislation to prevent expropriations.
MAMDANI AN EXAMPLE
Compared by some to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose campaign to make the city more affordable saw him win an unexpected victory last year, the 45-year-old Eralp is the child of left-wing Turkish parents who sought asylum in Germany after a military coup in 1980.
Like Mamdani, her campaign focused heavily on personal campaigning and social media and she scored particularly strongly among the young, while winning support from thousands of Berliners who previously did not vote.
"As a woman, I'm reluctant to compare myself to a man. But naturally Mamdani's success was a big example for us," she said. "And we were very happy about it, because that election victory sent a very clear signal — not just to New York, but to the entire world."
Little known outside left-wing circles before the campaign, she now stands poised to lead the German capital at a time when the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made increasing gains across the country and posted its best-ever result in liberal Berlin.
Potential coalition partners in the centre-left Social Democrats and the environmental Greens have indicated they are ready to talk about forming a government.
But both have demanded Eralp address the longstanding accusations over antisemitism that have been levelled against some local branches of the Berlin party, often in connection with criticism of Israel.
The issue has been extremely sensitive in Germany, which has seen a surge in antisemitic incidents since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by the militant group Hamas and the Israeli campaign that has laid waste to Gaza and killed tens of thousands.
Merz said the rise in antisemitism was a "disgrace for Germany" and pledged action to combat incidents in Berlin that he said had caused concern to European partners.
Eralp said it was her "absolute priority" to ensure that Jewish people in Berlin along with Muslims and all other groups "feel safe and can lead a good life here".
"It is absolutely clear to me that the glorification of violence and terrorism is completely unacceptable," Eralp told a news conference. REUTERS

China expels 2 top generals from ruling party, military over discipline, law violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:08:15 UTC
01:08:15 KST

Faisal Mahmud
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
- With latest purge, China’s top military decision-making body left with only 2 members, including President Xi Jinping
China on Monday expelled two of its most senior generals from the ruling Communist Party and military service over "serious discipline and law violations," state media reported.
The Communist Party of China’s (CPC) Political Bureau approved the expulsions of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli after reviewing reports submitted by the Central Military Commission (CMC), according to state-run Xinhua News Agency.
Zhang, 75, served as a CPC Politburo member and CMC vice chairman, while Liu was a CMC member and chief of staff of its Joint Staff Department.
China’s top legislature removed both generals from the CMC last month after authorities opened investigations against them.
The Defense Ministry announced on Jan. 24 that Zhang and Liu were being investigated for suspected “serious discipline and law violations.”
The CMC, headed by President Xi Jinping, exercises overall command over the People’s Liberation Army.
Zhang had been China’s highest-ranking uniformed military officer.
The PLA Daily earlier accused the two generals of undermining Xi’s authority and Communist Party leadership over the armed forces and damaging military combat effectiveness.
Their removal follows investigations and expulsions involving several senior military officials, including former Defense Minister Li Shangfu and former CMC members He Weidong and Miao Hua, amid Beijing’s continuing anti-corruption campaign in the armed forces.
Who remains on CMC?
The latest expulsions leave the seven-member CMC formed at the Communist Party’s 20th National Congress in October 2022 with only two of its original members: Xi, who chairs the commission, and Gen. Zhang Shengmin, secretary of the CMC’s discipline inspection commission.
The other five original members — Zhang Youxia, He Weidong, Li Shangfu, Miao Hua and Liu Zhenli — have all been removed following investigations.
Zhang and Liu had been under investigation since Jan. 24 and were formally removed from the state CMC by China’s top legislature in August before Monday’s expulsions from the party and military.
The US-based Wall Street Journal reported in January, citing people familiar with a high-level briefing, that Zhang was accused of passing information about China’s nuclear weapons program to the US and accepting bribes linked to official decisions, including the promotion of an officer.
Beijing has not publicly confirmed the nuclear-related allegation.

22 countries back call to keep AI ‘under human control’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:06:51 UTC
01:06:51 KST

The motto "The future is human", used prominently by "The Be Human Company", a Canadian AI strategy and transformation company, is seen during day two of the "ALL IN 2026" conference at the Palais des Congres de Montreal in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, on September 17, 2026. | Andrek Ivanov / AFP via Getty Images
NEW YORK — Several European countries were among a group of 22 nations that adopted a declaration Monday saying that artificial intelligence “must remain under human direction, oversight and control” and suggesting to create a global supervisory regime.
The declaration, adopted on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week, acknowledged AI’s “potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen our economies” but warned that “the rapid development of frontier AI models poses serious risks to safety and security if not appropriately managed.”
The push comes ahead of the meeting of U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the leaders of the world’s leading AI-developing nations, in Washington Thursday.
Advertisement
Neither the U.S. nor China are part of the new declaration. But Finnish President Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board: “I think it will be in the interest of both China and the United States to have some kind of guardrails. And our message here is that we need human intervention, so humans need to be in charge,” he said in an interview.
Referring to the recent cyberattack by rogue AI agents on the Hugging Face platform, the declaration urges to “address these risks” by obliging AI companies “to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation, with qualified evaluators granted sufficient access to assess risks.”
Yet the document falls short of calling for slowing down or pausing AI development, with organizers saying they want to focus on managing risks instead.
Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board: “I think it will be in the interest of both China and the United States to have some kind of guardrails. | Alessandro Rampazzo/ AFP via Getty Images
To do that, countries should “further develop and coordinate common standards” and strengthen transparency, “including shared reporting of serious safety incidents.” Moreover, UN member countries should “build on existing international mechanisms and explore creating an international institution” to oversee AI.
Stubb, who spoke to POLITICO at Finland’s consular office in New York, said that “our preference personally” would be to create a new institution similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency “within the U.N. framework.” Yet he added, with a nod to Trump’s skepticism of the United Nations, “we have to leave it open-ended so that people don’t reject it just because it would be within the U.N. framework.”
Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who initiated the declaration together with Stubb and who joined the interview via video, said that, “we would be very encouraged to see both G7 and the upcoming G20 presidency of the United Kingdom take on this ... The U.N. is big, but the G7, G20 is a bit more focused.”
Advertisement
However, the U.K. has not signed up to the declaration yet. Among the big European countries, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz supports the initiative, while signatures from France, Italy and Poland are notably absent.
Stubb added that neither he nor Støre were “doomsdayers” about artificial intelligence but named three reasons why the lack of effective oversight is threatening: AI-created bioweapons, cyberattacks by AI agents and killer robots using AI for lethal attacks.
Stubb stressed that the upside of AI can be “much higher” — if the tech is used correctly — ranging from “the eradication of diseases, productivity, information and many other things.”

How to align AI development with global climate goals - Türkiye proposed an important agreement ahead of the COP31 summit
Kyiv • UNN
Türkiye initiated an agreement to align AI development with climate goals. It also proposed increasing the share of electricity\r\nto 35% by 2035.
Turkey, which will host the COP31 climate summit in Antalya in November, initiated the process of drafting a political agreement on Monday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Its goal is to address the rapid growth in energy demand from artificial intelligence (AI) by committing countries to align the development of AI infrastructure with global climate goals, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
A new "Antalya Declaration on Artificial Intelligence" is being developed jointly with the UN International Telecommunication Union; its draft will be published ahead of the COP31 summit, the Turkish side, which will chair the conference, said.
"We must openly discuss the increase in energy consumption by AI systems, and it is time for governments to begin establishing appropriate rules. We expect companies to ensure transparency regarding energy consumption data and to use clean energy for their operations," said Murat Kurum, Turkey's Minister of Environment and Urbanization, who has been appointed president of COP31.
Ahead of the UN's annual climate summit, Turkey also officially presented its key initiative — a call for a global agreement to increase the share of electricity in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. The initiative includes measures to electrify buildings, transport and industry.
The "35x35" initiative aims to encourage countries to use clean energy and energy storage systems, modernize power grids, and support developing countries in the process of moving away from fossil fuels.
Trump said that concerns about AI are being stoked by "negative forces"13.09.26, 18:01 • 4926 views
Electricity currently accounts for around 20% of global energy demand. The remainder is covered primarily by fossil fuels, as well as biofuels and waste, which account for around 10%.
The voluntary agreement also provides for the creation of a global mechanism to track joint progress in electrification.
Turkey said that one day of the COP summit would be dedicated to technology and artificial intelligence. An initiative will also be launched to create a "portfolio of AI-based clean technology pilot projects" that will bring together technology developers, industrial partners and investors, particularly in the automotive and heat pump manufacturing sectors.

How France’s 2027 election could reshape Palestine solidarity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:00:36 UTC
01:00:36 KST

Breadcrumb
How France’s 2027 election could reshape Palestine solidarity
France’s 2027 presidential election is, in many ways, a referendum on whether the country wants the far-right in power or a progressive left-wing future. The outcome will certainly shape how pro-Palestinian voices in France will be treated. Will they face more intense repression in the form of arrests, fines, dissolved organisations, and academic exile, or will they be able to organise, protest and speak out without fear of being criminalised?
The results of the race will also have a detrimental impact on Paris continuing to push for Palestinian statehood, a ceasefire and accountability for what happens in Gaza and the West Bank or whether it will instead fall fully behind Israel.
Whilst some might mistake the question of Palestine as a niche issue, in reality it is a test of how far a democracy will go in policing conscience and what role France chooses to play in the world beyond it.
Already a hostile climate
To understand what's at stake, it helps to remember that France did not wait for a far-right government to start restricting Palestine solidarity. Indeed, since October 2023, authorities have taken an increasingly restrictive approach towards Palestine activism. Police have used tear gas and water cannons against demonstrators, and the Interior Ministry even banned protests.
Under Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau, authorities have also sought to dissolve Urgence Palestine, one of France’s largest Palestine solidarity groups, accusing it of promoting and glorifying terrorism.
University students have also faced disciplinary and legal action over their involvement in Palestine solidarity protests. Some have even been accused of antisemitism linked to their anti-Zionist views. In May 2024, 88 Sorbonne University students were held in police custody after they took over a lecture hall in solidarity with Gaza.
Dozens of others have been handed criminal records and fined for “entering a school with the intent to disturb the peace or good order of the institution".
Concerns were also raised over the proposed Yadan bill that was introduced under the guise of strengthening the fight against antisemitism. However, it soon became clear that it was being used to repress criticism of Israel. One of its most controversial proposals would have made “incitement to the destruction of a state” a criminal offence, punishable by up to five years in prison and a €75,000 fine.
Critics warned that the broad wording used would restrict legitimate political speech or expressions of solidarity with Palestinians. Nevertheless, after significant pressure, the legislation was withdrawn.
What a far-right victory would likely mean
If the National Rally (NR) wins the presidency, the measures already available to the state could take on greater significance. NR leader Marine Le Pen, previously barred from standing after her fraud conviction, is now proving popular in early polling after her ban was lifted. Worryingly, this means she has a good chance of taking power, and would therefore inherit an extensive set of legal and administrative tools to restrict protests, prosecute certain forms of speech, and shut down solidarity groups.
We know this is highly likely under Le Pen because she has worked to present the RN as a defender of French Jews and a strong supporter of Israel, which marked a significant shift in the public image of a party that had a long history of antisemitism.
This repositioning has allowed the party to incorporate the fight against antisemitism into its broader emphasis on security, immigration and national identity. This has particular negative implications for Palestine and other forms of activism, young people, French Muslims and people of North African and Middle Eastern backgrounds who will likely face increased racism, Islamophobia, anti-migrant policies and a curtailment of civil liberties.
Given the party’s positions on public order, protest bans could also become more frequent through the weaponisation of counter-terrorism, as we’ve seen implemented across Europe and the US.
Online speech will also likely remain an important battleground. If legislation like the Yadan bill becomes law, one of the central questions will be where authorities draw the line between antisemitism, anti-Zionism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government. After all, under a far-right administration, these boundaries are likely to widen rather than be clearly defined.
On the international stage, a far-right government would almost certainly pull France closer to Israel's positions, making it harder to advocate for aid to Gaza, a real ceasefire or accountability for Israeli crimes without that advocacy being cast as disloyalty or extremism.
It seems impossible to imagine that France will remain a country that recognises a Palestinian state under an RN presidency.
A different direction
On the other side of the political spectrum is Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise (LFI), a party that has made support for Palestinian rights a prominent part of its platform and has attracted significant support among younger and more diverse voters. This position stands in sharp contrast to the RN’s increasingly pro-Israel stance and reflects a wider political divide over how France should approach both the genocide and Palestine activism at home.
When the left-wing New Popular Front emerged as the largest bloc in the 2024 legislative elections, Mélenchon declared that recognising a Palestinian state should be among the priorities of a left-led government. LFI has also consistently criticised restrictions on Palestine demonstrations, as well as the use of terrorism allegations against activists and political figures who express solidarity.
A government led by LFI or the broader left would more likely resist legislation that blurs the distinction between antisemitism and criticism of Israel.
On the foreign policy front, such a government would also likely impose an arms embargo on Israel over its continued crimes in Gaza, while pushing more overtly for an independent Palestinian state and humanitarian assistance, as well as apply greater diplomatic pressure on the occupation.
Next year’s election will show the world whether France will vote to defend its democratic rights, like dissent, or fall for the divisive rhetoric of the far-right that will likely weaken people’s liberties.
Palestine activists and the Palestinian diaspora are understandably worried, given they are already in fear of the legal and professional repercussions that come with expressing their solidarity. A country led by the far-right will likely worsen their ability to exercise free speech, and criminalise them for daring to.
Ultimately, a democracy is tested not only by its willingness to protect speech it agrees with, but by how it responds to speech that challenges, unsettles and divides it.
Oman Alyahyai is a writer and journalist based in Paris.

Daily variations in salivary cortisol may predict cognitive decline in older adults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:00:19 UTC
01:00:19 KST

An analysis of the Chicago Health and Aging Project data found that cortisol level variations may be used to predict cognitive decline in older adults. Longitudinally, individuals with medium to high cortisol intraday variability showed slower cognitive decline whereas individuals with the highest average cortisol levels tended to show faster cognitive decline. The paper was published in JAMA Network Open.
As people grow older, their mental functioning gradually worsens. This is called age-related cognitive decline. Changes are typically seen in memory, processing speed, attention, and executive functioning, although the extent of decline varies considerably between individuals. Chronic stress may contribute to this process by repeatedly activating the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (the neural mechanism responsible for reactions to stress) and altering the regulation of the stress hormone cortisol.
Cortisol can influence brain regions that are especially important for memory and higher-order cognition, including the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Persistently elevated or dysregulated cortisol has therefore been investigated as a possible contributor to poorer cognitive functioning and greater risk of neurodegenerative disease.
Aside from cortisol, other systemic processes, such as inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and vascular health, may also affect the course of cognitive aging. Because many of the factors shaping these processes are potentially modifiable, age-related cognitive decline is increasingly studied within the broader field of dementia prevention.
Study author Ted K. S. Ng and his colleagues explored daily variations in salivary cortisol in a large and racially diverse group of older adults over an 11-year follow-up period. They chose to test saliva because it specifically measures physiologically active “free” cortisol and avoids the acute stress response caused by needle pricks during blood draws. They examined the associations between these variations and participants’ cognition, Alzheimer’s disease occurrence, and cognitive decline over time.
The study used data from the Chicago Health and Aging Project (CHAP). CHAP is an established population-based longitudinal study of aging and Alzheimer’s disease among community-dwelling older adults on the South Side of Chicago in four Chicago neighborhoods with substantial proportions of Black and White older adults. CHAP data were collected in three-year cycles, starting in 1993, and with later data collection waves conducted up to 2012.
Data used in this analysis came from 3,895 participants who provided saliva samples for the study. To be included in the analysis, they needed to have provided saliva that allowed at least one valid cortisol level assessment. Participants’ average age was 77 years. Sixty-four percent of them were women, and 64 percent were Black. Eighty-three percent of these participants provided three valid saliva samples.
From the cortisol level data derived from saliva samples (cortisol levels from three collection time points), multiple indices of daily variations in hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA axis) activity were created. The HPA axis is a hormone-regulating system linking the hypothalamus, pituitary gland, and adrenal glands that controls the body’s stress response, including cortisol secretion. Its activity level reflects how strongly the body’s stress-regulation system is operating. Daily variations in its activity can provide much more nuanced information.
The participants also completed in-home interviews at three-year intervals that assessed their cognitive functioning. Additionally, clinical evaluations of a smaller group of participants explored whether they were developing Alzheimer’s disease. This was done by a neurologist who was not informed about participants’ cognitive assessment scores.
The results showed that participants with middle to high intraday variability in cortisol levels—meaning how much their cortisol levels fluctuated over the course of a single day—had higher cognitive functioning at the start of the study and slower cognitive decline. Participants with the highest intraday variability in cortisol levels also tended to have better cognitive functioning at the start but did not show slower decline. Participants with the highest average cortisol levels tended to show faster cognitive decline compared to those with the lowest levels. Their cognitive function scores at the start of the study tended to be the lowest. People whose cortisol levels stayed relatively high across the day instead of dropping normally, and people who showed the largest overall change in cortisol across the day, had lower cognitive scores at the start of the study than those with the lowest values on these patterns.
These associations did not depend on the race of participants. However, Black participants tended to have lower cortisol levels, smaller daily change, and lower intraday variability in cortisol levels.
“In this cohort study of Black and White older adults, altered diurnal [daily] cortisol patterning was associated with faster cognitive decline but not short-term AD [Alzheimer’s disease] risk. These findings support salivary cortisol as a potential early biomarker of neurocognitive aging,” the study authors concluded.
The study sheds light on the utility of cortisol as a biomarker of cognitive health in older adults. However, the study did not assess the stress levels participants perceived, so it remains unknown how much the variations in cortisol levels reflect reactions to environmental stressors and how much they reflect intrinsic physiological differences or changes in the biochemistry of the body.
The paper, “Salivary Cortisol and Cognitive Decline and Alzheimer Disease in Older Adults,” was authored by Ted K. S. Ng, Todd Beck, Yashwanth Sudhini, Robert S. Wilson, Denis A. Evans, and Kumar B. Rajan.

Industry pushes to keep nuclear skills in Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:00:10 BST
01:00:10 KST

Babcock and Nuclear Restoration Services have co-chaired a showcase at the Scottish Parliament for the Scotland Nuclear Skills Hub, an initiative intended to build the workforce needed for defence and civil nuclear programmes and to keep those skills in Scotland, the company stated.
The hub brings together industry, academia, skills organisations and government in support of the United Kingdom’s ten-year Nuclear Skills Plan. According to Babcock, the nuclear sector in Scotland supports around 7,000 direct jobs across the Central Belt, the Highlands and the Islands.
The event drew MSPs, industry leaders, colleges, universities, STEM organisations and skills partners, and was sponsored by Liam Kerr, the Scottish Conservative Shadow Cabinet Secretary for Energy.
Mr Kerr said: “The opportunity for Scotland is enormous. The growth of the UK’s nuclear sector can create high-skilled, high-paid careers for people across Scotland, while developing expertise that is transferable and valuable across energy, engineering, defence and the wider economy.
“Our challenge is not just to develop that talent, but to create opportunities for people to build their careers and use their skills here in Scotland. The Scotland Nuclear Skills Hub shows what can be achieved when industry, education and government work together to make that happen.”
Debbie Joce, co-chair of the hub and Skills Director at Babcock, said: “Scotland’s nuclear sector is already making a significant contribution to the economy and supporting communities across the country. The challenge now is ensuring we have the skilled workforce needed to sustain that success and seize future opportunities.
“The Scotland Nuclear Skills Hub brings together industry, academia, skills organisations and government to take a coordinated approach to developing the talent Scotland will need in the years ahead. Through collaboration, we can create opportunities for people across Scotland while helping secure the skills needed to support the sector’s future growth.”
Mark Rouse, Director of the Nuclear Skills Plan, said: “Collaboration is at the heart of the Nuclear Skills Plan, and the Scotland Nuclear Skills Hub is playing a vital role in ensuring Scotland has the skills needed for the future. By aligning education, training and industry needs, the hub is creating opportunities for people across Scotland, supporting local economic growth and building the workforce required for the UK’s nuclear programme in the years ahead.”
The scale of the demand was set out in the Defence Nuclear Enterprise annual update to Parliament published this week, which recorded the combined civil and defence nuclear workforce growing from 83,000 in 2023 to more than 100,000 in 2025, with the defence nuclear workforce of over 47,000 expected to reach around 65,000 by 2030. Organisations signed up to the skills plan recruited more than 2,000 graduates and 4,000 apprentices in its first two years.
Much of that defence work sits in Scotland, where HM Naval Base Clyde employs around 6,000 people across Faslane and Coulport and is home to the Submarine Service, while Rosyth holds seven decommissioned submarines and is being prepared to defuel retired boats as part of the recycling programme.
The Scottish Affairs Committee warned in a report published this week that training provision in Scotland is not keeping pace with future workforce needs across the defence sector, and that major programmes will struggle to find enough skilled workers at current levels.
The civil side carries a political dimension in Scotland, where the Scottish Government opposes the construction of new nuclear power stations, while decommissioning at sites including Dounreay continues to require specialist nuclear skills for decades to come.

Ukrainian Drone Operators Target Russian Motorcycle Assault Troops Near Lyman
Ukrainian drone operators from the Signum unit struck Russian infantry on the Lyman front, including troops attempting to move across the battlefield on motorcycles, the unit reported on September 21.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

22 countries back call to keep AI ‘under human control’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

The motto "The future is human", used prominently by "The Be Human Company", a Canadian AI strategy and transformation company, is seen during day two of the "ALL IN 2026" conference at the Palais des Congres de Montreal in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, on September 17, 2026. | Andrek Ivanov / AFP via Getty Images
NEW YORK — Several European countries were among a group of 22 nations that adopted a declaration Monday saying that artificial intelligence “must remain under human direction, oversight and control” and suggesting to create a global supervisory regime.
The declaration, adopted on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week, acknowledged AI’s “potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen our economies” but warned that “the rapid development of frontier AI models poses serious risks to safety and security if not appropriately managed.”
The push comes ahead of the meeting of U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the leaders of the world’s leading AI-developing nations, in Washington Thursday.
Advertisement
Neither the U.S. nor China are part of the new declaration. But Finnish President Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board: “I think it will be in the interest of both China and the United States to have some kind of guardrails. And our message here is that we need human intervention, so humans need to be in charge,” he said in an interview.
Referring to the recent cyberattack by rogue AI agents on the Hugging Face platform, the declaration urges to “address these risks” by obliging AI companies “to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation, with qualified evaluators granted sufficient access to assess risks.”
Yet the document falls short of calling for slowing down or pausing AI development, with organizers saying they want to focus on managing risks instead.
Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board: “I think it will be in the interest of both China and the United States to have some kind of guardrails. | Alessandro Rampazzo/ AFP via Getty Images
To do that, countries should “further develop and coordinate common standards” and strengthen transparency, “including shared reporting of serious safety incidents.” Moreover, UN member countries should “build on existing international mechanisms and explore creating an international institution” to oversee AI.
Stubb, who spoke to POLITICO at Finland’s consular office in New York, said that “our preference personally” would be to create a new institution similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency “within the U.N. framework.” Yet he added, with a nod to Trump’s skepticism of the United Nations, “we have to leave it open-ended so that people don’t reject it just because it would be within the U.N. framework.”
Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who initiated the declaration together with Stubb and who joined the interview via video, said that, “we would be very encouraged to see both G7 and the upcoming G20 presidency of the United Kingdom take on this ... The U.N. is big, but the G7, G20 is a bit more focused.”
Advertisement
However, the U.K. has not signed up to the declaration yet. Among the big European countries, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz supports the initiative, while signatures from France, Italy and Poland are notably absent.
Stubb added that neither he nor Støre were “doomsdayers” about artificial intelligence but named three reasons why the lack of effective oversight is threatening: AI-created bioweapons, cyberattacks by AI agents and killer robots using AI for lethal attacks.
Stubb stressed that the upside of AI can be “much higher” — if the tech is used correctly — ranging from “the eradication of diseases, productivity, information and many other things.”

D&B integrates verified business data into Microsoft and IBM AI agents
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
18:59:57 EEST
00:59:57 KST

Dun & Bradstreet (D&B) is expanding the use of its global corporate data system in artificial intelligence-based solutions: in September, the company announced the integration of D&B Commercial Graph with Microsoft and IBM AI platforms.
On September 16, D&B announced new integrations via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) with Microsoft Copilot Studio and Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales AI agents. They make it possible to use verified information about legal entities, ownership structures, corporate relationships and risks directly in automated workflows.
As early as September 17, the company announced that D&B Commercial Graph had also become available in the IBM watsonx Orchestrate agent catalog via MCP.
The integration enables corporate AI systems to obtain verified business context while performing tasks in finance, credit analysis, compliance, procurement, sales, marketing and corporate data management.
A key element of the system remains the D-U-N-S Number — a unique nine-digit identifier for a legal entity that allows AI systems to unambiguously identify a company and link information about it from different sources.
Earlier in 2026, Dun & Bradstreet also announced the integration of its business data with OpenAI, Anthropic Claude and Gemini-based solutions. In particular, D&B’s cooperation with OpenAI makes it possible to use D&B Commercial Graph in ChatGPT and Codex via MCP for financial and analytical tasks.
“Artificial intelligence is moving very quickly from search and text generation to real corporate decisions — counterparty verification, supplier assessment, credit analysis or compliance. In such a model, it is critically important what specific data AI uses to make or recommend decisions,” said Maksym Urakin, Director of Development and Marketing at Interfax-Ukraine, Head of the D&B-Interfax-Ukraine business unit, and PhD in Economics.
According to him, publicly available information from the internet is insufficient for critically important business decisions.
“AI can process information very quickly, but speed alone does not guarantee its reliability. If the system has incorrectly identified a legal entity, failed to identify the parent company, beneficiary or a change in the ownership structure, automation will only accelerate the error. That is why verified corporate data are becoming the foundation of corporate AI,” Urakin emphasized.
Dun & Bradstreet reports that its global information infrastructure covers more than 600 million public and private companies in more than 200 countries.
For Ukrainian companies, the development of such technologies means that international business identification and the quality of corporate data will become even more important. Whereas previously information about a company was mainly checked by an employee of a bank, investor or procurement department, in the future part of such verification will increasingly be carried out by automated AI systems.
Discrepancies in a company’s English-language name, address, information about management or owners may, in such a situation, affect not only the speed of manual due diligence, but also the results of automated analysis.
“Ukrainian business must prepare for an environment in which it will increasingly be checked not by a person, but by an algorithm. For this, the corporate profile must be unambiguous, up to date and suitable for machine identification. The D-U-N-S Number and D&B’s global business data are effectively becoming one of the instruments of such digital trust,” Urakin added.
Dun & Bradstreet is an international provider of business data and analytical solutions whose history began in 1841. The company provides tools for business identification, counterparty verification, credit and commercial risk assessment, compliance, supply chain management and working with corporate data.
The official representative of Dun & Bradstreet in Ukraine is the Interfax-Ukraine news agency. The specialized D&B-Interfax-Ukraine unit helps Ukrainian companies work with international business data, verify foreign partners and obtain a D-U-N-S Number.
Questions can be submitted through the specialized D&B resource — dnb.ua, by email at [email protected], or by phone at +38 (044) 270-65-74.

Russia Could Use Properties in Sweden as Bases for Espionage and Sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:59:38 UTC
00:59:38 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Could Use Properties in Sweden as Bases for Espionage and Sabotage
Russian-owned properties across Sweden could potentially be used as bases for espionage and sabotage, according to politicians and security experts, as the country still lacks legislation capable of preventing such property acquisitions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to SVT on September 21, properties with Russian owners are located across Sweden, and the Swedish Security Service (Säpo) has identified foreign-owned real estate as a potential security concern.
A survey conducted by the Swedish Defense Research Agency (FOI) identified 247 properties across the country owned by Russian actors.
However, the actual number could be considerably higher. FOI researchers had to manually examine around 10,000 names of property owners registered as living abroad. Properties belonging to foreign owners who reside in Sweden do not appear in the relevant registers at all.
Swedish Defense Minister Pål Jonson said intelligence-gathering activities in Sweden have increased, while Peter Hultqvist, the Social Democrats’ defense policy spokesperson, noted that the security concerns extend beyond properties located near military facilities.
“Russia is waging a hybrid war against Sweden and other countries. This could involve properties that could be used for sabotage in Sweden, espionage, or other efforts to undermine Swedish society,” Hultqvist said.
He also criticized the pace of Sweden’s response to the issue, saying that the previous years “have not been used optimally.”
According to SVT, Sweden has spent nine years examining the issue, yet no legislation has been introduced to prevent such property purchases.
Concerns over Russian-owned real estate have already surfaced in a case involving a property near the Muskö naval base in the Stockholm Archipelago. The Swedish Armed Forces have submitted a formal request to the government to take control of the 600-square-meter property, which is owned by the family of Russian businessman Stanislav Aleshchenko.
SVT reported on August 25 that the military justified the request on national security grounds, noting that the property is the only plot bordering the strategically important naval base that remains outside military control.

EU Reportedly Set To Remove Sanctions On Russian Oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:59:38 UTC
00:59:38 KST

BRUSSELS -- The European Union looked set to remove Russian-Uzbek oligarch Alisher Usmanov and Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list while prolonging the asset freezes and visa bans for the near 3,000 other individuals and entities on the blacklist by an unprecedented three years.
EU ambassadors on September 21 agreed on the move after weeks of negotiations, diplomats told RFE/RL.
The list, which normally is prolonged by unanimity every six months, and contain several other oligarchs as well as the Russian President Vladimir Putin and his foreign minister Sergei Lavrov, risked falling altogether as Slovakia in early September pushed to get Usmanov and Fridman off the list by leveraging its veto.
While Bratislava did the same during the latest renewal of the sanctions in March, the initial belief among European diplomats was that another roll-over would be accomplished by the same compromise as in the spring: a green light to the extension by six months rather than the 12 months most other member states pushed for without any “political de-listings.”
The talks, however, became more complicated last week as first France indicated that it also wanted Usmanov removed from the list, notably due to indications from Azerbaijan that they would release two French citizens imprisoned in the South Caucasus country if this went ahead.
Then, Luxembourg stepped in, indicating that if Usmanov was delisted, Fridman must also be removed. Other EU capitals, meanwhile, were adamant that they wouldn’t entertain the two being deleted given their feelings that the legal case against both was solid.
Usmanov failed in his legal bid to be delisted in EU court in both 2024 and 2025. And while Fridman won a major case against Brussels in 2024, he remained blacklisted as the ruling concerned the sanctions as formulated back in 2022-23, with the bloc having updated the listing criteria with new evidence since then.
The deadlock resulted in EU member states prolonging the package by just seven days, from a deadline of September 15 to buy time to find a resolution.
Several alternatives were floated, including lifting just the visa bans but not the asset freezes of the two but no consensus could be found.
In the end, a compromise was reached for the pair to be completely struck from the list if the next renewal was moved to the autumn of 2029.
This is not the first time EU member states have managed to leverage their vetoes in order to get people delisted. Hungary and Slovakia successfully lobbied last year for the removal of oligarch Viatcheslav Moshe Kantor and Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov.

Ukrainian Zorelit v5 Drone Completes Testing to Intercept Jet-Powered Targets. Here is What We Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:59:32 UTC
00:59:32 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Zorelit v5 Drone Completes Testing to Intercept Jet-Powered Targets. Here is What We Know
Ukrainian defense company Vluchnyk announced on September 21 that it had completed internal testing of its Zorelit v5 interceptor drone, developed to counter high-speed aerial targets, including jet-powered strike UAVs.
The company disclosed the results to Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi, saying the drone had confirmed its declared performance characteristics during a full cycle of internal trials.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Zorelit v5 has passed a full cycle of testing and is ready for delivery to the troops,” Stepan Radibog, director of Vluchnyk, told Militarnyi. “We are open to direct contracts with military units already today.”
The v5 has not yet completed codification. Vluchnyk said the interceptor would become available through Ukraine’s e-Points procurement system after the process is completed.
According to specifications provided by the manufacturer, the interceptor is designed to engage reconnaissance drones along their flight routes, Russian Gerbera and Geran-2 strike and decoy drones, and high-speed jet-powered Geran-3 and Geran-4 UAVs.
Vluchnyk said the system is intended to intercept targets traveling at cruising speeds of 300 to 350 kilometers per hour.
Zorelit v5 is a high-speed interceptor developed from the earlier Zorelit v4 and designed to engage aerial targets directly along their flight path.
The manufacturer claims a maximum speed of 416 kilometers per hour and a range of up to 47 kilometers on a single charge. At a cruising speed of around 200 kilometers per hour, the drone can remain airborne for approximately 17 minutes.
It is designed to carry a warhead weighing between 300 and 600 grams.
The developer said the interceptor can optionally be equipped with an AI-based system for automatic target detection and highlighting, as well as automatic terminal guidance during the final stage of interception.
The drone can also be integrated with the SkyMap system, which guides it toward the target area and calculates an optimal interception trajectory while accounting for remaining battery charge.
According to the manufacturer, the system can also support remote drone control and video transmission over the internet.
The standard configuration includes a movable camera mechanism, an ELRS control system with a selectable operating frequency band, a 2.5-watt video transmitter, and a warhead initiation board equipped with remote detonation and a physical safety pin.
Vluchnyk said the new interceptor incorporates technical solutions tested on the Zorelit v4. According to the company, the earlier version has already seen successful combat use, has been accepted into service, and has received a NATO Stock Number, or NSN.
Before delivery, every manufactured interceptor undergoes a control test flight. Vluchnyk said it retains video footage of each test and marks individual airframes to allow specific builds and their components to be traced.
Vluchnyk's announcement fits a wider Ukrainian push to field fast, low-cost interceptors against Russia's expanding drone fleet. In early August, UV Military Cluster unveiled the Skazhenyi interceptor, a vertical-takeoff drone clocked at up to 365 kilometers per hour with a 45-kilometer range and a stated capacity of 5,000 units a month.

Documents from Russia’s state nuclear corporation show plans to expand output of carbon fiber used in Geran-2 attack drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:58:51 UTC
00:58:51 KST

Documents from Russia’s state nuclear corporation show plans to expand output of carbon fiber used in Geran-2 attack drones
European officials are increasingly worried about the growing number of sabotage attacks and Russian drone incidents in NATO countries. According to The Guardian, European intelligence agencies believe Russia may take more aggressive action in Europe in the coming months.
Michal Koudelka, head of the Czech counterintelligence service BIS, said Moscow could launch a small incursion into one of the NATO countries that border Russia. “It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said. Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned of a similar threat.
Officials in the Baltic states say they see no signs of an “imminent attack” yet, but they acknowledge that Russia may be preparing for more aggressive action. Jonatan Vseviov, secretary general of Estonia’s Foreign Ministry, said on social media that if the authorities had reason to fear a Russian attack, they would tell the public. “Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine.”
The debate over the likelihood of a direct escalation comes amid a very real rise in Russian hybrid operations in Europe. Last week, Bloomberg laid out in detail how those operations grew both more frequent and riskier over the summer. Their true scale may be much larger, since the authorities don’t publicly disclose many incidents. Bloomberg’s sources said Moscow intends to make life in Europe “hell” as punishment for supporting Ukraine.
Russia is also building up its capacity for further escalation, according to Politico. The outlet reviewed Rosatom documents on expanding production at the Alabuga-Volokno plant in Tatarstan.
In May, the Russian authorities approved building a new production line at the plant that would be able to produce up to 500 tons of carbon fiber a year. The material is used in the airframes of Russia’s Geran-2 attack drones, and the new line would allow Russia to expand drone production significantly. Experts estimate that 500 tons of carbon fiber is enough for 28,000 drone airframes a year. Ukraine currently puts Russia’s capacity at 36,000 Gerans a year.
Satellite images suggest that construction has already begun. It’s scheduled for completion in 2027. Serhiy Kuzan, chairman of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, which obtained the Rosatom documents, warned that the planned expansion at Alabuga should be seen not just as a problem for Ukraine’s front line but as a long-term threat to all of Europe.
The war in photos: Kramatorsk
Russia struck an evacuation center in Kramatorsk, in the Donetsk region. The center was housed in a school building, and evacuated civilians and staff were inside when the strike hit. Two people were injured.

Saudi forces fire more than 130 missiles, shells at northern Yemen in 12 hours — TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:58:40 UTC
00:58:40 KST

TUNIS, September 21. /TASS/. Saudi forces have fired more than 130 missiles and shells at populated areas in Yemen’s northern Saada province over the past 12 hours, the Al Masirah television channel affiliated with Yemen’s rebel Ansar Allah movement (Houthis) reported.
According to its sources, the shelling is continuing. Populated areas in the Az-Zahir and Haydan districts came under fire.
Meanwhile, Al Hadath television channel reported that Yemeni government forces had regained control of several positions in the south and west of Taiz province following fierce clashes with the Houthis.
The confrontation between Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis has been ongoing in Yemen since August 2014. The situation sharply escalated in early September, when the Ansar Allah movement launched an offensive in the southwest of the country. At the same time, the Houthis began carrying out missile and drone strikes on coastal areas of the Red Sea in western Yemen and on the outskirts of Taiz, a city in southwestern Yemen. They sought to cut off routes to Mocha, a port city on Yemen’s western coast, and advance toward areas near the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which separates Yemen from Djibouti and Eritrea. COVID cases are on the rise—here’s what you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:53:02 UTC
00:53:02 KST

Temperatures are dropping, and days are shortening, and that means we’re again barreling toward respiratory illness season. To kick things off, COVID infections are already on the rise.
The virus has been flying somewhat under the radar. “With the measles outbreaks that we’re seeing and all the foodborne illnesses that we’ve seen, the numbers of cases of COVID have not caught the attention of everyone the way they have in previous years,” says Jodie Guest, an epidemiologist at Emory University.
Nevertheless, now is the time to think about what’s happening with COVID and how to best protect yourself.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
How high are current COVID rates?
According to wastewater surveillance, levels of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID, have been steadily increasing nationwide since July, with the starkest upticks in the western and southern U.S. These are in line with what experts have seen in recent years, however.
Importantly, in places where rates of the virus are higher, indicators of serious illness aren’t rising yet, says Peter Chin-Hong, an infectious disease physician and a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco. Typically, he says, there’s an increase in rates of the virus in wastewater, then positive tests and then hospitalizations from infections. In recent months, the first two have happened, but the third hasn’t appeared yet.
What COVID variants are circulating?
Nearly half of current SARS-CoV-2 specimens represent closely related descendants of a strain called XFG. That might help explain the low hospitalization rates to date, Chin-Hong says; XFG first arose in early 2025 and has dominated infections for more than a year, meaning that most people’s immune systems probably have some familiarity with the viruses currently circulating.
Earlier this year experts worried about a mutation-rich variant officially designated BA.3.2 and nicknamed “Cicada.” But those fears are quieted now, and nothing new seems to be brewing yet. “We don’t have a blockbuster new variant like we’ve had in previous years,” Chin-Hong says.
What about vaccines?
Every vaccinated person reduces the spread of the virus. “We are all part of the support system for keeping people healthy from COVID,” Guest says.
For people without underlying risk factors, COVID infections are not outright dangerous but remain deeply unpleasant, Guest and Chin-Hong say. Symptoms remain wide-ranging, including fever, congestion, fatigue and gastrointestinal issues, with severe symptoms lasting up to a week, Guest says. Infection is also continuing to trigger long COVID, although incidence is difficult to measure.
This year’s updated vaccines are targeted to XFG variants, suggesting that immunization should be particularly protective. As in recent years, both mRNA and protein vaccines are available, and vaccination should be fully covered by health insurance despite continuing legal chaos surrounding the federal committee whose recommendations typically guide insurance companies.
Experts recommend getting a shot by mid-October, although people at higher risk may want to act faster, and there’s no such thing as too early. “Now is a great time to get a COVID vaccine—now is perfect,” Guest says. “But any time you get it is the right time.”
Guest and Chin-Hong encourage everyone older than six months of age to be vaccinated.
Parents should note that very young children will need a doctor’s appointment for vaccination and that there are reported delays in supplying the federal Vaccines for Children program, which covers one of every two kids. Despite these hurdles, vaccinating children—particularly those under two years old—is a key priority, given their increased risk of severe infection and lack of prior immunity. “It’s like 2020 for a child,” Chin-Hong says.
Other particularly vulnerable people include those over 65, those with compromised immune systems and pregnant people, whose vaccination will also protect children who are too young to be immunized themselves.
Are there other medications targeting COVID?
A key new development in the COVID landscape for this year is the approval of Xocova, also known as ensitrelvir. This five-day, seven-pill regime can reduce the likelihood of infection after exposure to the virus, although experts say it shouldn’t take the place of vaccination.
Two key caveats are that Xocova is not approved in the U.S. for children under age 12 and that it may interact with certain medications such that others shouldn’t use it. Although it requires a prescription, people can work with their doctors to have some on hand in case they need it, Guest says.
In addition, for people who do get infected with COVID, Paxlovid may be prescribed for those with moderate or mild symptoms who may be at risk of more severe disease. The drug stops the virus from multiplying in the body, effectively constraining its severity.

9 ‘boundaries’ keep Earth livable. We’ve breached 7 of them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:52:18 UTC
00:52:18 KST

Humans are continuing to push Earth beyond livable levels of heat, pollution and other conditions—both for us and for millions of species.
That’s the upshot of the annual Planetary Health Check, released on Monday by the Planetary Boundaries Science Lab at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) in Germany.
The report shows that seven of the nine chemical and physical “boundaries” we need to stay within to keep the planet habitable are at their worst recorded values since scientists first conceived of them in 2009.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“The diagnosis is unambiguous. Pressure is rising across every Planetary Boundary already outside the safe operating space,” said lead author of the report and PIK scientist Boris Sakschewski in a statement. “It means that the risk of large-scale, persistent and potentially irreversible change is increasing, while our margin for error in tackling these problems is shrinking.”
Sakschewski and other PIK researchers came up with these measures as a key to a sort of planetary life-support system—keeping within the boundaries they laid out is crucial to maintaining the environment we and other species have adapted to it over eons.
When they published the first Planetary Health Check in 2023, they found that human actions, from fossil fuel burning to excess fertilizer use, had pushed Earth past six of the nine boundaries. Last year we breached a seventh—ocean acidification.
Surpassing one of these limits isn’t a recipe for automatic doom, like flipping a switch. Rather “it’s like blood pressure,” said Katherine Richardson, an Earth systems scientist at the University of Copenhagen and lead author of the 2023 report, to Scientific American at the time of that report’s release. A high value is “not a guarantee that you’re going to have a heart attack,” but it raises the risks of one, she said.
Each measure is compared against a preindustrial baseline, or the period before humans began burning fossil fuels in earnest—roughly the mid-19th century. Beyond each boundary is a “zone of increasing risk,” in which the odds of moving away from those preindustrial conditions rise.
Among the boundaries that have been breached, according to the new report, are carbon dioxide concentrations, which reached a record 426 parts per million (ppm) because fossil fuel burning had not decreased at nearly the needed pace. That is compared with 280 ppm, which was the concentration prior to the industrial revolution, and 350 ppm, which many scientists consider a “safe” limit (and was surpassed in 1987).
Those rising CO2 levels are rapidly changing the planet’s climate, leading to weather extremes such as the unprecedented heat waves in Europe and other areas of the world this summer. Research has shown that many of these would not have happened without the influence of climate change. Earlier this month the United Nations acknowledged that global temperatures would blow past the goal of Paris Agreement’s target of no more than 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming.
Fossil fuels and the CO2 they release are also what pushed the planet past the ocean acidification boundary last year because the ocean absorbs some of the excess gas from the atmosphere, lowering the water’s pH. That increasing acidity can make it hard for shell-building organisms to develop their protective dwellings and could even causes shells and corals to dissolve. This would be a blow not only to biodiversity but also to economically valuable ecosystems; a 2020 report by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration found that ocean acidification would cost the country’s economy billions of dollars.
Humans are putting pressure on other aspects of the environment as well. Excess phosphorus and nitrogen from widespread fertilizer use flows into rivers and seas where they can spark toxic algal blooms. Artificial chemicals, such as plastics, dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) and “forever chemical,” or perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) , disruptively accumulate in food chains.
Just two of the nine limits remain intact: ozone depletion and aerosol pollution in the atmosphere. Only ozone shows clear progress away from the planetary boundary as a result of the success of the Montreal Protocol, which set up the phasing out of the chemicals that erode Earth’s protective ozone layer. Aerosol emissions have declined globally—partly from efforts to reduce pollution from global shipping—but are still high in some regions.
The new report’s authors underscored the urgency of maintaining momentum to keep below the boundaries where we are seeing progress and to reverse course where we are not.
“We do not have the luxury of time, but we do have the knowledge, capacity and solutions to change course,” said Johan Rockström, PIK’s director and a co-author of the report, in a statement. “Accelerating action to return to the safe operating space across all Planetary Boundaries is essential to protect lives and livelihoods, and to deliver on the promise of shared future prosperity.”
