The US Navy has awarded British defence company IrvinGQ a $14.7 million contract modification for further production of the MK-59 Floating Decoy System, with most of the work to be carried out in the UK.
The firm-fixed-price modification exercises Option Year One under an existing contract and covers continued production of the MK-59 system, according to the US Department of War. IrvinGQ is based in Llangeinor, Bridgend, where 64% of the work will be undertaken. A further 11% will be carried out in York, meaning three-quarters of the programme activity identified in the award will take place in the United Kingdom.
The US Department of War said: “IrvinGQ Ltd., Llangeinor, Bridgend, United Kingdom, is awarded a $14,743,469 firm-fixed-price contract modification for Option Year One production of the MK-59 Floating Decoy System.”
Additional work will be carried out in West Fargo, North Dakota, accounting for 16% of the contract, and Bloomfield, Connecticut, accounting for 2%. The remaining 7% will be spread across several locations, each representing less than 2% of the total. Production under the latest award is expected to be completed by March 2028.
The US Navy is funding the work through Fiscal 2026 Other Procurement (Navy) funding, with the full $14,743,469 being obligated at the time of award. The department said the funding “will not expire at the end of the current fiscal year.”
According to the contract notice, the award was made under provisions allowing procurement from a single responsible source where no other supplies or services will satisfy the requirement.
The US Department of War said: “This contract was not competitively procured in accordance with 10 U.S. Code 2304(c)(1) (only one responsible source and no other supplies or services will satisfy agency requirements).”

Why Egypt Is Looking Beyond Its Trade Deficit With China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:47:00 UTC
23:47:00 KST

When Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Egypt from September 1-2, much of the international attention focused on the security and geopolitical significance of the moment. The visit came amid continued instability across the Middle East and was widely interpreted in the context of China’s expanding regional engagement and growing diplomatic role in an area historically shaped by significant U.S. involvement.
Security considerations are undoubtedly an important dimension of the relationship. Yet they are not the only lens through which to understand China-Egypt ties.
Egypt’s importance in Africa-China relations is also rooted in the longevity of its diplomatic ties with China. On May 30, 1956, Egypt became both the first African and the first Arab country to establish diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China. That was more than two decades before the establishment of China-U.S. diplomatic relations. In 2014 China and Egypt elevated their relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
Beyond the diplomatic history, the China-Egypt economic relationship is nuanced, but hugely significant – something, in a sense, for other African countries to aspire to. That said, the aspiration should not necessarily focus on the trade relationship.
China has become one of Egypt’s most important trading partners, but even under the circumstances of an extremely mature relationship, the bilateral trade balance remains heavily tilted toward China. This is true even though Egypt is Africa’s second largest economy (the largest, South Africa, also runs a persistent trade deficit with China).
According to Chinese customs data., during the first half of 2026 Egypt exported around $596 million worth of goods to China, while imports from China reached $11.2 billion, leaving a substantial bilateral trade deficit.
But Egypt is not necessarily unhappy about this – certainly not to the degree that many G7 countries have been complaining about in their China relationship. Indeed, a large trade deficit is a problem, but it does not by itself determine whether the wider relationship is economically productive. Trade captures flows of goods; investment can influence where and how those goods are produced, creating value and productive capacity even when the resulting products can ultimately be sold to markets beyond China.
Egypt exported around $131 million worth of goods to China in June 2026, the first full calendar month after China introduced its zero-tariff treatment for products from African countries, compared with around $79 million in June 2025, an increase of 66.9 percent year-on-year. Although it is too early to establish whether the policy will produce a sustained shift in Egypt’s export performance, still the growth is encouraging. Monthly exports have historically fluctuated with recurring peaks and troughs across the year, but the broader trajectory has been upward.
Egypt realizes that agricultural processing, mineral beneficiation, and greater value addition are important not only for increasing exports to China, but for capturing more value along the entire supply chain.
This is where the Egypt and China investment relationship matters, and it tells a very interesting story. Chinese investment in Africa is spread across the continent; the share of China’s total investment stock within Africa in Egypt specifically is modest, at 3.2 percent in 2024. Yet the stock of Chinese direct investment in Egypt has increased consistently since 2017, unlike many other countries, reaching $1.4 billion in 2024.
More recent figures point to a significant acceleration in new investment. According to Mustafa Ibrahim, vice chairman of the Egyptian-Chinese Business Council, Egypt attracted between $1.5 billion and $2 billion in new Chinese investment during the first half of 2026 – more than the total Chinese investment stock in Egypt as of 2024.
This suggests that Egypt’s attractiveness to Chinese investors is not tied only to individual investment cycles, but increasingly reflects structural advantages, including its connectivity, market access and industrial platforms.
The key to Egypt’s attractiveness has been Egypt’s Special Economic Zones, particularly the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE). The SCZONE spans 461 square kilometers across six ports and industrial zones along the canal, offering port access, duty arrangements, and a location connecting producers to Europe, the Gulf, Africa, and Asia. Egyptian authorities frame this as access to 3.5 billion consumers across more than 100 countries.
Special economic zones are now common across Africa, but their sectoral strategies understandably differ. Where infrastructure, skills, or demand are concentrated, a narrower sectoral focus can be a practical way to build competitive clusters. Egypt is taking a broader route. SCZONE has identified 21 target sectors spanning manufacturing, logistics, and services, including textiles, automotive, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals, agribusiness, building materials, and digital infrastructure. The breadth reflects an ambition to develop a diversified, export-oriented industrial base and, in some respects, resonates with China’s industrialization experience: building a broad, interconnected industrial system spanning multiple value chains.
The scale is already substantial. SCZONE authorities report 305 operational establishments, 14 industrial developers and total investment costs of $18 billion, including infrastructure. Chinese stakeholders are an important part of this picture. Within SCZONE, the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone, established in 2008, hosts several flagship projects, including China Jushi’s fiberglass facility, which has annual capacity of up to 340,000 tonnes. More than 95 percent of its products are exported through the Suez Canal to markets in Europe and the Americas.
Importantly, the newer wave of investment into Egypt from China, including into the SEZ, is moving into more specialized intermediate inputs and multiple stages of production. In textiles, Chinese companies are now investing across polyester fiber, yarn, spinning, weaving, dyeing, fabric and garment production. Projects by Xinfengming, Lutai, Jasun, and others could create stronger linkages between upstream materials and finished products. A similar trajectory is emerging in automotive manufacturing, where investment extends from vehicle assembly and tires to steel cord and bead wire.
This is why Egypt is less focused on the trade deficit and more on investment – because that is the future. Egypt is working to strengthen and diversify its industrial base and increase exports worldwide – and this will improve its trade position. For Chinese companies, Egypt offers a strategic location from which to serve multiple markets, including the European Union, the United States, Middle East, and within the African continent. The convergence of these interests helps explain why economic cooperation between the two countries has accelerated.
No wonder then, that during Xi’s state visit, Egypt and China agreed to launch the third phase of the TEDA zone’s expansion, identifying renewable energy, automotive manufacturing, textiles, and chemical fibers as priority areas. The supply chains of these sectors could also intersect, creating additional demand for local inputs and services while opening scope to replace some imported intermediate inputs with local supply.
While few other African countries can boast the long historical and civilizational histories of China or Egypt – especially due to the border divisions made by colonial powers – nevertheless, many African countries can take a leaf out of their relationship in terms of asking the right questions about the future of the relationship, especially as the next FOCAC cycle approaches.
Yes, the unprecedented Africa-wide preferential trade scheme that China announced in May 2026 and followed up with numerous other policies designed to tackle non-tariff barriers are important, but actual investment patterns tell a great deal more about the future of growth and trade. The success of Egypt’s SEZs like SCZONE effectively demonstrate industrial strategy and planning beyond the zone: which parts of a value chain should be nurtured, where Chinese investment can help add productive capacity, and where a combination of domestic, regional African and global market consumers exist. The more specific African governments can become with these answers, the more likely they will be able to tell as strong a story as Egypt and China can.

Here’s what Russia’s election results really mean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:46:32 UTC
23:46:32 KST

Here’s what Russia’s election results really mean
Judging by the preliminary results, Russia’s new State Duma will look remarkably similar to the old one, after this weekend’s elections. Yet amid dramatically different domestic and international circumstances, that continuity is perhaps the most notable result of all.
The 2026 result has produced some changes, but the new is considerably less significant than the familiar.
Turnout, at around 57%, was the highest in a State Duma election for a decade, although hardly unprecedented as participation exceeded 60% four times in earlier elections.
United Russia was the clearest beneficiary, taking almost 58% of the party-list vote, up sharply from 49.8% in 2021. Even so, it remained below the party’s record 64.3% in 2007, during Vladimir Putin’s second presidential term.
The Communists again established themselves as Russia’s principal opposition party, comfortably finishing second with almost 14%, but that represented a significant retreat from their roughly 19% in 2021, and was far removed from the turbulent 1990s, when the party could attract almost a quarter of the electorate.
The ultra-nationalist LDPR improved from 7.55% to about 8.8%, but its hopes of overtaking the Communists proved misplaced, while liberals New People also advanced substantially, from 5.3% to around 7.9%, climbing from fifth to fourth. but the breakthrough suggested by some summer polling, when second place appeared possible, never materialized.
Fair Russia provided the late drama. After appearing in danger of losing its parliamentary status, the party eventually scraped across the 5% threshold, yet even this apparent resurrection was broadly consistent with pre-election polling averages.
The larger story, therefore, is how little Russian voting preferences have changed during five extraordinarily eventful years.
Since the previous Duma election, Russia has experienced the Ukraine conflict, unprecedented Western sanctions, sweeping economic changes, and a profound reorientation of its foreign relations. Such circumstances might reasonably have produced either a radicalization of political opinion or widespread political apathy, but instead, voters largely chose continuity. Thus, United Russia strengthened its position, but the familiar parliamentary opposition survived alongside it.
That may be the election’s real surprise, given amid unusually volatile conditions at home and abroad, Russians have largely preserved the existing balance of political forces, suggesting that while there has undoubtedly been consolidation around the flag, maintaining alternative voices within the established political system still matters to a significant part of the electorate.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was rewritten by the RT team.

Government to decide this week on measures to bring fuel prices down  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:46:31 UTC
23:46:31 KST

RIGA - The government plans to decide this week on measures to bring fuel prices down to an acceptable level, using all possible tools, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) announced on X.
According to the prime minister, the planned solutions include reducing excise tax on fuel, waiving fuel reserve requirements, and lifting biofuel requirements. As a result of these measures, the total potential reduction could be up to EUR 0.2 per liter.
The prime minister also writes that the goal is for the fuel price reduction to be in effect from October 1 through December 31. He promises that as early as Wednesday, the government’s plan will be submitted to the Saeima for further consideration.
Commenting on the current situation, Kulbergs acknowledges that the rise in fuel prices is a huge problem for Latvia and all of Europe.
It directly hits people’s pockets and makes almost everything more expensive, including private transportation, train and bus service, aviation, logistics, and the work of firefighters, police, and emergency medical services, the prime minister says.
He notes that the rise in fuel prices also means higher prices in stores and additional pressure on inflation. "This reduces the purchasing power of money and will directly affect both consumption and the cost of living this winter," the prime minister says.
Kulbergs also says that there is no direct correlation between the oil price on the exchange and fuel prices at the gas station, especially for diesel.
"Fuel retailers do not purchase finished fuel on the oil exchange. Prices for finished oil products are largely determined by the Platts international fuel price indices," the prime minister says.
He admits that diesel fuel is a particular problem. According to him, the price and availability of diesel fuel could become a long-term issue, as global refining capacity has been disrupted.
Kulbergs notes that a significant portion of Russia’s fuel refining capacity is currently out of operation. Russia has restricted fuel exports because it needs to provide fuel to its own market, and some products are also being purchased from China. "This increases tension in the global fuel market and demand for diesel," the prime minister writes, adding that this is particularly critical for Latvia, as approximately 67 percent of the country's vehicle fleet consists of diesel cars.
At the same time, an additional problem is about to arise in the winter, Kulbergs warns. Specifically, aviation fuel, or kerosene fractions of crude, is also used in the production of winter diesel fuel, so competition for these raw materials intensifies even further during the cold season.
Kulbergs notes that the greatest external risk at the moment is the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
He emphasizes that the Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important energy arteries, through which essential supplies of oil, gasoline, and diesel products, aviation fuel, LNG, and raw materials for mineral fertilizers are transported.
"Military action, uncertainty, damage to oil infrastructure, and disruptions at refineries in the Middle East directly affect global fuel prices," Kulbergs says.
He also notes that he is scheduled to meet with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Monday. One of the topics of discussion will be the Orlen refinery in Mazeikiai and fuel availability in the region.
The prime minister also warns that if the situation in the Middle East does not improve, the European Union (EU) could find itself in a situation where the issue will no longer be limited to fuel prices. According to him, a general fuel availability problem could also arise.
As LETA reported, the Union of Greens and Farmers has proposed reducing the value-added tax (VAT) rate on fuel from 21 percent to 12 percent until the end of this year, to mitigate the impact of the sharp rise in fuel prices on households and the national economy.
According to Greens/Farmers, the situation on the global oil market remains tense, while rising fuel prices in Latvia are significantly affecting the expenses of both households and businesses. The party notes that rising fuel prices increase costs in transportation, manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, and services, thereby contributing to overall rise in inflation.
On September 15, the Ministry of Economics informed LETA that a tax cut on fuel from 21 percent to 12 percent would decrease the diesel price by roughly EUR 0.156 per liter and the gasoline price by approximately EUR 0.146 per liter.
The Ministry of Economics adds that such a reduction in fuel prices would be possible if the tax cut were fully reflected in retail prices.

Procedure for extending EU sanctions against individuals close to Kremlin regime is an Achilles' heel - MEP  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:46:21 UTC
23:46:21 KST

RIGA - The European Union’s (EU) sectoral sanctions against Russia are working, but the procedure for extending sanctions against individuals close to the Kremlin regime is the "Achilles’ heel" of the sanctions regime, European Parliament member Rihards Kols (National Alliance) told LETA.
Kols said he does not believe there is a loophole in the sanctions regime, emphasizing that data indicate a deterioration in Russia’s economic situation. The Latvian MEP distinguished between sectoral sanctions, which target specific industries and products, and sanctions against individuals linked to the Putin regime or companies close to the Kremlin.
The MEP emphasized that sectoral sanctions are effective. He cited estimates of the costs imposed on Russia by the sanctions. Kaja Kallas, the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, noted in June that Western sanctions have cost Russia approximately EUR 1 to 1.3 trillion.
The MEP compared Russia’s war economy to a sprint, which can be sustained for a short time but cannot be maintained for a "marathon" distance.
Kols explained that Russia is seeking various types of allies, such as China and other authoritarian regimes. According to him, since the start of the full-scale war, China has paid Russia approximately EUR 320 billion for purchases of Russian fossil fuels.
The MEP mentioned EU regulations that call for a gradual phase-out of Russian gas imports. A complete ban on imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) is scheduled to take effect at the beginning of 2027, while a ban on pipeline gas imports is set to come into force in the fall of 2027. However, Kols considers the procedure for extending individual sanctions to be problematic, as it requires all EU member states to reach a new agreement on a regular basis.
The MEP emphasized that Latvia’s position so far has been to expand the sanctions by identifying new individuals, sectors, or companies to include on the lists, rather than assessing, during the extension period, which entities could be removed from the sanctions lists. He explained that Hungary has frequently raised objections on sanctions issues in the past, seeking to maintain, for example, the flow of Russian fossil fuels to Hungary.
Kols said that Hungary is not blocking the extension of sanctions anymore, but objections have come from Slovakia and France. The extension of individual sanctions was scheduled to be adopted by September 15, but member states failed to agree on a six-month extension due to disagreements over whether to keep certain individuals on the sanctions list. To give member states additional time to reach an agreement, the current regime of individual sanctions has been extended until September 22.
In Kols’ view, the regular extension of sanctions also poses risks because elections are taking place in EU member states, which means that political forces with differing stances toward Ukraine and Russia could come to power as a result. Kols emphasized that there have been proposals to change the duration of the sanctions and set them, for example, for two or three years.
The MEP explained that even so, the sanctions could be reviewed, but changes could only be made if all member states agreed to them. He compared this approach to the sanctions system in the U.S., where sanctions do not need to be renewed every six months because they remain in effect until another political decision is made. Kols also emphasized that the impact of sanctions is not immediate, comparing them to a mill that "grinds slowly but thoroughly," cutting off "the regime’s oxygen supply."
In the MEP's view, one of the problems is information leaks during the preparation of new sanctions. He noted that by publicly discussing an upcoming sanctions package and the areas it might cover, potential targets of the sanctions are warned in advance and gain time to seek ways to circumvent the upcoming restrictions.
Kols cited the flow of goods through third countries, including Kazakhstan, as an example of sanctions evasion. He referred to studies that have found disproportionately high sales of milk pumps in Kazakhstan relative to the country’s demographic indicators. According to the MEP, these devices contain components whose delivery to Russia is prohibited under sanctions and which can also be used in the production of drones and missiles.
In Kols' view, the situation has changed because Russia no longer needs to actively seek ways to circumvent sanctions through third countries, as it receives significant support from China. The MEP cited studies indicating that China supplies up to 90 percent of the sanctioned technologies that end up in Russia.
When asked how flexible the sanctions mechanism is in responding to attempts to circumvent sanctions, Kols noted that restricting the movement of goods would make Russia’s planning more costly and limit its options. He mentioned a proposal to completely close the border with Russia, even if only for half a year, to prevent any movement of goods. The MEP emphasized that there are still European companies trading with Russia in sectors not covered by sanctions. According to Kols' estimates, such trade contributes EUR 3 to 4 billion to Russia’s "war chest."
When asked why this solution has not gained sufficient support, Kols said that Western countries have long maintained economic ties with Russia. He explained that prior to the annexation of Crimea, the prevailing view in the West was that one should not confront the Russian regime but rather seek dialogue and bring Russia closer to the West through economic cooperation.
In the MEP’s view, Russia has deliberately created economic dependencies that are now painful for Western countries to sever. He concluded that the Kremlin is aware of this and exploits it, hoping that economic considerations will eventually prevail over a principled stance.
Kols noted that the goal of sanctions is not to provoke an uprising in Russia. He said that the aim of the sanctions is to make both the Russian regime and its citizens pay for the war. The MEP added that since the start of full-scale war, there has been a flow of Russian citizens to the West, and that one of the reasons could be the deterioration of living conditions.
The MEP indicated that the impact of economic pressure varies across different regions of Russia. Kols compared Moscow and St. Petersburg to poorer regions of Russia, including Dagestan, Ingushetia, and Buryatia, noting that in places where the standard of living has long been low, a further deterioration of the economic situation may be felt differently. He said that the "pain threshold" of Russian society may be much higher than is generally assumed in the West.
Asked about other sectors that could be subject to sanctions, Kols cited the aluminum industry as an example. He said that MEPs have raised this issue, and cited a company operating in Ireland that is linked to a sanctioned Russian oligarch and continues to export aluminum oxide to Russia. Exports of this product to Russia are not currently subject to EU sanctions.

"In reality, however, this is an assessment of all of Estonian engineering. The top experts and achievements in this field are highly visible in Europe and around the world through excellent applications."
According to Soomere, the success story of Estonia's e-state is just the tip of the iceberg, resting on a broad and solid foundation. "For example, the work of Ahto Buldas is one of the cornerstones for the creation of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, and Skype was founded and developed in our country."
The unique nature of engineering, according to Soomere, is the goal of creating and increasing tangible benefits. "True, a general benefit must be created first, but it must materialize as something specific as often as possible," he explained. "This is the golden rule of engineering, which largely directs the development of the field."
General and specific benefits are also inseparable in Academician Soomere's own research in coastal engineering. "More and more people have chosen to live near the sea, but rising ocean levels are constantly increasing the pressure, and waves bring enormous energy to the coast," he noted. "Therefore, coastal maintenance and protection are complex, requiring both a deep understanding of the processes and a great deal of common sense."
The impact of climate change is also becoming increasingly evident along the Baltic Sea, as exemplified by the recent floods in Pärnu. Consequently, Academician Soomere pays special attention to wave dynamics in coastal engineering and processes, as well as to marine meteorology. He was one of the first to recognize the role of ship wakes not only as a hazard but also as a significant source of information.
Tarmo Soomere has received international recognition in the field of engineering before. In 2022, the International Society for Engineering Pedagogy (IGIP) elected him as an honorary member.
Mart Saarma, president of the Estonian Academy of Sciences, highlighted the exceptionally high level of the EAE membership. "In 2026, a total of 147 new members were elected to the academy from around the world, 51 of whom are laureates of major international awards – including the Nobel Prize, Fields Medal, Turing Award, Breakthrough Prize, Wolf Prize, and Eni Award. Tarmo Soomere's election to this circle is a high professional recognition for both him and the achievements of Tallinn University of Technology in engineering science," he said. "It also very strongly supports the current strategy of the Estonian Academy of Sciences to promote engineering sciences in Estonia and to support technology transfer from universities to companies."
"Tarmo Soomere is an excellent example of a scientist who combines deep scientific competence, an engineering mindset, and a sense of responsibility to society," said Tiit Land, rector of Tallinn University of Technology. "The special recognition he has received also demonstrates that science in Estonia is world-class, and that our knowledge and experience are valued in Europe's most influential scientific networks."
Ülle Jaakma, rector of the Estonian University of Life Sciences, emphasized Tarmo Soomere's dedication and thoroughness in all his roles and endeavors. "We highly value his work as the chairman of the council of the Estonian University of Life Sciences and as a guiding figure in Estonia's higher education and research landscape. It is also important to mention Soomere's openness to collaboration, his ability to apply his knowledge in various scientific and economic fields, and his courage to stand by his principles," said Ülle Jaakma.
Founded in 1992 in Gothenburg, Sweden, the European Academy of Engineering brings together the world's leading scientists and experts. Its aim is to provide independent, authoritative expert advice on global, regional, and national issues.

Temporary bridge, worth around EUR 20 million, to be built over River Daugava in Riga for reconstruction of Vansu Bridge  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:45:32 UTC
23:45:32 KST

RIGA - Riga Mayor Viesturs Kleinbergs (Progressives) told reporters on Monday that a temporary bridge would be built over the River Daugava to facilitate traffic management during the reconstruction of Vansu (Suspension) Bridge.
At present, it is planned that the temporary bridge will have one lane in each direction.
Traffic will not be halted on Vansu Bridge until the temporary bridge is in place, said Kleinbergs. Major reconstruction works on Vansu Bridge are scheduled to commence in 2027.
According to Kleinbergs, building the temporary bridge could cost around EUR 20 million.
Kleinbergs plans to discuss with the prime minister and the finance minister in the near future who will cover the cost of such a temporary bridge and to what extent. Such a bridge could also be useful for civil-military purposes at the national level, not just for the municipality, he said.
Options are still being assessed as to where exactly such a temporary bridge could be located, but it will definitely be near Vansu Bridge, Kristaps Kaulins, Director of Riga City Council's Spatial Planning and Mobility Department, told reporters. Options for public transport that crosses Vansu Bridge on a daily basis are also being assessed. It is not yet clear whether public transport could be rerouted to use such a temporary bridge.
According to Riga City Council, approximately 55,000 to 60,000 vehicles cross Vansu Bridge each workday, as well as 759 Rigas Satiksme municipal public transport company's vehicles, which carry more than 20,000 passengers.
Traffic flows are currently being monitored at more than 50 intersections, and the necessary changes to traffic light operations and traffic management are being modeled, said Kaulins. There are also plans to use data from mobile network operators to work with Rigas Satiksme in order to prepare additional public transportation options in a good time.
In the meantime, and in accordance with Riga mayor's instructions, the necessary steps will be taken fir construction of the temporary bridge, said Kaulins.
The project will be implemented in three stages. In the first half of 2027, the riverbank reinforcements will be restored. This will be followed by reconstruction of a section of Krisjana Valdemara Street from Kronvalda Boulevard to Vansu Bridge. Reconstruction of Vansu Bridge itself is set to begin in late 2027 and to be completed in the second half of 2029.
According to Kaulins, there will be no significant traffic restrictions during the first two stages of the project, although such restrictions are expected during the third stage.
As reported, the reconstruction of the Vansu Bridge will cost EUR 69.8 million, according to information published in the Electronic Procurement System. The municipality has selected the supplier association Vansu Tilts as the winner of the tender for the reconstruction, design, and supervision of Vansu Bridge. The association consists of Hanza Construction Group, Tilts, and Baltijas Maksligo Buvju Projektesanas Birojs Vektors T.
The other bidder then contested the results of the tender at the Procurement Supervision Bureau, however, the Procurement Monitoring Bureau concluded that the other bidder's claim about the tender results was unfounded. Pursuant to the bureau's decision, the municipality has signed the contract with Vansu Tilts.
The total length of the Vansu Bridge is 593.6 meters, with the main pylon reaching a height of 108.7 meters. The project includes the resurfacing of the carriageway, construction of a divided pedestrian zone, and cycle infrastructure.
The project also includes replacement of the suspension cables. The total weight of the new cables will be 385.5 tons.
Riga has a total of 145 bridges, overpasses, and pedestrian tunnels. Some of them are in need of repair.

IN BRIEF: Key takeaways from Finance Minister Siluanov speech at Moscow Financial Forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:44:42 UTC
23:44:42 KST

MOSCOW, September 21. /TASS/. Russia’s draft federal budget for the next three years is challenging, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said speaking at the Moscow Financial Forum.
He stressed that the ministry's team would never allow a return to the "financial sloppiness" seen in the 1990s.
TASS has compiled the key statements made by the Finance Minister.
Attention to detail
The Finance Ministry team will never allow the "financial sloppiness" of the 1990s to repeat: "Our Finance Ministry team always strictly adheres to our capabilities and balances them carefully. We have absorbed the lessons of financial history and will never allow that financial 'sloppiness' of the '90s - if you can call it that - to happen again."
"Having learned from the history of the '90s - I lived through it myself and know how things happen. This can happen quickly and unexpectedly. One moment there are liabilities, and the next, they just vanish. Why? Either foreign currency debts have accumulated and the exchange rate shifted, or short-term government bonds require rapid refinancing but the financial market refuses to provide the funds. This understanding has been ingrained in me personally ever since those days."
US sanctions against Russia
Russia has built up an immunity to the US "sanctions from hell": "You know, we have probably already developed an immunity to all kinds of sanctions, whether they are ‘from hell’ or not. We just go about our business, and these ‘sanctions from hell,’ so to speak, bounce right off our financial policy."
Federal budget
The draft federal budget for the next three years is "challenging": "The government began working on the budget early in the year. We started in the very first months of this year, already understanding that the budget for the upcoming three-year period would be a difficult one. It has always been challenging in recent years, and it is no different now."
Russia's federal budget for next year will be drafted with a deficit of around 2% of GDP, but this "poses no risks."
National defense and security will be a key priority in the 2027-2029 budget: "The most critical task right now is defense and supporting the front line. Equally important is ensuring that our citizens do not feel the strain of this concentration of resources-that all social obligations are met and life goes on just as it did in previous years. I hope we have succeeded in achieving that."
The Finance Ministry is paying close attention to tax measures aimed at fighting the shadow economy: "When it comes to taxes, we are currently prioritizing the formalization of the economy. And, by the way, it is working."
The Ministry drafted the budget based on a cut-off price of $50 per barrel: "We have structured the current budget based on a cut-off price of $50 per barrel. Why so low? Although, in reality, it isn't low. That money could have been allocated to spending. But wait-we must not jeopardize the budget or create risks. What if the price drops below that? And it is highly possible that it will; in fact, it likely will. What would we do then? Drain our reserves? No, that would be a bad decision."
The importance of reserves
Having a reserve of resources is crucial: "We are building up reserves right now."
Every financial professional needs a "nest egg" - it is one of the rules of financial management: "I believe this is a hallmark of sound financial practice."
The Finance Ministry is not opposed to new spending, provided it yields results in the form of increased personal income or contributions to the economy: "We are not against new spending. First and foremost, this spending must deliver results. It needs to either generate more income for our citizens or ensure that for every kopeck of public money spent, businesses chip in three kopecks of their own. Ultimately, that would represent a real contribution to the economy. The Finance Ministry always supports that kind of spending."
Monetary Policy
The Finance Ministry has done everything on the fiscal side to enable the Central Bank to ease monetary policy: "It is crucial right now that inflation expectations and interest rates come down. We are constantly reviewing the projected budget deficit for the three-year period with the Central Bank; the Central Bank will base its monetary policy on these figures."
National Wealth Fund
The Finance Ministry plans to build up the National Wealth Fund (NWF) resources this year: "We expect-and prices are currently working in our favor-to take this opportunity to replenish the National Wealth Fund."
"Since 2019, we have spent 15 trillion rubles ($178 bln) from the NWF, our 'nest egg.' Out of that amount, only 4 trillion [rubles] ($47.5 bln) went toward investment. We advocate for putting this money to work in the economy so it generates additional revenue through tax returns."
Artificial Intelligence
Artificial intelligence is an interesting and "underrated" topic: "I recently attended a G20 financial meeting where finance ministers dedicated an entire session to this subject. After all, artificial intelligence helps save money and identify untapped reserves within the budgets we are discussing."

Edward Colston’s remains likely to stay at Bristol church that could become community space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:43:58 UTC
23:43:58 KST

Bones of the enslaver Edward Colston are likely to remain interred in a church in Bristol if and when the currently unused building is given a new lease of life as a community resource, it has emerged.
The dean of Bristol, the Very Rev Mandy Ford, said Colston’s remains would probably stay where they were in All Saints church on one of Bristol’s busiest streets.
Colston, who died in 1721, made headlines around the world in 2020 when his statue in the city centre was toppled during a Black Lives Matter protest and thrown into the harbour.
The diocese of Bristol has been consulting with Bristolians over what to do with All Saints on Corn Street, which has been closed since 1984.
While no final decision has yet been made, it seems likely it will be used as a space to reflect on the port’s connections with the slave trade – and Colston’s remains will stay where they are.
Ford said: “There is very, very clear guidance which assumes that you don’t disturb remains that have been given Christian burial, except in exceptional circumstances and so the presumption is that they will stay where they are.”
The dean said that if there was to be a radical rebuilding of the space there could be an argument to inter the remains elsewhere. “Otherwise the assumption is that Christian burial is permanent and that’s where they stay.”
Ford brings deep expertise to the job of helping decide what happens to Colston’s bones, as when she worked in Leicester she was closely involved in the reinterment of Richard III’s remains after they were found in a car park there.
She acknowledged people had different understandings of the theological or spiritual significance of human remains. “But it’s a Christian place of burial and we are a Christian church trying to do the right thing. This is the burial place of a human being who was involved in a practice which we recognise to be utterly sinful and wrong.”
The question of what to do about sites connected to Colston in Bristol is a thorny one.
After the Colston statue was thrown into the harbour, windows celebrating him were removed from two Bristol churches as the diocese declared the fall of the statue was a “signal” for it to take action. In the same year, Bristol’s concert hall was renamed Bristol Beacon, having previously been called Colston Hall.
It is likely to be many months before a final decision is made over the fate of All Saints.
But the dean said: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation. From the work that we’ve been doing in the cathedral and the relationships and the conversations that we have, I think there’s a strong sense that there’s huge potential in Bristol to have difficult conversations and to build a better future on the basis of truth-telling about the past.”
She added that work carried out at a new All Saints had the potential to sit alongside projects on Bristol’s history being done by institutions including the University of Bristol and Bristol Old Vic.
Ford said: “I think one can see it as part of a much bigger picture, which I think is really important if Bristol’s going to have a peaceful and flourishing future as a civic space and as a city.”
The Rev Anjali Kanagaratnam, who is leading the All Saints consultation, has been taking groups into the church.
She said there had been a huge range of views. “Each extreme was covered from: ‘I never want to come back into this building’ to ‘Why haven’t I been told that this building is here? I need to bring my children.’ Some people find it a hard space to be in. Some were annoyed by the fact that they didn’t know it was there.”
Kanagaratnam said it had been vital to hear the voices of people in Bristol that had been affected by transatlantic slavery but the church had also made sure it heard what people from other communities, such as white working-class areas in south Bristol.
Kanagaratnam said there was great potential for All Saints to be a place of “truth-telling”. She added: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation.”

Russia’s ‘Partial Mobilization’ Turns 4: Is Another Draft Coming?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:43:00 UTC
23:43:00 KST

On Monday, Sept. 21, 2026, exactly four years after Russian President Vladimir Putin announced “partial mobilization,” Moscow continues to insist that it can sustain its war against Ukraine without another mass call-up.
However, an examination of Russia’s legal framework, official recruitment figures, Ukrainian intelligence disclosures, assessments by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), and independent reporting shows that Russia is not relying solely on conventional voluntary recruitment. Instead, it has replaced one highly visible mobilization campaign with a permanent system combining contracts, large financial incentives, digital surveillance, and varying degrees of administrative pressure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
How Russia’s 2022 mobilization began
Putin announced the mobilization on Sept. 21, 2022, shortly after a Ukrainian counteroffensive forced Russian troops to retreat from large parts of the Kharkiv region.
Then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said 300,000 reservists would be called up. The campaign quickly became chaotic, with reports of summonses being sent to men who were medically unfit, too old, or lacked the military experience the Kremlin claimed it was seeking.
Members of ethnic minorities and residents of poorer regions were disproportionately affected. The uncertainty also triggered one of Russia’s largest wartime population movements. A EU Agency for Asylum estimate cited in an August 2026 UK government report said around 900,000 men left Russia after the announcement, although other estimates are lower.
Russia Hits 2 Gas Stations on Kyiv-Lviv M06 Highway
Shoigu declared the mobilization complete on Oct. 28, 2022, after the stated quota had been filled. Putin, however, never formally revoked the mobilization decree.
The decree does not mean that Russia has continuously conducted mass call-ups since 2022, but it allows mobilized troops to remain in service until the mobilization period is formally terminated. Many of those called up four years ago therefore remain in the military unless discharged for narrowly defined reasons.
Is Russia relying only on contract soldiers?
No. Contract recruitment is now the Kremlin’s main public method of bringing new personnel into the military, but it represents only one part of Russia’s manpower system.
The three main legal categories are different:
- Russia conducts routine compulsory military service for men aged 18-30. Around 300,000 are drafted annually for one year, according to the UK government’s military-service assessment.
- Mobilization applies primarily to reservists called into service during wartime.
- Contract service is officially voluntary and can include both first-time recruits and conscripts who agree to remain in the military.
In practice, the lines have become increasingly blurred.
The UK government report, which compiled evidence from European agencies, independent Russian media, and human rights groups, documented cases in which conscripts and other vulnerable men were deceived, threatened, or physically pressured into signing contracts. It stressed that this does not mean every Russian contract soldier was coerced, but it found that such practices were recurring.
Russian legislation also allows people facing criminal prosecution or serving prison sentences to sign military contracts. Regional authorities have targeted debtors, unemployed men, migrants, and people living in poverty, while companies have faced pressure to help meet recruitment targets.
A unified electronic military register now combines data from tax authorities, police, medical institutions, and other government systems. Electronic summonses can lead to restrictions on leaving Russia, receiving loans, conducting real-estate transactions, or holding a driver’s license.
Therefore, Russia can increase military intake without announcing a repeat of the nationally televised 2022 mobilization. It can raise enlistment bonuses, assign recruitment quotas to regions and employers, pressure conscripts to sign contracts, expand prison recruitment, and selectively summon reservists.
Is Russia’s recruitment system still working?
It continues to recruit hundreds of thousands of people, but at a rising financial and political cost.
Russian officials claimed that around 450,000 people signed military contracts in 2024. Deputy Security Council Chair Dmitry Medvedev said more than 422,000 did so in 2025, alongside around 32,000 recruits for volunteer formations, according to Reuters.
Medvedev subsequently claimed that about 200,000 contract soldiers and 16,000 volunteers joined during the first half of 2026. These figures cannot be independently verified and may include categories that overlap.
Russia’s reported 2026 target is approximately 409,000 contract recruits. In July, ISW assessed that Moscow was not on track to meet it.
The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine offered an even more pessimistic assessment. It said Russia recruited approximately 232,000 contract personnel between January and July while suffering about 240,000 casualties, including at least 140,000 “irreversible” losses.
Total casualty figures also include wounded soldiers, some of whom may return to duty, so they cannot be directly compared with recruitment totals.
The broader trend is clear: Russia is still finding recruits at scale, but recruitment is becoming more expensive and may no longer provide enough personnel to replace losses and expand the military.
Some regional enlistment packages reached approximately 4.1 million rubles (around $49,000) in 2026. Continued increases in payments suggest that the pool of people willing to sign at previous rates is shrinking.
Is the Kremlin preparing another mobilization?
Ukrainian intelligence says it is preparing the option, but there is no evidence that Putin has issued a final order.
In August, Ukraine’s military and foreign intelligence agencies said the Russian General Staff had developed a plan to mobilize an additional 600,000 people – 300,000 during 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027. Kyiv Post previously reported that the plan would prioritize replenishing units already fighting in Ukraine and staffing newly formed units.
The intelligence briefing cited several preparatory measures: tighter military-registration controls, expanded prison recruitment, possible quotas for law-enforcement agencies, and additional coercive penalties for ignoring electronic summonses.
It also said more than 2,500 job advertisements for employees responsible for military registration and mobilization work had appeared at Russian enterprises by late July.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had prepared the infrastructure to recruit at least 300,000 more people, either through an open call-up or a less visible campaign. He predicted that Moscow would deny such plans until the State Duma election was over.
Putin denied the reports before the vote.
“As of today, there is no scenario that would require a mobilization,” Putin said on Sept. 3, according to Le Monde. Medvedev later supported his claim saying Russia had “absolutely no need for mobilization.”
Why the State Duma election matters
Russia held its parliamentary election from Sept. 18-20, the first State Duma vote since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
According to Reuters, with more than 95% of ballots counted, the Kremlin-backed United Russia party received 57.83% of the vote and was projected to take 355 of the Duma’s 450 seats, preserving its constitutional majority.
AP also reported that the result should not be treated as reliable evidence of popular support for a new mobilization. The election was conducted in a tightly controlled political system, with genuine opposition suppressed, anti-war candidates excluded or marginalized, and voting also staged in occupied Ukrainian territories.
United Russia already controlled parliament, while the nominal opposition parties normally support the Kremlin on major military legislation. The vote therefore did not give Putin a power he previously lacked.
Another mass call-up before voting could have revived memories of the panic and exodus of 2022. With the election over, that immediate political constraint has disappeared. The Kremlin can also portray the official result as public approval of its wartime course, regardless of whether the vote accurately reflects Russian opinion.
Ukrainian intelligence said the most likely time for a decision would be after the election. That was an assessment, not confirmation that a mobilization order had already been signed.
Analysts interviewed by Novaya Gazeta Europe argued that selective regional call-ups and increased recruitment quotas may be more likely initially than another simultaneous nationwide campaign.
As the 2022 decree remains formally in force, Russian legal experts cited by the publication said the Kremlin might not require an identical new decree to broaden call-ups. Moscow could instead use regional administrations, employers, military commissariats, and the digital register to mobilize people gradually.
What would another 300,000 troops change?
A call-up of 300,000 people would not place 300,000 combat-ready soldiers on the battlefield immediately.
New personnel would have to be processed, trained, equipped, organized into units, and transported. Ukrainian intelligence estimates that Russia could provide only 15-60 days of training to many mobilized recruits. Larger numbers could also strain training grounds, commanders, equipment stocks, and logistics.
The additional manpower could still allow Russia to replace casualties, rotate exhausted formations, fill assault units, and release more experienced soldiers from rear-area duties.
It could also support longer-term offensive planning. According to Ukrainian official Pavlo Palisa, in August Russian commanders had been instructed to prepare possible operational plans toward Kyiv and Chernihiv. He stressed that Ukraine had not observed a strike force forming in those directions and that military planning did not mean an attack was imminent.
Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky has also warned against assuming that more Russian troops would automatically produce major territorial gains.
“More infantry means more losses,” he said, arguing that drones, sensors, and rapid strike systems now shape battlefield effectiveness. Nevertheless, Biletsky acknowledged another mobilization would create additional pressure on Ukraine.
Would mobilization mean Russia is preparing to attack NATO?
Not necessarily. European officials have issued increasingly serious warnings about Russian provocations. Czech intelligence chief Michal Koudelka told The Guardian that Moscow could test NATO within “months, not years” through drones, missiles, a limited incursion, or a false-flag operation.
Other Baltic officials offered a more cautious assessment. Latvian State Security Service chief Normunds Mežviets said there were no indications of an imminent conventional attack and noted that Russian resources remained stretched by the war in Ukraine.
Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs similarly predicted that Russia could increase mobilization after the election and use the winter to intensify pressure on Ukraine and its supporters. However, he said he would rule out a conventional Russian incursion for now, while warning about sabotage, cyberattacks, and drone or missile incidents.
French OSINT analyst Clément Molin argued that Russia currently lacks the forces for a conventional war with Europe because most of its military resources remain committed in Ukraine and its force posture around Kaliningrad is insufficient. In his assessment, another mobilization would more likely replenish forces fighting Ukraine, while hybrid attacks against Europe remain a more realistic near-term scenario.
Earlier, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said intelligence assessments indicate Russia’s plans in its war against Ukraine include “hybrid” drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Kyiv, including Poland.
He warned there was a “real risk” that drones or other missiles could enter the territory of one or several NATO countries on the alliance’s eastern flank and cause damage.
A new mobilization would primarily strengthen Russia’s ability to continue or expand its war in Ukraine. Over time, however, it could also help Moscow rebuild forces available for pressure against NATO, particularly if fighting in Ukraine decreases.
How mobilization currently works in Ukraine
Ukraine remains under a formally declared general mobilization and martial law, both extended through Oct. 31, 2026. Unlike Russia’s preference for avoiding the politically sensitive word, Ukraine’s mobilization is publicly acknowledged as a continuous national process rather than a sequence of separate “waves.”
In general, medically fit men liable for military service between the ages of 25 and 60 may be mobilized if they do not have a legal deferment or official reservation.
Men aged 18-24 who have not previously served and are not in the reserve generally join voluntarily under military contracts. Those who already have military experience, officer status or another legal status making them liable for service, can be mobilized before turning 25, according to a review of the current rules.
No new Ukrainian mobilization “wave” or general reduction of the mobilization age has been announced.
What is most likely to happen next?
The available evidence supports three conclusions.
First, Russia’s contract system is still producing large numbers of troops. Claims that Moscow has already exhausted its human resources are not supported by the available data.
Second, the system is becoming more expensive, coercive, and less effective at creating additional forces beyond replacing battlefield losses.
Third, Russia has created the administrative and digital infrastructure required for another call-up, but preparation does not prove that Putin has decided to order one.
The most plausible immediate scenario is an expansion of hidden or selective mobilization: higher regional quotas, intensified pressure on conscripts, broader prison recruitment, electronic summonses, and targeted reserve call-ups. A public nationwide campaign becomes more likely if those methods fail to satisfy battlefield requirements.

Poland and Ukraine will be partners in the so-called anti-ballistic coalition, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday during a joint press conference with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in western Ukraine.
Zelensky said Ukraine was working to establish a European anti-ballistic system and that Poland would be welcomed as a partner in the initiative. Tusk thanked Zelensky for his declaration on Poland's participation in the coalition.
The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established by Ukraine and nine European partners at a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Paris in July. Its members are France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, Spain, the Netherlands, Norway, Denmark and Sweden.
The coalition aims to develop new capabilities to help defend Ukraine against ballistic missile attacks.
Zelensky and Tusk met on Friday at a summit of regional leaders, where the Ukrainian president also announced the establishment of the Carpathian Eight (C8), a new regional cooperation format. (PAP)

Turkey launches AI initiative ahead of COP31 climate summit
- Turkey launched the Antalya Pledge on Artificial Intelligence to align AI infrastructure with global climate goals, focusing on transparency and clean energy use.
- Turkey introduced the 35x35 initiative to raise electricity's share of energy consumption to 35% by 2035, promoting clean power, grid modernisation, and support for developing countries.
- COP31 will feature a day dedicated to technology and AI, including an initiative to create AI-enabled clean-technology pilots linking developers, industry, and investors.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Turkey, which will host the COP31 climate summit in Antalya in November, launched a push on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Sept 21 to address AI’s skyrocketing energy demand through a political pledge that countries would adopt to align their AI infrastructure build-out with global climate goals.
The new Antalya Pledge on Artificial Intelligence is being developed with the UN’s International Telecommunication Union, and a draft will be shared ahead of COP31, the incoming Turkish COP presidency said.
“We must openly discuss AI’s growing energy consumption and it is time for governments to start setting the terms. We expect companies to be transparent about their energy use and to power their operations with clean energy,” said COP31 president-designate Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Minister for Environment and Urban Planning.
Turkey also formally launched its flagship initiative ahead of the annual UN climate summit, a push for a global pledge to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, which will include efforts to electrify buildings, transport and industry.
The 35x35 initiative aims to encourage countries to use clean power, storage and modernise grids and support developing countries as they shift away from fossil fuels.
Currently, around 20 per cent of the world’s total energy demand is met by electricity. The rest comes mostly from fossil fuels, plus around 10 per cent produced by biofuels and waste.
The voluntary pledge would also include a global mechanism to track collective progress on electrification.
Turkey said the COP will have a day dedicated to technology and AI, and will launch an initiative to develop “a portfolio of AI-enabled clean-technology pilots” that will connect technology developers, industry partners and investors in cars and heat pumps. REUTERS

MANILA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Fuel prices are set to go up in the Philippines starting Tuesday, due to tight global supply and continuing Middle East tensions, the country's Department of Energy (DOE) said on Monday.
The department announced at a press conference the price adjustments for the week of Sept. 22 to 28: gasoline, diesel and kerosene will increase by 4.88 pesos (about 0.08 U.S. dollars), 8.82 pesos and 6.47 pesos per liter, respectively.
Before the adjustment, the common retail prices of gasoline RON95, diesel and kerosene are 91.4 pesos, 94.5 pesos and 124.5 pesos per liter, respectively.

The Philippines is a net importer of petroleum products, significantly affected by global oil price swings, foreign exchange fluctuations, and disruptions in international supply routes, among others. ■

Feature: From Kampala to Shanghai, young Ugandan nurse takes first step onto WorldSkills stage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
22:39:18 CST
23:39:18 KST

KAMPALA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- For Ugandan nurse Flavia Nakaayi, who lives in Mpererwe, a suburb north of Uganda's capital Kampala, China was once a faraway country she knew mainly through TikTok videos.
It's a place of towering skyscrapers, a rich and colorful culture, and even robots serving guests in hotels. But that distant image is about to become a reality.
Nakaayi, 21, is set to fly to China to compete in the 48th WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai, which will take place this week. For her, the trip will mark not only her first flight and first journey abroad, but also her first time stepping onto the global stage as a vocational skills trainee.
The competition will bring together more than 1,400 young skilled competitors from over 70 countries and regions to compete in 64 official skill events under the theme "New Era, New Skills, New Dream."
Nakaayi's journey to Shanghai began far from the international spotlight.
The eldest of two children, she was raised by a single mother in Mpererwe. After completing Senior Four, the equivalent of lower secondary education in Uganda, she chose to leave the conventional academic path and pursue vocational training.
"Some of us are not from a well-off family, so I wanted something to do immediately after (school), start earning and relieve my mother the burden of tuition. When I finished school, I started working," she told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Nursing had been Nakaayi's passion since childhood, shaped in part by her own experiences with illness.
"I had a sickly childhood; I was this person who was always sick, moving to different hospitals. I was cared for when I needed help. So those people who took care of me when I was sick, it is now time for me to reward them," she said.
She later enrolled at Kabale School of Comprehensive Nursing and Midwifery in southwestern Uganda, more than 400 km from her home. There, she focused on her training and eventually earned a certificate in nursing.
Last year, WorldSkills Uganda, under Uganda's Ministry of Education and Sports, organized regional and national skills competitions involving trainees from technical and vocational education and training (TVET) institutions across the country.
Nakaayi competed against trainees from across the country, advancing through fiercely contested regional and national competitions to eventually become the national champion in the Healthcare/Nursing category.
Nakaayi will be joined in Shanghai by Elizabeth Mutoro, the national champion in Welding, and Paul Lugobe, the national champion in Cooking.
To prepare to compete against some of the world's top young skilled competitors, Nakaayi underwent intensive hands-on training at Kibuli Hospital in Uganda's capital, where industry experts provided detailed guidance on her nursing techniques and procedures.
Before their departure, the three competitors also received training in psychological resilience, international competition etiquette and cross-cultural communication.
Nakaayi said that regardless of whether she wins a medal, the opportunity to step onto the global skills competition stage in China, connect with peers from around the world and learn from one another is in itself an important step in her life.
"The major thing here is to learn. We are going to be nurses from different countries; each country has its own way of doing things. So what is taking me there besides competing is to learn new ideas, new techniques of nursing practice, improve areas like communication, critical thinking and safe patient health care delivery," Nakaayi said.
She said she is particularly interested in how China applies technology to healthcare and hopes to see how technological advances can improve nursing practice.
Jackson Kuucha, Team Leader of WorldSkills Uganda, told Xinhua that Uganda will send a delegation of more than 30 people, including senior government officials responsible for TVET, competitors, and heads of several TVET institutions.
Kuucha said the trip to Shanghai would not only be an opportunity to showcase Uganda's skilled talent, but also an important platform to benchmark the country's skills against global standards, build international partnerships and learn from other countries. The delegation hopes to bring the knowledge and experience gained back home to further strengthen Uganda's technical and vocational education and training system.
According to Ugandan government reports, vocational education is regarded as an important driver of industrialization and economic transformation, as well as a means of addressing youth unemployment. Nearly 1,000 technical and vocational education and training institutions across the country are currently overseen by the Ministry of Education and Sports.
For Kuucha, China's experience offers lessons for Uganda as it seeks to strengthen vocational education.
He said vocational training in China places greater emphasis on practical skills, while Uganda's system remains comparatively theoretical, creating gaps between classroom learning and workplace requirements.
"You realize that we are somehow delivering our content with talk and chalk and yet with vocational education, it is meant to be hands-on," the official said. "That's why we have engineers who don't know how to hold a spanner, how to unbolt nuts." ■

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli have been expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC) and military service for serious discipline and law violations, according to a decision made at a CPC leadership meeting held on Monday.
Zhang served as a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and vice chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC), while Liu served as a CMC member and chief of staff of the CMC Joint Staff Department.
A meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee approved the CMC's reports on the handling of Zhang and Liu's cases after deliberation.
With approval from the CPC Central Committee and the CMC, the CMC's disciplinary and supervisory authority launched investigations into their cases.
The investigations found that Zhang and Liu formed self-serving cliques, were disloyal and dishonest to the Party, took advantage of their positions to assist others in promotions and accepted a huge sum of bribes in return.
They also failed to fulfill the responsibility of exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance, said a statement released after the meeting.
They seriously violated Party discipline, were suspected of serious duty-related violations, and engaged in both corruption and dereliction of duties, it said, adding that their violations involved exceptionally large amounts of money, and were of extremely serious nature and with significantly negative impacts.
The cases related to their suspected crimes will be transferred to military prosecution authorities for legal review and prosecution in accordance with the law, according to the statement.
The decision to expel Zhang and Liu from the CPC awaits confirmation by the CPC Central Committee when it convenes a plenary session. Previously, the CMC had made a decision to expel Zhang and Liu from military service.
The statement noted the investigation and punishment of Zhang and Liu once again made it clear that no tolerance is shown for corruption, and that it represented a major achievement in the anti-corruption campaign waged by the Party and the military.
The people's military has become purer, more consolidated, with greater cohesion and combat effectiveness in the fight against corruption, the statement said. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- China has gained sound momentum in cultivating new quality productive forces in the first eight months of 2026, with high-tech industries and AI-related sectors leading the way, the country's latest tax data released on Monday revealed.
In the January-August period, sales revenue of China's high-tech industries increased by 15.7 percent year on year, with the high-tech manufacturing sector up 18.9 percent, according to the State Taxation Administration.
Notably, sales revenue of AI-related integrated circuit manufacturing and intelligent vehicle equipment manufacturing surged 67.7 percent and 38.8 percent year on year, respectively, the data showed.
Tax data also pointed to a deepening integration of the digital and real economies. In the first eight months, sales revenue of digital product manufacturing and digital product services went up 16.6 percent and 11.1 percent, respectively.
Meanwhile, China's industrial sales revenue rose 7.3 percent year on year during the period, with that of equipment manufacturing sector up 10.1 percent.
The tax data shows the Chinese economy maintaining a momentum, with new growth drivers and improved structure, an official with the State Taxation Administration said.
Quick growth of industrial sales revenue, especially in high-tech industries, came as China's industrial output growth continued to pick up.
Earlier data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed China's value-added industrial output expanded 5.2 percent year on year in August, accelerating by 0.7 percentage point from the previous month, with high-tech manufacturing output jumped 16.7 percent.

The platform helps prosecutors to more efficiently verify leads, assess ecological damage and corroborate evidence from multiple sources, he added.
Procuratorates also use other new technologies, such as drone photography, big-data comparisons and AI screening, to gather evidence and assess the results of ecological restoration in cases involving monitoring across large areas, the media conference was told.
Data from the SPP showed that, as of mid-August this year, procuratorial authorities across China had handled 73,000 ecological and environmental public interest cases since 2025, including 61,000 administrative and 12,000 civil cases. ■

How we protected the UK and space in August 2026
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
15:38:15 BST
23:38:15 KST

How we protected the UK and space in August 2026
This report was issued in September 2026 and covers the time period 1 August 2026 to 31 August 2026 inclusive.
August saw a reduced risk level to UK interests, with fewer uncontrolled re-entries, collision alerts, fragmentations and reduced space weather activity when compared with July.
All NSpOC warning and protection services were functioning throughout the period.
Re-entry analysis
There was a 13% decrease in the number of objects re-entering Earth’s atmosphere monitored by NSpOC in August, when compared with the previous month.
Of the 54 objects that re-entered, 47 were satellites, six were rocket bodies and one was likely a piece of debris.
Collision avoidance analysis
Collision risks to UK-licensed satellites were 25% lower in August than in July and sat well below the 12-month rolling average.
Registered Space Objects (RSOs) analysis
The in-orbit population increased in August, with a net addition of 248 objects to the US Satellite Catalogue.
The number of Resident Space Objects (RSOs) reported may be subject to small adjustments over time as the way objects are tracked is refined. Figures in this report reflect the most current available data and may differ slightly from those published in previous months.
Fragmentation analysis
One fragmentation incident took place in August involving a satellite in Low Earth Orbit. Assessments are ongoing to understand how many pieces of debris were released into orbit.
Space weather analysis
Space weather activity was lower in August when compared with the previous month, consisting of some solar flares and geomagnetic storms.
Comments
The National Space Operations Centre combines and coordinates UK civil and military space domain awareness capabilities to enable operations, promote prosperity and protect UK interests in space and on Earth from space-related threats, risks and hazards.

Nearly 130,000 people have been displaced across seven governorates in Yemen as families flee escalating insecurity, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Monday.
The UN agency's latest Displacement Tracking Matrix data showed that 129,438 people, or 21,573 households, have been forced from their homes.
"Nearly 130,000 people have been forced from their homes in just a few weeks. Many have already moved more than once to find safety," said Othman Belbeisi, IOM regional director for the Middle East and North Africa.
Belbeisi said the number had risen by 11,352 in just three days, from 118,086 on Sept. 18.
Taiz hosts the largest number of newly displaced people at 73,494, followed by Lahj with 33,828, Aden with 8,946, and Al Hodeidah with 8,244. Displacement was also recorded in Abyan, Hadramawt, and Marib.
"These are families who have lost their homes and their income," Belbeisi said, warning that communities receiving them were already struggling and needed greater support.
Meanwhile, 3,106 people had crossed the Red Sea from Yemen to Djibouti as of Sunday evening, according to IOM.
The agency said it is providing emergency assistance to arrivals and appealed for increased support.
