Giving low-income mothers a monthly cash stipend slows their children’s biological aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:00:27 UTC
23:00:27 KST

A new study suggests that providing low-income mothers with a substantial monthly cash stipend during their child’s first four years slows down the child’s biological pace of aging. The research, published in Nature Human Behaviour, indicates that while this financial support altered cellular markers of aging in young children, it did not have a similar effect on the mothers themselves.
The study focuses on DNA methylation, a biological process where small chemical tags are added to DNA molecules. These tags change how genes are expressed without altering the underlying genetic code. Over a person’s lifespan, these molecular changes accumulate in ways that reflect their biological age, which can sometimes outpace their chronological age depending on life experiences and environmental factors.
Scientists use algorithms called “epigenetic clocks” to measure this biological aging process. One such clock is DunedinPACE, which tracks the speed at which a person’s body is biologically aging. Another epigenetic tool, known as Epigenetic-g, attempts to quantify cognitive functioning and brain health based on these same DNA methylation patterns. Both tools offer a way to look at how life circumstances become biologically embedded in the body.
Growing up in poverty is consistently linked to poorer health, faster aging, and lower cognitive function later in life. The early years of childhood are thought to be an especially sensitive period where financial hardship might have the largest negative impact on a child’s developing system. A 2021 study found that children growing up in socioeconomically disadvantaged families tend to exhibit a faster pace of biological aging.
Research often explores how early life stress affects the body on a cellular level. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 observed that children with more emotional and behavioral difficulties also displayed DNA-methylation patterns indicative of accelerated biological aging. To test whether a financial boost could intervene in this trajectory, researchers examined data from the Baby’s First Years project. This initiative was designed to see if unconditional cash assistance could directly influence child development and family well-being.
“Our previous work, including a recent meta-analysis of 140 studies encompassing nearly 66,000 people across 23 countries, established a robust, global pattern: lower socioeconomic status is consistently linked to accelerated epigenetic aging,” Laurel Raffington, leader of the Max Planck Research Group Biosocial at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin, told PsyPost. “This biological weathering is visible in early childhood and seems to persist into adulthood decades later.”
“However, a major gap remains in the literature,” Raffington explained. “Existing studies show strong correlations, but they cannot prove that poverty causes faster aging, nor do they show whether relieving financial strain can slow it down. That is exactly what makes Baby’s First Years unique. By evaluating the impact of direct, unconditional cash gifts to mothers with low incomes, this study provides causal evidence that providing economic support can alter a child’s biology.”
The Baby’s First Years project enrolled mothers with low incomes shortly after they gave birth in hospitals across four U.S. metropolitan areas. The mothers were randomly assigned to one of two groups. The high-cash group received $333 per month, while the low-cash group received $20 per month. These unconditional cash gifts were loaded onto debit cards every month for the first four years of the children’s lives, with no restrictions on how the money could be spent.
When the children reached four years of age, the researchers collected saliva samples from both the mothers and the children. The final sample for the DNA methylation analysis included 735 children and 777 mothers. The research team used the saliva samples to calculate each participant’s DunedinPACE score to measure their pace of biological aging. They also calculated Epigenetic-g scores to estimate aging-related cognitive differences.
In their statistical models, the team controlled for several baseline factors to isolate the effect of the cash transfers. These factors included the mother’s age, education level, race, household income before the study, and the infant’s birth weight. They then compared the epigenetic scores of the families receiving the high cash amounts with those receiving the nominal amounts.
The results suggest that the higher cash gifts slowed the children’s pace of biological aging. Children in the group receiving $333 per month had a DunedinPACE score that was lower than the children in the $20 per month group. This difference provides evidence for a small but detectable deceleration in cellular aging among the children whose families received the larger financial support.
“The study demonstrates that larger cash transfers directly slowed children’s biological aging, as measured by epigenetic clocks,” Raffington said. “Because this study used a rigorous, randomized controlled design, we can confidently conclude that reducing financial strain caused this healthier biological trajectory.”
While the statistical effect size is modest, it carries weight for public health policy. “In medicine and social science, small individual effects can compound into large societal benefits when scaled across a whole population,” Raffington added. “These findings show that poverty leaves a biological footprint—and that providing direct financial support to families is a powerful public health intervention.”
However, the researchers found no evidence supporting their expectation that the higher cash gifts would increase the children’s Epigenetic-g scores. The results for this cognitive biomarker were ambiguous and did not show a consistent improvement linked to the financial assistance. The team also checked two other measures of biological age acceleration, known as GrimAge and PhenoAge, but found no group differences for these metrics.
The findings are generally in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that generous state-level anti-poverty programs mitigated the negative impacts of low income on children’s development. While that earlier study looked at brain volumes and mental health in 9- to 11-year-olds rather than epigenetic markers of biological aging in 4-year-olds, both indicate that financial assistance can buffer against the biological toll of childhood poverty.
When looking at the mothers in the study, the cash gifts had no observed impact on their epigenetic indices. Neither the pace of aging nor the cognitive biomarkers differed between the high-cash and low-cash groups for the adults. The authors noted that while the extra income helped the families financially, it did not seem to alter major adult environmental stressors, such as housing quality or food insecurity, which are typically associated with adult biological aging.
The team also explored whether the children’s epigenetic scores correlated with their concurrent behavior, brain activity, or physical health. The pace of biological aging was not associated with the children’s body mass index, executive functioning, vocabulary, or overall health as reported by their mothers.
“I was surprised to see that the epigenetic measures were not related to the children’s measured body mass index (BMI), cognitive task performance, or mother-reported socioemotional behaviors,” Raffington said, noting that prior studies found these associations. She suspects the young age of the participants plays a role in this discrepancy. “Epigenetic clocks at this early stage may be capturing subtle biological underpinnings that lay the groundwork for long-term adult health, even before they manifest as visible differences in standard childhood development or behavioral metrics,” she explained.
The lack of behavioral deficits also highlights the families’ strength. “These children are developing well because they and their families are resilient despite limited financial means,” Raffington told PsyPost. “The biological differences we observe suggest that accelerated aging may be a hidden, under-the-skin cost of that resilience.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “First, while these population-level effects are scientifically significant, they do not apply uniformly to every individual,” Raffington clarified. “Many people who grow up in financially strained families do not show accelerated epigenetic aging; population trends do not dictate an individual child’s destiny.” She also noted that epigenetic clocks are a population-level research tool and have not received scientific consensus support as an individual clinical diagnostic tool.
The children in this study are still very young, and it is unknown whether these early changes in the pace of biological aging will persist into adulthood. The cash gifts ended shortly after the children turned six, and it remains to be seen if the cellular benefits endure without ongoing economic support. “We don’t know if these differences will persist as children get older, nor do we know yet whether slower biological aging in early childhood predicts subsequent improvements in health or longevity,” Raffington said.
Additionally, scientists still disagree on exactly how to interpret epigenetic aging in young children. These epigenetic clocks were originally developed using blood samples from older adults. While they can be applied to saliva samples in children, some accuracy might be lost when translating the algorithms across different tissues and age groups.
The algorithms were also primarily developed using genetic data from populations of European descent. Expanding these epigenetic tools to be more globally representative is an ongoing priority for researchers in the field. Despite these limitations, the study offers a rare look at how a direct economic intervention can influence human biology in early childhood.
Looking ahead, the researchers are continuing to track the families to answer remaining questions. “Will we still see these epigenetic differences when the children are six and eight years old? Do they persist even after the cash transfers have ended? And, do these early epigenetic effects actually translate into tangible differences in health later in life?” Raffington asked.
She is also interested in exploring what would happen if financial support began even earlier. She pointed to a study evaluating the Rx Kids program in Flint, Michigan, which showed that providing unconditional cash support starting during pregnancy improved birth outcomes. “If the biological embedding of environmental conditions is most pronounced early in life, pregnancy is precisely the window where financial relief could yield the greatest long-term benefits,” she explained.
Reflecting on the work so far, Raffington praised the extensive collaboration required to conduct the trial. “The Baby’s First Years study is unique in its scope and scientific rigor,” she said. “It stands as a testament to the utility of team science—supported by a mix of research grants and philanthropy—and underscores the immense value of slow, careful science that requires some patience and long-term funding resources.”
The study, “Effects of a randomized controlled trial of unconditional cash transfers on epigenetic measures of ageing and cognition in children and mothers,” was authored by Laurel Raffington, Yayouk E. Willems, Jessica F. Sperber, Sepideh Zarandooz, Molly A. Costanzo, Daniel A. Notterman, Colter Mitchell, Elliot M. Tucker-Drob, Greg J. Duncan, Nathan A. Fox, Lisa A. Gennetian, Katherine A. Magnuson, Sonya V. Troller-Renfree, Hirokazu Yoshikawa, Elisabeth B. Binder, K. Paige Harden, and Kimberly G. Noble.

MRIs show brain changes linked to Alzheimer’s years in advance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

MRIs show brain changes linked to Alzheimer’s years in advance
A thickening cortex preceded known markers of Alzheimer’s disease by up to seven years
Brain imaging could reveal early changes linked to Alzheimer’s disease.
MRI scans show that the thickness of the outermost layer of the brain changes before the onset of the disease, detectable up to seven years prior, researchers reported August 19 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the differences are too subtle to use as a diagnostic tool, they could help researchers understand the early stages of Alzheimer’s.
Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia and can cause memory loss, disorientation and behavior shifts. But changes in the brain can occur long before these cognitive symptoms appear. Sticky protein fragments called amyloid-beta build up in the brains of people who go on to develop Alzheimer’s. These bundles, along with tangles of another protein called tau, slowly kill off brain cells and shrink the brain.
Under the current criteria, spotting A-beta buildups via positron emission tomography scans, or PET scans, is enough for an Alzheimer’s diagnosis even in the absence of cognitive symptoms. But most people do not receive PET scans without symptoms, so they won’t get diagnosed until later.
To better understand how the disease takes shape, Alzheimer’s researcher Yunpeng Wang and colleagues wanted to test whether they could spot brain changes before patients developed A-beta buildups.
The team examined MRI scans from over a thousand participants in long-term studies that track brain changes with aging. Wang and colleagues compared changes in the thickness of the cortex — the outermost layer of the brain, which averages around 2.5 millimeters thick— between people who later showed high A-beta levels and people who did not.
People who went on to develop high A-beta levels had thicker cortices than people who did not. Differences in thickness of a few hundredths of a millimeter were visible up to seven years before the participants were deemed to have high A-beta levels based on their PET scans. The cortices of people in both groups thinned naturally with age, but those of people who later developed high A-beta thinned less overall. The researchers didn’t observe any link between the thickness of the cortex and memory problems at this early stage of the disease.
The findings imply that “the trajectory of cortical changes is not [as] simplistic as we used to think,” says Victor Montal, a degenerative diseases researcher at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center who was not involved in the work. Rather than assuming the cortex thins consistently due to atrophy as the disease progresses, researchers will need to account for slower thinning in the early stages when studying Alzheimer’s, he says.
The relative thickening of the cortex might come from inflammation that occurs as A-beta first starts to accumulate, says Wang, of the University of Oslo. But MRIs can’t determine the cause of the thickening directly.
“I don’t think that this cortical thickness is something you’re going to use clinically,” says Frederik Barkhof, a neuroradiologist at University College London who was not involved in the study. The changes in cortex thickness are too subtle to use as individual diagnostic tools, he says, but they could help researchers understand the mechanisms behind Alzheimer’s disease and emerging treatments.
For example, some existing Alzheimer’s treatments remove A-beta but don’t stop the volume loss in the brain. The new findings could indicate that the current treatments reduce inflammation and not that a patient is losing excess brain tissue despite treatment, he says.

NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh minister Om Prakash Rajbhar has claimed that Prime Minister Narendra Modi assured him that the state would be divided into four parts, reviving a nearly two-decade-old debate over dividing the country's most populous state.Rajbhar, who heads BJP ally Suheldev Bharatiya Samaj Party (SBSP), claimed that PM Modi told him Uttar Pradesh could be divided after the caste census.“We want to assure you regarding the 27% reservation. I spoke with the prime minister about this,” he told the audience at an SBSP programme in Deoria on Sunday.“He (PM Modi) said, ‘Om Prakash ji, your point is justified, but some people are opposing it.’ I asked him how we could move forward, and he replied, ‘I will conduct a caste census, and once we have counted the castes, there will be no difficulty.’ The state will be divided into four parts. And on the day the Purvanchal is formed, if the chief minister is to be from any caste, then a Rajbhar’s son will become the chief minister,” he added.However, another UP minister and BJP ally, Sanjay Nishad, dismissed Rajbhar’s remarks as “misleading”, saying the Nishad Party was not in favour of a reorganisation.“There had been a demand to divide UP earlier, but now the state is progressing rapidly in all spheres.
Further, special development funds have been allocated for regions like Bundelkhand and Purvanchal that needed handholding,” Nishad told PTI.Rajbhar has advocated the division of Uttar Pradesh in the past as well, saying in October 2018 that the “state can be developed only after it is divided into four parts.”
When Mayawati proposed carving out four states from UP
With the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections due in early 2027, Rajbhar’s remarks have revived the long-running political debate over dividing the state.Ahead of the 2012 UP assembly elections, then chief minister Mayawati revived the demand, with the state assembly passing a resolution to split Uttar Pradesh into Avadh Pradesh, Purvanchal, Bundelkhand and Paschim Pradesh.In 2011, her government had sent a proposal to the Congress-led Centre seeking the creation of the four states.Before that, in 2008, Mayawati had proposed dividing Uttar Pradesh into three parts.Several parties, including the Rashtriya Lok Dal and Congress, have also backed demands for dividing the state at various points. There have additionally been calls for a separate Bundelkhand comprising parts of Uttar Pradesh and neighbouring Madhya Pradesh.
Uttar Pradesh was last divided in 2000, when the BJP-led central government carved out Uttarakhand, then known as Uttaranchal.
Why Uttar Pradesh matters
With a population of around 25 crore, Uttar Pradesh is India’s most populous state. If it were an independent country, its population would make it the fifth- or sixth-most populous country in the world.Geographically, Uttar Pradesh is the fourth-largest state in India.It sends 80 members to the 543-seat Lok Sabha, the highest representation of any state or Union territory. Its legislative assembly has 403 members.Six prime ministers were born in Uttar Pradesh, while several others, including Narendra Modi, have represented the state in Parliament.

Twenty Swiss pig herds culled due to lung disease
Pig herds at 20 Swiss farms are to be culled due to an outbreak of a contagious lung disease. In the canton of Lucerne alone, 11 farms are affected.
The measures are required to combat enzootic pneumonia effectively and prevent its spread. Pig herds on 20 farms located in the cantons of Bern, Lucerne, Solothurn, Schwyz, Thurgau and Vaud must be completely culled.
Around 1,500 breeding sows and their piglets are affected by the measure. The animals will be humanely euthanised, according to a statement. On 40 other fattening farms across 14 cantons, the movement of animals is restricted.
Last Wednesday, 60 holdings within a network of pig farms and breeding facilities were placed under quarantine.
The pathogen, which attacks the lungs of pigs, poses no danger to humans.

Fandoqlu: Grass skiing amid the mountain landscapes of Ardabil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:55:27 UTC
22:55:27 KST

Fandoqlu: Grass skiing amid the mountain landscapes of Ardabil
TEHRAN - High in the green mountains of northwestern Iran, where cool air lingers through the summer and broad meadows stretch across the landscape, Fandoqlu offers an unusual combination of outdoor sport and nature tourism.
Located near the Fandoqlu Forest, about 25 kilometers from Ardabil, the provincial capital, the Fandoqlu Grass Skiing Resort is one of the province's principal destinations for grass skiing.
The resort covers about 90,000 square meters and has facilities designed for the sport, including a cable car and skiing equipment.
Unlike conventional ski resorts, where snow determines the season, Fandoqlu relies on its mountain meadows. Its relatively cool climate makes it particularly suitable for summer outdoor activities, when much of the country experiences considerably warmer conditions.
Grass-skiing competitions have been held at the resort since 2014. During the first half of the year, the complex hosts competitions in disciplines including speed skiing and various spiral events. In recent years, camps for Iran's national grass-skiing team have also been held there. Depending on weather and snow conditions, the resort has occasionally hosted winter skiing competitions as well.
For visitors who are unfamiliar with grass skiing, the attraction is as much about the setting as the sport. The slopes run through a landscape of open green plains and mountain scenery, while the surrounding Fandoqlu region offers a range of natural attractions.
The resort lies in the Namin area, which has a cold climate during much of the year and relatively mild summers. Even in the warmer months, visitors can experience cool mountain air and gentle breezes, making the area a popular destination for escaping the heat of lower-lying regions.
Fandoqlu is also part of a wider tourism circuit that extends well beyond the ski slope. The surrounding area is known for forest landscapes, waterfalls, springs, flower-covered meadows and mineral hot-water springs.
Among the nearby attractions are the Meshe-Sui and Ali-Dashi hot springs, about 15 kilometers from the resort, while Lake Shourabil is about 27 kilometers away. Travelers approaching Fandoqlu along the Ardabil-Astara road can also visit the Heyran road and cable car, as well as the Heyran go-karting track. Bibi Yanlu Forest Park is another option for a forest excursion.
The region also provides access to Ardabil's cultural and historical attractions. The city's historic bazaar is adjacent to the shrine complex of Sheikh Safi al-Din Ardabili, a UNESCO World Heritage site. The Ardabil Anthropology Museum, housed in a historic bathhouse, and the city's archaeology museum offer further opportunities to explore the province's cultural heritage.
Accommodation and food are also available in and around the resort, with hotels, restaurants, barbecue outlets and fast-food establishments serving visitors.
For travelers, Fandoqlu therefore offers something different from a conventional ski destination. A visit can begin on a grassy mountain slope and continue through forests, hot springs and historic sites, turning a sporting outing into a broader journey through the natural and cultural landscape of Ardabil province.

Traditional vest from Yazd showcased in Mexico
TEHRAN – A traditional embroidered vest from Abarkuh, Yazd province, was showcased at the fourth international Soka exhibition in Mexico, where it received recognition from the event’s judges and experts.
The felt vest, regarded as a valuable example of Abarkuh’s indigenous clothing and embroidery traditions, was presented at the international event through the efforts of Hamed Akrami, a researcher and activist in the field of cultural heritage and traditional arts, with support from Abarkuh Municipality and the county’s Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Department, Miras Aria news agency reported on Monday.
The vest was accepted and commended during the exhibition’s judging process, offering an international platform for one of the lesser-known aspects of Abarkuh’s traditional clothing and handicraft heritage.
Featuring distinctive local characteristics and traditional embroidery techniques, the vests have potential for display at specialized exhibitions, as well as for the revival and reproduction of the craft. It could also help create new opportunities for employment and entrepreneurship, according to the report.
Research and documentation of the traditional craft are currently being completed. Once the documentation is finalized, a registration dossier will be submitted to the Abarkuh Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Department to undergo the required legal procedures.
The participation of the Abarkuh vest in the international event is seen as part of ongoing efforts to research, revive and promote the county’s traditional clothing and to introduce its traditional arts to audiences in Iran and abroad, the news agency said.
Abarkuh, also known as Abarqu, is known for its old earthen architecture and cultural heritage. Among its best-known landmarks is Sarv-e Abarkuh, an ancient cypress tree that has become a symbol of the city. Experts have variously estimated the tree’s age at between 4,000 and 5,000 years, although some estimates put it at as much as 8,000 years.

It is not officially known where Kravchenko is currently. According to unconfirmed media reports, he may be in Vienna, Austria, negotiating with local law firms over seeking asylum.

The 'rebel' hit by rebellion: How Mamata Banerjee's TMC journey has come full circle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:54:37 UTC
22:54:37 KST

Mamata built TMC through rebellion; 28 years on, revolt threatens the party she created
Mamata Banerjee's political journey in West Bengal has come almost full circle.In 1998, Mamata walked out of the Congress after years of differences with its leadership and formed the Trinamool Congress. She believed the Congress was not doing enough to challenge the Left Front, which had been ruling West Bengal for decades.28 years later, Didi, as she is fondly called, is now herself a step away from losing control of her party to a rebellion. Her Trinamool Congress has split, and rivals in the party, who once worked under her are now challenging her control. The Election Commission has temporarily frozen the party's original name and its well-known 'Jora Ghash Phul' (flowers and grass) symbol while it decides which faction has the “real” claim.
And what's more! In an interesting turn of events, Mamata is now desperately banking on the Congress’s support to survive the BJP’s political offensive against her in West Bengal.The change comes at a difficult moment for her.The BJP recently ended Trinamool’s 15-year rule in West Bengal in May, crossing 200 seats and forming its first government in the state. Mamata’s party, which had been in power for 15 years, fell below 100 seats.Mamata's troubles have only grown since then.The defeat was followed by a rebellion within the TMC and finally a battle over who has the right to use the party’s name and symbol.
For a leader who built her career as a rebel, Mamata is now facing a rebellion of her own.
Mamata on TMC symbol row
Congress: From bitter rival to 'sister party'
At the peak of her power-packed 15 years as chief minister of West Bengal, Mamata refused to acknowledge the presence of Congress in West Bengal. In fact, for Mamata, both the Congress and the Left were bitter political rivals and she would often accuse them of being the B-team of the BJP in the state. But that changed in the aftermath of her crushing defeat in May this year as the BJP swept the state’s political landscape and formed its first government.The shift in power dynamics was on display when Mamata announced support for the Congress candidate in the Nandigram bypoll to be held on October 6. "We are extending our support to Congress in Nandigram. We are doing this for the greater interest of the nation,” Mamata Banerjee announced. But what really surprised was her reference to the Congress as a “natural alliance” and a “sister party”. Words that would sound almost alien to those who have followed Mamata’s politics, especially the Congress leaders in the state.While the Congress has strongly backed her fight against the Election Commission, with Rahul Gandhi leading the charge, the help is unlikely to transform into a greater alliance, at least for now. The West Bengal Congress unit, which was at the receiving end of Mamata’s political aggression for many years, is very clear and categorical that it does not want any alliance with her party.
Rahul Gandhi backs Mamata Banerjee
Vendetta politics
Since losing power, Mamata has repeatedly accused the BJP of targeting her and trying to weaken her party.The irony is that Mamata herself faced similar accusations after she came to power in 2011, ending 34 years of Left rule. Both the Left and the Congress had accused the Trinamool of using political pressure and defections to weaken its rivals.The circumstances may be different, but the roles have now reversed. What is happening today to her is what she did to her opponents in the past in West Bengal.
Mamata's beginning in politics
Mamata started her political career with the Congress in the 1970s. The first glimpse of her aggressive political style was on display during Emergency days when she made headlines for her protest against Jay Prakash Narayan.She quickly rose through the Congress ranks and, in 1984, emerged as the giant killer when she defeated veteran Communist politician Somnath Chatterjee, to win the Jadavpur parliamentary Constituency in West Bengal. She was also among the youngest MPs elected that year.There has been no looking back since then. She lost in 1989, but came back strongly in 1991 from the Calcutta South constituency and retained the seat in 1996, 1998, 1999, 2004 and 2009 Lok Sabha elections.
From Congress activist and street fighter to TMC founder and three-term West Bengal chief minister
The protest politics and the birth of Trinamool Congress
Mamata's differences with the Congress grew through the 1990s. She believed the party was not aggressive enough in taking on the Left government in West Bengal.Her politics was built around street protests and agitations against the Left government.One of the most prominent moments of her political career came in 1993, as state Youth Congress chief, when she led a march to Writers’ Building demanding voter ID cards to prevent alleged electoral malpractice.Police opened fire during the protest, killing 13 Congress workers. By 1997, her differences with the Congress leadership had reached a breaking point. In 1998, Mamata walked out and formed the Trinamool Congress.Years later, the Singur and Nandigram movements turned that protest politics into a force strong enough to bring her to power for a good 15 years.
Nandigram challenge, once again
Nandigram has always had a special place in Mamata's political career. The land protests here in 2007 helped turn her into the strongest challenger to the Left. Four years later, she came to power.But Nandigram also became one of her biggest electoral setbacks. In the 2021 assembly election, Mamata chose to contest from the seat against her former aide Suvendu Adhikari, who had joined the BJP. Nandigram was Suvendu’s bastion and Mamata wanted to prove a point. That did not happen as she lost to Suvendu by around 2,000 votes. But her Trinamool Congress returned to power in the state with a thumping majority.Five years later, in 2026, it was Suvendu’s turn to challenge Mamata in her bastion of Bhabanipur, while also contesting from Nandigram. Suvendu not just reinforced his dominance in Nandigram but also humiliated Mamata in Bhabanipur.Suvendu retained Bhabanipur and vacated Nandigram, necessitating a bypoll. But this time around Mamata faced a setback even before the contest could begin. Her candidate for the October 6 bypoll in Nandigram withdrew from the contest after meeting chief minister Suvendu Adhikari, leaving Mamata without a candidate of her own. She then announced support for Congress candidate Milan Pradhan.For Mamata, Nandigram has now seen almost every phase of her politics. It helped her rise, handed her a personal defeat, and is now showing the challenges she faces after losing power.
The road ahead ...
For Mamata, the road ahead is not just about fighting the BJP. The former chief minister has a larger issue at hand at the moment. She has to hold her party together, fight for control of the Trinamool name and symbol, and rebuild her position as the main opposition force in Bengal.Congress support could help her on some issues, especially at the national level, but a wider alliance in Bengal seems unlikely, at least for now.Congress leaders in West Bengal remain wary of Mamata after years of on-and-off rivalry and large-scale defections from their party to the Trinamool under Mamata’s watch.That leaves Mamata at the junction of perhaps the most difficult phase of her political career.
She began as a Congress leader, broke away in rebellion, built a party of her own and eventually ruled Bengal for 15 years. Now, with rebels challenging that very party and she being forced to return to Congress for help, Mamata's journey has indeed come almost full circle.The future and fate of the original Trinamool Congress is now in the hands of the Election Commission. Mamata will be keeping her fingers crossed. And rightly so. Precedents from recent past in Maharashtra would worry her. Sharad Pawar lost control of the Nationalist Congress Party and Uddhav Thackeray of Shiv Sena, after the ECI ruled in favour of rebels who had split the two parties. So, will Mamata be lucky, or will she now be left with a “football player” to try another round of “khela” in West Bengal? Can Mamata once again fight adversity for a much-needed comeback? Well, we will have to wait and watch.

She also cares deeply about stories around women’s rights and social change, while two very opinionated dogs make sure she never truly switches off.

World leaders meet at UN as planet grapples with climate change, wars, runaway AI
As we face ‘three existential threats,’ says the UN chief, ‘international cooperation is more necessary than ever’
Under a global cloud of wars and bitter divisions, world leaders meet at the United Nations in New York this week facing new fears that runaway artificial intelligence could threaten humanity even as climate shocks and escalating prices are already making life much tougher for hundreds of millions of people.
The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth?
The future of the UN will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players.
The UN’s 193 member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful UN Security Council, where the US, Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power.

Secretary-General of Parliament Antti Pelttari charged over Supo intelligence activities
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:52:45 EEST
22:52:45 KST

The National Prosecution Authority announced on Monday that prosecutors have completed their consideration of charges in a criminal case concerning Supo's intelligence activities.
The case centers on allegations that Supo breached rules and regulations governing police powers, the use of intelligence-gathering powers and the handling of classified information.
The suspected offences include abuse of official position, breach of official duty and disclosure of a security secret.
The Deputy Prosecutor General has brought charges against seven people in total.
One of those individuals, former Supo chief Antti Pelttari, has been charged with disclosing a state security secret and abusing his official position.
According to the indictment, the charge of disclosing a security secret concerns suspected acts between 20 August and 7 September 2020. The charge of suspected abuse of official position covers the period from June 2012 to the end of 2023.
Pelttari has previously been charged with breach of official duty in connection with his time as head of Supo. That charge was brought last summer.
Other charges have also been brought in the case, with the latest filed at Helsinki District Court on Monday.
Initially, ten people were suspected of involvement in the case.
All those suspected in the case have denied wrongdoing.
Pelttari is currently the secretary-general of parliament, its highest-ranking civil servant. He has been suspended from his post since last summer, due to the criminal investigation.

Asian Games | Day 2: Yu, 13, sets swimming Asian record, Thai shuttler suspended for doping
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:49:36 CST
22:49:36 KST

by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese teenager Yu Zidi's sensational Asian record propelled China's gold-medal charge on day two of the 2026 Asian Games on Monday, while Thai badminton player Pitchamon Opatniputh became the first known doping case of the Games.
Pitchamon, 19, tested positive for the banned substance furosemide and was provisionally suspended.
The International Testing Agency said an out-of-competition sample collected from Opatniputh in Nagoya on September 17 returned an Adverse Analytical Finding for furosemide. The substance is listed by the World Anti-Doping Agency as a specified substance prohibited at all times under the category of diuretics and masking agents.
China claimed two shooting golds, including a world record, and five swimming titles, while Zhang Boheng won the men's gymnastics all-around gold to round off another prolific day for the delegation.
In the pool, 13-year-old Yu maintained her stunning form. She came from behind to win the women's 200-meter individual medley in an Asian record of 2 minutes, 6.10 seconds, with teammate and defending champion Yu Yiting second in 2:07.99. Japan's Mio Narita took bronze in 2:10.40.
Yu's winning time was just 0.40 seconds off the world record set by Canada's Summer McIntosh.
"I feel even happier winning this second gold medal than I did with the first one," Yu said.
Her performance produced the first Asian swimming record of the Games. Yu made her Asian Games debut by winning the 200 butterfly on Sunday.
The excitement peaked in the men's 4x200 freestyle relay. Japan led for the first 750 meters as China stayed close behind. Pan Zhanle narrowed the gap on the third leg before Zhang Zhanshuo took the lead in the closing stages to give China gold in an Asian record of 7:00.17.
Japan took silver in 7:01.05, while South Korea claimed bronze in 7:06.76.
Adding to China's swimming success, backstroke specialist Xu Jiayu successfully defended his men's 50 backstroke title in a Games-record 24.04, while Wan Letian and Wang Xue'er finished 1-2 in the women's 50 backstroke.
China's Dong Zhihao and Japan's Shin Ohashi shared gold in the men's 100 breaststroke in 58.64, while defending champion Qin Haiyang took bronze.
South Korea claimed its first swimming gold of the Games as Kim Yeong-beom won the men's 50 freestyle, while defending champion Siobhan Haughey of Hong Kong, China took the women's 200 freestyle title.
In shooting, China swept the men's 10-meter air rifle individual and team gold medals, setting a world record in the team event.
The trio of Zhang Changhong, Sheng Lihao and Ma Sihan combined for 1,899.0 points to take team gold, breaking the previous world record of 1,898.4. India won silver with 1,890.1, while South Korea claimed bronze with 1,884.2.
In gymnastics, China's Zhang Boheng retained the men's all-around title. Fresh from winning the same event at the Asian championships, the 26-year-old scored 85.065 points to take gold, while Japan's reigning Olympic champion Shinnosuke Oka and 2021 Olympic champion Daiki Hashimoto finished second and third, respectively.
Zhang had finished runner-up to Oka at the Paris Olympics and to Hashimoto at last year's World Championships.
"Gymnastics keeps progressing, and both Japanese all-around gymnasts have very high levels of difficulty and execution," Zhang said.
China's success extended to other disciplines, with Lin Xinyu, Li Mingxu, Huang Anqi and Zhang Xirui winning the triathlon mixed relay in 1:25:54.
Gong Li and Li Qiaoqiao added karate gold medals in the women's kumite 61-kilogram and 68-kilogram categories, respectively.
In team sports, China's women's football team thrashed the Philippines 5-1 in Group G, while the women's volleyball team edged Thailand 3-2 to avenge its defeat in last month's Asian Championship final and advanced to the gold-medal match. China's women's basketball team beat Indonesia 110-41 in Group A.
After two days of competition, China led the medal table with 23 gold, 10 silver and five bronze medals. Japan was second with eight gold, 12 silver and 12 bronze, followed by South Korea with five gold, 13 silver and 15 bronze. ■

'Scorched earth': How Israel is remaking south Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:49:22 UTC
22:49:22 KST

Breadcrumb
'Scorched earth': How Israel is remaking south Lebanon
Beirut, Lebanon - Israel’s military is continuing a “scorched earth” strategy in southern Lebanon, despite a framework peace deal and ongoing direct negotiations between Beirut and Tel Aviv, analysts told The New Arab.
Airstrikes and controlled demolitions have rocked southern towns and villages almost daily, while US-mediated talks aimed at securing an Israeli withdrawal and Hezbollah’s disarmament have stalled ahead of the Israeli legislative elections in October.
Earlier this month, Israeli ground troops took control of the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge - allegedly containing a Hezbollah command centre, tunnels and weapons stores - after months of fighting in southern Lebanon.
“Ali al-Taher is considered a linchpin for the Israeli security system of today,” Elias Hanna, a retired Lebanese army general, told The New Arab.
Hanna added that from this vantage point, Israeli forces can consolidate their position in the previously captured Beaufort Castle and dominate the area south of the Litani River.
But it is not clear whether the Israeli military’s seizure of the Ali al-Taher ridge signals an intent to expand its occupation deeper into Lebanese territory.
The subsequent destruction of the alleged Hezbollah command centre – Israeli troops detonated the hilltop, causing a 4.1-magnitude seismic tremor – has been touted as a strategic and symbolic victory by Israel.
However, Hanna said the Ali al-Taher ridge was not as valuable a stronghold for Hezbollah as it was before this war began, as the armed group has switched to guerrilla-style warfare that precludes the use of large bases.
According to Hanna, Israel’s military, for its part, is also pursuing a new strategy in the south.
“This time it’s totally different from the 1982 invasion – now they are destroying everything,” Hanna said.
Israel historically occupied a swathe of southern Lebanon from 1982 to 2000, when Israeli forces withdrew completely. This time, however, Hanna argued that Israel cannot afford to put a large number of boots on the ground and is opting instead for a “scorched earth” approach.
“If you want to destroy your enemy, you destroy the ecosystem of your enemy, so he won’t be able to ever recover and come back,” Hanna explained.
The remaking of south Lebanon
Israel has flattened entire villages inside the “yellow line”, a 10km-deep ribbon of land occupied by Israel along the Lebanese-Israeli border.
At least 46 of 54 towns and villages in this area have been heavily damaged or completely levelled by airstrikes and controlled demolitions, according to satellite analysis by Bellingcat. More than 340,000 people remain internally displaced.
In August, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz visited southern Lebanon and said the military was destroying underground infrastructure and “all the houses” in the area. Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has called the destruction a serious violation of international humanitarian law.
“Israel is consolidating its control over this dead security zone that it has demarcated in the south, in which it is attempting to erase any evidence of civilian life and then any possible social or infrastructural base for Hezbollah,” Sam Heller, a Beirut-based analyst with the Center for International Policy, told The New Arab.
The direct negotiations between Lebanon and Israel were announced in April, shortly before the latest ceasefire, despite heavy opposition from Hezbollah.
In June, a framework deal was agreed between Beirut and Tel Aviv that included a plan to launch “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon where the Lebanese army would disarm Hezbollah.
The last round of talks, held in Rome in August, reached a deadlock after Beirut failed to achieve either of its two key objectives: to secure a genuine ceasefire and to make progress on Israel’s withdrawal from the areas it occupies in southern Lebanon.
Israel, by contrast, prioritised Hezbollah’s disarmament and rejected a proposal to launch additional pilot zones.
Asked whether the Lebanese army was capable of disarming Hezbollah, which is widely considered to be the more powerful force, Hanna said: “It’s not about the Lebanese army’s capabilities, it’s about the political will of Hezbollah.”
One of the main obstacles to the negotiations has been the failure to appoint a third party to verify the agreement’s implementation on the ground. Italy and France emerged as potential candidates, but Israel objected to both options.
“The Israelis likely have basically nil confidence in Lebanese authorities’ ability or willingness to really confront Hezbollah or disarm it,” Heller said. “Instead, Israel will seek to legitimate internationally its continued direct role in Lebanon and to make that maximally sustainable politically,” he added.
“Israel has gotten most of what it wanted, which is a step towards the normalisation of relations, the opening of direct negotiations, and the legitimation by Lebanese authorities – as part of this agreement – of Israel’s indefinite presence inside South Lebanon.”
The diplomacy of an indefinite occupation
The next round of talks, which has been postponed to October, is due to take place as Israel gears up for what could be pivotal elections.
“The negotiations themselves have stalled, given the upcoming Israeli elections. The Lebanese President is hopeful that a change in government would yield positive results; the PM and his team are less so,” Mohanad Hage Ali, with the Carnegie Middle East Center, told The New Arab.
While progress on the negotiations before the end of October remains unlikely, Heller doubts that the Israeli elections will deliver a government more amenable to making the concessions Beirut is trying to secure.
The Lebanese government, which says it has no option but to negotiate, is seeking to garner international support for the Lebanese Armed Forces, especially as the UN peacekeeping mission in the south is set to withdraw at the end of the year.
Last week, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun met French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris, as well as Arab, European and US military officials.
While France affirmed its support, observers say this remains largely symbolic, as any meaningful change to the status quo in southern Lebanon will rely heavily on action and mediation from Washington.
“Regardless of how the Lebanese government feel about the prospects of negotiations, the process itself is now all about conflict management and de-escalation, buying time, and the fact is they have no other tools,” Hage Ali said.
Alex Martin Astley is a freelance journalist based in Beirut, covering conflict, foreign policy, and social justice issues

* Chinese manufacturers are taking a more targeted approach to global markets, moving beyond standardized products to create solutions tailored to specific needs in different global markets.
* Stronger R&D capabilities and faster responses to market needs are allowing Chinese manufacturers to play a bigger role in product design and development.
* From robotics and embodied intelligence to quantum computing, new applications are opening up a wide range of possibilities for manufacturing and creating new links with markets around the world.
HEFEI, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- As Europe was gripped by extreme heat this summer, a production base in Wuhu City, east China's Anhui Province, was racing to meet urgent orders from its European clients: 20,000 mobile air conditioners had to be produced and loaded in just seven days.
The tight deadline set an equally demanding task for the supply chain. More than 1,000 types of components had to be coordinated at the same time, with some rushed to the production line by air and high-speed rail to keep everything on schedule. Once completed, the air conditioners were transported overland across Eurasia to France.
The seven-day turnaround was made possible by a manufacturing system built for rapid shifts in demand -- from adjusting production lines to coordinating suppliers and logistics in real time.
Wuhu is just one part of Anhui's manufacturing landscape. Across the province, manufacturing runs at a scale that can be measured by the minute.
"Every minute, about 190 home appliances, 50 laptops and four new energy vehicles roll off production lines across the province," said Liang Yanshun, Party chief of Anhui, at the ongoing World Manufacturing Convention in Hefei, the provincial capital.
Increasingly, Chinese manufacturers are taking a more targeted approach to global markets, moving beyond standardized products to create solutions tailored to specific needs in different global markets.
TARGETED SOLUTION
In late March, Wuhu-based Tri Waters New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. signed a strategic cooperation agreement with the Maldives' transport authorities to export 32 electric sightseeing boats, each capable of carrying 100 passengers.
Taking into account the Maldives' island geography and demand for greener transport, further plans are in the pipeline to build a photovoltaic energy storage system, charging and battery-swapping networks, and a vessel maintenance base.
"This is a green mobility solution tailored to the Maldives," said Liu Yang, deputy general manager of the company, who noted that the Maldivian side had discussed and planned with the company before reaching a final deal.
"The shift from simply 'taking orders' to 'solving problems' reflects a profound restructuring of the logic of global industrial division of labor," said Han Junhui, an associate researcher at the Chinese Academy of Science and Technology for Development.
For decades, Chinese manufacturers have been engaged in global production networks primarily because of their strong industrial base and cost efficiency, often making products designed by overseas brands, Han said.
"Now, stronger R&D capabilities and faster responses to market needs are allowing Chinese manufacturers to play a bigger role in product design and development," he added.
FORWARD-LOOKING TECH
The same shift is also visible in emerging sectors, where new technologies are still taking shape. From robotics and embodied intelligence to quantum computing, new applications are opening up a wide range of possibilities for manufacturing and creating new links with markets around the world.
At the robotics and embodied intelligence exhibition area of the 2026 World Manufacturing Convention, nearly 200 robots are on display, showcasing applications in logistics, elderly care, services and other fields.
Data from the General Administration of Customs of China show that China exported more than 12 million robots of various types in the first half of this year, with exports valued at 24.85 billion yuan (about 3.68 billion U.S. dollars), reaching more than 160 countries and regions.
"China has a rich range of application scenarios and a strong manufacturing base. The rapid development of artificial intelligence has further strengthened the competitiveness of Chinese-made robots in international markets," said You Wei, chairman and general manager of EFORT Intelligent Robot Co., Ltd., a robotics manufacturer exhibiting at the conference.
Guo Guangcan, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said quantum technology worldwide has accelerated its transition from laboratory research to engineering validation, real-world applications and commercial deployment at scale.
Hefei has now developed a complete technological system covering quantum chips, cryogenic cooling, measurement and control systems, operating software and cloud services, Guo noted.
Through a quantum computing cloud platform open to users worldwide, its computing services have reached 192 countries and regions, with more than 55 million visits and over 1.16 million scientific research and industrial computing tasks completed.
"These applications have demonstrated the feasibility of commercializing quantum computing at scale and provided a practical path for the global open sharing and cross-sector application of quantum technologies," Guo said. ■

Nuclear power is back on Southeast Asia's energy agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:47:00 UTC
22:47:00 KST

Nuclear power is back on Southeast Asia's energy agenda
September 21, 2026
Southeast Asian governments are revisiting nuclear power as electricity consumption raises, exposing the region's dependence on fossil fuels.
The rise is largely driven by new factories, electric vehicles and the region's rush to host data centers against the backdrop of countries trying to reduce carbon emissions.
No Southeast Asian nation currently operates a commercial nuclear power plant, but several are placing their bets on nuclear energy and reviving plans that had been stalled for years.
On September 8, Vietnam's state-owned Petrovietnam and South Korea's KEPCO agreed to deepen cooperation on the planned Ninh Thuan 2 nuclear plan in Vietnamt. Six days later, Singapore's government said it was studying nuclear power and small modular reactors (SMRs)with an "open mind", though it stressed that it had not made a decision.
Vietnam wants to bring its two Ninh Thuan plants into operation by 2035 and pursue at least one SMR project.
Indonesia plans an initial 500 megawatts of nuclear capacity, with units targeted to begin operating in 2032, while the Philippines is working towards its first 1,200 MW of nuclear capacity from the same year.
Thailand's latest draft power plan proposes its first SMR in 2037, while Malaysia and Singapore remain at the study stage.
Energy shocks vs. the shadow of Fukushima
The renewed interest marks a sharp reversal from the caution that followed Japan's Fukushima nuclear disaster in 2011.
The accident stalled several Southeast Asian countries' plans to pursue nuclear energy, Alvin Chew, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS) at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, told DW.
But a string of geopolitical shocks in recent years has changed the energy debate.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) says Southeast Asia's electricity generation has risen by around 60% since 2015. Coal supplied most of that increase, pushing its share of regional generation from 37% to 47%.
The war in Ukraine and the current Middle East crisis have heightened energy-security concerns for developing countries, even as most Southeast Asian governments have committed to net-zero emissions by 2050 or 2060, Chew said.
The region's electricity demand is forecast to grow by an average of 5.3% a year between 2026 and 2030.
"Nuclear energy is deemed to be the viable solution to address both challenges of climate and energy security," Chew said.
Appeal of modular reactors
One reason governments are reconsidering nuclear power is that today's technology is starkly different from what was used 15 years ago in Fukushima.
SMRs have broadened the range of possible projects. Unlike conventional reactors, SMRs are designed as smaller units that can potentially be added in stages.
"In the past, deploying nuclear energy generally meant building very large conventional reactors, involving long construction periods, enormous upfront investments and requiring electricity grids capable of absorbing very large generating units," Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo, assistant professor and director at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy in Singapore, told DW.
"SMRs have changed the nuclear conversation in Southeast Asia because they potentially make nuclear compatible with smaller grids, smaller countries and more incremental investment," he added.
That does not mean SMRs will solve nuclear power's economics. Many designs remain at an early stage of deployment, meaning promises of cheaper construction through mass production have yet to be demonstrated on a broad commercial scale.
Another force pushing nuclear energy back onto the agenda is the rapid expansion of data centers, which require large quantities of reliable electricity, Julius Cesar Trajano, a research fellow with the Centre for Non-Traditional Security Studies at RSIS, told DW.
The IEA expects electricity consumption from Southeast Asian data centers to more than double by 2030.
More than 70% of existing regional data-center capacity is concentrated in Singapore and Johor in southern Malaysia.
"Countries are therefore approaching nuclear energy with greater emphasis on governance and regulatory capacity than during earlier attempts," said Trajano.
Building a nuclear safety net
The hardest problems, however, remain much the same. Nuclear plants, even SMRs, still require a lot of time and money, and newcomer countries must establish independent regulators, train specialist workforces and develop credible systems for radioactive waste and emergency response.
Geography adds another layer of difficulty. Parts of Southeast Asia are vulnerable to earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis, making site selection and emergency planning particularly sensitive.
Nuclear power also places unusually heavy demands on state institutions, Tan-Soo said. Governments need institutions that take a long time to establish and must remain reliable for decades.
"For countries developing nuclear power for the first time, building this ecosystem can take as much effort as building the plant itself," he added.
Long road to wielding nuclear power
Public support is another matter. A Philippine government survey released last year found that more than 70% of respondents supported nuclear energy's potential role in providing electricity.
By contrast, the Indonesia Energy Transition Outlook 2026 reported that 78% of respondents placed nuclear as their least-preferred energy source.
"The biggest obstacle is the political will to proceed with adoption of nuclear energy, which, to a certain extent, is dependent on public perception," said Chew.
Southeast Asia's highly varied national capacities and electricity systems also make a common pathway unlikely, Trajano said.
Vietnam has revived plans for large conventional plants, Indonesia and Thailand are giving greater attention to SMRs, while Singapore is still building the expertise needed to determine whether nuclear power is suitable at all.
"There is clearly much more political momentum behind nuclear power in Southeast Asia today than there was a decade ago, and I think some countries could ultimately deploy it," Tan-Soo said.
"But moving from announcing a nuclear ambition to financing, licensing, constructing and safely operating a reactor is an enormous step."
Edited by: Wesley Rahn

Timeline: ‘Mysterious explosions’ and blasts since al Sharaa took charge in Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:42:34 UTC
22:42:34 KST

Since Ahmed al Sharaa assumed leadership of Syria in late 2024, a string of “mysterious explosions” at ammunition depots and military storage sites has unsettled communities and prompted official investigations.
Many involve civil-war munitions and temporary facilities, with causes often listed as under review or later tied to improper storage.
Following the fall of Bashar al Assad’s rule on December 8, 2024, Israel expanded its occupation of Syrian territory and took control of the buffer zone and positions on the Syrian side of Mount Hermon.
Since then, Israel has conducted hundreds of strikes on Syrian military assets, claiming they are aimed at preventing military weapons from “falling into hostile hands”.
Israel has occupied Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967 and unilaterally annexed the territory in 1981, a move not recognised internationally.
Here’s a rough timeline focused on verified incidents of “mysterious explosions” since al Sharaa took charge of Syria.
December 2024 — Tartus countryside
Days after Bashar al Assad was overthrown on December 8, a massive explosion tore through a former Syrian military ammunition site in the Tartus area. The blast was so large that seismic monitoring stations registered what appeared to be a roughly magnitude-3 event. Videos showed a huge fireball and successive secondary explosions.
This occurred amid an intensive Israeli campaign against Assad-era military infrastructure. The Institute for Science and International Security subsequently examined satellite imagery and concluded that an ammunition depot northeast of Tartus was the most likely source of the enormous explosion. The organisation noted that satellite imagery showed fires at the site and that the facility contained bunkered ammunition storage.
December 29 2024 — Adra weapons depot explosion
A major explosion tore through a weapons storage site near Adra, northeast of Damascus, killing 11 people, most of them civilians.
The explosion was likely caused by an Israeli strike, and the incident was widely reported at the time as a suspected Israeli attack. But an Israeli military source told AFP at the time: “We are not aware of IDF [Israeli army] strikes in the area. The IDF did not strike in the area.” A local official described it simply as an explosion of unknown origin.
January 2-3 2025 — al-Safira, south of Aleppo major explosions from confirmed Israeli strikes
Large explosions were reported near al-Safira following what Syrian state television and Reuters described as an Israeli strike targeting military facilities.
Residents reported a series of exceptionally powerful explosions, while Israeli aircraft struck defence factories and research facilities.
January 5 2025 — Kisweh ammunition depots south of Damascus
Explosions hit former-regime ammunition depots around Kisweh, south of Damascus. The blasts may have resulted from an Israeli airstrike. AFP reporters on the ground observed fires and destruction at the site.
Again, however, Israel denied responsibility, telling AFP that its military had not attacked the site.
February 2, 2025 — Deir Ezzor’s former-regime underground weapons depot
A powerful explosion occurred at an underground weapons depot belonging to the former Syrian regime on Mount Harabesh in Deir Ezzor. The site was then under the control of the new administration. No casualties were initially reported.
February 8 2025 — Israeli strike in Deir Ali
The Israeli military said it had struck a Hamas weapons depot near Deir Ali, south of Damascus, saying the weapons were intended for attacks on Israeli forces.
In a brief statement, the army said the weapons depot was hit in the Deir Ali area in southern Syria, claiming that the weapons were stored to carry out attacks against Israeli targets.
Hamas did not publicly respond to the claim at the time.
February 26 2025 — Israeli strikes in Kiswah/Izraa
Israel carried out air strikes against locations around Kiswah south of Damascus and Izraa in Daraa. One strike hit a weapons depot and caused a fire.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz publicly confirmed the strikes and said Israel was targeting weapons in southern Syria.
March 18 2025 — Israeli strikes on former Syrian military sites
Israeli aircraft struck former Syrian army positions around Shinshar and Shamsin south of Homs, according to Syrian security sources cited by Reuters.
Israel had previously acknowledged similar strikes against military headquarters and sites containing weapons and equipment.
April 2–3 2025 — Israeli bombardment in Hama, T4 and Damascus
This was one of the clearest Israeli episodes after Assad's fall.
Israel admitted to striking the remaining military capabilities at Hama airbase and T4 airbase, as well as military infrastructure around Damascus. Reuters reported that the strikes destroyed or badly damaged runways, aircraft, hangars and weapons depots.
The Syrian foreign ministry explicitly blamed Israel, saying Israeli forces had attacked five locations within 30 minutes and had nearly destroyed Hama Military Airport. Damascus called the strikes a violation of Syrian sovereignty and appealed to the international community to stop them.
Israeli Defence Minister Katz subsequently described the strikes as a warning to al Sharaa and said Israel would not allow Syria to become a security threat.
May 2 2025 — Israel strikes near Syria's presidential palace
SANA reported Israeli strikes around Damascus, Hama and Daraa. Israel's military said it had struck a military site, anti-aircraft guns and surface-to-air missile infrastructure.
The same day Israel also struck an area adjacent to al Sharaa's presidential palace in Damascus. Reuters described this as a particularly explicit warning to the new authorities.
The Israeli military confirmed the strike, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz described it as a clear message that Israel would not allow Syrian forces to deploy south of Damascus or threaten the Druze community
June 3–4 2025 — projectiles from Syria followed by Israeli strikes
Two projectiles were fired from Syria towards Israel. Israel responded with strikes on Syrian territory and said it held President al Sharaa responsible.
The Syrian foreign ministry disputed the attribution. It said reports that projectiles had been fired toward Israel had not been verified, and said various parties could be seeking to destabilise the region for their own interests.
A Syrian official specifically mentioned remnants of Assad-era militias linked to Iran as possible actors seeking to provoke an Israeli response.
July 2025: the clearest cluster of unexplained ammunition-depot blasts
July 2 — Kafraya/al-Fu'ah area, Idlib
Explosions were reported at a military site near Kafraya and al-Fu'ah. Syrian state television, citing the defence ministry, attributed successive explosions to high temperatures and said there were no civilian or ambulance casualties.
July 8 — north of al-Fu'ah, Idlib
An ammunition depot containing mines and rockets left from the war exploded about one kilometre from residential areas. The interior ministry confirmed the existence of the depot and said there were minor injuries and fainting cases, but initially did not give a direct cause for the explosion.
July 24 — Maarrat Misrin, Idlib
A much more serious explosion occurred at an ammunition depot, killing at least seven initially and eventually 11 people, with more than 140 injured according to Syrian reporting.
AP reported that the cause was initially unclear; state television referred to the material as remnants of the war.
September 1 2026 — Binnish, Idlib: ammunition-laden vehicle explosion
An ammunition-laden vehicle exploded in Binnish, Idlib countryside, killing at least five people and injuring others. 
SANA reported the explosion but did not establish its cause or identify the vehicle's owner. Other reporting said the munitions were being transferred/unloaded at a warehouse belonging to a local arms dealer, who was reportedly among those killed. 
September 9 2026 — Sarmada, northern Idlib explosion
An explosion occurred at a temporary defence ministry storage facility near Sarmada used to collect and store weapons and remnants of war before their transfer. The death toll rose to 14 defence ministry personnel, with more than 10 others injured, including civilians.
Secondary explosions complicated the emergency response. The defence ministry said it assumed full responsibility and launched an investigation into the cause and circumstances.
At the time of reporting, no external actor was blamed and the cause remained undetermined.
September 18–19 2026 — Ayyash, western Deir Ezzor
An explosion occurred at a Syrian army position in Ayyash, west of Deir Ezzor. SANA initially reported that the cause was under investigation. By September 19, the defence ministry had held a funeral for 11 personnel killed in the blast.
September 21 2026 — Al-Eis, southern Aleppo countryside
A series of powerful explosions struck a Syrian army weapons depot near Al-Eis in the early hours of September 21. Secondary detonations continued for an extended period, sending rockets and other projectiles into the surrounding area.
At least four people were injured, including one by shrapnel. Authorities closed roads, including the Aleppo–Damascus highway, evacuated nearby residents and placed emergency teams on alert. The cause remained under investigation, and no external actor was officially blamed in the initial reporting.
Reuters described it as the fourth similar incident in Syria during September.
While many of the earliest post-Assad explosions were widely linked to or occurred amid intensive Israeli air strikes, the more recent cluster of depot blasts has largely been treated by Syrian officials as accidents or storage failures still under investigation, with not many confirmed to external attributions in official statements.

Why gender-based violence persists in Southern Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:42:00 UTC
22:42:00 KST

Why gender-based violence persists in Southern Africa
September 21, 2026
On Thursday, police in South Africa found the pattially naked body of Dineo M. The 38-year-old had been beaten and stabbed to death in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city.
This is one of a series of killings of women in their 20s and 30s in Ekurhuleni over the past two months.
But for Dineo's sister, Carol, this is much more than another statistic in a country where gender-based violence (GBV) was declared a national disaster in 2025.
"We sit here today and we will never see her walk through the door. Her 2-year-old has no idea what is going on," Carol told DW. "How do you explain to her [...] your mother was brutally murdered, dumped behind shrubs, left unrecognizable? [...] That is why you don't have a mother today."
A community on edge
Authorities said it was not yet clear whether the killings were linked. However, they said they have identified similarities, and have issued an alert for women in Ekurhuleni to take precautions.
Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said on Sunday that so far there was no conclusive evidence that the killings were carried out by a serial killer, "but nothing has yet been excluded while investigations continue."
For families and communities, the deaths have raised fresh questions about whether existing measures are enough to protect women.
South African Minister in the Presidency for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities Sindisiwe Chikunga said at a protest march in Johannesburg that violence against women often starts behind closed doors.
"Please, stop it. Stop raping women. Stop insulting women. Stop financially abusing women," she said, warning that verbal abuse can escalate. "They start with insults. They proceed to assault and then to murder. It cannot be."
Why laws fall short
For Naledi Masipa, campaigns manager at Gender Links, an NGO promoting gender justice across Southern Africa, the problem encompasses all of society.
"Having laws and policies does not automatically change what happens in communities and households," she told DW, adding that the entire support system must work, from reporting and policing to health services, psychosocial support and legal assistance.
If one part fails, she said, women continue to carry the burden. "The real test is whether a woman in an ordinary community feels safer."
Amnesty International South Africa said the response to the crimes must recognize the gendered nature of killings.
"Femicide itself is not recognized as a crime. It's just seen as another murder," said Tegan Snyman, a research assistant at the international non-governmental organization, pointing out that South Africa had declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis. She argued that more resources were necessary as well as a sense of urgency.
A regional challenge
The neighboring country of Botswana also struggles with high levels of gender-based violence.
Natasha Rampa, a permanent secretary in Botswana's Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs, said that "at least 37% of women in Botswana have experienced violence in their lifetimes."
In June, Botswana and the United Nations launched a joint program focused on prevention, survivor-centered services and stronger institutions.
"Violence is unacceptable, and we must work together as a society to address this issue," Minister of Youth and Gender Affairs Lesego Chombo told parliament. He said that tackling gender-based violence (GBV) requires action beyond government.
Turning policy into protection
Zambia also faces persistent gender-based violence — despite laws and national programs aimed at tackling it.
Anne Mbewe-Anamela, the executive director of the Non-Governmental Coordinating Council, an umbrella organization in the country that champions gender equality, said the response must put survivors at the center.
"GBV is deeply rooted in power, inequality, and social expectations," she told DW. "We can have strong laws, but if communities still believe violence is a private matter or a normal part of marriage, then survivors remain silent and trapped."
For activists across the region, the challenge is, therefore, not simply creating more policies. It is making protection, support and justice work in practice. And for families like Dineo's, that difference is painfully personal. Carol knows her sister will never walk through the door again.
She wants Dineo's daughter to grow up understanding that what happened to her mother was not normal and that women deserve to be safe.

2026-09-21
13:42:00 UTC
22:42:00 KST

Hundreds of thousands of Gaza children returned to in-person classes over the weekend for the first time in nearly three years, attending lessons in tents or damaged buildings as many families struggled to afford uniforms and supplies.
The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) says 98% of schools in Gaza were either destroyed or damaged during the war and Gaza education officials say about 660,000 students have been deprived of in-person learning and regular participation in education.
The reopening is a fragile milestone for Gaza after a conflict that has killed around 22,000 students and more than 770 education workers, including 532 teachers, according to Ibrahim Ramadan, director of education for East Khan Younis.
"The last time I have been to school was three years ago. Now, we are starting the school year, it is year of joy, happiness and success," said Moayed Abu Mustafa in Khan Younis.
Mustafa said he was determined to learn even though he will sit on the floor in a tent lacking ventilation, he has no decent shoes, nor a notebook and pen, and lost friends during the war.
"Despite all of this we will learn, we will learn even in a tent."
Fifteen-year-old displaced student Samar Abu Salmi, who lives with her family in a tent, is also returning to class.
"We studied on phones and we haven’t seen our teachers ... now, we are back pursuing our dream ... from one tent to another," she said, speaking in the yard of her new makeshift school.
She also lacks much of the essential equipment, which has become unaffordable for her family.
"Before the war, everything was available for us – notebooks, pens, goods, clothes, outings, things that we could get cheaply," Salmi said.
Despite the devastation in the enclave, the Education Ministry, backed by international and local organizations, has moved ahead with the 2026-27 academic year, establishing dozens of temporary schools made of tents, tarpaulins, sheet metal and wood to accommodate pupils.
Some are built on sandy ground, others have classrooms with only some mattresses and a blackboard, into which students cram. Others are still housing dozens of displaced families.
Attending another school was 14-year-old Yamen Abu Samra.
"We used to wake up happy to go to school ... Now, when we come to school, we’re afraid of stray bullets, rockets, strikes, everything," he said.
"Now, I’m sitting in a tent that has absolutely nothing, just the sun and the heat," he added.
At least 540,000 students are expected to attend in-person classes this year in makeshift private schools, temporary learning centers and educational points, with UNICEF support, according to education officials. Online learning will continue for those who can't attend classes or who left Gaza during the war.
Israeli forces remain in control of more than 70% of Gaza despite last year's cease-fire, which halted major fighting but failed to end the conflict.
Israel's 2-year genocidal war killed over 73,000 people, mostly women and children, Palestinian authorities say. The war was triggered by the October 2023 Hamas incursion that caused around 1,200 deaths.
Stationery trader Khaled Aliyan, 30, said Israeli import restrictions have reduced supplies and hiked prices.
"This notebook, which used to cost 3 shekels ($1), now costs 15 (shekels). All stationery items are expensive," he said.
