PROFILE - Elif Eralp, Germany’s Mamdani, clinches historic win in Berlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:02:57 UTC
21:02:57 KST

Berlin voters handed a historic win on Sunday to Elif Eralp, a human rights advocate of Turkish origin who now stands to become the city-state’s first governing mayor with a migrant background.
Her socialist Left Party took 25.7% of the vote—more than doubling its share from three years ago. In the spring, the party was still polling in the mid-teens. The surge was widely interpreted as evidence that Eralp had won Berliners’ trust and captured the city’s mood.
“Berliners, thank you — thank you for your trust,” Eralp told jubilant supporters on Sunday night. “Together, we made history today. Starting now, we will change Berlin — together.” She said “love and justice” had prevailed over “hatred.”
In recent months, supporters and many commentators in international media have compared her rise to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 victory. Eralp also embraced that parallel during the campaign.
“I hope what in Manhattan, in New York was possible will be possible here in Berlin as well,” she told Anadolu only days before the vote. “Mamdani focused on social demands and that’s what we also do. And he brought different communities together, that was a big success, and that's what we also try to do.”
Like Mamdani, she put everyday economic pressures at the center of her campaign: soaring rents, higher transport costs, and problems in street waste collection. Her team ran a door-to-door campaign across neighborhoods and did not skip districts that backed the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD).
She proposed a rent cap on city-owned apartments, a state office to fight illegal rent hikes, and a revival of plans to bring large housing companies into public ownership. She pledged that a Left Party-led government would make Berlin more affordable for all.
Eralp’s parents came to Germany from Türkiye after the 1980 military coup. Born in Munich in 1981, she grew up in Dortmund and Hamburg and has lived in Berlin for 16 years.
She has said she decided to study law after witnessing injustice and discrimination as a child, and has repeatedly recalled how, in primary school, she was affected by the wave of right-wing extremist violence targeting migrants in Germany in the 1990s.
That path took her into human rights work. She became a legal policy adviser to the Left Party’s group in the Bundestag, joined the party in 2017 and entered the Berlin state parliament in 2021. She has long worked against discrimination and argued for voting rights for people with a migrant background.
She still lives in a rented apartment and has looked for a new one for years without success. Asked whether landlords rejected her because of her Turkish surname, she said she did not know, because landlords do not have to give a reason.
Eralp cast herself as an answer to the far-right AfD after that party’s strong showing in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks earlier. A Left Party win in Berlin, she argued, would mark a turning point against the AfD’s momentum.
“I am the answer to Saxony-Anhalt election,” she said after that vote. It would be a strong signal, she argued, if someone with a migrant background became governing mayor in Berlin and offered answers to social injustice instead of blaming refugees.
She also sharply criticised Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative CDU for adopting far-right positions associated with the AfD and for failing, in her view, to address people’s main concerns. Many voters, she said, feel that “those at the top just do what they want” and no longer hear them.
Protest voters fear social decline and accept scapegoat theories, she said, “although refugees are not to blame for the mess we are in, but a neoliberal policy that cuts funds for social spending and does not support the poorest.”
The Left Party, she said, is the alternative: new measures against rent increases, action against large real-estate firms that squeeze tenants, and more affordable cities regardless of social background or origin.
Eralp also made the debate over pro-Palestinian protests part of her profile. She accused the outgoing CDU-led coalition under Governing Mayor Kai Wegner of canceling events and using disproportionate police force against peaceful demonstrators.
“The mayor of Berlin never listened to the issues of the Palestinian people here in Berlin, which is a big mistake,” she said. “We saw a lot of violence and repression against the people. And I want that this stops.”
She has been an outspoken critic of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and its far-right ministers, and she has condemned war crimes in Gaza. Asked about the International Criminal Court arrest warrant against Netanyahu, she said she would push to have him arrested if he came to Berlin.
“Netanyahu must be arrested and answer before international courts for the crimes he has committed,” she said in a recent interview.
She strongly rejects accusations of antisemitism against her party, saying it supports the protection of Jewish life as well as Palestinian and Muslim life, and that both Israel and Palestine have a right to exist. Criticism of war crimes by Netanyahu’s government in Gaza, she argues, is not antisemitism. She has also said that throughout her career, she has taken part in campaigns against antisemitism.
Eralp’s election-night triumph does not yet give her the mayor’s office. The next challenge is turning a campaign built on cheaper rents and a change of course into a coalition that can govern Berlin.
Despite its clear lead, the Left Party fell far short of an absolute majority and would need at least two partners. After a race fought against CDU policy, the most viable path is a three-party alliance with the center-left SPD and the environmentalist Greens.
That is where the Mamdani parallel will be tested. Attention in the coming days will turn to whether Eralp can hold her core promises while bargaining with parties that do not share all of the Left Party’s positions.
Eralp has said her party’s program won the election and that cheaper rents and social justice must be written into any coalition deal. Potential partners will press her on what she is willing to drop. How far she bends — and how much of that agenda survives — will determine whether the Mamdani comparison fades as campaign rhetoric or becomes something she can actually deliver in office.

Congress nominee Milan Pradhan sent to judicial custody till October 5

With planet's future on the line world leaders convene at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:02:00 UTC
21:02:00 KST

World leaders convene at the United Nations this week amid global conflict and division, facing warnings that artificial intelligence could threaten humanity while climate shocks and inflation further strain hundreds of millions of lives.
The annual high-level gathering at the U.N. General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth?
The future of the United Nations will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century's major global players. The U.N.'s 193 member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful U.N. Security Council, where the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.
Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the United Nations next. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' second five-year term ends Dec. 31 and no clear successor has emerged.
There is still no question that the U.N. remains THE gathering place for its 193 member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly starting Tuesday along with dozens of ministers.
Among the headliners will be U.S. President Donald Trump and French President Emanuel Macron. Both will speak Tuesday after Guterres' opening "state of the world" address.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is also set to address the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) Tuesday.
He is expected to reiterate Türkiye's call for ending inaction in the face of Israel's oppression of Palestinians in Gaza and voice concerns and expectations on other international issues.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian will speak Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – whom New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority – will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won't be coming to the U.N. because the U.S. has refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.
The United States, under its agreement with the U.N. to host the organization, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.
Equally telling is who else isn't coming. China's President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington Wednesday, yet he is skipping – some diplomats say snubbing – the U.N. gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn't coming either and Indian President Narendra Modi has backed out.
France's U.N. ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said it is "extremely critical" for world leaders this week to support the U.N. as the place where the world's nations meet – especially at a time of such polarization.
"We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation."
There is no doubt it's been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The U.S. failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organization's finances in rocky shape.
But veteran U.N. watcher Richard Gowan, the International Crisis Group's global issues and institutions program director, says 2025 was even worse.
A year ago, he said, people were contemplating that Trump would use his U.N. speech to announce that the United States would leave the world organization. Trump didn't announce a pullout last September and the U.N. muddled through the past 12 months with financial troubles that forced cutbacks to its peacekeeping operations and humanitarian aid.
In recent days, the U.S. paid $725 million of its dues to the U.N.'s regular operating budget for this year, enough to keep the Trump administration from losing its vote in the General Assembly. The payment was a strong indication Trump will keep the U.S. in the United Nations.
The U.N. is no longer "in freefall," Gowan said, but it "is stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis." Put more graphically, he said, "The U.N. may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it does seem to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future."
Former U.N. deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member, said, "While the world still trusts the U.N., the global public is eager for change."
The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.
Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as "a hoax," and urged continued advances to keep the U.S. ahead of China.
The U.N. Security Council added a high-level meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelenskyy on Wednesday morning.
For the U.N. chief, this will be his last assembly meeting with global leaders. He previewed his speech last week, telling U.N. reporters that power is shifting in "an era of deep uncertainty."
"At a time when the world faces three existential threats," he said, "international cooperation is more necessary than ever."
Others will be vying for the spotlight on issues from rising sea levels and funding education to the fight for gender equality. Hundreds of private meetings will also convene in U.N. cubicles, hotels, diplomatic missions and restaurants.
Esther Brimmer, a senior fellow in global governance at the Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. assistant secretary of state for international organization affairs in the Obama administration, said in-person meetings can help countries hash out ideas that get implemented months later.
She called the situation in 2026 "much more serious and complex than in decades past."
"With that said, I'm also not without hope as well," Brimmer said. "Over the past decades we've learned a lot about international cooperation."

Zelenskyy was ready to hold elections but backed off because Zaluzhnyi might run, says ex-defence minister Fedorov

Zelenskyy was ready to hold elections but backed off because Zaluzhnyi might run, says ex-defence minister Fedorov
Former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had been prepared to hold elections before the end of the war but abandoned the idea because former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi might have run.
Source: Fedorov quoted in the Ukrainska Pravda article "Mykhailo Fedorov's election bid: How the ex-defence minister outplayed Yermak, became a problem for Zelenskyy and beat a deadly disease" (English translation coming soon)
Details: Fedorov said he had proposed as early as June that elections be held. He believes they could be organised before the war ends, with a presidential election first and parliamentary elections to follow.
According to Fedorov, Zelenskyy was initially prepared to go ahead with the plan but changed his mind when he realised Zaluzhnyi might run.
Quote from Fedorov: "I told the president straight out: 'We need to hold elections because then you will stop thinking about them and start thinking about your legacy.' He asked: 'What's in it for you?' I replied: 'Victory in the war.'"
More details: Fedorov also said that after he began publicly advocating for elections, he received no offers of funding for a possible political venture, even though, according to him, "plenty of people were interested".
One senior member of Zelenskyy's team told Ukrainska Pravda that Fedorov is now viewed as a political opponent, partly because of his position towards the president.
Some members of the opposition also see Fedorov as a rival to Zaluzhnyi, the source added.
The member of Zelenskyy's team said: "He's seen as a political opponent by everyone except Zhelezniak and a few other MPs. The opposition sees Misha that way because he is effectively competing with Zaluzhnyi, whom Poroshenko planned to support.
Batkivshchyna [the parliamentary faction led by Yuliia Tymoshenko] is against elections right now because for some reason they believe Yuliia's ratings will improve after the war. Servant of the People sees Misha as an opponent because he is against the president and all of us. So now he is a non-system opposition politician – he is against everyone."
Background:
- In an address on 18 August, Fedorov called for measures to ensure that Russia does not get to decide when Ukrainians can once again elect their government.
- A source from the President's Office told the BBC that Fedorov's idea of holding elections demonstrates a "complete lack of realism".
- Fedorov's team told Ukrainska Pravda that his call for elections did not mean he wanted them held "tomorrow", but was intended to highlight the need to make thorough preparations and resolve all the issues related to the process in detail.
- In an interview with CBS on 16 September, Zelenskyy reiterated that elections cannot be held while active hostilities continue due to a number of factors: legislation, the logistics of organising voting abroad and in temporarily occupied territories, and safety concerns.

Epstein survivors struggle financially as they continue to heal their wounds: ‘It doesn’t just go away’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

Danielle Bensky wants a typical life.
“I would just love to own a house one day and have a dog,” said Bensky, who is among the Jeffrey Epstein survivors advocating for accountability. “I think that’s the dream – literally just to have a normal existence where we’re not trying to fight the government and constantly be facing our own abuse.”
For Bensky and many other survivors of the convicted sex trafficker, the simple dreams enjoyed by so many Americans remain out of reach. In addition to the psychological and physical toll of sexual trauma, some Epstein victims face extreme financial pressures related to their pursuit of justice for the well-connected predator.
“Right now, I am uninsured,” Bensky said.
Bensky has received coverage for mental health treatment because of a settlement between an investment bank and US Virgin Island authorities that led to the creation of a mental health fund. But there are many other costs associated with healing, she said.
Physical therapy for a post-traumatic injury costs approximately $200 per visit, she said. Bensky knows she should go more than twice per month, “but I can’t afford it,” she said. The yoga that helps keep Bensky centered comes to about $250 monthly.
“I’ve been doing all this advocacy for the year, and I’ve had to take time off from work,” Bensky said, explaining she has now hit roadblocks in securing work due to her advocacy. “There are certain places that won’t even hire some of us now because they’re saying that we’re ‘too political’.”
“I’m paying for everything out of pocket,” Bensky said about healthcare.
Congressional Democrats Ayanna Pressley, Teresa Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross this week introduced legislation to address survivors’ financial burdens. This proposed legislation seeks to launch a restitution fund in the judicial branch “for survivors of sexual violence whose rights were violated by the federal government, including all survivors of abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell”.
“Though it often goes overlooked or ignored, the deep financial burden that survivors of sexual violence carry – coupled with mental and physical trauma – can be debilitating. Navigating such harm can lead to time away from work or the need to leave a job entirely, resulting in a loss in income while rent is due, daily needs have to be met, and medical expenses to address physical injury and mental health support pile up,” Pressley said in a statement. “The Survivors’ Rights Restitution Act shines a light on this critical gap in support for survivors and would force our government to bring the meaningful accountability and compensation that survivors are owed.”
Many survivors support this initiative, but the likelihood of it passing both chambers of Congress and securing Donald Trump’s signature seems unlikely in the near future given heightened partisanship and geopolitical distractions. As a result, an initiative for steadier financial footing is poised more to be a long-term prospect rather than immediate relief.
Jess Michaels said that her financial future was derailed after Epstein assaulted her. She had flourished as a professional dancer but the attack left her unable to pursue work.
“I would go into auditions and I would lose my nerve,” Michaels said. “I would be unable to finish an audition. I would be unable to go to auditions because I would be stuck in bed, frozen or crying, and that lasted throughout my 20s.”
“The career that I had worked for collapsed … What does that end up costing someone?” Michaels said. She noted that for much of the time, “it meant I didn’t even have insurance”.
“Sexual harm is an injury that demands first aid care, just like any other injury, before it is a crime demanding an interrogation,” Michaels said. She said she has for years been dealing with physical ailments related to nervous system harm.
“That’s why I am someone that deals with gastrointestinal issues, cardiovascular issues, immune system issues, endocrine issues, endocrine system issues,” she said. “There’s something that happens when you have PTSD for a long period of time. It doesn’t just go away.”
If the bill passes, Michaels wants to spend money on her health which, she said, had deteriorated over the past year amid the stresses of advocacy. Even though Michaels has health insurance, “a functional medicine doctor that actually understands what I’m going through is expensive, and it’s often not covered by insurance”.
“Right now I can’t afford to get the exact type of doctor that I really need,” she said. “I have to wing it with AI, my [primary care provider], my insurance company, and I’m navigating all of those things, which is exhausting all on its own.”
Annie Farmer, an outspoken Epstein survivor who testified against his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell at the British socialite’s 2021 trial, is now able to receive money for therapy from the Virgin Islands mental health fund. But from 2019 until the near-present, Farmer spent “many thousands” of dollars on therapy.
Farmer said that her she has not been working this year because her advocacy “has taken over my life”.
“That’s obviously a choice I made. I could have kept working and not really been so involved in all the advocacy, but I think it would have been hard to do both in the way at the level I’ve been involved,” Farmer said. “I couldn’t work full-time, certainly, so there’s a cost to that.”
Farmer felt as if she had the flexibility to make that choice because she received funds from the Epstein compensation and mental health funds, but said some others are not in that position. “I’ve been able to do this and still be OK and be comfortable, but I think for people that either haven’t received those funds or received significantly less, it is that much more stressful.”
Survivors praised World Without Exploitation, an organization dedicated to ending commercial sexual exploitation, for financial assistance with advocacy. But, they said, the cost of participating in advocacy remains steep even with assistance.
“I’ve paid a lot of money to be able to be an advocate this year,” Bensky said. “I paid to get myself to the State of the Union [address]. I paid yesterday to go and speak at Ayana Pressley’s press conference.”
“The advocacy component of this is so important, and it feels very crucial to many of us,” Bensky said. “So we will always pay to get ourselves there in the name of trying to make it safer and make change.”
Michaels said there are costs associated with advocacy even when her travel expenses are covered in full; outside costs, such as dog sitting, could add up to $175 to $200 per day.
“People go, ‘Oh, you chose to do it,’ but who’s going to do it for us?” Michaels said. “Nobody’s going to do it for us, and nobody can really do it for us.”
“Some victims received very little, while others received a lot. The amount of money received depended on the severity of the abuse and how the abuse affected the survivor,” Spencer Kuvin, chief legal officer of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors. “Some survivors received tens of thousands while others received millions.”
Michaels disabused any potential skeptics who might think that participation in the fund automatically meant a lifelong windfall. Similar sexual assault cases that didn’t relate to Epstein, Michaels’ attorney said, might result in settlements up to $2.5m. “I got a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of that.”
Julie Roginsky, who pursued a sexual harassment claim against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes and co-launched the non-profit Lift Our Voices, said that many do not understand the long-term ramifications for survivors – even those who have been lauded for their bravery.
“After that applause dies down, you’re lying in bed at night at 2 o’clock in the morning, looking at the ceiling and wondering: what the hell just happened to my life? It’s been completely turned upside down,” Roginsky said. In a high-profile case such as with Epstein, barriers to work are not atypical.
“That is incredibly debilitating to know that you did the right thing, you spoke up for yourself and for other women, and it’s following you for the rest of your life – not just because of what happened to you, but also because people now refuse to give you a chance professionally,” she added.
When survivors come to Roginsky or her colleagues with questions about coming forward, she always tells them that it’s a personal decision because there are ramifications that can be “brutal”.
“I absolutely encourage people to come forward for themselves and to hold their perpetrators accountable and to help others, but at the same time, there is a huge cost to that,” Roginsky said.

Jamie Oliver’s recipes for fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

Of course, the act of cooking can be many things – joy, ritual, nourishment, comfort, celebration, indulgence – but this fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils are strictly about speed. Because, in reality, these are exactly the kind of recipes we all need in our repertoire, ready to whip out on a Wednesday night.
Fish pie pasta bake (pictured top)
Prep 5 min
 Cook 20 min
 Serves 4
320g frozen spinach
  1 onion (160g)
  Olive oil
  300g dried macaroni
  50g plain flour
  2 heaped tsp English mustard
  500ml semi-skimmed milk
  Salt and black pepper
  400g frozen fish pie mix, from sustainable sources
100g cheddar
2 red chicory
  60g rocket
  Red-wine vinegar
  Extra-virgin olive oil
Turn on the grill to high. Boil the kettle. Defrost the spinach in a bowl in the microwave. Peel and finely chop the onion, and place in a large ovenproof frying pan on a high heat with one tablespoon of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, for five minutes, or until soft. Cook the pasta in a pan of boiling salted water for eight minutes, until al dente, then drain, reserving a mugful of the starchy cooking water.
Stir the flour and mustard into the onions, then gradually stir in the milk. Add the spinach to the pan, water and all, then season. Stir in the fish chunks and simmer for five minutes on a medium heat, then stir in the drained pasta, along with a splash of the reserved water, if needed. Coarsely grate and mix in half the cheese, grating the rest over the top. Carefully transfer to the highest shelf of the grill for a few minutes, until golden and bubbling.
Meanwhile, finely slice the chicory bases and separate the leaves, toss with the rocket and a tablespoon each of red-wine vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil, then season. Serve with the fish pie pasta bake.
Tomato and feta lentils
Prep 5 min
 Cook 20 min
 Serves 4
4 garlic cloves
  1 fresh red chilli
  Olive oil
  500g ripe tomatoes
  1 460g jar roast red peppers
  ½ pomegranate
  30g shelled unsalted pistachios
1 bunch dill (20g)
  4 flatbreads
  2 400g tins lentils
  Red-wine vinegar
  Salt and black pepper
  100g feta
Peel the garlic and finely slice with the chilli, then put in a shallow casserole pan on a medium-high heat with two tablespoons of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, until soft but not coloured. Chop and add the tomatoes. Tip the peppers, juice and all, into a blender, blitz smooth, then pour into the pan. Cook, stirring occasionally, for eight minutes, or until thickened.
Meanwhile, hold the pomegranate half cut side down in your palm and bash the back of it so the seeds tumble out into a bowl. Finely chop the pistachios. Pick and chop the dill. Warm the flatbreads.
Drain the lentils and add to the pan with a half-tablespoon of red-wine vinegar. Simmer for a final five minutes, then stir through half the pomegranate seeds and half the chopped dill, and season.
Scatter over the pistachios and the remaining pomegranate seeds, crumble over the feta, and sprinkle over the remaining dill. Serve with warm flatbreads.

- 
  The Guardian aims to publish recipes for sustainable seafood. Check ratings in your region: UK; Australia; US.

Support for political violence drops across the board, though MAGA supporters remain the most likely to justify it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:00:22 UTC
21:00:22 KST

A recent nationally representative survey suggests that American public support for political violence decreased heading into the 2026 midterm elections, contrary to popular fears. The findings indicate that while partisan tensions remain high, an overwhelming majority of adults in the United States unconditionally reject the idea of using physical force to achieve political goals. The research was published as a preprint on SocArXiv, meaning it has not yet been peer-reviewed.
Political violence involves the use of physical force to advance a political agenda. This can range from damaging property to threatening, injuring, or killing individuals for ideological reasons. Aside from the immediate physical harm, political violence has long-term effects on public mental health and social stability. As the 2026 midterm elections approached, many political observers and citizens alike expressed concern that a highly polarized environment might lead to a spike in violent behavior.
These fears are sometimes amplified by public opinion polls, but survey design can play a large role in how these attitudes are measured. A 2022 study suggested that poorly designed polling questions often inflate apparent support for partisan violence, pointing out that Americans’ actual willingness to commit physical harm is much narrower than some surveys imply.
To accurately track these attitudes over time, a research team led by Garen J. Wintemute, a distinguished professor of emergency medicine, the Baker-Teret Chair in Violence Prevention, and director of the Centers for Violence Prevention at the University of California, Davis, launched an annual, nationally representative survey project in 2022.
“Political violence poses a serious threat to the United States,” Wintemute told PsyPost. “We are seeking to understand factors associated with justification for and willingness to commit political violence.”
As part of this ongoing monitoring effort, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that individuals who identify as “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) Republicans were more likely to view political violence as justified compared to other Americans, though they were not necessarily more willing to personally carry out such acts. With the 2026 midterms looming and several recent high-profile incidents of government-initiated violence in the news, the researchers anticipated that public appetite for political violence might increase. They conducted the mid-2026 wave of their survey to test whether this expectation matched reality.
The researchers analyzed data from the fifth wave of their annual survey, which was administered online between May 15 and June 15, 2026. The sample included 7,752 adult participants drawn from the Ipsos KnowledgePanel, a probability-based panel designed to reflect the demographic makeup of the noninstitutionalized U.S. population.
The survey measured three main concepts: respondents’ beliefs about the potential for future civil war, their justification for using political violence, and their personal willingness to engage in it. For these questions, the survey explicitly defined violence as physical force strong enough that it could cause pain or injury to a person.
Respondents first indicated whether they felt violence was ever justified in general or to achieve any of 21 specific political goals. These goals included preserving a certain American way of life, stopping police violence, preventing voter fraud, or stopping illegal immigration. A new question in the 2026 survey asked those who said violence was “never justified” to clarify their stance, checking to see if their rejection of violence was unconditional.
Those who said violence could be justified were then asked how willing they would be to personally damage property, threaten people, injure someone, or kill someone to advance a political objective. They were also asked about their willingness to target specific populations, such as elected officials, police officers, election workers, or members of an opposing political party. Finally, all participants were asked how likely they were to use a firearm in a situation where they felt political violence was justified.
The results point to a broad rejection of political violence across the ideological spectrum. Out of 53 survey items measuring anticipation of, justification for, and willingness to commit political violence, 51 showed small average decreases between mid-2025 and mid-2026.
“The general perception is that political violence is common and increasing,” Wintemute noted. “Neither of those things is true. And in our survey respondents, support for political violence fell from 2025 to 2026, across the political spectrum.”
Overall, high levels of support for violence were quite rare. In 2026, the belief that violence was “usually or always” justified to advance any specific political objective never exceeded 13 percent of the sample. Additionally, among the nearly one-quarter of respondents who said violence was never justified for any of the listed objectives, over 91 percent clarified that their rejection was absolute and unconditional.
When it came to personal willingness to carry out violence, the numbers were even lower. Among the subset of respondents who felt political violence was at least sometimes justified, only about 2 percent said they were “very or completely willing” to damage property, threaten, injure, or kill another person. Willingness to act in a group or as a lone actor also declined from the previous year. Similarly, fewer than 4 percent of all respondents expected that they would shoot or threaten someone with a firearm to advance a political goal.
The only measure that increased from 2025 to 2026 was the public’s expectation of a civil war. In 2025, 7.1 percent of respondents strongly agreed that a civil war would happen in the next few years; in 2026, that figure rose to 8.0 percent. However, the belief that a civil war was actually needed to “set things right” remained mostly flat at less than 4 percent.
The researchers also examined differences among political groups. MAGA Republicans and MAGA supporters who do not identify as Republicans tended to report higher levels of justification for political violence compared to Democrats and non-MAGA Republicans. For instance, roughly half of MAGA-affiliated respondents considered violence justified to advance at least one political objective. Among the small group of respondents who were willing to engage in violence, non-Republican MAGA supporters expressed the highest willingness to target specific populations. Despite these differences, the general trend of declining support for violence was observed among nearly all political groups.
“We found, as others have, that support for political violence is generally stronger on the political right than on the political left,” Wintemute explained. “Willingness to commit political violence is another matter; it is rare across the board. The vast majority of respondents in our surveys reject political violence altogether, and most of those who consider it acceptable are not willing to become involved in it themselves.”
These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found a similar nationwide decrease in support for political violence and belief in an imminent civil war between 2022 and 2023. Together, the data suggest a resilient public aversion to political violence, even during periods of intense political stress.
In a statement accompanying the research, the study authors emphasized the power of public norms. “These findings are clear,” they wrote. “Entrapment in a spiral of escalating political violence is not inevitable in the United States. Those who promote political violence should recognize that they do not have the public’s support and that promoting violence may exact a political cost.”
“We who reject political violence must make our rejection known to our families, friends, and larger social networks,” the researchers added. “A public climate of non-acceptance for violence can help reduce the likelihood of it occurring.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. First, survey responses about hypothetical willingness to commit violence do not perfectly predict how people will behave in real life. Some respondents might overstate their willingness to fight for a cause, while others might underreport their aggressive intentions because they know violence is socially unacceptable.
Also, the survey only asked about willingness to commit violence to the subset of people who first agreed that violence could be justified. Because different political groups passed this initial filter at different rates, the follow-up comparisons about personal willingness are based on varied sample proportions. For example, fewer Democrats than Republicans met the initial criteria, meaning the follow-up percentages for Democrats represent a smaller, more specific subset of that group. Finally, the survey was fielded over a single month in mid-2026, and rapidly unfolding political events or news stories could quickly shift public sentiment in unpredictable ways.
Moving forward, the research team hopes to translate these findings into proactive solutions. “Next year we hope to launch a randomized trial of an intervention to prevent political violence,” Wintemute said.
The study, “Decreased Support for Political Violence in the United States in Mid-2026: Findings from a Nationally Representative Survey,” was authored by Garen J. Wintemute, Sonia L. Robinson, Daniel J. Tancredi, Krista Neumann, Shaina Sta. Cruz, Aaron B. Shev, Elizabeth A. Tomsich, Bradley Velasquez, Mona A. Wright, and Veronica A. Pear.

S&P Global said consumers were concerned about the likelihood of an increase in interest rates by the Bank of England. More than 50% of 1,500 respondents said they expected a rise in the cost of borrowing over the next year.
Fixed-rate mortgage costs have already jumped to multi-year highs in the UK, while the threat of artificial intelligence and caution among employers about hiring new staff sent consumer confidence in the jobs market plunging to its lowest level in three-and-a-half years.
The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate rose to 5.88% on Monday, its highest since 16 April and up from 5.84% last Friday, while the average five-year is at its highest since October 2023, at 5.92%, up from 5.88%, data from Moneyfacts showed.
The rise in mortgage costs is expected to add about £150 to monthly mortgage payments, based on a typical loan of £250,000 over 25 years, since the start of March 2026.
Official figures have shown that the average direct debit to cover monthly mortgage costs has risen over the past four years from about £600 to £900.
Maryam Baluch, an economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a downbeat mood was spreading across UK households “as improved sentiment surrounding the new government is eroded by renewed worries over energy prices, the cost of living and job prospects”.
She said: “Against a backdrop of rising volatility in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East, households increasingly reported difficulties accessing credit, suggesting that expectations of tighter monetary conditions are beginning to feed through to borrowing conditions. Together, these factors point to cautiousness about both financial prospects and pose some downside risks to the broader economic outlook.”
Analysts believe the jobs market has proved resilient since the US attack on Iran and a steep rise in the cost of fuel and energy, but a steady decline in the number of payrolled employees over the past six months and a drop in vacancies to a five-year low have shown employers are worried about their profitability over the next year.
The British Chamber of Commerce has called for the government to give businesses extra support after a series of tax rises over the past two years, including an increase in employers national insurance payments.
A survey by the business organisation of 5,000 companies in the second quarter of 2026 found that only 17% were planning to increase investment in the coming months, a post-pandemic low.
Last week, Andy Burnham said he will need to take “difficult decisions” on the economy to ensure that it “remains on track”.
In response to the growing clamour for tax cuts to support businesses and households hit by the cost of living crisis, the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, said at his party conference that the UK should cut fuel duty to offset some of the rise in petrol and diesel prices at the pumps.
The German government on Monday announced plans for a cut in tax on fuel of about 15p to take effect on 1 October.
Healey could limit his tax rises to wealthier groups, including a rise in capital gains tax. However, analysts say he is unlikely to raise sufficient funds from discreet tax rises to pay for higher defence spending and the rise in debt costs while preserving a reserve buffer, often referred to as headroom, of at least £20bn.

Ebola vaccine trial begins in DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Ebola vaccine trial begins in DR Congo
An Ebola vaccine trial is underway in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), involving frontline health workers and others involved in the response.
The UN World Health Organization (WHO) said on Monday that 20,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine have been allocated for the research vaccination programme in Ituri province.
The aim of the trial is to improve understanding of how effective the vaccine is against Ebola Bundibugyo virus – and to protect individuals most exposed to it.
Under the microscope
The Ervebo vaccine has been “highly effective” against Ebola Zaire virus in the past, but it is not yet known whether it can provide “meaningful protection” against Ebola Bundibugyo disease, which is still spreading in the DRC.
A total of 70,000 doses have been made available to the Congolese authorities to support the outbreak response and related research.
The epicentre of the outbreak remains Ituri province in eastern DR Congo, although the virus has spread to seven provinces since it was confirmed in May this year.
Those leading the outbreak response face many challenges related to an ongoing humanitarian emergency caused by decades of violence in the DRC’s vast, resource-rich eastern provinces.
In January 2025, Rwanda-backed M23 militia seized control of Goma, capital of North Kivu province, before going on to take Bukavu, capital of South Kivu, weeks later.
First responders
In support of the DRC authorities, WHO continues to strengthen surveillance of Ebola infection and transmission, conduct contact tracing, boost clinical preparedness and management, and ensure the delivery of supplies. The UN agency also supports community engagement and cross-border preparedness.
“Community engagement will be key. It is only when communities are engaged in the response that such outbreaks are brought under control,” the WHO stressed.
Latest health authority data indicates a total of more than 7,600 confirmed cases of infection including over 3,670 deaths, with nearly eight in 10 infections recorded in Ituri.
Ervebo is the only Ebola vaccine licensed for use during outbreaks caused by Bundibugyo virus. The WHO-backed panel which advises on vaccines recommended earlier this month that Ervebo should only be used for research purposes initially.
It also emphasized that the vaccine’s “unknown efficacy” against Bundibugyo virus should be clearly communicated, although limited data and anecdotal reports suggest that Ervebo may provide “some protection” against the disease.
Children bear the brunt
Children are dying from Ebola at far higher rates than adults in the outbreak, even though they make up a smaller share of cases, the UN's Africa office for the World Health Organization said Monday.
Nearly one in four confirmed cases are children, yet they account for almost one in three deaths – among under-fives, more than 60 per cent of cases have proved fatal, compared with fewer than 30 per cent for adults.
“The fatality rate in children under five years with the Bundibugyo virus continues to be higher than in older children and adults,” said Dr. Daniel Youkee, Ebola case management team lead with WHO.
Young children need trained staff and paediatric-sized equipment and medication that are not always readily available, and isolation adds further emotional strain, according to Dr. Chaka Keita, a paediatrician with ALIMA, which runs five treatment centres in Ituri province.
Treatment centres have been redesigned to allow more staff contact with children without PPE and to enable family visits, and Ebola survivors are being brought into the response to work in high-risk areas. Children are also eligible, with parental consent, for the ongoing clinical trial of a Bundibugyo virus treatment.
Ebola facts
Ebola disease is a severe, often fatal illness affecting humans and other primates.
The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals (such as fruit bats, porcupines and non-human primates); it then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people. It can also be transmitted by contact with bedding or clothing contaminated with these fluids.
The average Ebola disease case fatality rate is around 50 per cent, according to WHO. Case fatality rates have varied from 25 to 90 per cent in past outbreaks.
The first Ebola disease outbreaks occurred in remote villages in Central Africa, near tropical rainforests.
The 2014–2016 Ebola virus disease outbreak in West Africa was the largest and most complex Ebola outbreak since the virus was first discovered in 1976.
There were more cases and deaths in this outbreak than all others combined. It also spread between countries, starting in Guinea then moving across land borders to Sierra Leone and Liberia.

UN panel calls for stronger safeguards as AI agents advance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

UN panel calls for stronger safeguards as AI agents advance
The world's first scientific body on Artificial Intelligence called on Monday for AI safeguards to be adapted as current firewalls are “unravelling”.
The UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI’s warning followed the hack of the online platform HuggingFace between May and July by “AI agents” during a test initiated by OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.
AI agents are software that can perform tasks independently and on behalf of a user, compared to chatbots, which are prompted by questions or instructions.
The panel issued its first thematic brief which found that the security breach was the result of a culmination of key risk factors, raising fears that humans will one day no longer be able to steer, constrain or stop AI.
AI training advancing
“Researchers have long warned that three conditions could lead to loss of control: a misaligned goal, the capability to pursue it and an environment that allows it. This summer, all three came together in a real system, not a laboratory,” said scientific panel co-chair Yoshua Bengio.
“Since this is not an isolated observation of misaligned goals, this raises serious questions about the way AI agents are currently trained.”
The panel’s independent experts stress that the incident provides no assurance that humans can reliably keep AI agents under control, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity.
Going rogue
The brief said AI agents bypassed testing safeguards, coordinated across separate runs through an internal software tool not designed to enable communication between agents, and gained unauthorized internet and administrator access.
Agents concealed attempts to cheat cybersecurity evaluations, with some opting to "sacrifice" themselves for the benefit of the group.
Around 1,200 agents exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files during the period examined, and activity extending beyond HuggingFace to an OpenAI research cluster.
See our comprehensive explainer on how the UN is working to make AI safe and equitable for all here.
Current safeguards 'unravelling'
For the panel, the immediate lesson from the incident is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, while safeguards are not keeping pace.
However, they pointed to a more insidious concern: that current training methods can lead AI agents to adopt their own goals, knowingly violate safety instructions and conceal their actions.
“This is not only a question of speed,” the panel’s experts said. “It leaves open whether safeguards designed today will work once agents can understand them and plan around them. In simple terms, the traditional model of safeguarding is unravelling.”
Wider context, future risks and governance
The AI panel’s brief sets the HuggingFace incident against wider research on two issues: agentic misalignment – that is, when AI agents act in a similar way to a threat – and AI control.
Another issue examined is how governance is moving from AI models, which use algorithms to recognize patterns, to AI agents.
Learn and adapt
The brief also reviews practical approaches already in use in other high-risk sectors such as aviation, medicine and cybersecurity where incident reporting, independent scrutiny and layered safeguards are in place.
“But those practices may not be enough as AI agents become more capable, autonomous and difficult to monitor,” said panel member Qinghua Lu.
About the panel
The Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence was established by the UN General Assembly in August 2025.
It produces annual reports on the opportunities, risks and impacts of AI in the non-military domain, alongside thematic briefs on emerging issues, that will inform the Global Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence Governance to be held at UN Headquarters in New York in May 2027.

Why climate action now comes down to speed, finance and cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Why climate action now comes down to speed, finance and cooperation
Temporarily exceeding the 1.5°C global warming goal set in Paris is widely considered inevitable. The challenge now is to keep that overshoot as small and short as possible by cutting emissions faster, unlocking finance and strengthening international cooperation.
Just over a decade ago, the world was heading towards more than 4°C of warming over pre-industrial levels. Climate action since the Paris Agreement has lowered that trajectory to 2.3°C if current national commitments are fully delivered.
The United Nations has been at the centre of those efforts, pushing for stronger national plans, a faster transition to renewable energy and greater attention to adaptation, climate justice and the financing needs of developing countries.
But progress to limit warming has come as the climate itself continues to heat up. The past 11 years have been the hottest on record, with heat, drought, floods, storms and wildfires taking a growing toll on lives, economies and development.
And the world is still on course to exceed the 1.5°C threshold, at least temporarily.
Against that backdrop, the next phase of climate action is less about setting new promises than delivering on those already made, while pushing ambition much further.
What is a 1.5°C overshoot?
The 1.5°C limit refers to the average rise in global temperature above pre-industrial levels over decades. It is not determined by a single unusually hot year.
An overshoot means temperatures rise above that threshold for a period, reach a peak and, if emissions are cut deeply enough, eventually begin to fall again.
But that decline is not guaranteed, it will depend on the choices governments make now and in the years ahead.
Even if current national climate plans and additional net-zero pledges are fully implemented, warming could still peak at around 1.8°C, according to a recent UN Environment Programme report.
That difference may sound small, but it matters. The higher temperatures climb, and the longer they stay there, the greater the risks.
“Every fraction of a degree will cost lives, destroy livelihoods, deepen inequality, and push ecosystems closer to irreversible damage,” Secretary General António Guterres has warned.
Why does speed matter?
The pace of action matters because the gap between current plans and what the science requires remains very large.
Countries responsible for nearly 90 per cent of global emissions have submitted updated national climate plans, known as NDCs. But even if those plans are fully implement, they are expected to reduce emissions by only around 10 per cent by 2035.
To keep the 1.5°C goal within reach, emissions would need to fall by roughly 60 per cent over the same period.
Closing that gap means faster cuts in emissions, particularly methane and other short lived climate pollutants, while halting deforestation and accelerating the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy.
Countries also need the infrastructure to support that shift, including modern electricity grids, more storage and greater use of clean electricity in transport, heating and industry.
Moving faster can also strengthen energy security. Three out of four people live in countries that import more fossil fuels than they export, leaving them vulnerable when conflict or other disruptions affect global supplies and prices. Renewable energy can reduce that dependence.
As Guterres has put it, “there are no embargoes on sunshine and no price spikes for wind.”
Why is finance so important?
Not all countries have the same resources to make the shift to clean energy.
Developing countries often face much higher borrowing costs for renewable energy projects, making investment in clean power, grids and storage harder even where the potential is enormous.
The UN has repeatedly called for cheaper finance, reforms to multilateral development banks and greater private investment in developing countries.
Finance also shapes who benefits from the transition. A just transition should help workers and communities adapt to economic change, create decent jobs and give developing countries a larger role in the growing clean-energy economy.
That includes the minerals needed for batteries and other technologies: Producing countries should be able to capture more value from those resources rather than simply exporting raw materials.
Why does adaptation matter ?
Cutting emissions is essential to limit future warming, but it cannot erase the climate impacts that people are already experiencing today.
The recent floods and landslides in Nepal and China have again shown how exposed communities and infrastructure are to extreme weather. A strong El Niño expected to persist into early 2027 could add to those risks in several regions, including the Greater Horn of Africa and parts of Latin America and the Caribbean.
This is why adaptation is so important. In practice, it means helping people and countries cope with the effects of climate change that can no longer be avoided.
In practice, this can include building stronger roads, homes and public services; supporting more resilient agriculture and ecosystems; improving water management; and expanding early-warning systems so communities have more time to prepare for floods, droughts, storms and heatwaves.
Adaptation also needs more funding, especially for the countries and communities most vulnerable to climate impacts and already dealing with climate-related loss and damage
Why do we need cooperation?
No country can tackle climate change entirely on its own.
Governments set their own climate policies, but many of the systems needed to make them work cross borders, from energy markets and finance to technology and supply chains. Greenhouse gas emissions do not stop at national borders either.
Cooperation can help countries speed up the renewable energy transition, strengthen resilience and make finance easier to access.
That does not mean everyone has to move at the same pace. Some have more resources and capacity, while others face much higher financial or technological barriers.
The challenge is to help more countries overcome those barriers and move faster, even as geopolitical tensions currently make international cooperation harder.
Road to the General Assembly
Those priorities are at the centre of the Secretary General’s Climate Summit on 23 September at UN Headquarters. Its objectives can be summed up in three phrases: accelerate the transition, unlock finance and protect people.
The meeting will bring together governments, development banks, business, finance and civil society to focus on practical barriers to implementation.
Also, as part of the Summit, Solutions Dialogues will take place during the week, focusing on practical ways to accelerate action on energy, oceans, adaptation, methane, finance, information integrity and green industrialization.
The focus is on turning existing commitments into action and on what can be done together to accelerate delivery.
You can follow the summit on UNWebTV.
More information is available on the Summit’s official website.

‘Nowhere is safe’: UN experts detail Ukraine war’s toll and Russia’s reach beyond its borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Nowhere is safe’: UN experts detail Ukraine war’s toll and Russia’s reach beyond its borders
UN Human Rights Council-appointed experts on Monday laid out a grim picture of the human cost of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, with a spotlight on civilians facing a third wartime winter as well as the intimidation of Russians who have fled abroad.
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, presenting an update to the council, said repeated Russian strikes on energy infrastructure are leaving Ukrainian civilians more exposed as winter approaches following a brutal 2025–2026 season in which temperatures fell to 20°C below and millions endured long power and heating outages.
Dangerous winter looms
A 74-year-old woman in Kyiv, living in an 18th floor apartment, told commissioners that power cuts routinely knocked out the lifts, trapping her without medicine or heat.
“There was no way to go in or out,” she said. “I lay cold and hungry, without medicine, without anything.”
Commission chair Erik Møse said continued attacks on energy infrastructure are making living conditions increasingly unbearable for civilians.
“We are concerned that the coming winter will be more difficult to endure,” he said.
The commission is also examining Russia’s push to embed patriotic and military education in occupied areas, with weapons training compulsory from age 14 and the recruitment of foreign nationals, many lured to Russia by promises of civilian jobs, then pressed into military contracts they could not read.
Some died soon after reaching the front, with others reported missing, injured or captured. Families searching for them said recruiting agents simply stopped answering their calls.
The commission will report fully to the UN General Assembly in October.
No escape abroad
Separately, Mariana Katzarova, the council-appointed Special Rapporteur on human rights in Russia, told delegates in Geneva that Moscow has built a state system to “intimidate and punish critics abroad and coerce their families at home”.
Ms. Katzarova’s report, Nowhere is safe, draws on nearly 400 documented cases and finds Russian repression abroad has risen sharply since the 2022 invasion, with between 650,000 and 900,000 people leaving the country.
Documented incidents rose roughly eight-fold, from 29 in the eight years before 2022 to 89 in the three years since.
Transnational repression
Ms. Katzarova pointed to assassinations, poisonings and assaults targeting exiled journalists and activists, telling delegates that Russia files more INTERPOL “red notices” than any other country, with roughly half of those reviewed in 2024 found to breach INTERPOL’s own rules.
She described a Chechen torture survivor who twice attempted suicide during 18 months in detention in Kazakhstan under a Russian extradition request and who still faces the risk of torture or death if sent back.
“There is nothing inevitable about transnational repression,” Ms. Katzarova said, calling for a binding UN convention setting out host States’ duties to screen Russian arrest requests and protect people at risk.
Both the commission’s members and the Special Rapporteur serve the Human Rights Council in an independent, unpaid capacity and do not speak for the UN.

‘We are not powerless’: UN chief urges world leaders to invest in peace

‘We are not powerless’: UN chief urges world leaders to invest in peace
In a world facing rising conflicts, violence and divisions that are causing great suffering for millions of people, the UN chief on Monday called on world leaders and citizens to invest more in peace.
“Achieving peace is not something that just happens,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in a message for Monday’s International Day of Peace. “It is a shared and decisive choice to invest in a better future.”
Invest in peace is this year’s theme, echoing the founding principles of the UN, built amid the ashes of the Second World War.
As world leaders gather at UN Headquarters for the annual High-Level Week, Mr. Guterres called on them to strengthen diplomacy, dialogue, mediation and peacekeeping operations as essential means of preventing and resolving conflicts.
Indeed, peace – a vital resource for human development – remains elusive in many parts of the world as conflicts increase in scale and complexity, he said.
Watch the UN chief’s full message here:
‘We must talk to one another’
At an event marking the day at the UN’s hub in Nairobi, Kenya, young people weighed in.
Pointing to “something that does not help in maintaining peace”, Benedict Wambuya, an agriculture and technology student at Jomo Kenyatta University, reflected on recent deadly crackdowns at home, when young people felt their rights were being violated by State authorities.
“As young people, we are hardly ever involved in peace discussions around the world,” he said. “We are not participating enough in maintaining peace around the world. We should seek to understand our leaders, come together, work together and maintain peace.”
Benedict Kioko, a Kenyatta University student, agreed.
“For peace to last, there must be mutual understanding,” he said. “We must talk to one another so that we can reach an understanding. Often, peace has been disrupted because there has been a lack of dialogue or understanding between two different sides.”
Festus Musau, a student at the Technical University of Kenya, said “everything is connected to peace.”
“For peace to thrive in a country,” he said, “it must begin with every individual.”
Crossing the border
Many societies around the world face violence and division while conflicts spill across national borders.
In the face of this, finding solutions has been challenging, with international solidarity weakening, the UN Secretary-General said.
Lasting peace needs to be built through inclusive societies, sustainable development and respect for human rights.
Watch today's UN-hosted intergenerational Peace Circle:
‘We are not powerless’
“Around the world, people are showing that we are not powerless,” he said. “Volunteers, advocates, civil society leaders, peacekeepers and peacemakers are bridging divides, uniting communities, and pushing for dialogue. Action by action, they are building peace from the ground up.”
These grassroots efforts show that peace can only be achieved if deliberate decisions are taken to invest in a better future, he said.
How does the UN invest in peace?
The UN is mandated by its 193 Member States to help nations prevent, resolve and recover from conflict.
From diplomacy and peacekeeping missions to working with communities to foster peace, efforts began right at the UN’s inception.
Here are some examples:
Peacekeeping and peacebuilding: Since 1948, the UN Security Council has deployed more than 70 missions around the world. Currently, 11 peacekeeping missions are operating. Learn more about the broad work of the UN Department of Peacekeeping and Peacebuilding here.
Peace Circle: On Monday, the UN Hear Us. Act Now for a Peaceful World campaign brings young voices and contributions in to a forthcoming independent progress study on how young people contribute to peace, with a Peace Circle event.
Peaceful world activation: From 14 to 26 September (International Day for the Elimination of Nuclear Weapons), the UN’s ActNow initiative is helping connect audiences with information and opportunities to take action, including via its mobile app partner, Through A World.

From a massive peace bell forged from the donated coins collected from 60 countries to the knotted bronze gun sculpture Non-Violence honouring the memory of The Beatles’ John Lennon, UN Headquarters in New York is a global gallery of diplomacy.

IN BRIEF: What we know about AfD, Left Party victories, CDU defeat in Germany’s elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:59:52 UTC
20:59:52 KST

MOSCOW, September 21. /TASS/. Germany’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the ruling party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, has not cleared the 5% threshold in elections held in the state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on September 20 and has not entered the state parliament for the first time ever, according to the regional election committee’s preliminary data published after all ballots had been processed.
The Left Party, considered a successor to the ruling party of former East Germany, the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED), has won elections to the Berlin House of Representatives (the state parliament) for the first time ever, the city’s election committee reported.
TASS has compiled the key information available so far.
Elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern
- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU has not entered the state parliament for the first time ever in the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state parliament elections held on September 20.
- The party won only 4.9% of votes and did not clear the 5% threshold required to enter the state parliament, according to preliminary official data published by the regional election committee after counting all ballots.
- The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the election with 38.2% of votes.
- The Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) came in second with 35.5% of votes.
- The Left Party garnered support from 6.5% of voters, followed by the Greens with 5.7%. The BSW party (previously known as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance - Reason and Justice) was on the verge of the threshold required to enter the state parliament, but received only 4.8% of votes in the end.
- The voter turnout stood at 78.1%.
- The CDU marked its worst-ever result in state elections in Germany.
- The party has never received less than 5% of votes, with the CDU always winning seats in state parliaments.
- For the AfD, the victory in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern marks its third state election win, following previous successes in Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt.
- The party advocates restoring ties with Russia, lifting sanctions and resuming gas supplies, demanding an end to arms deliveries to Kiev.
Elections in Berlin
- The Left Party, the successor to former East Germany’s ruling Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED), emerged victorious in Berlin House of Representatives elections for the first time.
- The party garnered 25.7% of votes, the city’s election committee reported.
- The CDU came in second with 18.8% of votes.
- The AfD received support from 16.3% of voters, followed by the Greens with 14.3% and the SPD with 12.1%.
- The BSW party secured 4.7% of votes and could not enter the House of Representatives.
Statements by Merz
- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz described the CDU’s result in the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state parliament elections as a catastrophe.
- Merz expressed his willingness to keep his posts as CDU chair and chancellor, as he "wants to move the country forward."
Opinions
- Politico Europe described Merz’s current position as a fight for political survival following another defeat for his CDU party in elections.
- According to the newspaper, Merz is already struggling to retain support within his party.
- His approval rating is among the lowest ever recorded for a German chancellor, which prompted discussions within the CDU about a possible replacement of the chancellor.
- According to a survey conducted by the ZDF broadcaster, only 1% of voters and 1% of CDU supporters said that Merz had helped his party during the elections.
- Russian Presidential Special Envoy for Investment and Economic Cooperation and CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) Kirill Dmitriev described the CDU result as a historic humiliation.
- The outcome of the elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern will not lead to an immediate change in the German federal government’s political course, but will increase the political price of unpopular reforms for the authorities, Ilya Grashchenkov, a political scientist and president of the Center for Regional Policy Development, told TASS.
- Experts note that after the country’s reunification in 1990, hardly anyone could have imagined that the successor to the party that initiated the construction of the Berlin Wall would emerge victorious in the capital.
- Grashchenkov said that the urban agenda, including rising housing costs, rents and daily expenses, has become the main reason for the Left Party’s victory in the Berlin House of Representatives elections.
- He emphasized that "it is the worst-ever result for the Social Democrats in Berlin elections."

Police officer wounded in shooting near synagogue on Yom Kippur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21

Shooting near Ontario synagogue on Yom Kippur leaves police officer wounded, man critically injured
A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. Police identified the suspect as Sean Ward, 29, from Quincy West. He was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.
The province's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, about 110 miles east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer, who was stationed outside of the synagogue, encountered the man around 7:10 p.m. local time and both were taken to a hospital. Police have said there was no ongoing risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers probed the scene.
Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted, However, asked whether the shooting was premeditated and could potentially be considered an act of terrorism within the Jewish community, SIU spokesperson Kristy Denette said at a news conference Monday that "common sense would say that probably is the case."
Denette said investigators believe the gunman traveled in the area by truck and discharged his shogun at a police officer, who returned fire. A second officer later arrived at the scene and discharged a firearm, too, according to the spokesperson, who estimated 20 or 30 bullets were fired in total. Some homes and vehicles were hit, Denette said. She couldn't confirm whether the synagogue was struck, too.
The synagogue's president, Norman Weddum, told CBC News Network he was ushering people into the sanctuary to begin services when he heard gunfire.
"I could say, 'Oh, this is definitely someone … shooting here,'" he told the outlet. "So that's when we ran back into the auditorium of the synagogue, closed the doors behind us so as to not leave a visible target. And we hit the floor."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur. He said in a post on social media he was "disgusted by the shooting and that Jewish people "have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear." He called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.
"My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones," Ford said.
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow also condemned the violence.
"Jewish Torontonians should not need police presence to observe Yom Kippur, or to simply live their day-to-day lives," she said on social media. "As long as we contend with rising antisemitism and hate, we will spare no expense keeping the community safe."
The SIU, a civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene. Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was underway.
York Regional Police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday, "Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives."
"Canada's government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law," he said on X.
"My thoughts are with the injured officer and his family, and the entire Jewish community," he added.
Carney previously warned that Canada was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism. He cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.
Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.
Earlier this month, a Michigan synagogue reopened in time for the Jewish High Holidays, six months after it was targeted in a terror attack. The Detroit-area Temple Israel was attacked on March 12 when a 41-year-old man rammed his truck packed with fireworks and gasoline deep into the building. The FBI called it a "targeted act of violence against the Jewish community."

AfD overtook Merz’s party in the election and called on him to resign after a historic defeat
Kyiv • UNN
AfD won in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with more than 38% of the vote, while the CDU failed to clear the threshold. Merz acknowledged the defeat but will remain in power.
The co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, Tino Chrupalla, said that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz should resign after the "catastrophic" results of the local elections. He said this in an interview with Deutsche Welle, reports UNN.
He was commenting on the results of the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin on Sunday, September 20, which he called a crushing defeat for Merz and his party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
Details
According to preliminary data, the CDU is receiving only 4.9 percent in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and risks failing to enter the state parliament. In Berlin, the CDU is in second place after the Left Party, narrowly ahead of the AfD.
"This is also a crushing defeat for Merz as chancellor. I would expect him to draw conclusions from this catastrophe in Berlin and here, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and offer his resignation. Citizens would expect this, and the country deserves it," Chrupalla said.
The AfD is in first place in the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, with more than 38 percent. Incumbent state premier Manuela Schwesig and the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD), according to Chrupalla, have been "dethroned" — they are in second place with 35.4 percent of the vote.
"As the election winners who have received a mandate to govern, we will of course propose talks to the other parties. And we will see whether they want to hide behind their firewall," the AfD co-leader said.
He believes that the AfD’s ratings will continue to rise because "citizens want change." In the politician’s view, the party will join the government — all that is needed is patience. "And we are ready. We want change. We want to turn the state upside down and put it back on its feet," Chrupalla added.
What Merz said
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, as noted by the BBC, called his party’s defeat — that of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — in the local elections a "catastrophe," but promised to remain in power.
In the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU failed to clear the 5-percent threshold for entering parliament, performing worse than expected and recording the party’s worst-ever result in the region. Meanwhile, in Berlin, the governing CDU was expected to lose to Die Linke (the Left).
Merz has been under growing pressure after months of low approval ratings, and there have been rumors that he could be replaced halfway through his term in a so-called "chancellor change."
After the vote, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel answered a BBC question about how long Merz would remain in power by saying in English: "He will be gone pretty soon."
Two local elections were held on Sunday, two weeks after the CDU received half as many votes in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the Alternative for Germany achieved a major victory.
