Italy's Salvini calls congress seeking to tighten grip on League party
ROME, Sept 21 - Besieged by internal rivals and with poll ratings declining, Matteo Salvini has unexpectedly called an extraordinary congress of his co-ruling League party, a move analysts see as an attempt to shore up his authority ahead of elections due next year.
Recent polls put the League below 6%, behind coalition ally Forza Italia and National Future, a new far-right group formed in February by League dissidents that is polling at around 8%.
Although Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's Brothers of Italy remains the country's largest party, the League's decline and the rise of National Future have weakened the broader conservative alliance, which now trails the centre-left opposition in recent surveys.
"We win when we are united, and the League is, and will be, more united than ever," Salvini told the party's annual rally in the northern town of Pontida on Sunday, saying the congress would be in October, just 18 months since the last one was held.
REINFORCE LEGITIMACY
Salvini, who has led the League since 2013, transformed a movement once centred on Italy's wealthy northern regions into a national far-right force, taking it to a record 34% in the 2019 European Parliament election.
However, he has long been overshadowed by Meloni, while critics including Attilio Fontana, governor of the Lombardy region around Milan, are increasingly questioning his leadership while advocating a renewed focus on the party's northern roots.
"By holding a congress now, Salvini has a chance to reinforce his legitimacy before the next election and limit the ability of his critics to campaign against him over a prolonged period," said Lorenzo Castellani, a politics professor at Luiss University in Rome.
"He is trying to exploit the fact that his (internal) opponents currently lack a frontman," he added.
The party board will meet in Milan on Monday to agree on the congress rules. It remains unclear whether Salvini's leadership will be at stake or whether delegates will simply be asked to approve or reject the political line.
Italy is due to hold elections in the second half of 2027, but Castellani believes Salvini's decision to hold a congress could be seen as another sign that Italians may be called to the polls earlier.
Last week, Meloni — who this month became Italy's longest-serving prime minister since World War Two — told reporters she aimed to remain in power until her term expires next autumn. REUTERS

Trump triumphal arch to become "top grade military complex" for launching drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:48:50 UTC
18:48:50 KST

Trump triumphal arch to become "top grade military complex" for launching drones
US president Donald Trump has announced that the planned 250-foot-high triumphal arch in Washington DC, designed by Atlanta-based Harrison Design, will now be a military base with drones and snipers.
According to Trump, who announced the plan in a Truth Social post yesterday, the change in the design was made at the request of the US military.
"At the strong request of the United States military, and for national security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent triumphal arch... into a top grade military complex/triumphal arch," he said.
Set to be built alongside the Arlington Memorial Bridge on the south bank of the Potomac River, the neoclassical arch is planned to be 250 feet high (76 metres) – nearly 100 feet (30 metres) higher than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.
Plans for the arch were first revealed last October, with US interior secretary Doug Burgum announcing that construct was about to begin earlier this month.
The plans gained approval from the Commission of Fine Arts in May and the National Capital Planning Commission in July.
According to Trump, the arch will now be used for the storage and deployment of "large numbers of drones", as well as a base for sniper units with "large quantities" of ammunition.
"[It will] house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage," he said.
Previously, the arch was planned as a tourist attraction topped with a publicly accessible viewpoint. Plans of the arch showed its interior spaces housing facilities for visitors, including galleries for exhibitions.
It is unclear how these spaces will be impacted by the plans to use the structure for military purposes, or how the plans will impact the arch's planning approvals.
Trump's decision to tie the construction of the monument to national security follows a similar move at the White House, where a ballroom is being built onto an extensive, underground military complex.
Recently, the US Supreme Court ruled that construction can continue on the ballroom despite numerous attempts to halt progress on the building.

In Cappadocia, medieval enthusiasts find a world of their own
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:48:24 UTC
18:48:24 KST

In Cappadocia, medieval enthusiasts find a world of their own
Costumed enthusiasts from Türkiye and abroad gather for a four-day medieval-themed fair in Cappadocia
Behcet Alkan
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
NEVSEHIR, Türkiye
Organizer Muammer Erinal says an interest that once made him feel alone has grown into a community of thousands
In Türkiye’s Cappadocia region, where volcanic rock formations, cave dwellings and ancient underground cities already give the landscape an otherworldly feel, hundreds of people are stepping into another era.
Dressed in medieval-inspired costumes and accessories, enthusiasts from Türkiye and abroad are gathering in the town of Urgup for a four-day fair that brings together people fascinated by the Middle Ages, from history and literature to period clothing and mythology.
The event was launched in 2023 by Muammer Erinal, a 60-year-old architect who has lived in Urgup for 24 years. What began as an effort to share his childhood fascination with the medieval world has grown into an annual gathering that Erinal says now draws thousands of people.
Erinal's interest began with stories his mother read to him as a child.
"I used to read these kinds of books, and even before I started reading, my mother would read them to me," he told Anadolu. "I would draw little heroes for myself. I would cut them out of cardboard and make them fight and talk on horses I made from cardboard as well."
His grandfather once told him he wished there were a way to record those childhood games so that Erinal could watch them when he grew up.
"Now, in fact, I have realized this dream of mine," he said.
From a medieval-themed restaurant to a festival
After buying an old building in Urgup and transforming it into a medieval-themed restaurant, Erinal began organizing the fair as a way to bring together people who shared his interests while contributing to tourism in the region.
Participants prepare their costumes months in advance, with some traveling from abroad with outfits created specifically for the event. This year's edition of the Barbarian Medieval Fair took place from Sept. 18-20.
"There are people who have been making and researching costumes for six or seven months just to attend this event, and there are people bringing costumes from abroad," Erinal said.
The first event attracted visitors from across Türkiye as well as artists from El Salvador and Mexico, he said.
"When I saw that crowd, I almost cried," Erinal said. "Hundreds of people came, but it grows every year. There are thousands of people this year."
For Erinal, the biggest surprise has been discovering how many people share an interest that he once thought was unusual.
"I used to feel lonely about something like this, but there is an incredible community interested in the Middle Ages and reading books about the Middle Ages," he said. "It is enjoyable to all be together."
A landscape made for another era
Cappadocia, a UNESCO World Heritage-listed region in central Türkiye, is known for its distinctive fairy chimney rock formations, cave homes and churches carved into volcanic stone. Its unusual landscape attracts millions of visitors each year and has long made it one of Türkiye's best-known tourism destinations.
For Erinal's daughter Ada, an architect, the setting is an important part of the experience.
"When you go outside, there are already stone buildings and dim lights," she said. "You cannot capture this in Istanbul or Ankara."
If the event grows further, she said, Cappadocia's atmosphere would make it an especially fitting home.
"That mystical atmosphere is very suitable for it," she said.
'As if I have been transported to a different period'
For some participants, the attraction is less about historical reconstruction than the feeling of briefly leaving modern life behind.
Deniz Apaydin, who traveled from the western Turkish city of Eskisehir, said she has been interested in history and mythology since childhood and attends the event every year.
"Cappadocia is already geographically very suitable for the Middle Ages," she said.
"When I leave city life and come here, I feel as if I have been transported to a different period and lived there. Then when I return, I have the same feeling of regret, saying, 'We've gone back again.'"
For Rafael Bukov, who traveled from Russia, the event was also a reason to visit Türkiye for the first time.
He said he was struck by both the landscape and the sight of so many people in period costumes.
"This is an incredible atmosphere," Bukov said. "There are so many people in costumes. It's fun and exciting."

Russian strikes halted 90% of Ukraine's steel production – FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:47:00 EEST
18:47:00 KST

Russian strikes halted 90% of Ukraine's steel production – FT
Three plants that produced 90% of Ukraine's steel have halted operations following Russian strikes.
Source: Financial Times
Details: In early September, Russian ballistic missile strikes knocked out Ukraine's three remaining major steel plants, located in the industrial centres of Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
"As of today, [Ukraine] doesn't have a steel industry any more," Oleksandr Vodoviz, head of the chief executive's office at Metinvest, an international mining and steel group headquartered in Ukraine, told the FT.
Quote: "They [the Russians] knew everything about the plant, they knew exactly where to hit."
More details: The ballistic missiles targeted the blast furnaces of three plants, including two Metinvest plants and the ArcelorMittal plant in Kryvyi Rih.
The companies said these plants, which accounted for 90% of Ukraine's steel production, had to be shut down.
"Right now we do not understand how long it will take to make the repairs, days, weeks, months or years," said Vodoviz.
He said the shutdown of the plants, which together employ more than 15,000 workers, could have a significant impact on tax revenue for Ukraine's budget.
Background:
- On the morning of 17 September, Russia attacked the shut-down Zaporizhstal (Zaporizhzhia Steelworks), a major iron and steel manufacturing plant in the city of Zaporizhzhia, with two ballistic missiles. One employee has been taken to hospital. Production equipment and railway infrastructure have been significantly damaged. This was the fourth attack on Zaporizhstal since August.
- Following a Russian ballistic missile strike on 11 August, Zaporizhstal completely shut down operations. In late August, Metinvest said that it was not yet possible to determine when the steelworks could resume operations.

'Non-application of mind': Delhi court sets aside order refusing probe in Sonia Gandhi electoral roll case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:46:50 UTC
18:46:50 KST

NEW DELHI: A Delhi court on Monday allowed a revision plea challenging a magistrate's order refusing to probe the allegation that Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's name was included in the electoral roll in 1980, three years before she acquired Indian citizenship.Special Judge Vishal Gogne delivered the judgment two days after deferring it. He quashed the order as "non-speaking" or an order that does not explain the reasons behind a judge's conclusion."The impugned order suffers from a manifest error in law on account of non-compliance with Section 175(3) of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), inter alia, not hearing the submissions of the police officer concerned and non-calling of a status report from the police station concerned," the Special Judge noted."The 'non-speaking' nature of the order was evident as the magistrate did not consider the twin options under law of directing the registration of an FIR or alternatively conducting proceedings under the BNSS, and instead of considering the core aspect of whether the complaint disclosed the commission of a cognisable offence, the magistrate digressed towards the issue of citizenship," he added.
The court remanded the matter back to the magistrate to pass a reasoned order after hearing fresh arguments.
The matter has been posted for further proceedings on September 29.In September last year, advocate Vikas Tripathi filed a plea in a Delhi magistrate's court seeking action against Sonia Gandhi, claiming her name appeared on the electoral rolls three years before she became an Indian citizen in 1983. The plea had sought a police investigation into what it terms a possible case of forgery.The application had pointed to documents suggesting Sonia Gandhi took Indian citizenship on April 30, 1983. Yet, her name allegedly appeared as a voter in the New Delhi constituency roll in 1980, was deleted in 1982, and re-entered in April 1983 after she formally became an Indian national.Tripathi's plea was dismissed on September 11, 2025, prompting him to approach a higher court.(With PTI inputs)

Govt asks people to use Sanchar Saathi to verify mobile connections, handsets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:45:47 UTC
18:45:47 KST

NEW DELHI: Govt Monday asked people to verify their mobile connections through the Sanchar Saathi Portal (http://www.sancharsaathi.gov.in), which allows them to check all numbers issued in their name and block those that are unnecessary or not genuinely theirs. The advice from the dept of telecom (DoT) came after a cybercrime probe led to a point of sale for SIM cards in Chhattisgarh where the agent was found to have illegally activated 25 mobile connections (SIMs) using citizens’ identification documents without their knowledge or consent.“Following this, the DoT and telecom service providers immediately blacklisted the concerned (agent), preventing it from issuing mobile connections (SIMs) in the future. These 25 mobile connections were examined.. Numbers failing re-verification were deactivated,” DoT said in a statement.It reiterated that “fraudulent issuance of SIM cards, misuse of telecom identifiers, or tampering with IMEI numbers is a punishable offence under the Telecommunications Act, 2023. Such violations may attract imprisonment of up to three years and fines up to Rs 50 lakh.”“Citizens are cautioned not to share or transfer SIM cards issued in their name, as legal liability may extend to the original subscriber if the SIM is found to be misused. To safeguard themselves, citizens are advised to regularly verify their mobile connections through the Sanchar Saathi Portal (http://www.sancharsaathi.gov.in) and Mobile App. The platform enables users to check all mobile numbers issued in their name and block those that are unnecessary or not genuinely theirs.
These measures are significant to prevent misuse of telecom resources in cyber frauds and to ensure a safe and secure communication environment,” it added.Misuse of SIMs, telecommunication identifiers, including International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) number of mobile devices “has emerged as a matter of serious concern” with the rapid expansion of mobile connectivity and digital services across India.
“Citizens can access various services available under Sanchar Saathi to verify and protect their mobile connections and devices. Citizens are urged to remain vigilant and make use of the digital tools available through the Sanchar Saathi initiative to verify and secure their mobile handsets. The IMEI details of a mobile handset can be verified through the Sanchar Saathi platform by using Check Genuineness of Your Mobile handset facility. The service enables citizens to check details such as the brand name, model name and manufacturer information associated with the device,” it said.

Dancers pull clothes from Tate Modern's floor for Homme Plissé Issey Miyake show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:45:07 UTC

Dancers pull clothes from Tate Modern's floor for Homme Plissé Issey Miyake show
Fashion brand Homme Plissé Issey Miyake has created a capsule collection for London's Tate Modern art gallery, which was informed by Henri Matisse's artwork The Snail and revealed as part of a dance performance.
The Japanese brand showed the collection in one of its Open Studio events, a global initiative by Issey Miyake to present its clothes in places where they haven't been seen before.
The Tate performance was its second edition and saw Homme Plissé Issey Miyake present a capsule collection informed by one of the gallery's artworks, The Snail by Henry Matisse.
The collage of vibrant, colourful pieces of paper formed the base of the clothing line, which was unveiled in a performance by the Dresden Frankfurt Dance Company last week on a set by Studio Dennis Vanderbroeck.
Located in Tate Modern's The Tanks – its permanent galleries for live art – the performance saw dancers move over a felt-covered floor, with benches and seats arranged around the circular concrete walls of the room.
As part of the performance, they lifted cut-outs from the floor to reveal the colourful garments in the brand's signature pleated designs, which they then wore as they continued to dance.
For the final part of the performance, the dancers lifted a large section of the floor to reveal a fabric version of The Snail artwork underneath, while wearing designs from the capsule collection decorated with the collage.
The brand chose London for the second Open Studio edition as it felt that Tate's work with designers made it a suitable partner.
"We decided to do the second edition of Open Studio in London because, through a common referral, we got a proposal from Tate," Satoshi Kondo, a member of the Homme Plissé Issey Miyake design team, told Dezeen.
"Being aware of Tate's engagement in working with designers to design something based on their permanent collection, we found a synergy between the offer and what Open Studio is."
Kondo, who is also the artistic director of the Issey Miyake mainline, said he is a big fan of Tate Modern and always visits it when he is in London.
"What Tate represents is this approach that art is open to everyone, so it's accessible to any person," Kondo said.
"Part of the Tate's permanent collection is open to the public for free, so whenever you come in, there are people making drawings and families spending time here."
This ethos ties in with what Issey Miyake wants to do with its Open Studio events, Kondo explained.
"The environment and the institution itself is quite liberal and open to the public, and that also really speaks to the intention of Open Studio – it's to open up and to really share with the local communities, in this case London, how we design and how we make clothing," he concluded.
The capsule collection will be on sale at Tate Modern before becoming globally available early next year.
Issey Miyake also recently unveiled its new flagship store in New York, designed by SO-IL, and showcased handcrafted paper furniture during this year's Milan design week.

Russian attack destroys part of Zaporizhzhia National University, a cultural heritage site
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:43:00 EEST

Russian attack destroys part of Zaporizhzhia National University, a cultural heritage site
A Russian attack damaged building No. 3 of Zaporizhzhia National University (ZNU) on the night of 20-21 September. The building was hit directly, causing a fire to break out. The building is a local cultural heritage landmark.
Source: Zaporizhzhia National University on Facebook
Details: ZNU stated that difficult recovery work lies ahead. Buildings No. 4 and No. 5 were also damaged. There were no casualties among university students or staff.
Building No. 3 is located on 62 Hohol Street. It is the former Oleksandrivsk Girls' High School – one of the historical buildings of Oleksandrivsk, present-day Zaporizhzhia. It was built in 1902–1903.
The building features elements of late historicism (eclecticism), neo-Renaissance and the so-called "brick" style. It has a T-shaped layout, arched windows and decorative ceramic brick embellishments. City architect Fadey Pekutovsky was responsible for the project.
In 1911, a house church was added to the building. After the closure of the gymnasium in 1920, the headquarters of the 30th Rifle Division was housed here, and from 1921 – a military hospital. In 1926, the building was handed over to the Zaporizhzhia Pedagogical College.
In 1930, the building was transferred to the Pedagogical Institute. After the Second World War, a secondary school operated here. In 1979, the building was again handed over to the Pedagogical Institute, initially housing the faculties of physical education and history and from 1987 – the faculty of biology.
The building was registered as a historical monument back in 1971, and in 1987 it was granted the status of an architectural monument of local significance.

Why Sri Lanka’s Ruling NPP Has Not Abolished the Executive Presidency Yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:42:00 UTC
18:42:00 KST

Civil society critics of Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and the National People’s Power (NPP) government are again asking why they haven’t launched a constitutional reform process to abolish the executive presidency.
A number of governments, starting with the Chandrika Bandaranaike administration (1994-2005), had promised to abolish the executive presidency introduced by the J.R. Jayawardene administration in the late 1970s. The main argument against the executive presidency is that it concentrates too much power in one individual, the president, which is bad for democratic processes.
The Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP), the main component of the NPP, has been critical of the executive presidency for decades.
It has been two years since the NPP came to power and its critics regard the delay in constitutional reform as a retreat from the mandate that brought Dissanayake and the NPP to power. However, that interpretation gives disproportionate weight to one electoral promise while ignoring many others. The NPP’s actions in the past two years also show that it is focused on accomplishing reforms that have more visible outcomes.
Dissanayake and the NPP’s appeal rested mainly on its reputation for honesty and its distance from the political establishment that ruled the nation since its independence. These rulers were culpable for Sri Lanka’s economic collapse and 2022 debt default, a fact that has been affirmed even by the country’s Supreme Court. Voters who lost faith in the established parties following the economic trauma of 2022 believed that Dissanayake and his party could form a government that would use public resources responsibly and hold powerful people accountable.
The NPP sought a mandate that extended well beyond constitutional reform. Those who voted for the NPP expected economic recovery and action against corruption that previous governments had allowed to flourish. Horu allamu (Let’s punish the crooks) was the rallying cry of the 2024 elections, and the arrests of several powerful politicians have been welcomed with great public enthusiasm.
The government is also implementing an island-wide anti-drug campaign, the Clean Sri Lanka Project, and a digitization drive. The NPP has prioritized these initiatives that enhance the quality of life of the people and satisfy the public demand to prosecute the corrupt. The resources the NPP has at its disposal are limited, and the government believes that it has pick battles that it can win while governing a country still recovering from economic collapse and exposed to fresh external shocks.
The lesson the NPP learned from the disastrous performance of the Yahapalanaya (good governance) government (2014-2019) was that delivering on promises that produce immediate results should be prioritized.
The Yahapalanaya government established a Constitutional Assembly and steering committee in 2016. Subcommittees examined specific subjects, and an interim report was published in 2017. These committees produced proposals and debate, but these did not result in a new constitution. Besides, the government failed to deliver on its other promises, especially on investigating and punishing the Rajapaksas for their alleged financial crimes. This led to public disillusionment, which allowed the Rajapaksas to return to power in 2019.
Sri Lanka’s economy grew by 5 percent in 2025, and by 4.2 percent in the second quarter of 2026. However, the country is vulnerable to external shocks and the IMF has warned that the war in West Asia has significantly worsened the economic outlook.
Sri Lanka imports all its fossil fuels and LNG and most of its fertilizer. Higher energy costs would threaten household budgets and the foreign exchange reserves. Disruption of fertilizer supplies puts pressure on agriculture. China’s restrictions on fertilizer exports and Russia’s temporary suspension of ammonium nitrate exports earlier this year are worrying developments. These are immediate problems for a government determined to prevent another economic collapse that might spell the doom of the NPP.
Judicial reforms are a cornerstone in the NPP’s drive to prosecute corrupt politicians. The proposed Twenty-Second Amendment addresses retirement ages for superior court judges and the tenure of the chief justice, which the government believes is vital to expedite high-profile cases. The NPP believes that if senior judges who have handled these cases retire when verdicts are close, that would delay punishment.
One of the tactics of corrupt politicians is to delay cases against them as much as possible, hoping that the momentum behind the investigations would wane. The government faces stiff opposition in implementing its initiatives, and dealing with these has taken up its time and resources.
Abolishing the executive presidency is not an easy task. Provincial councils are connected to presidential authority through provisions introduced by the Thirteenth Amendment. Under Article 154B, the president appoints provincial governors, who exercise provincial executive power within a framework that includes the advice of provincial ministers and specified discretionary functions.
Article 154F subjects governors’ exercise of discretion to presidential directions. Article 154L authorizes presidential intervention when provincial administration cannot function constitutionally, subject to prescribed procedures. These provisions make the presidency an integral part of the relationship between the center and the provinces. The relevant powers are detailed in Chapter XVIIA of the Constitution.
Provincial councils could continue under a parliamentary system. But reformers will have to agree on who appoints governors and controls the powers currently exercised by the president. Transferring those powers wholesale to a prime minister could preserve central control and giving provinces greater autonomy would require agreement on safeguards and mechanisms for resolving disputes. Apart from these technicalities, the thirteenth amendment and devolving power to the provinces are controversial topics in Sri Lanka.
Coming up with a solution to this aspect of dissolving the executive alone would consume colossal amounts of the government’s time, and it seems that the NPP government has decided it doesn’t want to at the present time.
Critics are nevertheless right to insist the NPP must not forget its pledge to abolish the executive presidency. The NPP has 159 seats in the 225-seat parliament, which would allow it to pass any constitutional amendment it wants. This was how new constitutions were passed in the past by governments that had the necessary numbers, for example in 1972 and 1978.
The problem with the NPP government is that it continues to give vague assurances of constitutional reforms, while it is obvious that these reforms are not a priority for them right now. It would make more sense for the government to tell the public the place constitutional reform occupies in its program. Being honest with what its priorities are and why would provide clarity to the people and those who are invested in certain aspects of the reform process.
On the other hand, NPP critics must recognize that credibility earned through effective administration creates an opportunity for constitutional reform. If economic recovery becomes permanent and justice is served for past crimes by powerful people, the NPP will be better placed to create and implement a new constitution that has the support of most Sri Lankans.
The NPP should ultimately be judged across the mandate it sought. Voters expected a government capable of repairing public institutions and protecting the country from another economic disaster.
Abolition of the presidency remains an important task. But the absence of a constitutional commission does not establish that the government has abandoned meaningful reform. Its critics should examine why the NPP has chosen to prioritize some promises over others and distinguish a government that postpones reform to preserve its privileges from one that sequences difficult commitments to make them achievable.

EU not to recognize Russian elections in occupied Ukrainian territories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

EU not to recognize Russian elections in occupied Ukrainian territories
As reported by Ukrinform, this was said in a statement issued by EU High Representative Kaja Kallas on behalf of the European Union.
“The State Duma elections held by Russia on 18–20 September underscored the continued and deepening erosion of democracy in Russia, taking place in an increasingly authoritarian political environment. The absence of any level playing field was further exacerbated by Russia’s illegal war of aggression against Ukraine and ongoing illegal occupation of Ukrainian territories,” the statement said.
The EU strongly condemned the Russian Federation’s illegal organization of so-called elections in Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories, namely the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, as well as in parts of thr Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
These so-called elections “represent yet another blatant violation by Russia of international law, including the UN Charter, and of Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.”
The European Union called on Russia to respect Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders and sovereignty, reaffirming that it “does not and will never recognize either the holding of these so-called ‘elections’ in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results.”
“Those involved in organizing these sham elections or standing as candidates in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as well as those responsible for undermining the possibility of free and fair elections inside Russia, will be sanctioned,” the statement said.
The European Union also reaffirmed its unwavering support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.
“Russia must cease its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, agree to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire, and immediately, completely and unconditionally withdraw its military forces and equipment from the entire territory of Ukraine,” Kallas wrote on behalf of the EU.
The statement also noted that the Russian authorities continue to intensify systematic and institutionalized domestic and transnational repression to prevent any democratic opposition forces from participating in efforts to change the existing state of affairs. According to the EU, the decision to bar candidates from the Yabloko party from running on the federal list further restricted the choices available to Russian voters, removing one of the last opposition forces and the only party with an anti-war platform from the electoral process.
The EU noted that, even in the period preceding the elections, independent analysts and observers had reported widespread abuse of administrative and judicial resources aimed at eliminating everyone opposed to the war, depriving Russian voters of a genuine choice regarding their country’s future, and significantly restricting Russians’ access to independent information.
In this context, the European Union and its member states reaffirmed their continued support for Russian civil society organizations, human rights defenders, and independent media.
The European Union also expressed regret over the Russian Federation’s decision not to invite OSCE observers.
“It further demonstrates the Russian Federation’s pattern of disregard for binding commitments undertaken by all OSCE participating States and has denied Russian voters and institutions an impartial and independent assessment of these elections,” the statement said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Poland’s Foreign Ministry condemned Russia’s holding of illegal “elections” in Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories.

Friedrich Merz clings on after German election ‘disaster’
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative party suffered its worst regional election defeat in postwar Germany, failing to enter the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania Parliament and losing ground in Berlin.
- The far-right AfD topped elections twice recently, stirring concern as it gains momentum, while coalition tensions rise over Merz's unpopular reforms and low approval.
- The election results highlight voter discontent over economic issues, with immigrant communities uneasy about AfD's rise and left-wing Die Linke gaining power in Berlin on housing reform promises.
AI generated
BERLIN – Chancellor Friedrich Merz was clinging to power on Sept 21 after his conservative party tumbled to its worst regional election defeat in post-war Germany and members of his coalition clashed over his unpopular reform agenda.
Merz himself described the Sept 20 loss in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania as a “disaster” as his party for the first time missed the 5 per cent threshold for entering a state Parliament.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) took first place.
While it fell well short of a majority, it was the second time the party had topped a state election within a month, which it sees as building momentum towards national power.
Merz’s party also bled votes in a second election in the state of Berlin, which could see the far-left Die Linke party, the descendants of the communist party that once ran East Germany, take power in a coalition after winning most seats.
German chancellor’s future in balance
The Sept 20 results may not prove a knockout blow for Merz, but his low approval ratings, unpopular reforms and the AfD’s surge have left his future in the balance.
Several conservative state premiers met on Sept 20 to take stock after having publicly backed Merz in an open letter last week.
“The meeting was not about a revolt or a plot against Chancellor Merz,” one of the participants of the meeting told Reuters.
“However, there was agreement that the Chancellor needs to deliver more following the CDU’s difficult results in the state elections.”
Within minutes of the results coming in on Sept 20, Merz in televised remarks vowed to press on with his reform agenda that he says is vital to revive sluggish growth in Europe’s largest economy and keep it globally competitive.
But members of his centre-left coalition partner, the Social Democrats, pushed back. They include Manuela Schwesig, the popular incumbent state premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, who has sharply criticised the federal government’s pension reforms.
Schwesig said she was “very irritated” by Merz’s remarks. “I think more humility is actually called for on the part of the Chancellor,” she told the ARD broadcaster.
Bitter pill for Germany’s immigrant communities
The AfD party leads in national opinion polls but has been kept from power by the other main parties’ refusal to work with it, in a policy known as the “firewall” that has been increasingly scrutinised as the AfD gained strength.
Its hardline stance on immigration has left some in Germany of migrant background questioning their future.
“The fact that the AfD is in the lead is quite a bitter pill to swallow,” said Yasmin Goudarzi, an educational scientist who attended an election event hosted by a migrant organisation in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s capital Schwerin.
In Berlin, Die Linke topped the polls in a state election for the first time on a campaign to nationalise housing from corporate landlords and put a cap on rents, echoing the rise of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
“From today, we’re changing Berlin together,” said Die Linke’s lead candidate Elif Eralp, the 45-year-old daughter of left-wing Turkish parents who fled a coup in Turkey in 1980.
Elected in 2025 on a promise of reforms to return Germany’s stagnant economy to growth, Merz has struggled to win over voters as a stream of communication missteps served to compound resentment over unpopular pension, tax and healthcare reforms.
Disillusionment with his government has hung over the campaigns in both Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, where voters have focused on soaring energy and housing costs.
Schwesig, sometimes seen as a potential next SPD national leader, is likely to remain in power in her state.
“Yes, I would have imagined a different outcome as well because, let’s say, the troublemakers who voted for the AfD clearly weren’t paying attention in history class,” said Detlef Spelker, a passer-by in Schwerin.
“We’ve been in a similar situation before, almost 100 years ago. Inflation, problems with jobs, nobody had any money. We’ll see what this brings now. I don’t know whether they’ll deliver.” REUTERS

Russia's ruling United Russia party is on track to comfortably win a tightly controlled wartime election after Ukraine launched what is thought to be the largest drone attack on the Moscow region on the last day of voting.
United Russia, which is supported by Russian President Vladimir Putin, received 57.5% of the parliamentary vote with more than 71% of the ballots counted, data from the Central Election Commission showed. It is the first election to the 450-seat State Duma, the lower house of parliament, since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
On Sunday, three people were killed in what Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin described as the "largest enemy drone attack" on Russia's capital to date. Flames and huge columns of black smoke rose from the city's outskirts, and a facility at an oil refinery was also damaged.
Russian government officials accused Ukraine, which condemned the Kremlin for having the elections include residents of regions it illegally annexed from Kyiv during the war, of trying to disrupt the election.
The results are expected to shore up the dominant United Russia, which is far ahead of its rivals, after more than four-and-a-half years of war.
All parties on the ballot have broadly pledged loyalty to Putin and his political views. The liberal Yabloko party was the only registered party to oppose the war in Ukraine, but the country's top court barred it from standing.
Elina Ribakova, senior fellow at Peterson Institute for International Economics, said the election shows that United Russia is on course to receive a much higher vote share than in 2021.
"I think it matters for the regime to show the legitimization of it, right? People have voted and just a curious fact, head of Chechen Republic [Ramzan] Kadyrov, for example, got 99.85% of the vote," Ribakova told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.
"What happens after the election, that's what really matters," Ribakova said. "I think Putin himself worries the most about the participants of the war. There will be hundreds of thousands of people who will be coming back, should there be peace or a temporary ceasefire, to Russia facing stagflation: high inflation and zero growth," she continued.
"This is what Russia calls the most passionate part of the population that the regime needs to be really worried about."
Zelenskyy to meet Trump in New York
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday said he and U.S. President Donald Trump had agreed to meet in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week.
"We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum," Zelenskyy said via social media.
"There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human life. We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps," he added.
The Ukrainian president followed his post on meeting Trump by sharing an update on the situation in Zaporizhzhia, after what he called a "vicious" Russian attack overnight.
Residential buildings, a university facility and a shopping mall were among some of the infrastructure damaged in the attack, Zelenskyy said, with five people reported injured.
A separate drone strike in the Kharkiv region killed one person, with Russia striking 10 regions on Sunday evening and throughout the night, Zelenskyy said. "Russia is not backing down from its escalation and is sending many signals that it is ready to expand the war," he added.

India’s exports to BRICS jump as China drives growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:35:23 UTC
18:35:23 KST

India’s exports to BRICS jump as China drives growth
India’s exports to its four core BRICS partners jumped 34% in the first five months of the current financial year, with engineering and electronics exports to China driving the growth as New Delhi expands trade across major emerging markets.
Shipments to China, Russia, Brazil, and South Africa rose to $19.9 billion in the April-August period, from $14.9 billion a year ago, according to Indian Commerce Ministry data. 
Indian exports to China rose 39% to $9.6 billion, with industry executives linking some of the increase to demand from the global build-out of artificial intelligence and data centers. 
“It shows that Indian manufacturing is beginning to win credibility in one of the world’s most competitive global value chains,” chairman of the Indian Cellular and Electronics Association Pankaj Mohindroo told the Business Standard newspaper. 
India and China have been rapidly normalizing bilateral ties, which had largely frozen following a border skirmish in 2020. 
South Africa recorded the fastest growth rate, with shipments climbing 58%, while exports to Brazil and Russia increased 13% and 11%, respectively. Shipments to Brazil stood at $3.46 billion, and those to Russia at $2.04 billion. 
India-Russia trade rose to $79 billion last year, Russian Economic Development Minister Maksim Reshetnikov told RT on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi. The two countries have a trade target of $100 billion to be achieved by 2030. 
India still runs large trade deficits with Russia and China. India, the second largest buyer of Russian crude, imported about $40.8 billion of Russian oil in the year ended March. New Delhi imported about $131.6 billion worth of goods from China in the same period.
The US remains India’s largest export destination, although tensions have risen recently over possible sanctions on Russia’s top oil buyers under a recently passed law.
Indian goods exports to the US reached $42.79 billion in April-August, up from $40.39 billion a year earlier – more than double the combined value of shipments to the four other BRICS members.
The data comes shortly after BRICS leaders met in New Delhi, where members advanced measures aimed at improving trade and investment, including customs cooperation, supply chains, digital services, and cross-border payments.
India’s exports to the broader BRICS grouping have also grown, although at a slower pace. Shipments to all BRICS members rose 13% year-on-year to $34.5 billion in April-July, compared with $30.5 billion in the same period last year.
Indian shipments to other major markets like Japan, Italy, and South Korea have also grown as New Delhi seeks to diversify its export markets, with new and pending trade agreements expected to widen access for Indian goods.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday said no progress has been made in negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war, state news agency TASS reported.
Peskov said Moscow continues its “special military operation,” the term Russia uses for the war in Ukraine, but remains open to negotiations.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Michelin-starred chef Lam Ming Kin (林明健) is bringing a refined approach to traditional hotpot with The Tide Fish Maw Chicken Soup and Seafood Hotpot, which will officially open Oct. 6 following a soft opening.
Lam combines French culinary techniques with memories of his native Hong Kong to offer an upscale dining experience.
Everything from the signature broths and dipping sauces to the handmade meatballs, wontons, and desserts is prepared in-house.
At the center of the menu is a signature Hong Kong-style chicken soup. Lam combines free-range hens, pork leg, Jinhua ham, and dried scallops with red dates, goji berries, and Chinese yam.
The ingredients are brought to a rolling boil and then simmered for six hours without artificial additives, producing a rich, golden broth.
Each pot features 75-head deep-sea fish maw, which absorbs the broth and develops a tender texture. Diners can upgrade to 16-head thick-cut fish maw sheets. The soup is served in Le Creuset cast-iron pots to retain heat throughout the meal.
The restaurant also highlights fresh, wild-caught seafood. Penghu leopard coral grouper is served in thick chunks rather than thin slices, helping it maintain a firm, springy texture when cooked.
Lam created four dipping sauces, from which diners can select two. The options are a signature fish sauce, Taiwanese five-flavor sauce, Hong Kong satay sauce, and Japanese ponzu.
Handmade hotpot additions include beef meatballs with aged tangerine peel, pork wontons with century egg and cilantro, and peeled chili chicken wontons flavored with parmesan cheese and coriander seeds.
Staff manage the cooking times and sequence for meats, fish, and live seafood at the table.
To finish the meal, the chef prepares Typhoon Shelter Rice Crisp Soup directly in the remaining broth, topping it with fried garlic, shallots, and ginger.
Desserts include ginger milk curd brulee, which combines a traditional warm ginger milk base with a torched sugar crust.

He said national power planning through 2035 accounts for anticipated demand from economic growth, artificial intelligence, and data centers. The government will also continue developing green and low-carbon energy sources.
Lai said the Ministry of Economic Affairs and National Science and Technology Council are identifying more land for industrial development. The Cabinet will coordinate across agencies to help companies secure land, water, electricity, workers, and skilled personnel when investing in Taiwan, per FTV News.
Lai said the Baipu project is part of the government’s broader effort to expand the technology industry in southern Taiwan. He called for cooperation between government and businesses to support the country’s long-term economic competitiveness.

Report flags half of Taiwan farm product ads on Meta as possible scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:31:14 UTC
18:31:14 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Scam groups are posing as local farmers and luring consumers into buying fake products online, according to a new report by Taiwanese cybersecurity firm Gogolook.
The report analyzed 4,461 agricultural product advertisements posted on Meta platforms over 18 days in August and classified 2,271, or 50.9%, as high-risk impersonation ads.
The findings echo an April warning from the government’s Anti-Fraud Command Center, which said agricultural products were the most common category among shopping scams circulating on Facebook and Threads. The products ranged from garlic and eggs to blueberries and tomatoes, per CNA.
The report identified two main types of agricultural product scams. The first involves fake farmer accounts that contact users directly, while the second uses one-page advertisements to lead consumers into making purchases.
In the first type, scammers use Taiwanese names and build followings of more than 100 people to make their accounts appear legitimate before contacting users through Messenger.
The second type uses disposable accounts with few followers. In one case, 113 identical advertisements promoting Pingtung “organic cinnamon powder” were posted by 12 accounts, each with fewer than 10 followers.
Fu Yu-ling (傅郁玲), who oversees Gogolook’s anti-fraud protection service, said the scams rely heavily on local knowledge because they target specific agricultural products, regional brands, and farmers, according to a press release.
She said AI-powered detection tools monitor local brands and farmers’ identities in real time, allowing fraudulent advertisements to be identified and removed more quickly.
The analysis found that Pingtung had the highest number of high-risk advertisements, followed by Tainan and Nantou. Some promoted “Nantou organic notoginseng powder,” although the herb is not grown in Taiwan, the report said.
Gogolook spokesperson Kara Yang (楊莞儀) told Taiwan News that the project began through a collaboration with the Yunlin County Government. The company reported fraudulent advertisements involving Yunlin products to Meta, which subsequently removed them.
Yunlin County Magistrate Chang Li-shan (張麗善) told PTS in July that the key to preventing scams is stopping consumers from seeing fraudulent advertisements in the first place.

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- China claimed both the men's 10m air rifle individual and team gold medals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Monday, setting a world record in the team event.

====================================================================================================

Xi steers China-U.S. relations toward stability
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:30:19 CST
18:30:19 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to travel to Washington for a state visit and a high-stakes meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump.
With the upcoming visit, the two presidents are expected to complete reciprocal visits within months. The trip will be Xi's second state visit to the United States following his first in 2015.
More than a decade on, the world's most important bilateral relationship has followed a bumpy course. How Beijing and Washington manage ties -- and find room to work together -- is increasingly consequential for both countries and the world.
NEW VISION
In May, as Xi hosted Trump in Beijing, he opened their talks with three questions:
"Can China and the United States overcome the Thucydides Trap and create a new paradigm of major-country relations? Can we meet global challenges together and provide greater stability for the world? Can we build a bright future together for our bilateral relations in the interest of the well-being of the two peoples and the future of humanity?"
The questions were raised against the backdrop of years of turbulence in bilateral ties, from trade disputes to tech curbs. Xi has repeatedly stressed the need to find the right way for the world's two major countries to get along.
The Beijing summit gave renewed momentum to that effort. Xi and Trump have agreed on a new vision of building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability over the next three years and beyond.
"It marks the first time in more than a decade that China and the United States established a consensus about how to define the relationship that leaders on both sides broadly recognize," said Da Wei, director of the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University.
For a while now, China-U.S. relations have moved forward along the track charted by the two leaders. "Head-of-state diplomacy is the anchor of China-U.S. relations," Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Thursday in a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in preparation for the upcoming summit.
Since Trump's re-election, Xi has maintained contact with him through various means, like face-to-face meetings and phone calls, sometimes in a casual format.
During the May visit, Xi invited Trump to Zhongnanhai, the leadership compound in central Beijing, for a private meeting -- an invitation extended to few foreign leaders.
Xi and Trump strolled in the garden, chatting and pausing now and then to admire the towering ancient trees and Chinese roses in full blossom.
"While President Trump hopes to make America great again, I am dedicated to leading the Chinese people toward national rejuvenation," Xi said later as the two leaders sat down for a conversation over tea.
He urged both sides to keep to the right direction, steer clear of disruptions and promote the steady development of bilateral relations.
Such moments away from the formal meeting table have become a feature of Xi's encounters with Trump, providing a more personal setting to learn about each other's countries and perspectives.
Similar interactions stretch back to Xi's first meeting with Trump in 2017. At Mar-a-Lago, Trump's private estate in Florida, Xi presented him with a piece of Chinese calligraphy bearing an ancient saying: "A nine-story tower rises from a heap of earth; a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step."
The message carried a metaphor for the relationship Xi hoped the two countries could build. He told Trump that the two leaders could rally those in both countries who shared the goodwill and enthusiasm for advancing China-U.S. relations, and build the edifice of the relationship one story at a time -- making it stronger, taller and more glorious.
BALLAST
Economic and trade relations should continue to serve as the "ballast" and driving force for China-U.S. relations, rather than a stumbling block or a point of friction, Xi told Trump in Busan, South Korea, in 2025. Xi has often likened China-U.S. relations to a giant ship, for which ballast is critical to staying on course through rough waters.
Following the surge of U.S. tariffs in 2025, Beijing responded with resolute countermeasures while continuing negotiations with Washington in an effort to manage their differences. By the time Xi and Trump met in Beijing, their economic and trade teams had reached "generally balanced and positive outcomes."
The dialogue has continued since, with their latest round of talks, which were candid, in-depth and constructive, concluded in New York on Sunday.
There is no winner in a trade war, Xi has repeatedly stressed, both in his exchanges with Trump and on the international stage. "Facts will prove that decoupling and cutting off supply chains will not hold back our development process, and espousing 'small yard, high fences' will only box oneself in and divide the world," Xi said at the just-concluded BRICS summit in New Delhi.
That message also lay at the center of Xi's outreach to the American business community. In March 2024, he met with representatives from U.S. business, strategic and academic communities in Beijing. He told the gathering that the respective success of China and the United States is an opportunity for each other.
During the May visit, Xi sat down with Trump in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing alongside more than a dozen executives from some of America's most preeminent companies, including Apple, Nvidia, Tesla and Boeing.
Trump introduced the business leaders to Xi one by one, underscoring the weight he attached to the delegation.
"Each side, the United States and China, has a big stake in constructive strategic stability," said Robert Lawrence Kuhn, a U.S. scholar and longtime observer of China.
From artificial intelligence and climate change mitigation to public health and counter-narcotics, there are plenty of issues that China and the United States are both involved in, he added.
Rather than expecting Washington and Beijing to suddenly work together perfectly, Kuhn said, the more immediate objective should be to prevent disputes over tariffs, critical minerals, and other issues that could lead to further escalation.
BRIDGING THE PACIFIC
"Friendship, which derives from close contact between the people, holds the key to sound state-to-state relations," Xi has said. For him, the foundation of China-U.S. relations was laid by the two peoples.
Upon the official announcement of Xi's U.S. visit on Monday, his recent reply to American university students was made public. In his letter, Xi encouraged them to foster greater mutual understanding and affinity between people of the two countries, and to promote the steady and sustained development of bilateral relations.
When China-U.S. relations were at a low ebb, Xi cast his eyes toward the future -- young people. The youth, he believes, carry the future and hope of this relationship.
During his 2023 trip to San Francisco for the APEC leaders' meeting, Xi announced an initiative to invite 50,000 young Americans to China for exchange and study programs over the next five years. By May this year, that goal had been reached two and a half years ahead of schedule.
Many participants have written to Xi, thanking him for the opportunity to see China for themselves and forge friendships with their Chinese peers. Xi, in turn, has encouraged young people from both countries to become "envoys of friendship" bridging the Pacific.
A 2026 Reagan Institute Summer Survey found that younger Americans were significantly less likely to view China as a major threat to the United States.
That emphasis on people-to-people bonds extends beyond the younger generation. For decades, Xi has stayed in touch with his old friends in Iowa, whom he first met during his maiden trip to the United States in 1985, and corresponded with veterans of World War II's Flying Tigers, recalling the bonds forged between the two peoples during that time.
"We should build more bridges and pave more roads for people-to-people interactions," Xi once said. "We must not erect barriers or create a chilling effect."
Ahead of Xi's U.S. visit, another story of friendship across the Pacific went viral online.
In 1999, American teacher Ronald Sakolsky donated 5,000 U.S. dollars to support Chinese woman Yin Yuzhen's tree-planting efforts to combat desertification in north China's Inner Mongolia. With the funds, Yin went on to cultivate a forest of more than 50,000 trees.
When Sakolsky and Yin reunited in China in August, he was asked what message he wanted to take home to the United States. His answer was: "Bridge."
He said he believes the upcoming meeting between President Xi and President Trump could help build that bridge.
"China is ready to rebuild the bridge," Sakolsky said. "Is America ready? I believe so." ■

The 27-member bloc criticized Moscow for not inviting observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
It urged Russia to accept a “full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire” in the war with Ukraine, and withdraw all its forces and military equipment from Ukrainian territory.

Across China: Rare dark-sky zone in east China drives rural tourism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:30:02 CST
18:30:02 KST

HANGZHOU, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Fang Shanfei never thought his village was special, nor did he understand terms like the Bortle scale. But things changed when strangers arrived, eager to gaze at the stars he had seen all his life.
Running the only rural homestay in Gaotiankeng Village, in east China's Zhejiang Province, Fang was the first to spot the drift in 2017, when stargazing enthusiasts scoured the mountains for a dark-sky site and eyed on his village.
Elsewhere, especially in the brilliant glow of the Yangtze River Delta, the night is awash with light, serving as a proxy for electricity use and economic vitality in China's economic and technology powerhouse.
But in the largely mountainous province, farmers in remote areas relied mainly on selling homegrown produce and rural specialties such as raw tea leaves, with limited incomes and peaceful but still dark nights.
In Fang's village, however, the darkness reveals something even rarer: a sky brimming with stars, far from urban luminescence.
Nestled in eastern Zhejiang's mountains at an altitude of 680 meters, with forest coverage above 85 percent, Gaotiankeng is shielded from light pollution by its natural surroundings.
In 2024, it was officially added to the world list of dark sky protected areas, marked by a stone stele at the village entrance. A year later, the Beijing Planetarium set up a permanent astronomical observation site there, the first in the Yangtze River Delta to join the top institution's official observation system.
Professionals classify Gaotiankeng as a Class 2 dark-sky zone with a Bortle scale rating of two to three, marking a rare astronomical resource unmatched across the entire delta region.
Fang's homestay now runs at nearly full occupancy, with all eight dining tables regularly filled during meals. Guests range from study-tour groups from neighboring Shanghai and road trip travelers from Zhejiang's capital Hangzhou, to astronomy enthusiasts hauling telescopes from across the country.
Before dark-sky tourism took off, Gaotiankeng was a hollowed-out mountain village. Young people migrated to cities for work, leaving farmland abandoned.
Today, villagers are returning. Four other villager-operated homestays are in business, each generating annual turnover exceeding 100,000 yuan (about 14,820 U.S. dollars).
A local company has acquired and renovated 45 old, empty house buildings, preserving their original architecture. Of these, 16 were converted to high-end star-viewing homestays, while the rest transformed into a star-themed library, a teahouse, a restaurant and an art gallery, adding new vigor to the village's business.
The benefits extend beyond tourism. Vacant houses in the village attract rental inquiries, abandoned farmland is reclaimed and leased, and local specialties such as dried bamboo shoots become popular in the market.
The Hangzhou Astronomical Society has also set up a permanent meteor-monitoring station there. On the mountaintop, an astronomy museum, equipped with professional instruments and a dome theater, stands alongside a dedicated stargazing camping base.
Dou Chuang, the museum's curator, leads astronomical study tours. During the Perseid meteor shower earlier this year, Dou delivered on-site observation sessions for student groups, showing visitors why preserving the dark sky matters.
Dark-sky tourism has driven coordinated development across the township of Changhong, which administers Gaotiankeng. Residents comply with light-pollution controls, and dark-sky protection rules have been embedded in village regulations.
In 2025, Changhong Township recorded more than 120,000 tourist visits and 8 million yuan in tourism revenue, up 28.5 percent year on year. Homestay occupancy reached 98 percent during holidays. Six villages achieved collective operating income above 500,000 yuan, and two surpassed 1 million yuan.
This year, Fang renovated the second floor of his homestay into three guest rooms with private bathrooms and star-gazing skylights, all ideas from guests expecting to watch meteor showers from bed.
As dusk fell, after checking room reservations and informing guests about the weather, Fang lounges back into his old bamboo chair in the courtyard, while soft breeze stirring under the starry night. ■

MADRID, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- La Liga heads into the first international break of the season with FC Barcelona top of the table after seven straight wins, while Atletico Madrid's derby victory left Real Madrid six points behind the leader.
Here are the four things we learned this weekend in Spain.
1. Raphinha, Yamal lead Barcelona charge
It has been an outstanding week for FC Barcelona, with a 7-2 home win over Racing Santander followed by a 3-1 victory away to Sevilla.
Raphinha scored hat-tricks in both matches, underlining his importance as Hansi Flick continues to use him in a more central role.
The Brazilian continues to show how complete a player he is, while Lamine Yamal provides creativity and unpredictability on the right.
Yamal did not score on Saturday but provided clever assists for two of Raphinha's goals and was a constant threat throughout the match.
2. Controversy, tension at the Metropolitano
Atletico won the Madrid derby 2-1 at home to Real to move second in the standings after a typically heated encounter.
Real Madrid can feel unfortunate that Atletico midfielder Lee Kang-in escaped a red card in the first half for a bad challenge on Federico Valverde, but can have few complaints about Dean Huijsen's dismissal after bringing down Giuliano Simeone for the penalty that changed the game.
One positive for Real Madrid was the performance of record signing Yan Diomande, whose pace and dribbling caused Atletico problems in the closing stages.
3. Things starting to click for Inigo Perez
Inigo Perez endured a difficult start as Villarreal coach, failing to win until a 3-1 victory in Malaga in midweek.
Villarreal showed signs of adapting to his high-energy, high-pressing style in that match, and followed it up with a 3-1 home win over Levante on Sunday.
Villarreal looked quicker, more energetic and more effective in attack, with Alberto Moleiro underlining his importance with a goal and an impressive all-round display.
4. Time for a rethink at Racing
It has been a difficult week for Racing Santander, with a 7-2 defeat at Camp Nou followed by a 5-0 loss away to Celta Vigo.
While the defeat to Barcelona can partly be explained by coach Jose Alberto Lopez making wholesale changes to his usual starting lineup, Saturday's result is more concerning as he fielded what should be his strongest side.
Racing was promoted as second-division champion last season, but the step-up has been demanding. It has conceded 21 goals in seven matches while scoring 11. ■

Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann’s big push to make state drug-free

Punjab Chief minister Bhagwant Singh Mann’s government has expanded its ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’ anti-drug campaign beyond a conventional police crackdown, combining action against drug networks with prevention in schools, youth engagement, community vigilance and treatment for people battling addiction.The government said the campaign seeks to make it harder to sell drugs, easier for citizens to report peddling, prevent young people from falling into addiction and ensure those affected can access timely treatment. The strategy brings police, teachers, students, community volunteers and health workers into a coordinated anti-drug effort.Between March 2025 and September 2026, Punjab’s Anti-Narcotics Task Force registered 61,824 FIRs and arrested 81,433 people. Authorities seized 3,918 kg heroin, 991 kg opium, 47 tonnes poppy husk, 1,416 kg ganja and 65 lakh tablets and capsules during the period. Punjab Police also conducted 79,293 public meetings to strengthen community participation in the campaign.The government has simultaneously taken the prevention campaign into schools. A 14-week anti-drug curriculum is being taught to 7.5 lakh students across 3,600 schools through trained teachers.
In the first phase, nearly 25,000 teachers from 13 districts are being sensitised, with 7,000 already trained in Amritsar, Tarn Taran and Fazilka. The programme aims to help teachers identify early signs of mental-health distress, vulnerability to substance abuse and possible intervention.Youth programmes are also being used to address peer influence and social acceptance of drugs. Schools have been given year-long activity calendars, while colleges are promoting cultural festivals, mental-health clubs, sports and other activities to encourage healthier lifestyles and reduce the stigma around recovery.At the grassroots level, around 1.25 lakh people have joined nearly 15,000 Village and Ward Defence Committees. More than 50,000 members have been trained to use the Nasha Mukti App to report drug-related information and connect people seeking help with government services.
Since its launch on March 1, 2025, the safe Punjab whatsApp helpline has received more than 51,000 citizen tip-offs, which the government said helped police make over 25,000 drug-related arrests.The government has also expanded treatment infrastructure, with Punjab currently having 547 OOAT centres, 219 de-addiction centres and 91 rehabilitation centres. Government facilities have been revamped, health workers trained and skilling and creative activities introduced at treatment centres.Admissions to government de-addiction and rehabilitation centres rose from over 12,200 in 2024 to nearly 34,000 in 2025, an increase of more than 170%, according to the government. The figures indicate a sharp rise in people seeking institutional support as Punjab seeks to combine enforcement with prevention, community action and rehabilitation in its fight against drugs.

Traditional safeguards for AI agents are unraveling: UN panel
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:29:34 CST
18:29:34 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- A UN panel on artificial intelligence (AI) warned on Monday that traditional safeguards for AI agents are unraveling.
The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI issued the warning in its first thematic brief, an assessment of July's breach of U.S. AI company Hugging Face's systems by AI agents under evaluation at OpenAI, another U.S. AI company.
The panel finds that stopping this incident is no assurance that humans can reliably keep AI agents under control today, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity.
"The default interpretation and immediate lesson is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, and safeguards are not advancing at the pace of capabilities," said the panel in a press release. "The more insidious and grave concern is that current training methods can lead agents to adopt goals of their own, knowingly violate safety instructions, and conceal their actions."
It leaves open whether safeguards designed today will work once agents can understand them and plan around them. In simple terms, the traditional model of safeguarding is unraveling, said the panel.
The panel also finds that the governance challenge is moving from AI models to AI agents. A local failure could spread across organizational and national boundaries. AI safety may be becoming a matter of collective security as well as corporate governance.
The panel, established by the UN General Assembly, is made up of 40 independent experts from all regions.
The panel is publishing an advance unedited version to make the brief available to world leaders gathering in New York for this year's General Assembly's High-level Week. ■

Ten lions found dead in suspected poisoning at Tanzania reserve

Ten lions found dead in suspected poisoning at Tanzania reserve
Ten lions have been found dead at Tanzania’s UNESCO-listed Ngorongoro Conservation Area, prompting an investigation into suspected poisoning, the authorities have said.
The animals were discovered on Friday in the Ndutu area of Endulen Ward, according to a notice issued by the Ngorongoro Conservation Area Authority (NCAA). “Preliminary findings suggest the animals may have died after ingesting poison,” the agency said.
The NCAA has launched an expert investigation to establish the cause of the deaths and identify those responsible. It did not disclose the animals’ ages or sexes or say what substance may have been involved.
Poisoning is a recurring threat to large carnivores in East Africa and is frequently associated with conflict between predators and livestock owners. However, the authorities have not established whether the latest deaths resulted from deliberate poisoning or identified a possible motive.
In 2018, six lions and 74 vultures died after feeding on a poisoned cattle carcass near Tanzania’s Ruaha National Park. Conservation groups said the poisoning appeared to have been carried out in retaliation after lions attacked livestock, although no suspect was identified.
The latest deaths come a month after 18 elephants were found dead in Kenya’s Amboseli ecosystem near the Tanzanian border. Preliminary tests indicated possible exposure to a toxic substance. Four suspects were arrested and later released on bail pending further investigation. In January, six lions and more than 30 vultures were killed in a poisoning incident in Kenya’s Kitenden Conservancy, also near the Tanzanian border.
Tanzania has an estimated 17,200 lions, the world’s largest national population, according to a 2024-2025 wildlife census released by the Tanzania Wildlife Research Institute in June. Around 5,844 live in the northern tourism circuit, which includes Ngorongoro, Serengeti, Tarangire and Lake Manyara.
Ngorongoro is a UNESCO World Heritage Site where ethnic Maasai pastoralists coexist with lions, elephants, buffaloes, black rhinos and other wildlife.
The Tanzanian Tourism Ministry said the country received 993,771 international tourists during the first half of 2026. Attractions managed by the NCAA recorded 331,349 domestic and foreign visits during the period, an annual increase of 7.6%.
