Three postponements in a week: who is delaying the hearing of the medical negligence case involving Odrex doctors?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:51:42 EEST
17:51:42 KST

Three postponements in a week: who is delaying the hearing of the medical negligence case involving Odrex doctors?
Kyiv • UNN
Last week, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa was supposed to continue hearing the case involving Odrex doctors; however, all three scheduled hearings were postponed. Two of them were postponed at the request of the defense.
Last week, three hearings were scheduled at the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa in the case of private Odrex clinic doctors Vitaliy Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, who are accused of improper performance of their professional duties, which, according to the investigation, could have caused the death of businessman Adnan Kivan. All three hearings were postponed, two of them following procedural actions by the defense. Why the case, which has been heard for more than nine months, has stalled again was examined by UNN.
One of the hearings did not take place following a motion by Maryna Bielotserkovska’s lawyer to postpone the hearing because of her participation in another court proceeding. The court granted the motion and scheduled the next hearing for September 18.
However, even then it was impossible to proceed with further examination of the evidence. Vitaliy Rusakov’s defense once again moved for the recusal of the presiding judge, Viktor Chaplytskyi. The court considered the recusal motion and denied it, but was unable to continue examining the merits of the case because Rusakov himself failed to appear.
These are far from the first postponements. Since the beginning of the trial, dozens of hearings have been postponed or failed to take place following motions or failures to appear by the defense. Presiding Judge Viktor Chaplytskyi responded to the defense’s actions and appealed to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar.
Oleksandr Sytnykov, a retired judge of the Supreme Administrative Court of Ukraine, explained to UNN that ensuring a case is heard within a reasonable time is the court’s responsibility. Therefore, if lawyers’ repeated failures to appear or motions effectively block the progress of the case, the presiding judge must respond to the situation, since responsibility for compliance with procedural time limits also rests with them.
Undoubtedly, if a lawyer’s actions lead to the protraction of proceedings, the judge must respond. The judge is subject to procedural time limits and may also face disciplinary liability for failing to comply with them. Therefore, a situation may arise in which, due to constant postponements, the judge themselves comes under scrutiny regarding compliance with the time limits
Andriy Misiats, acting chair of the Higher Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar, also draws attention to the possible consequences of systematic failures to appear.
A combination of failures to appear may indicate not an accidental violation, but a certain pattern of a lawyer’s behavior and their unfair attitude toward their professional duties
He emphasizes that a lawyer’s participation in another proceeding may indeed be a valid reason for failing to appear if it is genuine and properly documented. At the same time, being occupied with another case alone does not automatically mean that a hearing must be postponed. Whether the actions of the lawyers for the Odrex doctors show signs of a disciplinary offense must be determined by the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar.
Why are the accused afraid of hearing the medical expert’s testimony?
All these postponements are taking place at the stage when the court is to hear the medical expert. The expert is to provide professional explanations regarding the medical documentation, expert conclusions, compliance with treatment protocols, and the medical aspect of the question of a possible causal relationship between the doctors’ actions and the patient’s death. The guilt of the accused, however, is determined exclusively by the court.
In May, the expert had already appeared in court, but at that time Rusakov’s lawyers initiated the issue of changing jurisdiction. Now that the case has once again approached the examination of the key medical component of the evidence, a series of so-called "procedural maneuvers" has continued.

Merz in for rough ride after historic state elections losses for CDU

2026-09-21
08:50:00 UTC
17:50:00 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz begins the week weakened by his center-right CDU party’s bruising losses to far-right and far-left rivals in two regional elections.
Just 16 months in office, Merz has seen his approval ratings plummet while his party has suffered a string of regional election losses against the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which also leads nationwide polls.
Fighting speculation that his CDU/CSU bloc may try to oust him, 70-year-old Merz took the unusual step of addressing the nation on TV Sunday, just minutes after the first exit polls were announced.
Merz admitted that his CDU had suffered a "disaster" in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state – and that was before the CDU dropped below five percent there in the ongoing count, meaning it got kicked out of parliament altogether.
While the AfD came first there, the center-left SPD party looks set to continue governing the state by forming a coalition with left-wing allies.
After the CDU was also soundly defeated by a far-left Die Linke in Berlin, Merz charged that "trust in our country's institutions is waning" and being "actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right."
"What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience," Merz said. "I will demonstrate this as CDU party chairman and, above all, as chancellor of our country."
Analysts saw it as an attempt to gain the advantage before another hailstorm of criticism comes raining down.
"His extremely early move shows that Merz is staking a claim to define the narrative," political scientist Oliver Lembcke of Ruhr University Bochum told AFP.
Lembcke labeled this "leadership from a defensive position – and an attempt to prevent a personnel debate with an uncertain outcome from gathering steam."
ING bank economist Carsten Brzeski said about Merz's unusual TV address: "Read the appearance for what it was, an attempt to choke off the speculation about his possible resignation that has been building in recent weeks."
After Sunday's CDU crisis meeting, the chancellor has also cleared his calendar for the following days and skipped a trip to New York for the U.N. General Assembly, to deal with potential aftershocks from the votes.
Merz has been fighting off rumors for weeks he may be ousted by his center-right CDU/CSU bloc.
Names of hopefuls for the top job that have been floated include Hendrik Wuest, state premier of populous North Rhine-Westphalia, and Markus Soeder, the Bavarian state premier and head of the CSU, the regional sister party of the CDU.
However, no contender has made an open move for the job – perhaps fearing the act of disloyalty could backfire, or intimidated by the tough task of trying to revive the party's fortunes during one of its worst-ever crisis.
When Merz took office in May last year, he vowed to reboot a flagging economy, rebuild the military to deter Russia and reduce irregular immigration to soothe voters' fears and lure them away from the AfD.
But the AfD now leads nationwide polls and Merz's personal approval ratings hover just above 10%, not helped by his occasionally blunt and abrasive comments.
The latest elections came two weeks after the far-right, pro-Trump and Moscow-friendly AfD also dealt a stunning defeat to the CDU in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The string of election debacles comes as Merz has struggled to push through promised economic and social welfare reforms with his coalition partners the SPD.
Under-fire Merz received some badly needed support from CDU power brokers last week when eight state premiers declared jointly that Germany needs "stability now more than ever" rather than "discussions about personnel."
They refrained, however, from issuing a personal endorsement for Merz.

Egypt rejects European plans for refugee camps in 'return hubs'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:48:02 UTC
17:48:02 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt rejects European Union's plans for refugee camps on Egyptian shores
Egypt has categorically rejected a proposal by some European countries to create camps for the reception of refugees and asylum-seekers in non-European countries south of the Mediterranean.
During a meeting with European diplomats in Cairo on 10 September, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said his country refuses the mere discussion of such a proposal under all circumstances.
Egypt, he said, bears a huge refugee burden already.
The Egyptian rejection comes as some European nations actively discuss and advance plans for the creation of what has come to be known as "return hubs".
These are deportation or repatriation centres that could receive irregular migrants and rejected asylum-seekers who cannot be returned to their home countries.
The European nations advancing these plans, including Germany; Austria; the Netherlands, and Greece, suggest creating the aspired centres in African countries, including in North African countries southern Mediterranean.
Discussions about the creation of such hubs come almost four months after the European Parliament approved new legislation that allows member states to establish these centres in non-EU countries via agreements, provided that human rights and international law standards are met.
The new legislation and the aforementioned discussions highlight the intensity of the refugee and asylum problem in Europe, analysts in Cairo said.
Nevertheless, the same discussions also come at a tough time for North Africa where the refugee problem is equally intense, being exacerbated by escalating conflicts in the Middle East and Africa, they added.
"These conflicts have put North African countries at the receiving end of a large number of refugees," Mona Omar, a former assistant to the Egyptian foreign minister and a retired ambassador, told The New Arab.
This refugee burden, she added, comes with heavy economic pressures, given the fact that North African governments have to provide these refugees with all types of support, including food, healthcare and education.
"These pressures translate into higher inflation, public anger, and consequently domestic security threats," she said.
Heavy burden
Egypt hosts millions of refugees already, highlighting one of the reasons for its rejection of European discussions about the establishment of return hubs in it, observers said.
Sitting at the crossroads of a series of regional and continental conflicts, the Arab country is one of the world's largest refugee receiving states, they added.
Leading economic Khaled al-Shafie said Egypt's reception of such a large number of refugees puts a drain on its economy.
"The refugee burden saps the economy in general by depleting state resources and overstretches basic services," he told TNA.
He attributed part of Egypt's current economic hardships to the same burden.
Egypt hosts over 10 million refugees and asylum-seekers who have converged into it from neighbouring and regional states, escaping conflict and economic hardships back home, according to the Egyptian government.
Despite this, only 1 million of the foreigners the populous Arab country hosts are registered with the United Nations refugee agency, with the Sudanese constituting the largest number of these refugees and asylum-seekers.
Egypt prides itself, meanwhile, on building its distinct refugee and asylum-seekers hosting model by allowing those foreigners to live side by side with its own citizens, sharing services offered to these citizens by the Egyptian government.
Over the years, however, the same pride has shrivelled up to give way to a feeling of the real burden of hosting such a huge number of refugees, comparable to almost 9% of Egypt's overall population of 120 million.
Such a feeling of being weighed down by the refugee burden also came as the Egyptian economy felt the heat from regional unrest, including because of the war in Gaza, the current war in Iran and the unfolding unrest in the Red Sea.
This might explain the Egyptian leadership's repeated plea for the international community to share with Egypt its refugee burden, analysts said.
Treating symptoms
Whether the Egyptian government's refusal to host refugee deportation centres will affect relations with the EU remains to be seen.
Apart from its geostrategic importance, its influence in the Arab and Islamic worlds, the presence of the Suez Canal in it, and its role in brokering regional peace, Egypt acquires part of its appeal to Europe from its ability to function as a barrier for waves of illegal migrants to Europe, specialists said.
Perhaps the same appeal was the reason why the continent was keen to strengthen its relations with Cairo in different fields over the years, something that has grown quite noticeable in the past few years, they added.
The two sides upgraded their relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2024.
The first Egypt-EU summit was held in Brussels in 2025 to seek ways to help the economically-struggling Arab country, in the light of a 2024 multibillion dollar aid package.
The second Egypt-EU summit is expected to be held in Egypt next year. The third edition of the Egypt-EU Investment Conference is also expected to be held on the sidelines of the summit.
During his 10 September meeting with European diplomats, the Egyptian foreign minister said his country is committed to managing the refugee issue in a comprehensive manner.
He called for addressing the root causes of migration by advancing development, creating jobs and enhancing border management.
In Cairo, analysts believe that EU states are only treating the symptoms, rather than the cause by planning to create repatriation centres in other countries.
Addressing the root causes of the refugee problem, they added, would come through a more active European involvement in conflict resolution in refugee-sending countries.
"You can't prevent migration waves to Europe without putting an end to conflicts in countries sending these migrants or refugees," Ambassador Omar, the former assistant to the Egyptian foreign minister, said.
"This is why I believe the creation of the planned return hubs in non-European states will solve the problem as long as these conflicts keep raging," she added.

Russia election results show Putin’s party winning: What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:47:06 UTC
17:47:06 KST

Russia election results show Putin’s party winning: What we know
With more than 90 percent votes counted, Putin’s United Russia appears poised for a landslide win. But analysts say warning signs for the Kremlin may lie in the results.
Early results emerging from Russia’s first parliamentary elections since the launch of the full-fledged war on Ukraine show President Vladimir Putin’s party dominating the vote — an outcome widely predicted.
The election, which began on Friday and ended on Sunday to elect members of the lower house of parliament, the State Duma, is projected to see Putin’s United Russia maintain its hold amid a tightly controlled election in which opposition to the president’s policies remains limited.
Despite the lack of alternatives to United Russia, the Kremlin had positioned the vote as a chance for residents to have their say since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and amid economic hardship.
Most antiwar candidates have been barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party said they feared for their freedom after two senior party figures were handed long jail terms before the election due to comments made about the Russia-Ukraine war.
Still, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “For peace”.
Here’s what we know:
What have early results shown?
The state news agency TASS reported on Monday that 90.43 percent of ballots had been counted, according to data from the Central Election Commission (CEC). As counting progressed, The Associated Press reported later in the day 95 percent of results had been tabulated.
The CEC found that, as of Sunday night, voter turnout stood just below 57 percent.
United Russia led with 57.86 percent of the vote, with 225 deputies apportioned from party lists. In single-seat races, another 225 lawmakers will be chosen, and Putin’s party is also projected to win most of them.
So far, no surprises or upsets have been recorded.
TASS also reported, citing the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media, that more than 3.6 million people voted online.
Those voting included residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed in 2022 – Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhia – as well as those in Crimea, which was taken in 2014. The United Nations and most of the world do not recognise Crimea and other occupied Ukrainian regions as part of Russia.
How have other parties fared?
Other parties, like the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the ultranationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR), New People and A Just Russia, all of which largely vote the same way as United Russia in parliament, trailed behind in the early election results but were still on course to win seats in the State Duma.
The vote breakdown showed the CPRF at 13.84 percent, the LDPR at 8.9 percent, New People at 7.94 percent, and A Just Russia at 4.95 percent, according to TASS.
But while the early results paint a predictable outcome, the Berlin-based think tank NEST, cofounded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, said the vote could produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.
NEST said the votes received by the CPRF and New People might in many cases amount to a silent protest against Putin and United Russia — even if these parties do not actually challenge the president on most issues.
“The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot,” it said in a note.
What were previous outcomes and when are final results expected?
During the 2021 State Duma elections, United Russia kept an absolute majority in the 450-seat lower house, holding 326 seats.
The CPRF was the second-largest party, winning 57 seats. It has remained a major force in Russian politics since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The CEC will announce preliminary results and turnout on Monday, but the final results are unlikely before Friday, by which time all ballots are likely to be counted and other procedures required by law are completed, TASS reported.
What has Ukraine said on the Russian election?
Ukraine had denounced the election, which involved voters from the annexed regions, with officials calling it illegal.
Moscow accused Ukraine of attempting to sabotage the election after a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks targeted Moscow and other regions on Sunday, which TASS called the biggest of its kind since the war began in February 2022.
The attacks killed three people in the Moscow region and two in the Russian-held part of Kherson, including an election official, according to the regional governor and the election commission.
Moreover, a facility at Moscow’s oil refinery, which has been targeted before, was also damaged.
On Monday morning, a man was killed and three others were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Bryansk region, according to acting Governor Yegor Kovalchuk.

The European Union has condemned the holding of elections to the Russian State Duma in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, assuring that it will never recognize them, and that sanctions will be applied to those involved in their organization.
A corresponding statement by High Representative Kaja Kallas on behalf of the EU regarding the elections to the State Duma of Russia held on September 18-20, 2026, and their non-applicability on the territory of Ukraine, was distributed in Brussels on Monday.
The European Union strongly condemned the illegal organization by the Russian Federation of so-called "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, namely in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, as well as in parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson regions, stating that these votes represented another blatant violation by Russia of international law, in particular the UN Charter, as well as the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine.
In this regard, the EU called on Russia to respect Ukraine's internationally recognized borders and sovereignty, reiterating that it does not and will never recognize either the holding of these so-called "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results. It assured that sanctions would be applied to persons involved in organizing these fictitious elections or running as candidates in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as well as to those responsible for undermining the possibility of holding free and fair elections in Russia itself.
In addition, the European Union reaffirmed its unwavering support for the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, urging that Russia must stop its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, agree to a full, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire, and immediately, completely, and unconditionally withdraw its troops and equipment from the entire territory of Ukraine.
Regarding the elections in Russia itself, the High Representative stated that they once again highlighted the ongoing and deep erosion of democracy in Russia, which is taking place in an increasingly authoritarian political environment, noting that the lack of a level playing field for all participants was further complicated by Russia's illegal war of aggression against Ukraine and the ongoing illegal occupation of Ukrainian territories.
The statement emphasized that the Russian authorities continue to step up systematic and institutionalized domestic and transnational repression to prevent any democratic opposition forces from participating in the struggle against the status quo, and that the decision to bar candidates from the Yabloko party from participating in the elections on the federal list further limited the choice for Russian voters by removing one of the last opposition forces and the only party with an anti-war program from the electoral process.
The text also pointed to such facts as the large-scale abuse of administrative and judicial resources to eliminate all those who opposed Russia's illegal war of aggression, deprive Russian voters of a real choice regarding the future of their country, and significantly limit Russians' access to independent information, adding that the European Union and its member states will continue to support the important work of Russian civil society organizations, human rights defenders, and independent media.
Furthermore, the EU expressed regret over Russian's decision not to invite OSCE observers to these elections, stating that this once again demonstrated Russian’s disregard for the commitments undertaken by all OSCE participating states and deprived Russian voters and institutions of the opportunity to receive an impartial and independent assessment of the elections.

China Focus: Exhibition showcases AI-powered manufacturing, int'l cooperation opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:42:22 CST
17:42:22 KST

HEFEI, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- At an exhibition booth, a dual-arm robot works with remarkable precision, gripping a delicate test tube with one arm while handling reagents with the other.
"It is more than a robot that simply executes pre-programmed commands," said Wang Wandong, assistant director of the Center for Scientific Intelligence and Innovation. An onboard foundation model for scientific research enables it to understand a research task, generate an experimental plan, and carry out tasks on its own.
The "thinking" robotic arm, according to Wang, offers a glimpse into how Chinese manufacturers are combining sophisticated hardware with increasingly capable homegrown artificial intelligence (AI).
At the Binhu International Convention and Exhibition Center in Hefei, capital of east China's Anhui Province, more than 1,200 companies are showcasing over 15,000 products across a 70,000-square-meter exhibition area as part of the 2026 World Manufacturing Convention that opened Sunday.
Humanoid robots play rock music, practice boxing and sing traditional Chinese operas, while sleek electric vehicles sit alongside displays of chips, electronic panels and other key components. Around them, exhibitors display technologies ranging from quantum applications to artificial intelligence.
China's manufacturing value-added accounts for nearly 30 percent of the global total, the largest share worldwide for over a decade. The country's manufacturing sector is placing greater emphasis on improving quality and efficiency, aiming for high-end technology and smarter, greener production.
Anhui, an inland province, has in recent years seen rapid growth in manufacturing sectors such as electric vehicles, semiconductors, quantum technology and robotics.
From January to July this year, the output value of Anhui's strategic emerging industries grew 17.3 percent year on year. During the period, the output of new energy vehicles, integrated circuits and robots increased 27.5 percent, 28.6 percent and 32.8 percent, respectively, year on year.
At the opening ceremony, Hefei-based Chinese memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) announced its latest fifth-generation technology platform, which improves product capacity, power consumption and stability.
The company, which went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's STAR Market in late July, became the most valuable listed company on the A-share market. Luo Xiaodong, vice president of CXMT, said that, in developing the new platform, the company introduced a tailored AI large model and digital simulation covering the entire production process, significantly improving R&D efficiency.
This year's convention also puts a greater emphasis on showcasing entire industrial chains, shifting from individual products to broader ecosystems, the event organizer said.
Anhui ranked first nationwide in automobile production, new energy vehicle production, automobile export volume and export value in the first half of this year.
In the intelligent connected new energy vehicle section of the exhibition, displays span the full chain, from complete vehicles and power batteries to chips and chassis. Industrial data showed that more than 3,000 core parts suppliers now support automobile manufacturing in the province.
The province's growing industrial clusters are bringing manufacturers, technology companies and suppliers closer together, strengthening links between innovation and production, analysts noted.
"Anhui is helping shape the future of manufacturing," said Peter Wilson, the British ambassador to China. He added that Anhui has developed a globally significant manufacturing base, built world-class industrial clusters and is a center for emerging technologies.
Xin Guobin, vice minister of industry and information technology, said at the opening ceremony that China welcomes industrial enterprises from around the world to share opportunities here.
China will continue to expand high-level opening-up and create a world-class business environment that is market-oriented, law-based and internationalized, he added.
China removed all market access restrictions for foreign investors in the manufacturing sector in 2024, and in its latest edition of the Catalog of Encouraged Industries for Foreign Investment, effective Feb. 1, it added and expanded relevant items in the advanced manufacturing sector.
"Partnership creates opportunity," said Wilson, adding that Chinese and British businesses have been contributing to each other's manufacturing sectors.
"Let's learn from each other, work together, empower each other, and succeed together," the ambassador said. ■

====================================================================================================

Cambodia's fuel prices continue to surge amid ongoing Middle East tensions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:42:03 CST
17:42:03 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Retail fuel prices in Cambodia continued their upward trajectory on Monday, driven by a surge in global oil prices fueled by ongoing tensions in the Middle East, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
In its latest announcement, the ministry said that the price of regular gasoline has risen to 5,250 riels (about 1.29 U.S. dollars) per liter. This marks a 9.3-percent increase from 4,800 riels just 10 days ago.
Diesel prices saw an even sharper jump, climbing 11.9 percent to 6,100 riels per liter, up from 5,450 riels in the previous period.
The ministry's data highlights a staggering long-term trend, showing that since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict, the retail prices of regular gasoline and diesel in Cambodia have skyrocketed by 36.3 percent and 58.4 percent, respectively.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, warned that these hikes directly inflate transportation and production costs.
"This drives inflation and erodes consumer purchasing power, particularly for food and agricultural products," he told Xinhua. "Ultimately, this dampens overall economic activity and pushes food prices higher."
He added that the burden falls disproportionately on vulnerable segments of the population.
"The most affected are low- and middle-income households, informal workers, and small and medium enterprises, as they are forced to confront rising living and operational costs with very limited financial cushions," he said.
Cambodia remains highly vulnerable to global oil market volatility. The Southeast Asian nation relies entirely on imported petroleum and diesel, as its own offshore oil reserves have yet to be commercially exploited. ■

====================================================================================================

Dementia survey highlights diagnosis delays, carer burden in Australia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:41:47 CST
17:41:47 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- A national survey has found that many Australians living with dementia report positive wellbeing and support from family and friends, but face complex pathways to diagnosis and difficulties accessing support services.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) survey, conducted between May 2025 and January 2026, collected responses from 266 people living with dementia and 1,648 carers, an AIHW statement said Monday.
Three in five people living with dementia reported receiving a diagnosis within three years of first noticing symptoms, while fewer than half said they were diagnosed within the first year, the survey found, adding that barriers included delays in seeking advice, delays in tests and specialist appointments, symptoms being attributed to other causes, and appointment costs.
The survey also highlighted the burden on carers. Nearly one-third spent 70 hours or more each week caring for someone living with dementia, while more than seven in 10 women and six in 10 men reported feeling overwhelmed by their responsibilities.
Around two-thirds of carers recorded low wellbeing, with those providing 70 hours or more of care a week reporting lower wellbeing than those providing fewer hours, it said.
Nearly 459,000 Australians are estimated to be living with dementia in 2026, with the number expected to exceed 1 million over the next 35 years, said AIHW spokesperson Bronte O'Donnell, noting that the findings would help Australia better understand how dementia affects people's everyday lives.
Monday marks World Alzheimer's Day, observed as part of World Alzheimer's Month. Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, accounting for an estimated 60-70 percent of cases worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. ■

Asian Games | Feature: Pan Zhanle swims past self-doubt
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:41:40 CST
17:41:40 KST

by sportswriters Zhang Can, Gao Meng, Liu Yichun
TOKYO, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Pan Zhanle had already accepted defeat before he touched the wall.
With just one meter to go in the men's 100-meter freestyle final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sunday, the Chinese world record holder thought he was going to lose.
But Pan found the finish first.
He edged South Korea's Kim Young-beom by just 0.04 seconds to win the title in 47.61, with another South Korean, Hwang Sun-woo, taking bronze in 47.79.
"I thought I was going to lose at 99 meters," Pan said.
Before the medal ceremony, Pan asked Kim about his wingspan. Kim told him it was 2.16 meters, while Pan's is just over 1.9 meters.
"So I really thought I was going to lose in that last meter," Pan said with a smile. "Maybe I was just lucky."
The relief was visible. Pan climbed onto the lane line to celebrate, a rare display of emotion for a swimmer who has often kept his post-race comments brief.
Minutes later, he was equally candid in the mixed zone, talking about the challenges he had faced over the past two years.
Three years ago at the Hangzhou Asian Games, Pan broke 47 seconds for the first time by winning the 100m freestyle in 46.97. In 2024, he set a new world record of 46.40 at the Paris Olympics.
But those performances became harder to reproduce. He won the 100m at the 2025 national championships in 47.77, missed the final at the Singapore world championships after clocking 47.81 in the semifinals, and won the National Games in 48.01. In March this year, he finished third at the Chinese Swimming Open in 48.05.
"Over the past two years, I have become less and less confident," Pan said.
He changed his training methods and competition habits and spent time training overseas. The experience, he said, did not necessarily produce immediate results, but changed the way he understood swimming and his own career.
"Training overseas gave me a better understanding of the sport and swimming," he said. "That kind of improvement is difficult to show directly, but it will affect my entire career."
The biggest change, however, was mental.
"Enjoy life, enjoy the competition, give my best in training and leave no regrets in the race," Pan said.
For him, enjoying competition does not mean losing the desire to win. It means accepting whatever the race may bring.
"I don't think I'm a naturally gifted or genius athlete," he said. "Winning is of course good, but losing can give you experience."
Pan still has three relay events to come in Tokyo, but for now his focus remains on the immediate task.
"I don't want to talk too far ahead," he said. "I just want to fully show my training level and form in competition, and leave no regrets." Enditem.

17:41:34 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Singapore will introduce fines of up to 500 Singapore dollars (392 U.S. dollars) for disruptive behavior on public buses from Sept. 23, including putting feet on seats, playing audio loudly and littering, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) said on Monday.
The LTA said in a statement that the new regulations will apply to public buses, as well as bus interchanges and terminals, and are intended to foster a safer, more considerate and pleasant public transport environment.
More serious offenses, such as causing obstruction or danger to commuters at bus interchanges or terminals, or soiling any part of a public bus, interchange or terminal, carry a maximum penalty of 5,000 Singapore dollars.
Authorized staff, including ticket inspectors and bus interchange staff, may issue Administrative Notifications of Offenses to people suspected of committing an offense. The LTA will conduct follow-up investigations.
Bus captains will not be empowered to issue the notifications, so as not to affect their core duty of safely operating the bus. However, they may advise passengers to stop disruptive behavior or require them to alight if they fail to comply.
The LTA said it would continue to exercise discretion and fairness, particularly in cases involving commuters with physical or mental health conditions. ■

China's grain industry to see annual output value exceed 4.5 trln yuan during 2026-2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:41:30 CST
17:41:30 KST

The State Council Information Office holds a press conference on safeguarding China's granaries to ensure food security in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Xu)
BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The annual industrial output value of China's grain industry is expected to exceed 4.5 trillion yuan (666.8 billion U.S. dollars) during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), an official said on Monday.
The grain sector will better meet people's demand for higher-quality, more nutritious and healthier food, said Liu Huanxin, head of the National Food and Strategic Reserves Administration, at a press conference.
China's grain industry has maintained steady growth in recent years, with the total industrial output value of grain enterprises rising from 3 trillion yuan at the end of the 13th Five-Year Plan period (2016-2020) to over 4 trillion yuan at the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025).
Liu said that despite current fluctuations in the international grain market, China's grain market has remained generally stable and the country's food security is well guaranteed.
Liu pointed to a recent forecast by the World Meteorological Organization, which showed that El Nino will continue to strengthen and could impact global food production. Meanwhile, geopolitical conflicts are disrupting transport routes, driving up fertilizer prices and production costs, and adding to uncertainties around global food security.
He said China's food security is underpinned by stable production, ample reserves and strong processing capacity.
On the production side, China's grain output has been supported by steadily improving production capacity and the country's vast territory, which allows different regions to offset each other's harvest fluctuations, Liu said.
China's annual grain output has stayed above 650 million tonnes since 2015, exceeding 700 million tonnes for the first time in 2024 and reaching 715 million tonnes in 2025. Per capita grain availability has surpassed 500 kg, higher than the global average, providing a solid foundation for the country's food security.
On the reserves side, China's grain stock-to-use ratio remains well above the international grain security threshold of 17 to 18 percent, Liu said. If abnormal market fluctuations occur, reserves can be used to regulate supply and demand and help stabilize the grain market.
China also has strong grain processing capacity. The country has about 24,000 grain processing enterprises engaged in grain and edible oil processing, food and condiment production, feed processing and deep processing, among other businesses. Processing capacity for flour, rice and edible oil is sufficient to meet domestic demand, Liu said. ■

Three South Korean officers injured in blast near North Korea border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:40:18 UTC
17:40:18 KST

An explosion near South Korea's heavily fortified border with North Korea has injured three South Korean military officers, Seoul has said.
South Korea's Defence Ministry said on Monday that the explosion occurred during an unspecified operation in the Demilitarised Zone, a border buffer zone separating the two nations that is commonly referred to as the DMZ.
The cause was not immediately clear, the ministry said.
Officials did not say whether the explosion could have been caused by a landmine planted by North Korea, which has added mines, anti-tank barriers and other frontline fortifications in recent months as relations between the two countries have sharply deteriorated.
Two of the officers were airlifted from the site by helicopter, while the third was transported by land before being airlifted, according to the ministry. The officers are being treated at a military hospital near the capital Seoul.
The DMZ, which stretches 248 kilometres and is four kilometres wide, is one of the world’s most heavily armed borders. An estimated two million mines lie inside and near the border alongside barbed wire fences, tank traps and combat troops on both sides.
The zone is a legacy of the 1950–1953 Korean War, which ended with an armistice but no peace treaty.
Border tensions
Increased activity by North Korean soldiers near the military demarcation line has raised concerns in South Korea as Pyongyang strengthens its border defences amid prolonged tensions.
The South Korean military has not officially confirmed media reports that North Korean soldiers crossed the line more than 20 times during frontline operations in August alone.
In April 2025, South Korean troops fired warning shots after around 10 North Korean soldiers crossed the line in the eastern section of the DMZ. The North Korean soldiers retreated following audio warnings and the shots, with no clashes reported.
North Korean troops also crossed the border three times in June 2024, prompting South Korea to fire warning shots.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has suspended virtually all cooperation and diplomacy with Seoul in recent years, declaring South Korea his country’s most hostile enemy amid a stalemate in nuclear negotiations with Washington.
Landmines have caused casualties on the southern side of the border before. North Korean mines have occasionally washed down swollen rivers into South Korea, killing or injuring civilians.
In August 2015, landmine blasts maimed two South Korean soldiers and triggered a sharp rise in tensions between the two countries.

Old balloons, new drones: U.S. Army tests both in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:40:16 UTC
17:40:16 KST

- U.S. Army soldiers launched micro-High-Altitude Balloons, one carrying an APOLLO-R drone, in Hokkaido, Japan, on Sept. 18 during Exercise Orient Shield 26.
- It is at least the third U.S. Army exercise this year with balloon-carried drones, after Morocco and Guam.
U.S. Army soldiers launched micro-High-Altitude Balloons at the Yausubetsu Training Area on Hokkaido, Japan, on Sept. 18, including one that carried an APOLLO-R drone. Observers from Japan, the United Kingdom and Australia watched the demonstration during Exercise Orient Shield 26, according to the title of the U.S. Army’s video.
Balloons are often seen as relics of earlier wars. The Hokkaido launch is at least the third U.S. Army exercise this year to feature balloon-carried drones. Earlier this year, during African Lion 26, the U.S. Army launched drone-carrying micro balloons from a vessel off Morocco, Naval News reported. On June 24, soldiers from the 3d Multi-Domain Task Force launched an Apollo R on an Urban Sky balloon at Orote Airfield, Naval Station Guam, during Valiant Shield 2026. That test looked at sensing from the stratosphere and at extending joint communications networks.
A micro-High-Altitude Balloon is a small balloon that lifts equipment high into the atmosphere. In the Hokkaido photos, one rises with the APOLLO-R attached. A second U.S. Army video shows soldiers recovering the balloons on Sept. 19.
Icarus, a Los Angeles aerospace company, builds the APOLLO-R. The Defence Blog reported in June that it is an autonomous, solar-powered aircraft designed to fly indefinitely at altitudes above 18,300 meters (60,000 feet). The balloon does the initial lifting. TWZ reported that the U.S. Army has supported the aircraft’s development through its xTech innovation challenge.
Russ Van Der Werff, vice president of stratospheric solutions at balloon maker Aerostar, has argued that balloons offer survivability advantages over aircraft such as the Global Hawk and the Reaper.
Orient Shield 26 is the 41st edition of the annual exercise and the largest so far, with about 3,700 personnel from U.S. Army Pacific, the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force and the Australian Army. The opening ceremony took place Sept. 17 at Camp Higashi-Chitose.
The U.S. Army has not said how high the balloon climbed, whether the APOLLO-R separated and flew on its own, or how many balloons were launched. The captions do not name the balloon’s maker or the unit that ran the launch, and they do not say what the drone collected or relayed.
Ukraine offers a wartime example with a different platform, the tethered aerostat, which stays anchored to the ground while it holds equipment aloft. The Defence Blog reported in March that Ukrainian company Aerobavovna had delivered specialized aerostats to Ukrainian forces for surveillance, communications relay and electronic monitoring linked to drone operations.
“To control a drone at long distances and at low altitude, the relay needs to be raised into the sky,” said Aerobavovna CEO Yuriy Vysoven.
Vysoven said another drone can do that job, but its time in the air is limited, while an aerostat can operate around the clock. He expects the market to move toward larger numbers of smaller, cheaper platforms instead of single systems costing hundreds of millions of dollars, because large radar aerostats placed near the front become targets.
The Defender reported in May that the company’s AB12TC aerostat can lift equipment to altitudes of 100 to 700 meters (330 to 2,300 feet) and operate for up to 72 hours in field conditions. According to company data cited in that report, more than 50 aerostat systems have been delivered to units of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, Special Operations Forces and National Guard. Vysoven said in March that Aerobavovna was preparing its first export sale, to a customer in the European Union.

Construction began in February 2022, and engineers broke through the tunnel in December 2023 after overcoming difficult geological conditions, including unstable slopes and shallow rock cover.

'Rules need to be upheld': Australia's push to change a contentious UN power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:33:32 UTC
17:33:32 KST

Australia would push to reform the United Nations if given a seat on its Security Council, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Monday, as she joined Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in New York for the United Nations General Assembly.
Speaking with SBS News, Wong said Russia's use of veto powers to exempt itself from repercussions during its invasion of Ukraine was an example of where Australia would seek reform.
"We've had a longstanding position as a country of reform of the veto, and we know it's been misused previously," Wong told SBS World News chief political correspondent Anna Henderson in New York.
"What happened in relation to Russia's invasion of Ukraine was that a permanent member of the Security Council used its veto to prevent any action being taken for its own breach of the charter. That was an example where we would like reform."
Fifteen countries sit on the Security Council, and its five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — have the right to veto any resolution or decision.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In 2022, Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution that described its attempts to unlawfully annex four regions of Ukraine as “a threat to international peace and security”, demanding Russia “immediately, completely and unconditionally withdraw all of its military forces” from Ukrainian territory. Ten of fifteen members had voted in favour of the resolution, while four abstained.
Wong said that Australia was "for reform", but that Australians were "very practical people".
"We recognise rules need to be upheld; the UN needs to be reformed.
"We want to make sure, where it really matters, that we continue to be part of setting the direction about that reform."
Wong has backed Albanese's bid for a seat on the council, which Australia has not held since 2014. Asked whether the veto powers in their current state rendered the campaign redundant, Wong stood by the pursuit.
"We might be distant from New York, but we are not distant from the rest of the world, and the world does have an effect on what happens in our economy, in our lives.
"So what I would say is we want to be able to advocate for Australia's interests in every forum that matters, and the UN Security Council matters."
International law under 'pressure'
International law is under a "great deal of pressure", Wong said, but the best response would be for countries to "come together" and advocate for the observance of international law.
"You've got two options, don't you? You can throw your hands up and say, 'I give up'. Or you can say, 'This actually matters to many countries.'
"We're not a superpower, but we're a country with substance and power to work with others to try and ensure that we hold onto the rules that matter."
Asked whether Australia could hold the United States to account over accusations around the war in Iran, as well as its actions in Venezuela, Wong said it was a task for the international community to work out the rules that "we really want to hold on to, that matter to us".
"I think trading arrangements matter to us. They certainly matter to Australia, and we've been very clear about our difference with the Trump administration."
But Australia does not intend to join its like-minded international partners in broader sanctions on Israeli settlements on the West Bank, Wong said, referring to "targeted sanctions" announced earlier this month as the UK banned trade in the occupied territories, and nine European countries said they were considering the same.
"I've announced already that we would engage in targeted sanctions," Wong said, noting that no country that had announced it would engage in the sanctions on a blanket basis had yet implemented them.
"And we certainly will be working with them as they do that to understand how they intend to deal with that," she said, and added that she has a "very clear intention" of engaging in more action against settlements, "which are an obstacle to peace", and "engaging in behaviour which makes two states less likely" in the case of the E-1 settlement, a contentious development plan for a 12-square-kilometre corridor in the West Bank.
"We'll continue to work closely with our like-minded countries just as we did a year ago, when, with others, we recognised the state of Palestine, which was part of the precursor to the peace plan, which we want to see implemented."

Ukraine Urges Global Shutdown of Russian House Centers, Citing Security Threat
Germany closed the Russian House cultural center in Berlin on September 18, ending years of what Ukraine describes as malign Russian influence. Despite the shutdown, similar centers still operate in at least seven European countries, Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, warned on September 19.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Sybiha set out the assessment in a post on X on September 19, framing the network as a front for hostile operations. He identified Rossotrudnichestvo and the so-called Russkiy Dom, or "Russian House," centers as instruments of disinformation, destabilization, and espionage.
"Our shared European home is not the place for 'Russian houses' promoting war propaganda," Sybiha wrote. He commended the measures European authorities have taken to block the network across the continent.
The network's reach extends well beyond Europe, the minister noted. Its scale is even greater in Africa, Central and Eastern Asia, the Asia-Pacific, and South America, he added.
In several countries, the official infrastructure remains intact, Sybiha stated, and in some it is woven directly into Russia's diplomatic presence. He characterized the centers as part of a comprehensive Russian effort to wage a global battle for public opinion.
Ukraine has formally appealed to governments worldwide to recognize the network as a national security threat, the minister explained. Kyiv has presented arguments for restricting the centers' operations and closing them entirely.
The Berlin shutdown extends a steady contraction of Russia's overseas cultural network. At least 13 Russian Houses have closed worldwide since Moscow's full-scale invasion began in 2022, down from roughly 15 centers operating across the European Union before the war.
Slovenia became the first EU state to expel its branch in April 2022, followed by Romania's closure of the Bucharest center in February 2023 and the shuttering of houses in Slovakia, Croatia, North Macedonia, and Montenegro that same year.
Moldova's center ceased operations entirely on July 4, 2026, with officials citing subversive activity conducted under the guise of culture.

Türkiye begins serial production of first domestically developed high-speed train
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:30:45 UTC
17:30:45 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye has begun serial production of its first domestically developed high-speed train, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu said, as the country moves to expand its indigenous rail manufacturing capabilities.
The train, developed by Turkish Rail System Vehicles Industry (TÜRASAŞ), is designed to operate at speeds of up to 225 kilometers per hour. The first train set is currently undergoing testing, reaching 250 kilometers per hour during dynamic running safety tests, Uraloğlu said.
Production of the second train set has now begun, marking the transition to serial production, according to the minister.
Türkiye aims to manufacture 14 electric high-speed train sets over the next two years, with seven planned for 2027 and another seven in 2028. Each eight-car train will have a capacity of 577 passengers and will be developed using domestic engineering capabilities.
Critical components, including the Train Control and Management System and traction system, are also being designed and manufactured domestically in cooperation with Turkish defense and technology company ASELSAN.
Uraloğlu said serial production will eventually be carried out at Türkiye’s first dedicated high-speed train factory, which is currently 90 percent complete. The 18,000-square-meter facility will bring production, assembly and testing operations under one roof once completed.
The factory is designed to have a production capacity of one high-speed train set per month, allowing Türkiye to scale up manufacturing as it seeks to strengthen domestic capabilities in railway technology and reduce reliance on imported systems.
The project is part of Türkiye’s broader efforts to expand its high-speed rail network.

Iran shuts down French cultural center over security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:25:45 UTC
17:25:45 KST

Iran shuts down French cultural center over security concerns
Iran has shut down a French-language center in Tehran, accusing the embassy-affiliated institution of operating illegally and engaging in activities which threaten the country’s national security.
Relations between Paris and Tehran have deteriorated despite France staying out of the war which the US and Israel launched against Iran in late February and denouncing the initial strikes as a breach of international law.
In July, two French diplomats were detained by Iranian security services, which accused them of interfering in the country’s internal affairs. They were subsequently expelled from the country. France retaliated in August by expelling two of Iran’s diplomats.
“Based on the Tehran prosecutor’s office’s order, the illegal center affiliated with the French Embassy in Tehran, which has operated for years under the guise of language instruction, has been closed,” the Iranian judiciary’s Mizan news agency said on Sunday.
Iranian authorities claimed that the institution had repeatedly ignored warnings to obtain the licenses required under the country’s laws and had conducted activities that “violated diplomatic conventions.” They also accused it of using language instruction as cover to promote projects opposed to Iranian-Islamic culture, identify and build networks, and facilitate the departure of skilled Iranians from the country.
France has condemned the closure as an attack on its cultural presence in Iran and said it would take “appropriate measures” in response. Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has ordered the Iranian ambassador to be summoned.
The French Language Centre (CLF) offered French language courses in Tehran, with thousands of Iranians attending its classes each year, according to the French Foreign Ministry.
In January 2023, Tehran closed the French Institute for Research in Iran after the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo published dozens of cartoons mocking then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and Iran’s religious establishment. The images, some of which were graphic or sexually explicit, were selected through an international contest called “Mullahs Get Out” and were intended to support anti-government protests in Iran.

Kalin, Libya’s acting defence chief discuss deepening Türkiye-Libya ties
Unknown

The head of Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization (MIT), Ibrahim Kalin, met with Libya’s acting defence minister, Abdussalam Zubi, in Istanbul, as Ankara and Tripoli seek to deepen cooperation and support efforts to unify Libya’s divided institutions.
The Saturday meeting came as negotiations aimed at bringing Libya’s military and political institutions together have gained momentum, according to Turkish security sources.
Kalin and Zubi discussed developments in Libya and the wider region, steps to maintain Türkiye-Libya cooperation, and ongoing efforts to achieve political and military unity and preserve stability in the North African country.
Zubi thanked Türkiye for its efforts to advance unity in Libya, while Kalin reiterated Ankara’s determination to continue supporting Libya’s security and stability.
A relationship built around security, trade and the Mediterranean
Türkiye’s engagement with Libya has expanded considerably over the past several years, encompassing security, energy, trade and maritime cooperation.
A landmark step came in November 2019, when Türkiye and Libya’s then Government of National Accord signed a memorandum on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean.
The agreement, registered with the United Nations, defines a maritime boundary between the two countries’ continental shelf and exclusive economic zone areas.
The accord has remained a central element of Türkiye-Libya relations and the wider geopolitical debate over maritime boundaries in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Ankara maintains that the agreement protects the maritime rights of both Türkiye and Libya and was concluded in accordance with international law.
The maritime understanding was followed in October 2022 by a separate memorandum on cooperation in hydrocarbons, covering scientific, technical, technological, legal, administrative and commercial cooperation on land and at sea.
The agreements have helped broaden the relationship beyond security cooperation, placing energy and the Mediterranean at the heart of Ankara-Tripoli ties.
Ankara backs efforts to consolidate Libya’s institutions
Türkiye has also increasingly framed its engagement around Libya’s territorial integrity, political unity and institutional consolidation.
In August, Kalin said Türkiye would continue supporting efforts to bring Libya’s eastern and western administrations together under a single Libyan framework, while Turkish and Libyan officials discussed measures to strengthen security and stability.
International and regional efforts have sought to establish unified institutions and pave the way for lasting political stability.
Against that backdrop, Ankara’s contacts with figures from different Libyan institutions have become an important component of its engagement with the country.
The latest Kalin-Zubi meeting underscores the breadth of that engagement, linking security cooperation with the broader effort to help Libya achieve political and military unity.

zuckoff uses bluetooth to let you know when smart glasses are nearby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:15:18 UTC
17:15:18 KST

ZUCKOFF RECOGNIZES CAMERA GLASSES THROUGH BLUETOOTH
Created by Polish developer Paweł Szydłowski, ZuckOff is an independent app that makes the otherwise invisible presence of camera-equipped glasses more legible through Bluetooth. The app listens for signals emitted by devices including Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, and Snap Spectacles, alerting users when compatible hardware is nearby while showing the evidence behind each detection.
As cameras and other sensors appear disguised as objects that resemble ordinary eyewear, their technological capabilities can become difficult for people nearby to recognize. ZuckOff approaches that problem at the level of the device’s wireless communication, turning Bluetooth advertisements into information that can be inspected on a phone, watch, or computer.
image by Sadjad Frogh
Paweł Szydłowski’s APP SHOWS USERS WHY A DEVICE is FLAGGED
ZuckOff exposes the wireless signals that can indicate the presence of a potentially recording device, responding to a particular ambiguity created by camera glasses. Paweł Szydłowski’s app currently identifies Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta through their manufacturer signature, as well as Snap Spectacles. It can also record other Bluetooth devices it encounters, including display glasses and headsets such as Quest and Vision Pro, but does not flag those devices as camera glasses.
The app assigns confidence levels, including possible, likely, and strong. A Ray-Ban Meta detection, for example, can show its manufacturer ID, the advertised service, signal strength, approximate distance, and other identifying information. Users can therefore inspect the reasoning rather than receiving an unexplained notification, making ZuckOff an interface for interpreting an increasingly dense wireless environment.
image courtesy of Meta
seeing why a device was flagged
The app’s Sightings interface keeps a record of every Bluetooth device heard nearby, whether or not it is identified as camera glasses. Individual devices can be followed through a signal timeline, creating a record of when they appeared and how their signal changed. Users who own compatible glasses can also mark their own devices, preventing them from repeatedly generating alerts.
The interface deliberately communicates uncertainty. Signal strength can suggest proximity but cannot establish direction, while Bluetooth advertising cannot reveal whether a camera is actively being used.
ZuckOff also has limitations. Camera glasses are easiest to detect when they power on, pair, or leave their case, and most continue broadcasting while they are being worn. Some standalone models can remain silent, however. This means that not detecting a pair does not necessarily mean there are no camera glasses nearby, while detecting one does not mean that its camera is being used.
The app does not require an account, and users can export the full Bluetooth log as a CSV. Its detection rules are based on real device captures. ZuckOff is asking people to share short scans from camera glasses that are not yet supported, or to lend hardware for testing. The team is also open to working with privacy groups. This means the list of detectable devices can grow as new camera glasses appear. Each new device adds another Bluetooth signature that the app can learn to recognize.

The US deported more than 25,000 migrants to third countries under secret agreements - investigation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

The US deported more than 25,000 migrants to third countries under secret agreements - investigation
Kyiv • UNN
An investigation by Forbidden Stories uncovered secret US agreements with 35 countries on the deportation of more than 25,000 migrants. $410 million was allocated for the program.
The United States deported more than 25,000 people under secret agreements with 35 countries that agreed to accept migrants who have no ties whatsoever to those states, according to an investigation by Forbidden Stories. Agence France-Presse (AFP) reports this, writes UNN.
Details
As the publication notes, after U.S. President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, Washington began concluding agreements with developing countries to accept migrants who cannot legally be sent back to their countries of origin.
The Forbidden Stories investigation found that the U.S. administration had allocated $410 million to be paid directly to countries accepting deportees or to UN agencies to facilitate their relocation.
According to data collected by Forbidden Stories together with a consortium of international journalists, as of August 31, 2026, at least 25,447 people had already been deported to third countries.
The vast majority—about 20,000 people—were sent to Mexico. The rest were distributed among 27 other countries in Latin America, Africa, and the Pacific region, while agreements had already been finalized with seven more countries.
The terms of these agreements vary, including regarding citizens of which countries may be deported and whether people with criminal convictions may be accepted.
An AFP investigation conducted earlier this year found that Washington was using visa bans and restrictions against African countries to pressure them into agreeing to accept deportees.
Lawyers told the publication that deportees end up in a "legal black hole": they are held without being charged in countries with which they have no ties whatsoever and where they have very few or no rights at all.
Forbidden Stories reported that as many as 49 of the 54 African countries had been approached with an offer to accept deportees from third countries.
According to Forbidden Stories, most of the negotiations and payments were handled by a little-known unit of the U.S. Department of State—the Office of Remigration, established in May 2025.

31 years ago, Ganesha ‘drank’ milk and India went viral: How a September 21, 1995 claim spread from temple to temple, crossed borders within hours and became a global story without social media
31 years ago, Ganesha ‘drank’ milk and India went viral: How a September 21, 1995 claim spread from temple to temple, crossed borders within hours and became a global story without social media
Smita Mishra / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Sep 21, 2026, 13:42 IST
Thirty-one years ago, on September 21, 1995, I came home from school to find that something was strangely different. My aunt, who would diligently wait for me every day and was always the one to serve me lunch, was missing. She was more than just the person who fed me; she would sit with me, tell me interesting stories and make the afternoon feel special.I looked for her everywhere. Finally, the housemaid arrived with my plate of dal and rice and casually told me, “Didi has gone to feed milk to Lord Ganesha.”I was puzzled. What did she mean? After lunch, I called a friend from the landline. She had the same story. Her mother, too, was not at home. By evening, my aunt returned, visibly excited, and told my mother, who had just come back from work, what she had seen.“I took a spoon of milk to feed Ganesha, and the milk disappeared,” she said. My mother looked at her in disbelief. “Really?” she asked. “Really. I saw it with my own eyes,” she insisted, quite overwhelmed with emotions.The news spread fast, Ganesha idols were apparently drinking milk. There were no smartphones, social media platforms, WhatsApp groups or instant notifications to amplify the news.
India’s internet had only just arrived, television was still dominated by Doordarshan, and newspapers remained the primary source of next-day news. Yet, within hours, temples were overflowing, milk was disappearing from shops and the story had travelled beyond India.
The incident got global coverage
The morning India heard an extraordinary claimIt was not the age of viral news. In fact viral was the world synonymous with just one thing-the infectious disease of influenza. There was no way to immediately search the internet, watch a viral video or check social media posts from another city. Then what caused the spread of this frenzy? According to a contemporary Times of India report preserved in the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research's Bombay archive, Mumbai and several other parts of India were swept by reports that Ganesha idols were accepting milk offerings. The report described the news as spreading “like wildfire” as thousands of devotees rushed to temples. Astrologer Jayant Salgaonkar was quoted saying, “I myself witnessed it.” Times of India report preserved by TIFRThe crucial point was that people did not merely hear the claim. They went to temples and tried it for themselves. Devotees carried spoons filled with milk towards the trunks or mouths of Ganesha idols, and many reported seeing the milk disappear.India was still largely offlineThe episode becomes even more extraordinary when viewed against India's technological landscape in 1995. Public internet access had only just been launched by VSNL in August that year. According to historical International Telecommunication Union data, internet use in India in 1995 stood at just 0.026% of the population.Telephones were also far from universal. India had approximately 11.98 million fixed telephone connections in 1995, equivalent to around 1.24 fixed lines per 100 people.This meant that the mechanisms of mass communication were fundamentally different from those available today. A person could call a relative, but there was no instant group messaging system through which hundreds of people could receive the same information simultaneously. News moved through conversations, local networks, religious communities, radio, television and newspapers. And yet the Ganesha story moved extraordinarily quickly.Not an age of 24-hour newsIt would be inaccurate to suggest that India had only Doordarshan in 1995. The country's television landscape had already begun changing. Zee TV had launched in 1992, Star TV had entered the Indian market in 1991 and Sony Entertainment Television launched in 1995. But the explosion of private, round-the-clock news channels that would later transform India's news culture was still years away.Doordarshan nevertheless remained hugely influential. An academic study citing Ministry of Information & Broadcasting figures puts India's television universe in 1995 at approximately 40 million television households and 250 million viewers.There was therefore a very different relationship between an event and the news cycle. Newspapers generally reported what had happened the previous day, television had scheduled programming rather than today's constant breaking-news stream, and there was no digital ecosystem continuously refreshing itself. The Ganesha phenomenon had to travel through people before it could become a mass media story.When the milk became part of the storyThe reports quickly produced visible consequences. A contemporaryLos Angeles Times report published on September 23, 1995, said millions of Indians had rushed to test the phenomenon and reported that milk had “virtually disappeared” from shops in New Delhi by noon.
There was a milk shortage nationwide
That detail captures the extraordinary feedback loop created by the phenomenon. People heard that Ganesha was drinking milk, went out to buy milk, took it to temples and offered it to idols. The resulting rush itself became evidence of how seriously the story was being taken.Contemporary reports described crowds gathering at temples, with devotees carrying spoons, bowls and containers of milk.From one temple to the worldThe most remarkable part of the episode was perhaps how quickly it crossed India's borders. Reports soon emerged from Hindu communities in Britain, the United States, Canada, Nepal and elsewhere. A contemporary Los Angeles Times reportnoted that the reports had spread beyond India to Hindu communities in other countries, including Britain and Los Angeles.Hinduism Today later recalled receiving telephone calls and fax messages from different parts of the world reporting similar experiences. Its contemporary account provides a fascinating glimpse into how an international religious community communicated before email, social media and messaging apps became commonplace.The technology may appear primitive by today's standards, but the human network was remarkably effective. Someone in India could telephone a relative abroad, that person could contact a local temple, and within hours another community could be trying the same experiment.The story did not need an algorithm to travel. It travelled through relationships.The science behind the phenomenonAs the reports spread, scientists and sceptics began examining what devotees were observing. One of the principal scientific explanations involved capillary action and surface tension. Rather than the idol literally consuming the milk, the liquid could move along the surface of the material, creating the appearance that it was being absorbed by the idol.For devotees, however, the scientific explanation did not necessarily invalidate what they had experienced. The same physical observation could be interpreted through very different frameworks: as a religious sign by believers, as a scientific phenomenon by researchers, and as an extraordinary mass social event by journalists.
People queuing up in temples for offering milk to Lord Ganesha
What made the episode so unusualLooking back from the age of smartphones, the 1995 episode is remarkable not simply because of what people believed they were seeing, but because of how quickly the information travelled.India's public internet had only just begun. Fixed telephone connections were limited, television was expanding but had not yet become the 24-hour news environment of today, and newspapers operated on a fundamentally different news cycle. Yet within hours, a local report had become a national phenomenon and then an international story.A telephone call led to another telephone call. A conversation at one temple led to another. Newspapers carried the story forward, television added another layer of coverage and international media transformed what had begun as a local religious phenomenon into a global news story.The first great pre-social-media viral phenomenon?Calling the Ganesha milk episode the world's first viral phenomenon would be too absolute. Stories travelled internationally long before 1995, through newspapers, radio, television and word of mouth.But the episode offers a remarkable case study of mass communication before the social-media era. Millions of people participated in the same rapidly spreading story without having access to the tools that today make such mass participation almost instantaneous.
That is what makes September 21, 1995, worth remembering 31 years later. The question is no longer simply whether Ganesha idols were actually drinking milk. The episode has another story to tell, about technology, faith, communication and human networks.In 2026, information can travel around the world in seconds. In 1995, it travelled from person to person, from telephone to telephone, from temple to temple and eventually from newspaper to newspaper.And somehow, by the end of that extraordinary day, a spoonful of milk had become a global story.(All images are AI Generated)

Injuries reported after blast at Syrian military site in S. Aleppo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:11:00 UTC
17:11:00 KST

At least four civilians were injured and three families evacuated early Monday after a series of powerful explosions at an ammunition depot at a Syrian military site near al-Eis in southern Aleppo province, according to preliminary reports.
More than 10 blasts were reported at the site, with the explosions heard across parts of western and northern Aleppo countryside. The blasts briefly subsided before resuming, accompanied by heavy flames at the site, locals authorities said.
The Civil Defense, operating under the Emergency and Disaster Management Ministry, said one civilian was injured by shrapnel, while two others suffered temporary breathing difficulties. Another civilian was injured in a traffic accident while trying to leave the area.
"Military police have deployed in the area surrounding the site of the explosion to secure it in cooperation with the relevant authorities, while military engineering units have begun securing the site and surrounding areas," the ministry said, according to SANA.
Emergency teams later entered the area after continuing explosions initially prevented ambulances and rescue crews from reaching the site. They evacuated the four injured people and three families living near the location, while emergency teams remained on alert.
Aleppo's local security forces placed personnel on alert and closed the Aleppo-Damascus highway and roads leading to the site as a precaution. Authorities also established a security cordon around the area and barred traffic and civilians from approaching.
Aleppo Gov. Azzam al-Gharib urged residents to remain in their homes and avoid approaching or gathering near the site. He said hospitals, ambulances and emergency services were on standby and called on residents to rely on official information and avoid circulating unconfirmed reports.
The Emergency and Disaster Management Ministry warned residents in al-Eis and surrounding areas against approaching the site because of the risk of shrapnel, unexploded ordnance and other hazardous objects.
"Due to explosions occurring in the al-Eis area and its surroundings south of Aleppo, we urge everyone not to leave their homes and not to approach the sites of the explosions," al-Gharib said in a statement.
He added that "hospitals and ambulance and emergency teams are on standby, while the relevant authorities are monitoring the situation on the ground and responding to any emergency."
The ministry's Early Warning and Preparedness Department advised residents to move to a safe area when possible without putting themselves at risk, keep roads clear for emergency teams and shelter inside buildings if they could not leave safely. It also urged residents to stay away from windows, doors, glass, rooftops and other exposed areas.
Authorities were investigating the cause of the explosions.
The explosion came amid a series of blasts at military weapons and ammunition sites in Syria in recent weeks, including incidents in Idlib and Deir el-Zour.
At least 14 people were killed and 11 wounded on Sept. 9, when an explosion ripped through a temporary storage for weapons and war remnants in the northwestern province of Idlib.
