Xiplomacy: Five years on, China's Global Development Initiative delivers tangible progress
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:12:50 CST
12:12:50 KST

by Xinhua writers Liu Bowei, He Yixuan
BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- "Stay committed to putting development first, and open up the prospects for shared prosperity." At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek this year, Chinese President Xi Jinping once again called on countries to make development a priority.
In September 2021, Xi proposed the Global Development Initiative (GDI) at the 76th session of the UN General Assembly, bringing a vision of shared development to the global agenda and calling for the benefits of development to be more widely shared.
Five years on, the initiative has evolved from a vision into concrete cooperation, with more and more countries joining forces in the pursuit of a better future for all.
FROM VISION TO SHARED ASPIRATION
The GDI was put forward at a critical moment when the global development agenda was facing unprecedented challenges.
In the Sustainable Development Goals Report 2021, the United Nations underscored the scale of the setback: global extreme poverty rose for the first time in more than 20 years, with 119 million to 124 million people pushed back into extreme poverty in 2020, while 101 million children fell below the minimum reading proficiency level.
It was against this background that Xi proposed the development initiative, emphasizing the necessity to put development high on the global macro policy agenda.
The initiative calls for staying committed to development as a priority, to a people-centered approach, to benefits for all, to innovation-driven development, to harmony between man and nature and to results-oriented actions.
"It was both timely and strategically far-sighted. At a time when the international agenda is increasingly dominated by differences and dividing lines, the initiative brings a fundamental question back into focus: how to achieve development and stability and create a dignified future for people," said Serik Korzhumbayev, editor-in-chief of the Delovoy Kazakhstan newspaper.
In January 2022, when the Group of Friends of the GDI was launched at the UN Headquarters in New York, delegates from more than 100 countries attended the meeting, voicing support for the initiative and willingness to join the group.
"Development holds the key to people's well-being." Over the past five years, Xi has continued to promote the implementation of the initiative at the SCO, BRICS, the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, the G20 and other multilateral platforms, calling for building political consensus to ensure everyone values development and all countries pursue cooperation together.
"This is where I see particular value in the GDI: it links development with people, and national needs with the shared responsibility of the international community," Essam Sharaf, former Egyptian prime minister and founder and chairman of the Sharaf Foundation for Sustainable Development, told Xinhua.
As of now, nearly 100 countries and international and regional organizations have signed cooperation documents with China on the initiative, while the Group of Friends of the GDI has grown to 88 countries.
Reflecting on the GDI's progress over the past five years, Abdulaziz Alshaabani, a Saudi researcher at the Al Riyadh Center for Political and Strategic Studies, said the initiative "has evolved from a Chinese proposal into concrete mechanisms for international cooperation."
"One noticeable change since the launch of the GDI is that more and more countries have begun to place development and related issues higher on the international cooperation agenda," said Alshaabani.
PROGRESS IN ACTION
In Rwinkwavu, a rural area in Kayonza district of Rwanda's drought-prone Eastern Province, a bank of solar panels enclosed by a blue fence stand among the hills. The solar-powered borehole is one of 200 drilled under a China-funded project benefiting about 110,000 people across the province.
Magnifique Habimana, head teacher of GS Rwinkwavu school, one of the beneficiaries, told Xinhua that "the project came at the right time to address a serious water problem."
"It was a very big inconvenience to the school in terms of sanitation and running costs," said Habimana.
Over the past five years, stories like this have unfolded in communities across the developing world. While projects involving infrastructure, energy and water have made everyday life easier, agricultural cooperation has expanded to more than 140 countries and regions, with over 1,000 agricultural technologies shared with developing countries and more than 14,000 technicians trained in hybrid rice technology.
"For developing countries, development is not an abstract political formula. It means new roads and railways, reliable energy supplies, modern enterprises, jobs, education, digital connectivity, food security, access to technology and better prospects for the younger generation," Korzhumbayev told Xinhua.
Backed by more than 23 billion U.S. dollars in funds it has mobilized, the initiative has implemented over 1,800 "small and beautiful" projects and trained more than 200,000 professionals, delivering concrete benefits to local communities in over 120 countries.
At the SCO Bishkek Summit, Xi announced plans to implement 100 technological cooperation projects with other SCO countries in the next three years and nurture more green industry talents through China-SCO cooperation, building on his pledge a year earlier at the SCO Tianjin Summit that "China plans to implement 100 'small and beautiful' livelihood projects in member states with such need."
A defining feature of the GDI is its emphasis on action and tangible results, said Hussein Askary, vice-chairman of the Belt and Road Institute in Sweden. "China not only discusses development issues, but also takes concrete action to advance common development."
A PATH FORWARD
Five years on, development remains as an urgent priority as ever, as geopolitical conflicts, economic uncertainty and climate change compound the pressing challenges facing the international community.
The latest UN data show that only 36 percent of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets with available trend data are on track or making moderate progress, and 15 percent have even regressed below their 2015 baselines.
"This is precisely why, in my view, the significance of the GDI has actually increased over the past five years," said Emin Gasimov, director of Azerbaijan's Center for the Study of China's Global Initiatives, Development and Culture.
While emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), are creating new development opportunities, they also pose a risk of widening existing gaps.
Sharaf noted that the GDI presents a major opportunity to help shape an important principle for the next phase. "The future of technology should not be a future for a limited number of countries, but a shared future for humanity," he said.
Xi has described AI as "a new engine of world economic growth and an accelerator for the shift of growth drivers." As a new round of technological revolution and industrial transformation gathers pace, he has called for bridging the digital and AI divides, so that technological revolution and development achievements can benefit all nations.
In July, during the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in Shanghai, an upgraded version of MAZU was officially handed over to Djibouti, marking a new step in China-Djibouti cooperation on AI-powered climate resilience.
MAZU, short for multi-hazard, alert, zero-gap and universal, is an AI-driven meteorological early warning platform developed by China and named after the Chinese guardian goddess of the sea.
Currently, MAZU has been deployed on the ground in seven countries and is providing cloud-based services in more than 40 countries, making it an important international public good serving countries across the Global South.
At the 2026 WAIC, Xi announced that China will provide developing countries with 5,000 opportunities in AI training and seminar programs in the next five years, and said that 30 countries can use the AI-powered meteorological warning system to safeguard homes around the world.
Projects such as MAZU offer a stellar example of how digital technologies can support the implementation of the GDI, said Alshaabani. "Its value lies not simply in providing a technology, but in helping countries strengthen their capacity for disaster early warning, risk management and emergency response."
Beyond MAZU, China has been building a broader framework for international AI cooperation, including establishing the World AI Cooperation Organization with 28 other countries and setting up international AI application cooperation centers with major regional and multilateral organizations.
If such emerging technologies can be made more accessible to the Global South, the role of the GDI will expand significantly, Alshaabani told Xinhua. "It will not only help developing countries address today's development challenges, but also help them build the capacity to adapt to future technological change."
"In my view, this is one of the most promising transformations of the GDI: from development assistance to jointly building the capacity to develop. For the Global South, this capacity could become one of the most important resources of the next decade," said Gasimov. ■

Italian Serie A: Frosinone vs. Como

====================================================================================================

Younger Australians face a harder path to wealth, report shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:55:13 UTC
11:55:13 KST

Intergenerational Report charts falling fertility, aging population and housing divide
In short:
Australia's latest Intergenerational Report shows younger generations are working longer and finding it harder to build wealth and buy a home than those before them.
Falling fertility and an aging population are also expected to reshape the economy and put greater pressure on government spending in the next 40 years.
What's next?
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the government is tackling these challenges through housing tax changes and measures to boost Australia's workforce, skills and productivity.
Younger Australians face working longer and struggling more to buy a home without the same early gains in income and wealth experienced by the generations before them.
The latest Intergenerational Report released on Monday by Treasurer Jim Chalmers has laid out how an aging population and falling birth rate would reshape Australia's economy in the next 40 years.
Fertility is expected to fall to just 1.34 children per woman by 2065, which has sparked debate about what, if anything, could be done to persuade younger Australians to have more children.
The report, which is produced by Treasury every three years, found Australians born in the 1990s and after are better educated and likely to live and work longer, but the traditional path of accumulating wealth through home ownership has become harder.
The economy is expected to more than double in size in the next 40 years, with living standards continuing to rise, and the long-term budget outlook has had "significant" improvements since 2023.
But an older growing population, weaker productivity growth and rising costs in areas such as defence and health will put increasing pressure on government finances.
Handing down the report, Mr Chalmers said the global and generational risks faced by Australia were "serious" but argued the country was well-placed to deal with them.
"Australia's opportunities are endless," he said.
"Every page … [of the report] justifies, validates, and I hope one day vindicates the difficult decisions that we've taken reforming the housing market and reforming the tax system."
Fewer home owners now
There would be about 250,000 more home owners aged between 25 and 34 if ownership rates had held up at 1981 levels.
House prices have risen about 400 per cent since 1999, which was more than twice as fast as the average income.
Australia is also building homes at roughly half the productivity of 30 years ago.
Mr Chalmers was asked if the Australian dream of owning house with a backyard and Hills hoist was dead.
"Not on our watch," he said.
"We've taken some very substantial political risks in order to meet our intergenerational obligations and responsibilities.
"The pointiest part of that … is really the housing market, which has locked young people out for too long."
Treasury said population growth and smaller households have increased demand for housing, while weak construction and productivity has constrained the supply response.
The report also specifically identified investor tax concessions, like negative gearing and the 50 per cent capital gains tax (CGT) discount as contributing to the problem.
"These tax advantages have increased the share of housing owned by investors, at the expense of Australians looking to buy a home," it said.
Treasury noted between 80 to 90 per cent of investor housing lending since 2019 had gone towards the purchase of existing housing stock rather than new dwellings.
Young Australians not achieving early wealth gains
The new report found fertility had fallen in Australia due to "complex economic, social and cultural factors" including more time in education, and career establishment, living with parents longer, as well as delayed partnership and childbearing.
Those demographic shifts have occurred as the economic fortunes of younger Australians have started to diverge from the generations before them.
Treasury said younger millennials were reaching their 30s without experiencing the early-career real disposable income increases compared with those born in the 1980s.
The average real household net worth rose from $0.5 million in 1993-94 to more than $1.3 million in 2019-20, but much of this wealth growth was concentrated among older households.
It is a trend that has been emerging for decades, with only about two-thirds of Australians born in the 1960s onwards doing better than their parents, compared with 80 per cent of people born in the 1950s.
Birth rates spark baby bonus debate
Australia's declining fertility rate has prompted discussion about the return of financial incentives to encourage more people to have children.
Mr Chalmers said more people were having kids later and that there were fewer with three or more children.
"I do not and will not give free advice about these very personal decisions that [people] make about whether to start a family and when to start a family," he said.
Mr Chalmers said the government's responsibility was to make it easier for people to make that choice.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said Australians who did have children should be supported.
"That can be through our investments in early education and care, our three-day guarantee, our extending (paid parental leave) … ensuring that dads or second parents can take it, putting super on that so that people don't have that economic hit when they have children," she said.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has called for greater support for families but said he did not think a revival of the "baby bonus" was the right way to encourage more Australians to have children.
"I think anything that we should do should be more … designed around the idea that if you … work for yourself, if you're helping yourself, we'll help you some more," he said.
"The baby bonus, it was just 'Here's some cash', without you having to put in the effort as well."
Australians to work for longer
Australia has more people participating in the workforce than Treasury expected thanks in large part to women working at increasing rates.
Female workforce participation is expected to continue rising until the mid-2040s, with the gap between men and women shrinking from 7.7 points now to a projected 5.4 points by 2065-66.
Older Australians are also working substantially more than previous generations, with participation among people aged over 65 rising 9.5 per cent since the 2002 Intergenerational Report.
Since 2023, an extra 1 per cent of Australians have continued to work beyond the age of 65, which the report has linked to the physical aspects of modern jobs and changes to retirement settings.
In his speech, Mr Chalmers said an aging population means a proportionately smaller workforce, and broader demand for health and aged care.
He said the number of Australians over 85 will triple by 2066, and a third of new healthcare spending over the next 40 years will be because of aging.
But he said Australia's workforce participation would continue growing while most OECD countries would see a decline.
Migration is also helping Australia maintain a workforce, with Treasury expecting the actual working-age population to continue growing due to overseas arrivals.
AI has potential to help economy grow
Despite worse demographics, Treasury now thinks Australia will spend less, run smaller deficits and carry substantially less debt than was forecast in 2023.
Looking at the budget long term, officials have projected Australia would run a surplus from 2029-30 for twenty years before aging and other pressures would push it back into deficit.
Health would remain a significant spending pressure, rising from 4 per cent to 6.2 per cent of GDP.
Public hospital funding is expected to account for more than 60 per cent of additional Commonwealth health spending.
At the same time, Australia's transition to electric vehicles (EVs) is expected to have a significant impact on budget revenue as fewer motorists would pay the fuel excise charged on petrol and diesel.
The net fuel excise was projected to collapse to just 0.1 per cent of GDP by 2065-66, which is expected to drive the case for some form of EV road user charge to replace it.
Australia's productivity growth is expected to remain below its historical average, however Treasury said artificial intelligence (AI) presented a major opportunity to lift economic output.
AI is expected to be a significant force impacting Australia's economy in the next 40 years, but the potential benefit would depend on how effectively the country adopts and takes advantage of the technology.

Xi rolls into Trump summit with China’s trade engine roaring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:54:01 UTC
11:54:01 KST

News analysis
Xi rolls into Trump summit with China’s trade engine roaring
BEIJING – In the four months since the leaders of the two global superpowers last met, Chinese President Xi Jinping has overseen a surge in China’s trade with the world while US President Donald Trump has struggled with falling approval ratings at home.
That shift in fortunes has tempered expectations for their summit in Washington this week, analysts say, with Xi in no rush to make concessions and Trump constrained by a costly war with Iran that has hurt both his popularity and Americans’ wallets.
While thorny issues such as Taiwan may surface, the main focus of the Sept 24 meeting is whether the leaders will signal an extension of the 2025 trade truce that averted a major shock to the global economy.
“Xi is not really looking for anything tangible. He wants to extend the gentleman’s agreement with Trump so that China has time to fortify itself,” said Jon Czin, a foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution who formerly served as China director at the US National Security Council.
White House officials have sought to downplay the potential for major breakthroughs.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng helmed preparatory talks in New York on Sept 20 aimed at teeing up some potential agreements on artificial intelligence guardrails and trade in non-sensitive products.
That is a far cry from Trump’s vow when he returned to office in 2025 to use tariffs to address a trade imbalance with China that was “killing” the US.
But since agreeing to the truce with Xi in October, his attention has been divided among a myriad of other foreign policy battles, from the wars in Iran and Ukraine to disputes with Europe over free speech.
China has faced its own challenges, such as slowing domestic demand and a protracted property crisis, but the export juggernaut that Trump sought to tame has kept roaring in what economists are increasingly referring to as China Shock 2.0.
China’s global trade surplus is on pace to top US$1 trillion (S$1.28 trillion) for a second straight year.
While US efforts to curb the cheap parcels that online retailers such as Shein and Temu rely on have worked, more than half of the roughly 6,500 product categories China sold to the US so far in 2026 have grown compared with 2025.
A delegation of Chinese business leaders, potentially including firms facing US regulatory scrutiny as they seek greater market access, is set to accompany Xi to Washington.
The Trump administration “thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions, and that did not occur”, said Scott Kennedy, an expert on the US-China economic relationship at Washington-based think-tank CSIS.
“Now, this is Xi Jinping’s world, and we’re all living in it.”
Taiwan and trade wins
If Xi is in the driver’s seat as analysts suggest, it will further unnerve US allies in Asia who expect the Chinese leader to push Trump to soften Washington’s support for Taiwan, the democratically governed island claimed by Beijing.
When they met in Beijing in May, Xi repeatedly asked Trump about Taiwan, including about arms sales and Washington’s resolve to defend the island, the US leader told reporters.
Trump described a pending US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan as a “negotiating chip” with Beijing.
Some officials in Taipei and Tokyo worry he may be tempted to cash in that chip for political wins ahead of November’s midterm election, which could prove challenging for his Republican Party.
These could include Chinese purchases of Boeing jets or farm goods, or commitments to curb the flow of fentanyl precursor chemicals that have fuelled the US opioid crisis.
“China-US ties have become more transactional,” said Wu Xinbo, a professor at Shanghai’s Fudan University who advises China’s Foreign Ministry.
While Washington may want to prioritise trade talks, for Beijing, the US approach to Taiwan could be key, he said.
“If you accommodate our concern on the Taiwan issue, then we would be willing to accommodate your concerns on other issues, be it law enforcement or on purchases of US agricultural products,” Wu said.
Putting pressure on Iran
Washington also sees Xi as uniquely able to exert pressure on Iran to bring an end to the war that has dragged Trump’s approval rating to the lowest of his political career.
But Xi has shown little inclination to do so. Reuters reported earlier in September that Beijing is selling billions of dollars’ worth of goods to Iran through a sanctions-evasion scheme. China’s Foreign Ministry says it is not aware of such a scheme.
US threats in August of secondary sanctions on countries doing business with Iran, which Bessent called an “Economic D-Day”, appear not to have yet been wielded against Tehran’s largest trading partner.
That is more evidence, analysts say, that Trump is eager to keep relations with Xi steady as he focuses his energies elsewhere, an arrangement that also suits the Chinese leader.
“Both Xi and Trump feel it’s quite helpful to have stability in the relationship so that they can focus on more pressing things,” said Ruby Osman, senior geopolitical researcher at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.
“For Trump, that is Iran. For Xi, that is building out China’s domestic resilience for whatever comes after Trump.” REUTERS

Cybercrime feud erupts on dark web as notorious group claims hijack of rival’s website
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:35:00 UTC
11:35:00 KST

Cybercrime feud erupts on dark web as notorious group claims hijack of rival’s website
WASHINGTON – One of the world’s best-known cybercrime groups said on Sept 20 it had hijacked one of its chief rivals’ sites on the dark web, bringing what it said was a long-simmering feud out into the open.
ShinyHunters, a digital extortion group known for aggressive data theft campaigns, said it broke into the dark web site of cybercrime gang cl0p on Sept 18 after discovering a vulnerability in cl0p’s software and using it to establish wide-ranging control over the group’s infrastructure.
“We basically own them now,” ShinyHunters said in an online chat with Reuters.
Cl0p did not respond to repeated messages seeking comment. The group’s dark web site was unreachable when Reuters tried to access it on Sept 20. On Sept 19 it displayed the words, “Domain Seized By ShinyHunters”, according to a screenshot preserved by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch.
Two cybersecurity experts told Reuters the clash appeared to be genuine.
“Street beefs on the dark web are a real thing,” said Brandon Parsons, a threat intelligence manager with Minnesota-based Ascent Solutions.
Joe Roosen, the senior director of security research at Texas-based SpyCloud, said that he had never seen one cybercrime group take another head-on so openly. “This was a twist for sure,” he said. “It is rare I get to see these criminals fight each other.”
Oracle software exploit clash
ShinyHunters said it had been at loggerheads with cl0p over the alleged theft in 2025 of a software exploit taking advantage of what was then an unknown flaw in Oracle’s E-Business Suite (EBS).
Such “zero days” – so-called because cybersecurity teams have had zero days to fix them – are particularly treasured by hackers because they can be used to gain sweeping access to vulnerable networks.
Cl0p, a Russian-speaking cybercrime gang, used the EBS vulnerability to steal data from what a Google analyst estimated was more than 100 companies, but ShinyHunters told Reuters it had discovered the zero day first.
As the dispute festered, cl0p threatened to reveal the identities of several of its rival group’s members, according to ShinyHunters.
ShinyHunters in turn threatened to reveal the details of cl0p’s internal workings.
Reuters could not immediately establish the veracity of ShinyHunters’ account of the feud.
Cl0p is counted as one of the most prolific and innovative cybercrime groups, largely because of its skill in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in enterprise software.
In 2023, cl0p leveraged a bug in MOVEit file management software to steal data on tens of millions of people from more than 600 companies. In August, it claimed to have stolen large volumes of data from nearly 50 companies worldwide, including Philips, Shell, Fiserv and GE.
ShinyHunters is similarly prolific. It drew media attention in April for its claim to have stolen millions of business records from video game developer Rockstar Games, the maker of the Grand Theft Auto series, and for a hack in May centred on education tool Canvas that caused widespread disruption across US schools.
Earlier in September, AI company Anthropic said it had caught ShinyHunters-linked hackers trying to use its tools. REUTERS

Migration to keep Australia growing as population turning point approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:30:03 UTC
11:30:03 KST

In brief
- Australia's population is projected to reach 39.3 million by 2065-66, despite deaths overtaking births.
- Economic growth is forecast to slow, while AI and the energy transition reshape the economy.
Australia is on track to record more deaths than births by the 2060s as the nation's fertility rate falls to a new low, the latest Intergenerational Report (IGR) has forecast.
However, Australia's population is still projected to grow to 39.3 million by 2065-66, driven by net overseas migration (NOM), giving the country what the report describes as greater "demographic resilience" than nations such as Germany, Italy and South Korea, where deaths already outnumber births.
Other forecasts include Australia's economy growing by an annual average of 2 per cent over the next 40 years, per capita income being 55 per cent higher, and life expectancy reaching 89.5 years for women and 86.1 years for men by 2065-66.
Published by the federal government every three years since 2002, the IGR outlines Australia's economic and budgetary outlook over the next 40 years.
The forecasts in the reports are predictions, some of which have fallen far off the mark, such as the first report projecting that Australia's population would reach 25 million in 2042 — a milestone reached 24 years earlier in 2018.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The latest report, published on Monday, predicts the most "consequential transformations" over the next 40 years include artificial intelligence, geopolitical fragmentation, the energy transition, population ageing and Australia moving further towards a services-based economy.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers remained positive about Australia's ability to confront future challenges, saying the country was better placed than comparable nations.
But he warned of the dangers of "accelerating change".
"If people are unmoored economically, generationally, they feel disconnected from, and disregarded in, our politics. At worst that's what we're seeing now, at best it’s what's at stake," he said in a speech to the Australian National University on Monday.
Demographics
Australia's population growth is expected to fall from an annual average of 1.4 per cent over the past 40 years to 0.9 per cent per year through to 2065–66.
For the first time in an IGR, deaths are projected to outnumber deaths by the 2060s.
But Australia's population is expected to continue to grow, reaching 39.3 million by 2065-66, largely driven by overseas migration.
The IGR assumes a long-term NOM rate of 235,000 per year; however, the Opposition and One Nation have promised a far lower number if they are in power.
The median age is projected to rise from 38.6 in 2025-26 to 45 by 2062-63. The number of Australians aged 65 and over will almost double, while the number of those aged 85 and over will almost triple.
Australia's fertility rate is projected to decline to 1.34 children per woman by 2065–66 — down from the 2023 IGR assumption of 1.62 — due to delayed family formation and smaller family sizes.
Fertility rates have now been below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman for more than 50 years.
Australians are expected to continue to enjoy some of the longest life expectancies in the world, with life expectancy projected to reach 89.5 years for women and 86.1 years for men by 2065-66.
Unlike many other developed countries, the IGR projects Australia's working-age population (15 to 64) will continue to grow due to migration.
The report notes the median age of a migrant today is 26, compared to 38 for the resident population, helping slow Australia's ageing population.
Capital cities will continue to absorb most of the population increase, growing at twice the rate of regional areas.
The economy
Australia's economic growth — which has averaged 3 per cent per year for the past 40 years — is predicted to slow to 2 per cent, largely due to Australia's ageing population.
Despite slower growth, Australia's economy is expected to be more than twice as large by 2065-66 as it is today.
Living standards are also expected to rise, with real per capita gross national income to grow by 55 per cent.
The pathway to future productivity remains "uncertain" and will depend on major transitions and on Australia's ability to respond to technological progress, with the IGR assuming a long-term productivity growth rate of 1.2 per cent per year.
The labour force participation rate is projected to peak at 67.7 per cent in 2039-40, then fall to 64.7 per cent by 2065-66.
The unemployment rate is projected to settle at 4.25 per cent over the long run.
The average weekly hours worked per employee is expected to decline from 31.4 hours today to 30.6 hours by 2065-66, reflecting a shift to more part-time work.
Australia's fiscal outlook will be challenged by rising demand for government services, pressure on the tax base and a slowing economy.
Health and aged care, the National Disability Insurance Scheme, defence, and interest payments on debt are expected to drive the majority of government spending.
Spending is expected to exceed revenue over the next 40 years, resulting in underlying cash deficits.
Australia's budget position is expected to improve over the medium term, with the underlying cash balance to reach a deficit of 0.3 per cent of GDP by 2036-37 before widening to 18 per cent of GDP by 2065-66.
However, the IGR notes this is an improvement over the 2023 forecast, which predicted a larger deficit.
Despite the challenges, the report is optimistic about Australia's position.
"The Australian economy is one of the best placed to benefit from the major transitions that will unfold over coming decades," it states.
"We have a resilient economy, a highly skilled workforce, a stronger and more sustainable budget position than most advanced economies and a younger population compared to other comparable nations."
The challenges
The IGR notes the global economy is "experiencing a period of remarkable change" which is only accelerating.
It outlines six major transitions expected to shape Australia's future: the AI revolution, geopolitical fragmentation, the energy transition, the ageing and care economy, the industrial transformation and inter-generational equity.
Artificial intelligence risks increasing inequality if the economic gains are not shared among everyone. However, it could reduce inequality by lowering consumer costs and making certain expertise and services more widely available.
"The overall effect will depend on factors such as how AI capabilities evolve, which workers and industries are most affected, how the technology diffuses and how society responds," the report says.
The report notes the energy transition is well underway as the country moves to a net zero economy by 2050. Australia has the potential to become a "renewable energy superpower" through green exports, such as critical minerals, renewable hydrogen and green metals.
"If Australia seizes the export opportunities associated with the net zero transition and becomes a global renewable energy superpower, green exports could be $68 billion higher in 2050 than would otherwise be the case," it states.
Geopolitical fragmentation is another factor, with the report noting there were eight conflicts between countries as of 2025 — the highest level since World War Two.
It says strategic competition is increasing between major powers, with global trade becoming less predictable as governments prioritise security.
"The government is preparing for a more uncertain world by better understanding where vulnerabilities exist, how they could affect the economy and where resilience measures may be warranted," the paper states.
Australia's ageing population is driving a major industrial transformation toward the care economy, increasing demand for health services while placing long-term pressure on labour supply and public finances.
The IGR notes younger generations face mounting barriers to home ownership, driven by supply challenges and generous tax concessions to investors.
However, they will benefit from a maturing superannuation system, which will become the primary source of retirement income and reduce reliance on the aged pension.
"Nonetheless, without reform, the long-term pressures on housing, the tax system and from an ageing population will intensify concerns about intergenerational equity and risk eroding Australia’s strong democratic and social cohesion as well as economic security," it states.

Former Kremlin political prisoner Mykola Karpiuk killed in action
As reported by Ukrinform, several politicians and bloggers, including politician Artur Palatnyi, public figure Yurii Honcharenko and former SSU Deputy Head Viktor Yahun, reported his death on social media.
“Mykola Karpiuk has been killed... (...) This is a loss that cannot be measured or described in words. A man who devoted his entire life to Ukraine, who never chased fame, money or positions. A man who endured torture in a Russian prison. He was abducted in 2014 because they understood his importance to Ukraine’s national movement,” Yurii Honcharenko said on Facebook.
Viktor Yahun wrote on Facebook that Mykola Karpiuk was one of those people for whom Ukraine was not just a word, but part of life itself.
“He made his choice long ago and remained faithful to it under any circumstances. He went through a great deal of hardship. What could have broken another person did not break him. He remained true to himself – straightforward, principled and caring,” Yahun said.
Artur Palatnyi also reported Karpiuk’s death. He said he knew him personally and described him as a man who had devoted his life to the struggle for Ukraine.
As reported, on September 7, 2019, Ukraine and Russia conducted a 35-for-35 prisoner exchange. Eleven Ukrainians who had been illegally convicted returned home: Oleh Sentsov, Roman Sushchenko, Mykola Karpiuk, Oleksandr Kolchenko, Volodymyr Balukh, Stanislav Klykh, Oleksii Sizonovych, Pavlo Hryb, Edem Bekirov, Yevhen Panov and Artur Panov, as well as 24 sailors who had been captured by Russia near the Kerch Strait in November 2018.
On May 26, 2016, a court in Chechnya sentenced Karpiuk and Klykh to 22.5 and 20 years in prison, respectively. They were accused of killing Russian servicemen in Grozny in 1994–1995.
According to the Russian investigators’ version, Klykh and Karpiuk were members of the UNA-UNSO organization and, in late 1994 and early 1995, fought against Russian federal forces as part of the armed formations of the self-proclaimed Chechen Republic of Ichkeria. At the hearings, the prosecution provided no evidence that Klykh and Karpiuk had been in Chechnya during that period.

Hong Kong, ASEAN sign protocol to amend investment agreement
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:24:53 CST
11:24:53 KST

MANILA/HONG KONG, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The First Protocol to Amend the Investment Agreement between ASEAN and Hong Kong was signed in Manila on Sunday, according to a press release from the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government.
The protocol, signed during the 58th ASEAN Economic Ministers' Meeting and Related Meetings, enables Hong Kong enterprises to enjoy treatment no less favorable than that accorded to local or foreign enterprises in 10 ASEAN member states.
The signing of the protocol is set to bring about legal certainty, enhancing the investment environment and creating more investment flows, according to the Commerce and Economic Development Bureau of the HKSAR government.
ASEAN has been Hong Kong's third-largest destination of outward direct investment for four consecutive years, with a stock of 671.2 billion Hong Kong dollars (about 85.56 billion U.S. dollars), according to the bureau.
An extension of the free trade agreement and investment agreement to Timor-Leste, the 11th member state of ASEAN, is pending ASEAN's internal procedures, according to the press release. ■

Fremantle Dockers great Shaun McManus has been named the club's cup presenter for the AFL grand final.

What's next?
ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.
Fremantle pioneer Shaun McManus will hand over the AFL premiership cup to captain Alex Pearce if the Dockers break through for their maiden flag.
Part of the inaugural 1995 Dockers squad, McManus has been named as Fremantle's cup presenter ahead of Saturday's grand final against back-to-back reigning premiers Brisbane.
Loading Twitter content
The Lions are yet to name their presenter after three-time premiership player Jonathan Brown did so for last year's decider win over Geelong.
McManus was brought to tears when he was told he was the club's cup presenter during a segment on Perth radio this morning.
Peter Bell was named the club's presenter for the eventual 2013 grand final loss to Hawthorn.
Dockers chief Simon Garlick described McManus as a perfect embodiment of the club's values.
McManus began his AFL career as a 19-year-old, going on to play 228 games across 14 seasons.
He captained the team alongside Adrian Fletcher from 2000 to 2001, and played alongside current coach Justin Longmuir.
"Shaun perfectly sums up what a Fremantle person is," Garlick said in a club statement.
"He had a remarkable career as a Fremantle player, but beyond that he has been a champion of this club since our humble beginnings back in 1995.
"Those early foundation years weren't easy, and as a 19-year-old he came in, showed great qualities which resulted in him being named captain at just 24.
"The courage he showed on field speaks for itself, but ever since retiring he's been a passionate and positive influence, someone who purely lives and breathes Freo.
"If we are good enough to get the job done on Saturday, it will be a great moment to see Shaun present the cup to Alex, and his old teammate Justin."
McManus is the ninth-highest game record holder in the club's history and was the second behind Shane Parker to reach the 200-game milestone.
Retiring after the 2008 season, McManus remained at the club as a player development coach and transitioned through various off-field roles.
The 50-year-old became a Dockers life member in 2004.

Miguel Gutierrez (L) of Bayer 04 Leverkusen shoots to score during the German first division of Bundesliga football match between Bayer 04 Leverkusen and RB Leipzig in Leverkusen, Germany, Sept. 20, 2026. (Photo by Ulrich Hufnagel/Xinhua)
BERLIN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Patrik Schick struck just before halftime as Bayer Leverkusen beat RB Leipzig 2-0 in the Bundesliga on Sunday.
Leipzig threatened early at the BayArena, with Neil El Aynaoui and Ezechiel Banzuzi both testing goalkeeper Mark Flekken, and thought it had broken the deadlock in the 34th minute when Romulo released Christopher Nkunku, who finished past Flekken. The goal was ruled out after a VAR review, however, with Romulo adjudged offside in the build-up.
Leverkusen struck shortly before the interval. Miguel Gutierrez sent in a cross and Schick stretched out his right leg to turn the ball home in the 44th minute.
The host improved after the restart and doubled its advantage in the 57th minute. Ibrahim Maza initiated the move before Leipzig failed to clear the danger, allowing Gutierrez to score with a deflected effort.
"With the result we cannot be satisfied, but in the first half we were the better team," Leipzig coach Martin Demichelis said. "Football depends on small details and then the goal does not count. We must learn to play consistently until the last minute."
Leverkusen coach Carles Martinez said his side had read the game well. "We showed a lot of passion and worked well as a team. I think we were the better side," he said.
The victory lifted Leverkusen to fifth on seven points from four matches, while Leipzig dropped to ninth on six. Dortmund leads the standings with 12 points.
After the international break, Leverkusen will visit Mainz on October 10, while Leipzig hosts Eintracht Frankfurt.
Elsewhere on Sunday, promoted Schalke and Elversberg played out a goalless draw in their first Bundesliga meeting, while Paderborn beat Hoffenheim 3-1 to claim its first league victory of the season. ■

Egypt calls Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam 'illegitimate', reserving right to act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:22:07 UTC
11:22:07 KST

Egypt has declared the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) "illegitimate" and reserved the right to take any measures necessary to safeguard its national water security, Irrigation and Water Resources Minister Hani Sewilam announced.
Speaking at a briefing for foreign media in Cairo organised by the State Information Service, Sewilam emphasised that the dam's physical completion does not mean Cairo has accepted a fait accompli or relinquished its historic riparian rights.
Sewilam said the 2015 Declaration of Principles signed by Egypt, Ethiopia, and Sudan established mutual commitments on dam filling, operations, and data exchange.
He affirmed that the accord provides Addis Ababa no mandate for unilateral actions, characterising continued filling and operation without a binding deal as a direct breach.
"The dam is illegitimate and will remain so. Egypt has the right to take appropriate action to remove the harm caused to it," Sewilam said.
"We gave Ethiopia more than one opportunity and tried every possible way to reach understandings, but it did not respond and also violated the Declaration of Principles."
Downstream operational risks
Sewilam warned that uncoordinated operations risk abrupt fluctuations in downstream river flows, posing operational hazards for downstream dams across both Egypt and Sudan.
He added that official statements from Addis Ababa suggest the primary purpose of the project extends beyond electricity generation.
Sewilam noted that Cairo's annual quota of 55.5 billion cubic metres represents barely 2.7 percent of the roughly 2 trillion cubic metres of rainfall across the Nile Basin.
In contrast, Ethiopia received more than 1 trillion cubic metres of rainfall in 2023—including 467 billion cubic metres over its Nile catchment—with renewable water resources reaching 122 billion cubic metres annually.
He noted that Ethiopia has over 18 million hectares of agricultural land compared to Egypt's 4.03 million hectares, with rain-fed Ethiopian farming using 148 billion cubic metres of green water annually alongside 9.68 billion cubic metres of blue water.
While Cairo and Khartoum demand a legally binding agreement covering drought protocols, Addis Ababa maintains that an accord is unnecessary.

Qatar's Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani called Sunday for a regional security framework bringing Gulf countries and Iran together, saying the recent war should serve as a "wake-up call" for the region.
"We are hoping that this war is a wake-up call for everyone that it's time for it to happen," Al Thani said, speaking at the Qatar Economic Forum on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York.
He also noted that the recent regional crisis had tested assumptions about security and stability, describing the crisis as having effects extending beyond the region.
"Iran is our neighbor," Al Thani said. "We need to understand that without having a security framework that brings us all together as Gulf countries with Iran, ensuring that none of us is posing a threat on the other, this region will not just be continuing in the same way as it used to be."
"We have to act together responsibly as a region and to make sure that we are having good relations with Iran and Iran has good relations with the Gulf countries," he added.
Al Thani said Qatar and its regional partners were working toward such an arrangement and expressed hope that the conflict would prompt greater cooperation.
"We are working toward that. Our regional partners believe in this, and we are hoping that this war is a wake-up call for everyone that it's time for it to happen," he said.
He also said that Qatar would continue its mediation efforts, maintain communication channels and work with regional and international partners to reduce tensions and support diplomatic understandings.
On the economy, Al Thani announced the launch of the Doha Investment platform aimed at managing and expanding the Qatar Investment Authority's domestic portfolio and increasing private-sector participation.
Qatar expects to tender about $38.5 billion in infrastructure projects over the next five years, while real estate and hospitality projects are expected to attract $22.5 billion in private investment, bringing the combined potential value above $60 billion.
The remarks came as world leaders gathered in New York for the high-level week of the UN General Assembly, with the war involving the US, Israel and Iran and its regional consequences among the central issues facing Gulf states.

F-35 parts diversion to Hong Kong under probe in US Congress

Diversion of F-35 jet components to Hong Kong under probe in US Congress
- A US House committee is investigating the diversion of sensitive F-35 fighter jet parts from Australia to Hong Kong in 2026, raising security concerns.
- The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin are working to retrieve the components and prevent future incidents but have not disclosed specific details about the parts.
- The shipment included a stealth technology canopy, and the investigation highlights ongoing challenges in tracking F-35 inventory and safeguarding classified components.
AI generated
NEW YORK – A US House committee that oversees defence policy is investigating the diversion in 2026 of potentially sensitive F-35 fighter jet components from Australia to Hong Kong, a spokesperson said.
“The committee is aware of this issue and we’ve received multiple briefings on it,” said House Armed Services Committee spokesperson Heather Vaughan, adding that the group is “continuing to look into the incident and conduct oversight”.
The Pentagon’s F-35 programme office said in a statement that “we are aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 components, and we are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence”.
Politico reported on Sept 18 that a shipment of F-35 parts bound for the US for repairs was rerouted from Australia and ended up in Hong Kong, sparking concerns over reverse engineering of classified components of the fighter jet.
The programme office declined to disclose the components or explain the term “unserviceable”, including whether the items were damaged beyond repair. Programme officials are scheduled to brief committee staff as early as Sept 22, a US official said.
When asked to comment on the report, a spokesperson for Australia’s Department of Defence said Canberra “takes the protection of classified and export-controlled technologies extremely seriously”.
The diversion of the parts is separate from the longstanding problem of inadequate Pentagon visibility into the programme’s inventory.
For the sixth straight year, failures in tracking spare parts and equipment for the fighter jet were a “material weakness” contributing to the continuing inability to achieve a successful account of the military’s finances, according to the Pentagon comptroller and inspector-general.
Politico said an intermediary transported the parts on behalf of manufacturer Lockheed Martin.
The shipment ended up in Hong Kong, though it is not clear why it was rerouted or who currently possesses the components.
The shipment included one of the jet’s canopies, which covers the cockpit and contains stealth technology accessible only by the US and its allies, the publication said.
Lockheed Martin manages the programme’s overall supply chain and uses commercial shipping providers to transport parts.
It said in a statement that the company, “for security reasons, can’t discuss the status of specific shipments or shipping procedures. Our teams handle every shipment with the utmost diligence and safeguards to ensure the integrity of the programme and the security of our allied partners”.
Australia is the Indo-Pacific inventory hub for parts and maintenance of F-35s flown by Asian allies in the world’s largest aircraft programme. BLOOMBERG

Bessent hails 'successful' meeting with He Lifeng
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:11:28 UTC
11:11:28 KST

Chinese and US teams on Sunday held candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges during consultations on economic and trade issues in New York.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the meetings with Vice Premier He Lifeng were "very successful", adding that both sides discussed greater communication on artificial intelligence (AI) threats.
"We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese," Bessent said after the all-day meeting with Vice Premier He Lifeng.
The discussions, which also included top US trade official Jamieson Greer, lasted around eight hours and saw the two sides engage in exchanges on economic and trade issues of common concern, as well as the implementation of consensus reached in previous talks.
The meetings set the stage for possible agreements on trade, AI and other issues before a summit of the countries' top leaders this week.
President Xi Jinping is due to meet his US counterpart Donald Trump in Washington DC.
Bessent said the United States proposed a notification mechanism between the two countries for incidents such as security threats.
"What we discussed was setting up a mechanism. So it's going to be called the US-China AI dialogue," he said. 
"We've agreed to meet again."
Bessent and He also spoke one-on-one during the gathering that took place at JPMorgan Chase's headquarters in New York.
Li Chenggang, Vice Minister of Commerce, who was elevated to a top-level international trade representative post shortly before the meetings, was present too.
Greer said US export controls on sophisticated AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment were not on the agenda for the AI mechanism talks.
Greer added that Sunday's discussions would prepare the groundwork for a "successful summit" between Trump and Xi on Thursday and Friday in Washington.
"These are the two most powerful countries on earth, whether it's in trade or AI, and it's imperative that they're able to work together. It doesn't mean there aren't challenges in the relationship. A lot of these are obvious," Greer said.
The meeting covered other key topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process agreed in May for each side to identify potential tariff cuts on non-strategic goods, called the "Board of Trade."
Greer did not identify a specific list of products that could see such reductions, but he repeated his desire for a "relatively small subset of American and Chinese goods that can be traded in a balanced way, that are non-sensitive."
These would be considered as "a class unto themselves."
Potential candidates among Chinese exports include "consumer goods, low-tech items," he said, while US exports for this treatment could include energy, agricultural goods and medical devices, he added.
Greer and Bessent did not mention any progress on improving the flow of critical minerals to US companies, which US officials have said are insufficient despite Beijing's prior commitments to ease restrictions under last year's US-China trade truce.
The discussions point to more incremental progress in avoiding an escalation of tensions in a delicate trade relationship that has major consequences for the global economy.
"I think status quo is probably both sides' general best expectation," Anna Ashton, a China trade analyst and founder of Ashton Intelligence said prior to the meeting.
Bessent and Greer did not provide updates on other issues that are unresolved after the May meeting in Beijing between Trump and Xi, including Chinese pledges to increase purchases of US agricultural goods by US$17 billion a year and to purchase more than 200 Boeing aircraft. (Xinhua/Agencies)

Facebook, Instagram down for thousands of users, Downdetector says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:00:35 UTC
11:00:35 KST

Meta’s Facebook, Instagram recover after brief outage
SAN FRANCISCO - Meta’s social media platforms Facebook and Instagram recovered after a brief outage disrupted service for thousands of users in the US on Sept 20, according to Downdetector.com.
The disruption began around 8.55pm ET (8.55am on Sept 21 Singapore time) and peaked at more than 17,000 reports of outages on Facebook and more than 5,000 reports on Instagram, according to Downdetector, which tracks outages by collating status reports from multiple sources.
Reports of outages had fallen sharply by about 10pm ET, indicating the services had largely recovered.
Meta did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on the outage.
Since the numbers on Downdetector are based on user-submitted reports, the actual number of affected users may vary.
Facebook and Instagram experienced a similar outage in July, when Downdetector logged as many as 4,808 reports of issues on Facebook and 2,829 on Instagram.
In Singapore, reports on Downdetector for Facebook spiked at 9.26am with 229 complaints, while there were 109 reports for Instagram at 9.25am.
More than half of the complaints for each platform were for problems with their websites. REUTERS

As the US weighs restrictions on cloud computing, how will China’s AI sector adapt?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:00:26 UTC
11:00:26 KST

In FocusAs the US weighs restrictions on cloud computing, how will China’s AI sector adapt?
If Washington expands its tech blockade to include cloud networks, China’s AI sector will face its most severe choke point since the chip bans
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.
However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.
By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.
Under contracts signed by non-Chinese entities, models have been trained on cutting-edge Nvidia processors housed thousands of miles, away outside the reach of US authorities, he said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked four military aircraft, seven naval vessels, and four official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Sunday and 6 a.m. on Monday.
Three of the four People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s central, southwestern, and eastern air defense identification zone, according to the MND.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems to monitor PLA activity.
So far this month, the MND has tracked Chinese aircraft 184 times and ships 214 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

Endangered black robin wins 2026 Bird of the Year in New Zealand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:34:44 CST
10:34:44 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Karure black robin, a critically endangered bird native to New Zealand's Chatham Islands, has won the 2026 Bird of the Year competition after receiving 25,610 votes, Forest & Bird said on Monday.
The closely contested election attracted a record 105,000 voters, with about 88 percent of votes cast from within New Zealand, according to the New Zealand's conservation organization.
Kakapo, a flightless, nocturnal parrot native to New Zealand, finished second with 19,445 votes, followed by karearea, or New Zealand falcon, with 17,423 votes, according to the results.
Karure black robins are a conservation success story. In 1980, only five birds remained, including the only fertile female. A recovery effort by the Chatham Islands community and the Wildlife Service, now the Department of Conservation, began with a single breeding pair, Forest & Bird said in a statement.
There are now about 350 adult black robins living on two pest-free nature reserve islands. However, the suitable habitat on the islands is nearly at capacity, with all suitable territories occupied, it said, adding that a third population on another island is needed for the species to continue growing.
Forest & Bird said that conservation work on Pitt Island, which sits right between the two nature reserves, could provide safer habitat for the black robin and benefit the wider biodiversity of the Chatham Islands, which supports 20 percent of New Zealand's threatened bird species. ■

====================================================================================================

Malaysian King Approves Imprisoned Former PM Najib’s House Arrest Bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
01:29:00 UTC
10:29:00 KST

On Friday, Malaysia’s king granted imprisoned former Prime Minister Najib Razak a royal pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his prison term under house arrest, prompting an outcry and creating another potential political headache for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Najib, 73, has been imprisoned since August 2022, when Malaysia’s top court upheld a conviction in a case linked to the multi-billion-dollar looting of the state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
In a statement, the government confirmed that Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar had granted Najib a “conditional pardon.” This will allow him to serve the remainder of his prison term under house arrest if he pays a 50 million ringgit fine ($12 million) imposed by the courts. Najib’s sentence expires on August 23, 2028.
The 1MDB state investment fund was established shortly after Najib’s election in 2009. In the ensuing years, Malaysian investigators claim, at least $4.5 billion was drained from the fund and laundered by Najib’s associates through a labyrinth of dummy corporations and bank accounts across the globe. The 1MDB scandal helped bring down Najib’s government at the general election of 2018, and has since led to criminal investigations in a number of other countries, including the United States, Switzerland, and Singapore.
Najib’s original conviction was handed down in 2020, when a court sentenced him to 12 years in prison and fined him 210 million ringgit ($51.5 million) for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust, and money laundering. The charges related to Najib’s illegal receipt of around $10 million from SRC International, a former unit of 1MDB.
Since then, Najib has pursued a range of legal and political tactics in order to reduce his sentence. In early 2024, he succeeded in gaining a royal pardon from Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah of Pahang, the country’s previous king, which halved his prison sentence and reduced his fine to 50 million ringgit. He has also mounted a legal bid to serve his sentence under house arrest, claiming that the royal pardon contained a royal “addendum order” that entitled him to serve the remainder of his sentence at home. Accusing the authorities of deliberately ignoring or concealing the order, he initiated legal action aiming to compel them to confirm its existence and to execute it. His legal bid was shot down by the Kuala Lumpur High Court in December 2025.
This royal pardon, based on the sweeping powers granted to the king under Malaysia’s constitution, effectively overrides that decision. As the Associated Press noted, the king’s decision “marked an unprecedented use of house arrest as a form of royal clemency in Malaysia and could renew debate over the rule of law and the treatment of Malaysia’s most prominent corruption convict.”
Indeed, much Malaysian social media commentary about the decision has been shot through with a resigned and weary acceptance that the rich and powerful will always manage to evade accountability.
G25, a prominent civil society coalition, said in a statement that it was “deeply shocked and dismayed” by the decision.
“This does nothing to strengthen public confidence in our criminal justice system. It is a travesty of justice,” the group said, adding that it was difficult to reconcile with the government’s stated commitment to strengthening the rule of law and combating corruption.”
Indeed, the decision has placed Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in a tricky position. While he has spent much of his career crusading against corruption, he is currently governing in a marriage-of-convenience coalition with Najib’s party, the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the primary component of the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition.
Given the various corruption scandals that have swirled around UMNO and its key figures, this has been a source of growing discontent within Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) and among its supporters, who argue that the Malaysian leader has been forced to compromise his principles in order to mollify his coalition partner.
This has reached a tipping point over the past year due to a string of corruption scandals, including the dismissal in January of 47 corruption charges against UMNO head Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, a key Anwar ally, and subsequent reports of widespread misconduct at the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission. This disillusionment arguably contributed to PH’s defeat in a string of important state-level elections over the past year.
In the wake of Najib’s pardon, Transport Minister Anthony Loke announced that he would tender his resignation, stating that the king’s decision, while legitimate, was “difficult to accept” for his Democratic Action Party (DAP), an important member of the PH coalition. The DAP, a party associated with Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese population, has performed poorly in the recent state elections due in part to the growing disillusionment with Anwar’s administration. In the wake of the recent state election results, some within the party have called for it to withdraw from the unity government in order to maintain its credibility as a liberal and reformist party. Last month, the DAP called a special congress to vote on the question. While the party’s members chose to stick with Anwar for now, it remains to be seen whether it will do so over the longer term.
At the same time, Najib’s release into house arrest would be a boon for UMNO and BN, which, while remaining in coalition with PH at the federal level, have competed with it in the recent state elections. In Negeri Sembilan, UMNO cooperated closely with the Islamist party PAS, a key member of the opposition Perikatan Nasional coalition, on a joint Malay unity platform, and won a significant majority in the state assembly. This offered a possible preview of the next general election, which is due by February 2028 – unless the growing PH-BN tensions prompt Anwar to call an earlier snap election.
On Friday, Anwar urged the public to accept the king’s decision, which he said would not weaken the government’s fight against graft and abuse of power.
“I want to stress that the principle of the rule of law remains intact,” he said, according to the AP. “Our commitment to taking action against all cases of corruption is not affected, and this does not mean the country should bow to practices of embezzlement and corruption.”
It remains unclear for now whether Najib will be able to fulfill the conditions necessary to secure his release from prison. A statement issued by Najib’s legal team yesterday said that the former leader was “profoundly grateful” to those who had offered their support and assistance. However, the question of whether he will be able to pay the required fine “does not lie in his own hands” given that many of his assets have been frozen due to the ongoing court cases.
“In those circumstances, our client is presently taking advice and considering his options as to how best to give effect to the condition,” the statement added.
After the royal clemency was announced, UMNO launched a “solidarity fund” in order to help, which had raised more than 1 million ringgit as of Saturday.
In the statement, Najib’s lawyers said that their client “does not wish the party, its members and supporters, or members of the public to feel burdened or obliged on his account.” He nonetheless remained “profoundly grateful” to all those who had “chosen to offer their support and assistance.”
As things stand, a lot of uncertainties surround Najib’s house arrest situation. Legal experts say that Malaysia does not have rules governing house arrest, and even if these are hastily put in place, it remains unclear how any potential breaches would be monitored or enforced.
However, there is a broad consensus that the pardon is unlikely to apply to the separate 15-year prison sentence handed down to Najib in a larger 1MDB-related trial late last year. In this case, judges found Najib guilty of 25 charges, including four counts of abuse of power and 21 counts of money laundering relating to 1MDB funds worth 2.27 billion ringgit ($574 million). Najib was also hit with a massive fine of 11.38 billion ringgit ($2.9 billion).
That prison term is due to begin after he completes his current sentence. Najib has appealed the verdict.

Trump administration readies sweeping sanctions against ICC, reports say
Measures targeting the court itself could disrupt payments, IT services and investigations.
The Trump administration is reportedly preparing sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) that could disrupt the tribunal’s finances and day-to-day operations.
The US sanctions would prohibit most transactions with the ICC after a grace period of six to seven months, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.

- list 2 of 2Duterte in person at ICC for first time over ‘war on drugs’ killings
The move would mark a sharp escalation in Washington’s campaign against the Hague-based court by targeting the institution itself rather than individual judges and prosecutors.
The Trump administration plans to announce the sanctions soon, according to the Reuters news agency, quoting two sources familiar with the matter.
The Journal, citing anonymous officials, said a decision could be finalised during this week’s United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York or soon afterwards.
If imposed, the measures would generally bar US citizens and companies from providing the ICC with money, goods or services without a licence from the US Treasury.
Banks and other companies often take an especially cautious approach to US sanctions because they rely on access to the American financial system.
The ICC president and registrar have previously warned that sanctions on the organisation as a whole could interfere with its ability to buy information technology and insurance services, hire investigators and make routine payments, including salaries for American employees.
The ICC was created in 2002 to prosecute individuals accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when national authorities are unable or unwilling to do so.
Washington has already sanctioned more than a dozen ICC judges and prosecutors under an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in February 2025.
In August, it added the court’s President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye to the list, with restrictions on them taking effect on September 17.
The United States has never joined the court.
The Trump administration says the court has exceeded its authority by pursuing officials from countries that are not ICC members.
Relations deteriorated sharply after the court issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Israel, like the US, is not an ICC member and rejects the court’s jurisdiction.
Washington has also objected to an earlier ICC investigation into alleged abuses in Afghanistan involving US personnel.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a campaign in July to further isolate the court and urged other countries to withdraw from it.
Trump’s move adds to growing opposition to the ICC in recent months.
Chad and Venezuela moved in July to withdraw from the court, following Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.
Four US-based rights groups sued the Trump administration in August, arguing that existing sanctions obstruct their legal and human rights work.

Egypt calls Ethiopian Renaissance Dam ‘illegitimate,’ reserves right to act to protect water security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
01:19:30 UTC
10:19:30 KST

Amer Solyman and Mohammad Sio
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Egypt considers the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) “illegitimate” and reserves the right to take any measures it deems necessary to protect its water security, Irrigation and Water Resources Minister Hani Sewilam said Sunday.
Sewilam made the remarks during a briefing in Cairo with representatives of foreign media in Egypt organized by the State Information Service.
Egypt and Ethiopia have been at odds for years over the GERD, which Addis Ababa began building on the Blue Nile in 2011. Cairo has repeatedly demanded a legally binding agreement regulating the dam’s operation to safeguard its water security.
Sewilam said the completion of the dam and the passage of time did not mean that Egypt had accepted the situation or relinquished its rights.
He said the 2015 Declaration of Principles signed by Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan was intended as a roadmap that established commitments on cooperation, reaching an agreement on the dam’s initial filling and annual operation as well as coordination and data sharing.
The declaration does not give Ethiopia the right to take unilateral measures concerning the dam, Sewilam said, adding that Egypt considers continued filling and operation without an agreement a breach of those commitments.
“The dam is illegitimate and will remain so. Egypt has the right to take appropriate action to remove the harm caused to it,” he said.
“We gave Ethiopia more than one opportunity and tried every possible way to reach understandings, but it did not respond and also violated the Declaration of Principles,” he added.
Potential risks
Sewilam warned that uncoordinated operation of the dam can lead to sudden increases or sharp declines in water flows, potentially affecting dams in both Egypt and Sudan.
He said Egypt’s main concern is the timing and quantity of water releases and the rules governing them, rather than simply Ethiopia’s use of the dam to generate electricity.
“Ethiopia’s actions and statements by its officials indicate that the primary purpose of building the dam is not electricity generation,” he said.
Sewilam stressed the need for a legally binding agreement setting out procedures for periods of prolonged drought or repeated flooding.
He also rejected Ethiopia’s claim that Egypt receives the “lion’s share” of the Nile's water.
Egypt’s annual allocation of 55.5 billion cubic meters represents about 2.7% of the roughly 2 trillion cubic meters of rainfall across the Nile Basin, he said.
Ethiopia received more than 1 trillion cubic meters of rainfall in 2023, including about 467 billion cubic meters over the Ethiopian portion of the Nile Basin, while its renewable water resources amount to around 122 billion cubic meters annually, according to Sewilam.
He said estimates of groundwater recharge in Ethiopia range from 51 billion to 81 billion cubic meters annually and are linked to rainfall, unlike Egypt’s deep groundwater reserves, which he described as non-renewable.
Sewilam said Ethiopia has more than 18 million hectares of agricultural land compared with about 4.03 million hectares in Egypt.
Rain-fed agriculture in Ethiopia uses around 148 billion cubic meters of what is known as “green water” annually, in addition to around 9.68 billion cubic meters of “blue water,” he said.
Green water refers to rainfall, while blue water refers to water from rivers and groundwater sources.
Sewilam said Ethiopia’s total agricultural water use reaches around 158 billion cubic meters annually, while the water footprint of its livestock sector amounts to around 85.5 billion cubic meters, most of it green water.
He called for greater cooperation on rainwater harvesting, groundwater and improving agricultural water-use efficiency.
He also pointed to Ethiopia’s potential in solar and wind power, arguing that diversifying its energy mix could ease water-related pressures.
Cairo and Khartoum have called for a legally binding trilateral agreement between Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia governing the filling and operation of the GERD to ensure their water rights and interests are not harmed.
Ethiopia, however, says operating the dam does not require a binding agreement and maintains that it does not intend to harm the interests of other countries.
The dispute led to negotiations among Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia being suspended for three years in 2020 before resuming in 2023 and stalling again in 2024.
